p.x: These pages explain how to install EiN, use it day to day, look after it and build on it. This one says what EiN is, where to start, whoever you are, and how the pages are divided between core and the modules. EiN ( Everything is a Node ) is a system you host yourself, on your own Linux machine (x86-64). Everything it keeps is a node in one tree, with an owner and permissions as a file has: files and folders, accounts, logs, queues, even its own commands, and with the Archive installed, photos and albums, people and places. The web interface, a bash-compatible shell in the browser or over SSH, and SFTP all work on that one tree, as you and under the same permissions. Modules decide what EiN is for, and bring the pipelines that do the work each change starts. The first is the Archive , for a family's photos, videos, recordings and letters: as files come in, its pipelines make thumbnails, find faces, read text, transcribe speech and prepare everything for search. The assistant module adds a chat that answers your questions by running EiN's commands for you. On your machine EiN runs as a few containers under podman or Docker. EiN itself serves the web interface on port 8080 and SSH and SFTP on port 2222 by default, and keeps every node in a PostgreSQL database beside it and the files themselves in a data folder. Two more services are optional: the media service , which does the work on pictures, video and sound and which the Archive needs, and a language model for the assistant. A graphics card makes both faster, but nothing needs one. How EiN works explains the whole model in one page. Only EiN is reached from outside; the database, the media service and the language model answer EiN alone.

These pages come in two parts, as EiN does: Core holds for every EiN, whatever modules it has: installing it, the web interface, the shell and SSH, looking after it, the ideas it is built on, and the reference. Where a core page shows something a module adds, such as an entry the Archive puts in the sidebar, it says so and links to that module's pages. Modules has a section for each module. Read a module's section once that module is installed on your EiN, and leave it aside otherwise. Each section opens with an overview of what the module adds and what it needs. Module What it adds The Archive Albums of photos, videos, recordings and documents, people and their family tree, locations, devices, and staging, where uploads wait to be sorted The Assistant The chat that answers your questions by running EiN's commands for you, with a language model The media service EiN's side of the media service, the container that does the work on pictures, video and sound which the Archive needs

You want to try EiN. Install EiN puts it on a Linux machine with one command, and First steps takes you from the first sign-in to a family using it. You use EiN day to day. Finding your way around shows the web interface, and Search and the finder and Sharing cover what every EiN offers. With the Archive installed, Getting your photos in and Albums cover what you do most. You run EiN for others. Installing in detail explains every part of the installation, Configuration and Modules how to change what it does, Health and the dashboard how to tell that it is keeping up, and Troubleshooting what to do when something is wrong. You work in the shell. The terminal opens EiN's shell in the browser, and SSH and SFTP connects to it from your own computer. You build modules. Writing a module shows a module's folder, what each part becomes and how EiN finds it.

Under Core , the sidebar groups the pages in sections: Section What it holds Getting started What EiN is, installing it, and setting it up for a family. Using EiN The web interface, page by page, for everyone with an account. The shell and SSH The terminal, the shell language, the commands by task, the editor, SSH and SFTP, and reaching other machines from EiN. Administration Installing, configuring, watching and maintaining EiN, for the person who looks after it. Concepts Nodes, the tree, links, files and pipelines, in depth. Reference Every command, setting, environment variable and node type; the configuration files, keyboard shortcuts, the web interface's addresses and a glossary. Developing Writing a module, its manifest, and building EiN from source. Under Modules , each module's section holds its guide pages and a page of its commands. The Commands , Settings , Environment variables and Node types pages are written from what a running EiN with all its modules says about itself; an installation with fewer modules has fewer of them. Words EiN uses in its own way, such as node, softlink or staging, are in the Glossary . Every installation also carries these pages: Documentation , under System in EiN's sidebar, shows this guide as it was when EiN was built, without reaching the internet. Beside it, under This installation , its reference ( Commands , Settings , Environment , Node types and Modules ) is read from that installation as you open it: the commands on your PATH, each setting with its current value, the modules installed there. A link here to one of the reference pages opens that one there. In the shell, <command> --help describes a command. Note EiN is a work in progress. Nothing is released yet: the installer runs the newest EiN, and these pages describe it. Where they and the documentation inside your installation differ, the one inside describes what you run.

This page explains the few ideas EiN is built on: one tree of nodes, one set of commands that works on it from every interface, pipelines that act on every change, and modules that decide what it is for. Read it first, whether you are going to use EiN, run it or build on it. It also says how these pages are divided: Core for what every EiN has, and a section under Modules for each module.

EiN keeps everything in one tree, the way a computer keeps files in folders. A photo is a node, and so are the album that holds it, a person in the family tree, a place on the map, an account, the system log, a queue of work waiting to be done, each of EiN's own commands and the file that holds the system's settings. Each has a path from / , as a file does: What Path Type A photo /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg file The album it is in /archive/albums/christmas-2019 album A person /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield person A place she lived /archive/locations/Highbury location An account /etc/users/admin user The group everyone who signs in belongs to /etc/groups/users group The system's settings /etc/config file The system log /var/logs/system log The pipeline engine's queue /var/queues/pipeline-engine queue A command /usr/bin/ls command The photo, the album, the person and the place come with the Archive and are there once it is installed; the rest is in every EiN. A node has a type, a name in its folder, an owner, a group and permission bits, and the attributes its type needs: a photo's name, size, checksum and the time it was taken; a person's names and dates. Some types hold content as well: a file its bytes, a log its lines, a queue its messages. Any node can have children, a file included. With the Archive, a photo keeps what EiN works out about it beneath itself: its EXIF in metadata/exif , its thumbnails in thumbnails/ , the faces found on it in regions/ . Delete the photo and they go with it. A person is a node like any other. The Nodes page, in an administrator's sidebar, browses the whole tree. The type decides what a node is and how EiN treats it. Core has 17 types of its own, and modules add theirs, such as the archive's album , person and location . Nodes and node types describes a node part by part, and Node types lists every type. The top of the tree is divided by what each part is for. The tree has every standard path. Folder What it holds /archive The content EiN is for: the labels folder tags , and with the Archive its albums, people, locations and devices /home/<you> Your own space: your settings, shell history, favourites and trash, and with the Archive the uploads waiting for you to sort them /etc Accounts and groups, settings, and the services EiN runs /var What the system writes as it runs: logs, sessions, queues, pools and pipeline runs /usr Commands, modules and the built-in guide /dev , /tmp Event channels and scratch space

p.h: Owners and permissions, as with files
p.x: Every node has an owner, a group and permission bits that say who may read it, change it, and go into it or run it, written the way chmod writes them: 0750 , or rwxr-x--- . A node may also give access to more users or groups through an access list. A node belongs to whoever made it and takes its group from the folder it is made in. The administrator bypasses every permission check. Two things work differently from a computer's files: What you may not read is not listed at all : not in a folder, not in search, not in ls . Two people can see the same folder or album differently, and it can look emptier to you than to its owner. You can share anonymous links : A link can be created that opens it without an account. It works on any node from the Nodes explorer, and with the Archive installed its pages offer it on an album, a picture, a person, a location or a device. Someone who has not signed in is the guest. The guest can sign in or open a share link and nothing more, unless an administrator turns on Visitors may browse , and the guest never changes anything. Sharing shows the dialog, and Permissions in depth has the exact rules.

p.h: Links put one thing in many places
p.x: A softlink is a node that points at another node by its path; opening it opens what it points at. EiN uses softlinks wherever one thing belongs in several places: being in a group is a link under /etc/groups/<group>/users/ ; your favourites are links in /home/<you>/stars ; with the Archive, an album's cover is a link to one of its pictures, and a picture added to an album from somewhere else is a link to where it lives; with the Archive, a label is a folder under /archive/tags/ holding a link to everything that carries it, and how two people are related is a pair of links, one on each person. Moving or renaming a node re-points every softlink to it, so an album can change its name without losing its cover or its labels. A hard link is the other kind: the same node under a second name in another folder, as on Unix. Links covers both, and what deleting and the trash do to them.

At the heart of EiN is a shell that speaks bash. Core brings more than 200 commands, and each module adds its own. All data access, from the web or over SSH, runs these commands, except SFTP, which moves files and nothing else: Interface How you get there What happens The web UI A browser at http://ein.local:8080 Each page runs commands as you and shows what they answer The terminal The terminal button in the top bar, or Alt + T , once you are signed in A shell of your own in each tab SSH ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local from your own computer, with your EiN username and password The same shell, or one command at a time SFTP sftp -P 2222 helen@ein.local , sshfs, or a file manager that speaks SFTP Files and folders without a shell, with the same permissions The assistant Chat in the sidebar, with the assistant module It runs commands as tools, as you; a command that would change something waits for you to accept it Every interface upholds the same permission checks, and all but SFTP go through the same commands. The web interface is no exception. Each page gets what it shows by running commands over one connection to the server, as you, with JSON_OUTPUT=1 so that they answer in JSON; renaming a folder on the Nodes page runs mv . Only the bytes of files, uploaded or downloaded, take a way of their own, through the same permission check. You can run the same commands yourself; these two list the root: # in EiN's terminal ls / JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l / | jq '.[].name' Because every interface acts as the same person under the same check, the rules are the same everywhere. What you cannot see in the browser you cannot see in the shell, over SFTP or through the assistant either, and a command only an administrator may run is refused to anyone else whichever interface they use. The terminal works on the tree the pages show: people, albums and photos are paths. The terminal , SSH and SFTP and Chatting with the assistant describe each interface, and Commands lists every command.

Every change to the tree, a node made, changed, moved or deleted, is announced as an event once it is saved. Pipelines act on these events: a pipeline is a definition of the change it waits for and the steps, each a command, that it then runs on the node that changed. A module brings its pipelines with it. Core brings none, so without a module EiN keeps what you give it and works nothing out. With the Archive installed, uploading a photo sets off a chain: The Archive notices the uploaded photo, video or recording and announces it. media-ingest reads the file's metadata, such as the camera, the time it was taken and where, through the media service. Its result starts the rest, each a pipeline of its own: thumbnails and display sizes, video and audio the browser can play, the faces on it, a picture vector for searching by meaning, text read from the picture, a transcript of what is said in a video or recording, a fingerprint that finds copies, the address of its GPS position, and a link to the location that contains it. What these write are changes too, and they start what depends on them, such as matching the faces to the people they show. Work waits in queues and pools, which are nodes like everything else, so nothing is lost when EiN restarts, and a node that changes ten times while it waits is worked on once. When the media service is busy or down, its steps wait for it rather than fail. Work that fails anyway is tried again after an hour, six hours and a day, and then marked as needing a person; a file that no decoder can open is not tried again. The Dashboard , an administrator's page, sums all this up in one word: Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person . After a large upload it reads Catching up for a while, which is expected. Changes and pipelines follows a change from event to finished work, Processing and pipelines is the administrator's side, and Health and the dashboard explains the four words.

p.h: Modules decide what EiN is for
p.x: Core is the tree, the shell and its commands, the pipeline engine, accounts and sharing, and the frame of the web interface. On its own, its sidebar holds Home , Search , Settings , Statistics and Documentation , and for an administrator Nodes and Dashboard . Everything else comes from modules. A module is a folder with a manifest, mod.json , kept in a repository of its own. What it adds is what its folders hold: commands, services that run in the background, pipelines, pages and sidebar entries, settings, node types and its own documentation. It also joins core features by the names of its commands: every command whose name starts with search- is asked when you search. The published modules are in the einhq organisation on GitHub, each named module-<name> : Module What it is for What it needs archive The Archive: albums of photos, videos, recordings and documents, people and their family tree, locations, devices and the tracks they recorded, and staging, where uploads wait to be sorted The ems module, installed along with it, and the media service assistant The chat that answers questions about EiN by running its commands for you A language model ems EiN's side of the media service: the client the Archive calls it through, the media service's health and graphics card readings on the Dashboard, and the text vectors that search by meaning compares The media service An administrator installs, updates and removes modules on Settings → Modules , with mod install , or with the installer's --module option. Modules explains all three. These pages are divided the same way. The Core part of the sidebar holds for every EiN, with or without modules; where a core page shows something a module adds, it says so and links to that module's pages. Under Modules , each module has a section of its own that opens with its overview, linked in the table above. Read a module's section once it is installed on your EiN, and leave it aside otherwise.

EiN itself is one process: the web interface, the shell, SSH and SFTP, the pipelines and the modules' services all run in it. The installer sets it up on one machine with podman or Docker and compose, each part in a container of its own: EiN, PostgreSQL and, if you choose them, the media service and the language model. Only EiN is reached from outside; the database, the media service and the language model answer EiN alone. Container What it is When you need it ein EiN itself, the only container with ports open to other machines Always db PostgreSQL 18 with TimescaleDB, pgvector and PostGIS. It holds every node, link and permission, the logs, the vectors that search by meaning compares, the shapes on the map and GPS tracks. Always ems The media service: every media tool and model, for thumbnails and video renditions, faces, voices, text in pictures, transcripts, search vectors and fingerprints. It keeps no data of its own and knows nothing of the tree: it reads the files EiN stores and answers EiN. It uses an NVIDIA graphics card when there is one, and the CPU otherwise. With the Archive: the installer's --ems llm The language model the assistant asks: Qwen3.5-4B in llama.cpp, on the graphics card or the CPU. A hosted provider with an OpenAI-compatible API can take its place. With the assistant: the installer's --llm , unless you use a provider Only EiN is reachable from other machines: port 8080 for the web interface and 2222 for SSH and SFTP. The database, the media service and the language model answer only EiN, on the network compose makes for them. Your files are on the machine's disk, in the data folder ( ~/ein/data unless you chose another): the originals in files , the thumbnails and renditions EiN makes from them in files-volatile . The database is the container engine's volume ein_db . The two belong together, as Files and storage and Your data explain. Without the media service, EiN still takes in, keeps and shares what you upload, but the files you add get no metadata, thumbnails, faces or transcripts: that work waits until the media service answers. Without a language model, everything except the chat works, though the search box then reads what you type by its own rules alone, without picking out the people and places you name. The media service and The language model say more about each.

Install EiN puts EiN on a machine of your own, and First steps takes you from the first sign-in to a family using it. Finding your way around is a tour of the web interface. The Archive , The Assistant and The media service open each module's section, for the modules installed on your EiN. The Concepts pages take each idea above further: Nodes and node types , The tree , Links , Files and storage and Changes and pipelines . The terminal is the place to start with the shell. Writing a module is for building a module of your own. Glossary defines the words these pages use.

This page takes you from a Linux machine to an EiN you can sign in to: what the machine needs, the one command that installs EiN, what you see while it runs, and what to do first once it is up. It is the quick path for trying EiN on your own machine. Installing in detail covers everything else.

EiN runs as a few containers on one Linux machine. The installer downloads their images, which GitHub builds from the newest source: there are no releases. It needs no root, but the tools it uses must be installed first. What the machine needs depends on whether you install EiN on its own (EiN Core) or with the media service, which the Archive needs to make thumbnails, find faces, read text and make pictures searchable: EiN Core With the media service ( --ems ) System Linux on x86-64 Linux on x86-64 Container engine podman, run as your own user (rootless), with podman compose ; or Docker with its compose plugin the same Tools git , curl and openssl the same Processor 2 cores 4 cores; 6 or more recommended Memory 4 GB 16 GB; 32 GB recommended Free disk 10 GB, plus your files about 100 GB, plus your files Graphics card not used optional: NVIDIA, 16 GB recommended, 8 and 12 GB work Cores are counted as physical cores, not threads. The language model for the assistant ( --llm ) takes several GB more, on the graphics card or in memory. With 16 GB of memory, leave it out or use a hosted model instead; The language model explains both. A few more things to know before you start: No macOS, Windows or ARM. The installer stops at once on anything but Linux on x86-64, a Raspberry Pi included. Internet access. The install downloads EiN's images from GitHub's registry, ghcr.io . At its first start EiN downloads the modules you named from GitHub, and the language model downloads its model from Hugging Face. Docker needs your user to have access to its daemon , usually by being in the docker group. The installer does not check this. A graphics card is optional. Without one everything works, only slower. Only NVIDIA cards are used, with driver 610 or newer to encode video on the card. The graphics card has the setup. A current browser that shows AVIF and plays AV1 video: Chrome, Edge or Firefox, or Safari 17 and newer on an Apple device that decodes AV1 (M3, A17 Pro or later). On Ubuntu 24.04, for example, this installs the tools for the podman route: # on the machine that will run EiN sudo apt install podman podman-compose git curl openssl Note When both podman and Docker are installed, EiN uses podman. To use Docker, put EIN_ENGINE=docker in front of bash in the install command. setup.sh keeps the engine in .env , and every later run uses it. The installer's own checks still look at podman when it is there. Installing in detail explains what happens when the two are mixed.

There are two install commands. Both check the machine first and install nothing when it falls short. EiN Core is EiN and its database: the tree, the web interface, the shell, SSH and SFTP. You add the rest when you want it. # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash EiN Archive is the full Archive installation: EiN with the media service, the assistant's language model, and the Archive and assistant modules. # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- --ems --llm --module archive --module assistant Everything after bash -s -- is passed on to ~/ein/setup.sh , EiN's own setup script: Option What it adds --ems The media service: every media tool and model, in an image of about 30 GB. It uses the graphics card when the first install found one ready for containers. --llm The language model the assistant answers with, Qwen3.5-4B in llama.cpp. --module <name> A module, such as archive or assistant , which EiN installs at its start with the modules it needs. Give it once for each module. --no-ems , --no-llm Leave the media service or the model out again on a later run. Its data stays. Note The Archive module needs the media service. Installed with --module archive but without --ems , it still installs: the installer's archive line says low , and setup.sh ends with The Archive module needs the media service, which is not installed here: ./setup.sh --ems adds it. Nothing you upload then gets thumbnails, dates, faces or searchable text: that work waits until the media service is there. Modules lists what each module needs.

EIN_CHECK=1 runs the checks for the options you give and stops. A variable for the installer goes in front of bash , not in front of curl : # on the machine that will run EiN curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | EIN_CHECK=1 bash -s -- --ems --llm You can read the installer before you run it: it is at einhq.eu/install.sh , and its source is on GitHub .

EiN goes in ~/ein , and your files in ~/ein/data unless you name another folder with EIN_DATA . The folder holds your originals, so put it on a disk with room for them, in a folder your user can write to: # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | EIN_DATA=/mnt/photos/ein bash -s -- --ems --llm --module archive --module assistant EIN_DATA is read only by the first install, when ~/ein/.env is written. Later runs keep the folder named there.

Open a terminal on the machine as your own user. Do not use sudo or a root shell: the installer and EiN are meant to run as your own user. Paste one of the install commands above and press Enter . Read the report. Each line is one check, its result, and why: EiN: checking this machine against the system requirements system ok Linux on x86-64 podman ok 5.4.2, rootless compose ok podman compose, with podman-compose git ok curl ok openssl ok processor ok 8 cores memory ok 31 GB disk ok 870 GB free under /home/anna/ein/data (not made yet; measured on /home/anna), plus room for your own files graphics ok NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070, 12282 MB, driver 610.31 card memory low 12282 MB: works; 16 GB is recommended, room for the media models and the assistant side by side container GPU ok nvidia-container-toolkit 1.18.1, CDI spec in /var/run/cdi This machine can run EiN; 1 item(s) are below what is recommended. The graphics lines appear only with --ems or --llm , and the thresholds for processor, memory and disk are the higher ones only with --ems . On a terminal the results are coloured: Result Colour What it means ok green The machine meets it. low yellow Below what is recommended. The install goes on. Every graphics line is at most low : without a usable card, the media service and the model run on the processor. missing red A requirement is not met. The reason says what to install or how much is needed. The last line is the verdict: Verdict What happens <n> requirement(s) not met, so nothing was installed. The installer stops before it fetches anything, and your machine is as it was. Fix what the missing lines name and run the command again. This machine can run EiN; <n> item(s) are below what is recommended. The install goes on. The low lines tell you what would make EiN faster or roomier. This machine meets the recommended requirements. The install goes on. The disk check measures the free space where your files go. The images and the database are kept in the container engine's own storage (for rootless podman, usually under ~/.local/share/containers ), which is often the same disk but need not be: that disk needs the room too.

One command does all of it: the installer downloads and starts EiN, and EiN sets itself up at its first start Once the checks pass, the installer: Fetches ein/deploy into ~/ein , or updates it when it is there already, and runs ~/ein/setup.sh with your options. setup.sh writes ~/ein/.env the first time: your options, the folder for your files, and the passwords it makes for the database, the media service and the admin account. It downloads the images of EiN and its database, and of the media service and the model when you chose them. Their sources, for the media service and the model, it fetches into ~/ein/src . From an organisation of your own ( --source ), it fetches the sources into ~/ein/src instead and builds the images on your machine; Where the sources come from explains it. It starts everything with podman compose or docker compose , and waits for EiN to answer. At its first start, EiN sets up its database, makes the admin account, downloads the modules you named and the modules they need, sets them up, starts its services, and gives admin the password INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env . setup.sh prints the address of EiN and the admin password, which it prints again at the end of every run until you delete its line from .env . It makes EiN start again when the machine does, where your user may: under podman it turns on podman-restart.service for your user and lets your user's services run without a login. What it may not do, it prints as commands for you to run, such as sudo loginctl enable-linger anna . The end of a run looks like this: Fetching https://github.com/einhq/deploy into /home/anna/ein Wrote .env: your files go under /home/anna/ein/data == Fetching the sources ems 93fa61b 2026-10-21 llm 2e8b4d7 2026-09-30 == Getting the images (the media service the first time: about 30 GB) … == Starting EiN … Waiting for EiN to answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/; its first start takes a minute or more … EiN is up at http://ein:8080/ Sign in as admin with the password 5e0c9a2f71b3d846 and change it, then delete the line INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD from /home/anna/ein/.env. Enabled podman-restart.service, which starts EiN's containers at boot Enabled lingering for anna, so podman-restart.service runs at boot without a login EiN starts again when the machine does.

Most of the time goes into downloading the images, and how long that takes depends on your connection. EiN Core is a few hundred MB. With the media service, its image of about 30 GB takes by far the longest. The container engine prints its own progress as it goes. Built from your own source instead, the media service's image takes about an hour more. After == Starting EiN , setup.sh prints Waiting for EiN to answer at … and then, every 10 seconds, EiN's newest log line when it has changed. The first start takes longer, as EiN also downloads the modules you named. It waits up to 10 minutes, and stops sooner when EiN's container stops or keeps restarting. With the media service and the model, two parts are still getting ready when the password appears. The media service loads its models for a few minutes after it starts; until then the Dashboard's health check for ems says http://ems:8181 is not answering; work that needs it waits , and the work resumes by itself. The language model downloads its model the first time it starts, so the assistant may not answer for a while.

Where What it holds ~/ein setup.sh , the compose files, the sources under src/ , and .env ~/ein/.env your options and the passwords made at the install, kept nowhere else ~/ein/data , or your EIN_DATA your originals, the thumbnails and other renditions, scratch space, the language model and the installed modules the ein_db volume the database: every name, folder, album, person, setting and account, in the container engine's storage Keep .env safe. EiN has no backup command; Your data explains what to copy and why the database and the data folder belong together.

Open the address setup.sh printed, such as http://ein:8080/ , in a browser. On the machine itself, http://localhost:8080/ works too. If another computer cannot find the machine by that name, use its address instead, such as http://ein.local:8080/ or http://192.168.1.20:8080/ . In Username or e-mail , type admin . In Password , type or paste the password setup.sh printed, and click Sign in . The sign-in page. Browse without signing in appears only when visitors may browse, which is off after an install You land on the home page, Welcome . What it shows comes from the modules: with the Archive it fills as pictures come in, and on EiN Core alone it stays empty. There is no setup wizard: First steps walks you from here to a family using it. EiN listens on port 8080 for the web and 2222 for SSH and SFTP, on every address of the machine, over plain HTTP. That is fine at home. Before you make EiN reachable from outside your home, read Ports, HTTPS and remote access . When something else on the machine already uses 8080 or 2222, setup.sh gives EiN the next free port instead, says so ( Port 8080 is taken on this machine: EiN uses 8081 instead (EIN_HTTP_PORT in .env) ), keeps it in .env , and prints the address with it.

p.h: Change the admin password straight away
p.x: Do this before anything else: The password is in ~/ein/.env , as INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD , readable by anyone who can read that file, and setup.sh prints it at the end of every run while the line is there. Once you have changed it, delete that line from .env . Changing the line does not change the password: EiN reads it only at its first start. EiN has no way to recover a lost administrator password. Only another administrator can set a new one, and a fresh install has no other.

Click your picture at the top right to open the account menu, and choose Profile . Open the Security tab. In Current password , enter the password setup.sh printed. Enter your own password in New password , and again in Confirm new password . Click Update password . Password updated appears beside the button. Profile → Security: the form asks for the new password twice, so a typing mistake is caught

Open the terminal with the terminal button in the top bar, or Alt + T , and run: # in EiN's terminal user passwd admin It asks Password: , sets what you type, and answers Password updated successfully . It asks only once, so type carefully. The name is required: user passwd on its own answers user passwd: missing username . The reference lists its options. Your profile, favourites and trash has more on the profile, and Accounts and groups on making accounts for your family.

Everything the Archive command installs can be added to EiN Core afterwards. Run setup.sh in ~/ein with the option: # on the machine EiN runs on ~/ein/setup.sh --ems # the media service ~/ein/setup.sh --llm # the assistant's language model ~/ein/setup.sh --module archive # a module, with the modules it needs An option is kept in .env once given, so a later run without it keeps it. Give each option only when you add it. Every run of setup.sh is also an update: it brings ~/ein itself up to date, fetches the newest sources of what is installed, builds again and restarts EiN, which is down while it starts. Updating has the details. A module given with --module is installed by EiN at its next start, which that same run brings about. --no-ems and --no-llm take the media service or the model out again. Their data stays. Modules can also be installed without a restart. In the web interface, open Settings → Modules , click the Published modules button beside the filter, and click Install on the module. In the terminal, mod install archive does the same ( reference ). Modules covers updating and removing them, and why a module you remove in Settings → Modules comes back at the next start while EIN_MODULES in .env still names it. Instead of --llm , the assistant can use a hosted model, set in ~/ein/.env : see The language model .

The commands here are written for podman. With Docker, write docker compose where they say podman compose . What you see What to do <n> requirement(s) not met, so nothing was installed. Nothing was changed. Install or free what the missing lines name, and run the command again. The podman line says low and run as root here: run the installer, and EiN, as your own user You ran the installer as root. Run it again as your own user, without sudo . The compose line says missing and install podman-compose, which 'podman compose' runs Install podman-compose , or for Docker its compose plugin, and run the command again. A line about an external compose provider each time podman compose runs podman's own notice that podman compose runs podman-compose . It is not an error. setup.sh: EiN stopped before it answered; its log is above: podman compose logs ein EiN's container stopped, or restarted three times. The last lines of its log are printed above the message; they name what went wrong. See Troubleshooting . setup.sh: EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/ in 10 minutes: podman compose logs ein Look at what EiN is doing with cd ~/ein && podman compose logs ein . A first start that downloads modules over a slow connection can take this long; podman compose ps shows whether it still runs. Starting fails with unresolvable CDI devices nvidia.com/gpu=all The container engine cannot hand the graphics card to the containers. podman before 5, such as 4.9.3 on Ubuntu 24.04, needs a fix once per machine, which the installer's container GPU line names: see The graphics card . No Sign in as admin line at the end .env has no INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD line: you deleted it, or .env was written before setup.sh kept the password there. In the second case a new EiN printed a random password to its log, below. When nothing is there, the database was there from an earlier install, so the admin already had a password, or the containers have been made again since. See Troubleshooting . some of INSTALL_MODULES could not be installed; continuing boot in the log EiN could not download a module, often for want of a connection to GitHub. Install it from Settings → Modules once EiN is up. The address does not open on another computer Use the machine's IP address instead of its name, and open ports 8080 and 2222 in the machine's firewall if it has one. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . EiN does not start again when the machine does until this has run: at the end setup.sh could not turn on what starts EiN at boot, such as lingering for your user. Run the commands listed below the line; until then, start EiN after a reboot with cd ~/ein && podman compose up -d . Installing in detail explains. Uploads in the Archive get no thumbnails The media service is not installed, or is not answering yet. Without it, the installer's archive line says low and setup.sh ends with The Archive module needs the media service, which is not installed here: ./setup.sh --ems adds it. Add it with ~/ein/setup.sh --ems , or see The media service . To find a random admin password in the log, as long as the containers have not been made again since: # on the machine EiN runs on cd ~/ein && podman compose logs ein | grep 'Admin password set to' Troubleshooting has more questions and answers.

First steps : from the first sign-in to a family using EiN. Installing in detail : every option and variable, podman and Docker, what runs where, and running EiN day to day. The graphics card and Ports, HTTPS and remote access , when you want EiN faster or reachable from outside. Modules : what each module brings and how to install, update and remove it. The Archive and The Assistant : the sections for the modules the EiN Archive command installs.

This page is for the administrator who has just installed EiN and is setting it up for a family. It goes from the first sign-in to the family using it, one short step at a time, and links each step to the page that covers it in full. The steps hold for any EiN, whichever modules it has; each module's own pages take over from there. Take the steps in order. Some of them depend on an earlier one: the sharing defaults in step 4, for example, apply to what is created after you set them, so set them before the family starts adding things. Sign in and change the admin password Check the dashboard Install the modules you want Decide who sees what Create accounts for the family Try the terminal Start with the modules Let the family sign in Keep EiN running Commands on this page are written for podman. With Docker, write docker compose where the page says podman compose .

p.h: Sign in and change the admin password
p.x: At its end the install printed the address and the administrator's password: EiN is up at http://ein.local:8080/ Sign in as admin with the password 5e0c9a2f71b3d846 and change it, then delete the line INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD from /home/anna/ein/.env. Open the address in a browser. If your computer cannot find that name, use the machine's IP address instead, such as http://192.168.1.20:8080/ . Enter admin under Username or e-mail , the printed password under Password , and choose Sign in . EiN opens on Home, titled Welcome . Open the account menu under your picture at the top right, choose Profile , then the Security tab. Fill in Current password , New password and Confirm new password , and choose Update password . EiN answers Password updated . Install EiN shows the form. You can change it in EiN's terminal instead. Open the terminal with the top bar's terminal button or Alt + T , and run: # in EiN's terminal user passwd admin It asks for the new password after Password: . The reference lists its options. If the install's output is gone, the password is still in ~/ein/.env , as INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD , and every later run of ./setup.sh prints it again at its end: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein grep INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD . env Once you have changed the password, delete that line from .env : the old password stays readable there for anyone who can read the file, and changing the line does not change the password, which EiN takes from it only at its first start. Warning Once you have changed it, nothing else keeps the admin password, and EiN sends no e-mail, so there is no "forgot password". Keep the new one in a password manager. If it is lost, only someone who can act as the administrator can set a new one. Step 5 shows how to give a second person that right.

Choose Dashboard under System in the sidebar. Only administrators have it. The page, System dashboard , shows a badge above its title for how things stand: Badge What it means What to do Healthy Nothing is waiting to be done. Nothing. Catching up Work is waiting, and some was done in the last hour, as after an import. Wait. It turns to Healthy when the work is done. Stuck Work is waiting, and none was done in the last hour. Look at the Work tab, and read Health and the dashboard . Needs a person A check failed. Read the failed check on the Overview tab, and see Troubleshooting . Healthy means nothing is waiting; this one reads Catching up, as work waits and is being done, and a fresh install reads Healthy within a minute or two For the first minute after EiN starts, the dashboard may show warming up while it takes its first readings. Below the badges, the Overview tab lists every check that is not fine. Warnings do not stop Healthy , and two are expected on an install without the optional parts: with the archive but without the media service, ems says http://ems:8181 is not answering; work that needs it waits ; with the assistant but without a language model, llm says http://llm:8190 is not answering; the chat cannot answer until it does . With the parts installed, the same warnings show for a while after a start, as the media service loads its models and the language model downloads its own the first time; they clear by themselves. Step 3 says how to add either part.

What EiN is for comes from its modules. Without any, the sidebar holds only Home , Search and the pages under System . These modules are published: Module What it adds What it needs archive Media , Staging , Year , Map , Albums , People , Locations and Devices in the sidebar, and Import media , Album , Person , Location and Device in the Create menu the ems module, installed with it, and the media service assistant Chat , in the sidebar and as a top-bar button a language model, your own or a hosted one ems the client for the media service, and the Media service tab on the dashboard the media service If you installed with the EiN Archive command from einhq.eu, the three are installed already. Open Settings → Modules , choose each module, and check that its panel says Active , not Not set up or Setup failed . To install a module: Open Settings → Modules . Choose the Published modules button beside the filter. Choose Install beside the module. EiN installs the modules it needs as well, and says so: "Installed, with ems". The module's pages appear in the sidebar without a reload. Each installed module has a panel that says whether it is set up and what it adds In EiN's terminal, mod install does the same: # in EiN's terminal mod install archive The archive's photos, videos and recordings need the media service , a separate container that reads dates and places, makes the previews, and finds faces, text and speech. Installing the module does not install the service. If you left it out at the install, add it on the machine: # on the machine EiN runs on ~/ein/setup.sh --ems It downloads the media service's image, about 30 GB, and starts EiN again. Without it, uploads arrive but wait in staging as being prepared . The assistant needs a language model the same way: ~/ein/setup.sh --llm runs one on this machine, and a hosted provider is set in ~/ein/.env . Modules , The media service and The language model have the details.

Settings , under System in the sidebar, is where you set up EiN. Its tabs are System , with every system setting by category, Users , Groups , Permissions and Modules . Each setting says what it does and which module brought it, and is saved on its own with Save change . Configuration explains the page and the same settings in the terminal. Start with who sees what. Open Settings → Permissions . Its four cards each say in a sentence what their settings come to. The demo shown here lets visitors browse; a family's own EiN keeps that off Visitors. Visitors may browse is Off on a new install, and the setting itself advises keeping it off for a family's own archive. Off, anyone who has not signed in is asked to sign in. A share link still opens what it was made for (see Sharing ). Turn it on only for an archive meant to be public. The setting is CFG_GUEST_BROWSING . Sharing sets what anything created as shared starts with. With the Archive installed, that is an album made with Create → Album , and a group filed from staging into a new album; the rest of this step speaks of albums for that reason. Its rows: Row New install What it decides Owner empty: whoever creates it who owns what is created Group Users, which is everyone with an account the group it is shared with Permissions Owner Edit, Group “users” View, Everyone else None ( as 0750 ) what the owner, the group and anyone else may do with it So on a new install the card reads: "Shared with Users: the owner can change it, members can see it, anyone else can't see it." Some common choices: You want Set Everyone with an account sees every album, and only its owner changes it nothing: the defaults do this The family adds to and changes each other's albums Group “users” to Edit Some accounts are not family, such as friends you share a single album with a family group as Group (see step 5), with Everyone else at None Each row is saved on its own with Save change . A change applies to what is created afterwards; albums that exist keep their sharing, which you change with Share , as Sharing shows. Each person can also narrow what they create, under Profile → Preferences → How widely what you create is shared . Sign-in sessions. A browser stays signed in for 1 day after its last visit ( Browser sign-in ), and a session unused for 12 hours ends ( Idle session ). Lengthen both if the family should stay signed in longer on their own devices. Sharing and Permissions in depth explain what each choice does.

Give each person an account of their own. With the Archive installed, what they upload waits in their own staging area, which only they see, until they file it into an album. Open Settings → Users and choose the New user button beside the filter. Type the person's Name , such as Helen Okafor. Username is suggested from it ( helen ). It is lower case and cannot be changed later. E-mail is optional: with one, they can sign in with it instead of the username. EiN sends no e-mail to it. Type a Password and Repeat it. You can leave both empty and set the password later, but they cannot sign in until you do. Under Groups , Users is ticked and greyed: everyone who signs in belongs to it. Tick any other group the person should be in. Choose Create user . EiN says "Created helen." and opens the account. The Users tab lists every account; the button beside the filter makes a new one If everyone with an account is family, the Users group already covers them, and you need no other group. If some accounts are not family, make a group for the family: Open Settings → Groups and choose the New group button beside the filter. Type a Name , such as family (it cannot be changed later), a Title , such as Family, and tick the Members . Choose Create group . On Settings → Permissions , choose the group as Group on the Sharing card, and add it under Groups on the New users card, so the New user form ticks it for each new account. Group changes reach a person the next time they sign in. Tip Tick Administrators on request for a second person you trust, or for an everyday account of your own. They can then choose Administer… in the account menu and enter their own password again to act as the administrator, until they sign out or choose Leave admin mode . Such a person can also set a new admin password if it is lost. Ticking Administrators does not do this: it is only the administrator account's own group. When someone forgets their password, open their account in Settings → Users , type a New password and Repeat it under Password , and choose Set password . Accounts and groups covers the rest: disabling and deleting accounts, groups, and the commands.

Everything the pages do, and more, can be done with commands in EiN's terminal, a shell that works on the same tree as the pages, as the person signed in. Open it with the top bar's terminal button, or with Alt + T wherever you are, and try a first command: # in EiN's terminal health It says in one line how EiN is doing, the same verdict as the dashboard's badge, and lists the checks behind it. --help after a command's name says how to use it, and docs find followed by what you want done finds the command that does it. Press Alt + T again to hide the terminal; what runs in it goes on. The terminal shows the rest, and SSH and SFTP how to reach the same shell from your own computer.

What comes next depends on the modules you installed in step 3: The Archive. The Archive takes it from here: importing the first photos, sorting them in staging into albums, and sharing an album, with or without an account. The Assistant. The Assistant says what it needs, what it adds, and where to start chatting.

Give each person: the address you opened in step 1, such as http://ein.local:8080/ , or the machine's IP address if their device cannot find the name; their username, or the e-mail address you gave the account, and their password. They sign in on the sign-in page with Username or e-mail , Password and Sign in . Ask them to change their password at once, under Profile → Security . Finding your way around is a good page to send them, with the overview of each module you installed, such as The Archive . EiN answers on your home network. Reaching it from elsewhere takes an HTTPS proxy of your own in front of it; Ports, HTTPS and remote access explains what EiN needs from one. On a phone, EiN runs in the browser; there is no app to install from a store. The page fits the screen: the EiN mark at the top left opens the menu. From the browser's menu, a phone can add EiN to its home screen, where it opens full screen, like an app, when EiN is served over HTTPS. EiN does not work offline. EiN on a phone shows what differs.

Look at the dashboard now and then. EiN sends no alerts, by e-mail or otherwise: what goes wrong shows on the dashboard and in the logs. Its Storage card shows how much room each part of the data folder has left, and says "full in ~N days" in red when a part fills within two weeks. EiN does not stop work for you when the disk fills. Update by running the installer again: # on the machine EiN runs on curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash It updates ~/ein , then downloads the newest images of EiN and its services and starts them again, keeping your options in ~/ein/.env , your data and the installed modules. ~/ein/setup.sh alone does the same, ~/ein included, without checking the machine. There are no releases: an update takes the newest code, and there is no going back to the previous one. Modules are updated separately, with Update in Settings → Modules → Published modules . Updating explains what an update touches. After the machine restarts , check that EiN came back. The installer makes EiN start at boot where it can: under podman it enables podman-restart.service , and lingering for your user, and with Docker it checks that Docker's own service is enabled. Where it cannot, its output ends with "EiN does not start again when the machine does until this has run:" and the commands to run, such as sudo loginctl enable-linger and your username. Until they have run, start EiN yourself after a reboot: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose ps podman compose up -d Back up. EiN has no backup command; you copy its data yourself, with your own tools. A backup needs three things, taken together: ~/ein/.env , which holds your options and the passwords made at the install, and nothing else keeps them; the data folder, ~/ein/data unless you chose another at the install, and above all its files folder, which holds your originals; the database, which is the container engine's volume ein_db (or the folder you gave --db-dir ), not part of the data folder. Note The database holds every name, album, person and setting, and the files folder holds the files themselves, stored by an id rather than by name. Neither is any use without the other, so copy them at the same time, and back up before each update. Your data: backup, moving and removing gives a procedure, and Troubleshooting helps when something goes differently.

This page shows the parts of EiN's web interface and what each one does: the top bar, the sidebar, the headers of pages, and the dialogs and side panel that pages open in. It also covers signing in and out. It is for everyone who uses EiN in a browser.

Open the address your administrator gave you, for example http://ein.local:8080 , in a current browser. EiN shows its sign-in page. The sign-in page. Browse without signing in is there only where the administrator lets visitors browse. In Username or e-mail , type your username, or the e-mail address of your account. In Password , type your password. The eye at the right of the field shows what you typed. Choose Sign in , or press Enter . EiN loads afresh and opens Home . If you followed a link to a particular page while signed out, you land on the sign-in page first and go on to that page once you are in. Note A fresh installation has one account, admin , whose password the installer prints once. Install EiN and First steps take it from there.

The sign-in page says what went wrong in a red box above the fields: Message What it means What to do Username or e-mail is required The first field is empty. Fill it in. login: authentication failed The username or e-mail, or the password, is wrong. EiN does not say which, so that nobody can find out which accounts exist. Check both and try again. If you have forgotten your password, ask an administrator to set another one. login: account disabled Your password is right, but an administrator has turned off sign-in for your account. Ask an administrator. login: password reset required Your password is right, but your account is waiting for an administrator to set a password. Ask an administrator to set one. login: too many failed sign-ins; try again in N s There have been too many wrong passwords from your network address. Wait the number of seconds it gives, then try again. A wrong password takes about a second to be answered. After five failed sign-ins from one network address, EiN makes that address wait before it checks another password: one second at first, doubling with each further failure, up to 15 minutes. After five failures on one account, each attempt on that account is slowed by up to 10 seconds, but the account is never locked, so someone guessing at your password cannot lock you out. Failures are forgotten an hour after the last one. Administrators find the rest in Accounts and groups .

An administrator can let people look around without an account, with Visitors may browse under Settings → Permissions (the setting CFG_GUEST_BROWSING ). It is off by default, and then anyone who has not signed in is sent to the sign-in page. Where it is on, opening EiN takes you straight to Home , and the sign-in page offers Browse without signing in . As a visitor: you see only what has been shared with visitors, and you cannot change anything; the top bar has a Sign in button where the terminal button and your picture would be, and no Create menu; the sidebar leaves out Settings , and with the Archive Staging ; a page that belongs to an account, such as Profile , Trash , Favourites , About EiN or a form that creates something, sends you to sign in, and back to that page afterwards. Someone can also send you a share link, an address with /s/ in it. It opens what was shared without an account, even where visitors may not browse. There, you see only the pages of what the link opens: no sidebar and no search box, and the EiN mark leads back to what was shared. Sharing covers share links, including the page that says This link no longer works .

Choose your picture at the right end of the top bar, then Logout . EiN signs this browser out, ends your terminal sessions and shows the sign-in page. Your sign-in also ends by itself. By default a browser stays signed in for 1 day after its last visit, and a session unused for 12 hours ends; an administrator can change both under Settings → Permissions . When your sign-in ends, or an administrator disables your account, the page reloads and shows the sign-in page.

Every page sits in the same frame: the top bar across the top, the sidebar down the left, the page itself in the middle, and the side drawer at the right when something is open in it. The frame stays the same on every page; only the page in the middle changes. Home, signed in as the administrator, with the archive and assistant modules installed. What you see depends on the modules installed on your EiN. EiN itself gives the frame, Home, Search, Settings, Statistics, Documentation and the administrator's pages. The Archive adds the pages for photos, albums, people and places, and the assistant adds the chat. This page describes the frame every EiN has and marks what each module adds; the screenshots show EiN with both installed. Without modules, the sidebar holds only EiN's own entries, and the top bar has no Random album , chat button or Create menu. The browser tab is titled with the page's name followed by · EiN , for example Albums · EiN ; on Home it says EiN alone. The interface is in English and always dark: there is no light theme and no other language.

From left to right: Part What it does The EiN mark and name Go to Home . On a phone the mark opens and closes the menu instead. The search box, Search for anything Finds pages, and with the Archive albums, people and places, as you type; Enter searches everything. Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) puts the cursor in it from anywhere. Search and the finder explains it. Random album (two crossing arrows) Opens an album picked at random; Alt + R does the same. Added by the Archive. Disconnected (with a red dot) Shown only while the page's connection to EiN is lost; on a phone it is a red crossed-out plug. EiN tries again by itself every second or two. Uploads Appears once you upload something, such as files dropped on the terminal . While files are going up it is a ring, with "Uploading N of M" in its tooltip; choose it for the files, Cancel , Retry failed and Clear . With the Archive, see Getting your photos in . Chat (a speech bubble) Opens the chat in the side drawer; choose it again to close the drawer. Added by the assistant; see Chatting with the assistant . Create (a plus) The Create New menu, below. Signed in only, and only where a module gives the menu rows. Toggle Terminal (Alt+T) Opens and closes the terminal, which drops down over the page. Signed in only, and not on a phone. See The terminal . Your picture The account menu, below. Its tooltip is your name. Sign in For visitors only, in place of the terminal button and your picture. A button that opens a page in the side drawer is lit while the drawer shows it, and it is left out on that page itself: on the Chat page there is no chat button. Warning Uploads run in the open browser tab. Closing or reloading the tab while files are still going up stops them, and EiN does not warn you first.

Choose the plus to make something. Each row opens a form in a dialog over the page you are on. EiN itself puts no rows in this menu; the modules do. Without a module that adds one, there is no plus in the top bar. With the Archive installed, the menu has these rows: The Create menu's rows come from the modules; these are the archive's. Row Opens More Import media Import media : choose a category in staging and the files or folders to bring in. Getting your photos in Album Create Album Albums Person Create Person People and faces Location Create Location Locations and the map Device Register Device Devices and GPS tracks

Choose your picture at the right end of the top bar. The menu is headed Account . The account menu holds your own pages and signing out. Row Shown What it does Me With the Archive, when your account is linked to a person Opens that person's page. Favourites With the Archive The pictures you have marked with a heart. Profile Always Your name, description, preferences and password. Trash Always What you have deleted, to restore or remove for good. Shortcuts ? Always Opens the list of keyboard shortcuts. About EiN Always A dialog with EiN's version, how long it has been running, the installed modules with their versions, the services it uses (the language model, the media service) and the versions of PostgreSQL and Deno it runs on. Administer… For members of the sudo group, outside admin mode Admin mode, below. Leave admin mode In admin mode Back to your own rights. Logout Always Signs you out. Your profile, favourites and trash covers Me , Favourites , Profile and Trash . With the Archive, your picture is the cover photo of the person your account is linked to. Without a linked person it shows the first letters of your username, as an image drawn by the outside service ui-avatars.com ; without a connection to the internet, the first letter of your name shows instead.

A member of the sudo group can act as the administrator for a while, the way sudo works on other systems, without signing in as admin : Choose your picture, then Administer… . In the Administer dialog, "Enter your password again to act as the administrator until you sign out or leave admin mode.", type your own password in Password . Choose Administer . The page reloads with the administrator's rights. While they last, your picture has an orange ring and a small orange shield at its lower left, and its tooltip ends in "(administrator)". A wrong password shows "That is not your password." Choose Leave admin mode in the same menu to go back to your own rights; signing out ends admin mode as well. Accounts and groups explains who is in sudo and the admin command that does the same in the terminal.

The sidebar lists the pages, in four sections. The first has no heading. Section Entry Opens Shown to Added by Home What the modules put there: Home and statistics ; with the Archive, On this day, News and Events: Memories, news and events on Home everyone EiN Chat Conversations with the assistant: Chatting with the assistant everyone assistant Media Every photo, video, recording and document: Media, Year and labels everyone archive Staging Your uploads waiting to be sorted: Sorting in staging signed in archive Explore Search What the modules make searchable; with the Archive, photos, videos, albums, people and places, by name, date or @mention: Search and the finder everyone EiN Explore Year One year's pictures: Media, Year and labels everyone archive Explore Map Pictures and tracks on a map: Locations and the map everyone archive Browse Albums Albums everyone archive Browse People People and faces everyone archive Browse Locations Locations and the map everyone archive Browse Devices Cameras, phones, scanners and trackers: Devices and GPS tracks everyone archive System Nodes A file manager over the whole tree administrators EiN System Dashboard How EiN is doing: Health and the dashboard administrators EiN System Settings How this installation is set up: Configuration signed in EiN System Statistics How the archive has grown: Home and statistics everyone EiN System Documentation EiN's own guide, and the commands, settings and modules installed on your EiN everyone EiN An entry added by a module is there once that module is installed; The Archive and The Assistant describe what each brings. "Administrators" means the admin account, or someone in admin mode. For anyone else Settings opens on its Modules tab, the only one they get. A section left with no entries is not shown. Where you are. The entry of the page you are on is lit, with a bar in the accent colour at its left. Fold a section. Click its heading ( Explore , Browse or System ) to fold it away, and again to unfold it. A folded section still shows the entry of the page you are on. This browser remembers which sections you folded. Collapse to icons. The button at the foot of the sidebar, Collapse to icons , narrows it to a column of icons; hold the pointer over an icon to see its name. The same button, then called Show labels , brings the names back. This browser remembers the choice. You and your administrator can rename, reorder, hide and add entries: see Your sidebar and top bar . On a phone the sidebar is out of sight until you choose the EiN mark or swipe right: see EiN on a phone .

Most pages open with a header: a band in EiN's coloured pattern with the page's title, a line under it, and often counts. Actions stand at the header's right: Upload , Share and Edit as buttons, in that order, on the pages that offer them, then ⋮ ( More actions ) with the page's other actions and Move to trash last. Where the header is narrow the buttons fold into ⋮ too. Actions that change something are offered only on what you may change. Tabs sit along the header's foot, such as Media , Map and Info on the Archive's album pages. The chosen tab is part of the page's address ( ?tab= ), so a link can open a given tab; see Addresses in the web interface . Scrolled down , the header's last row, its tabs or filters, stays in view under the top bar, with ⋮ holding every action of the page. On a wide screen the page's name appears at that row's left. Pages that are tools rather than things to look at, such as Nodes , Trash and Chat , have a header one line high instead, with the title at the left and the page's controls at the right. The Map page has no header; the map fills the page. Move to trash puts the thing in your trash and leaves its page. A message at the foot of the screen says it was moved, with Undo to put it back.

p.h: Pages, dialogs, the side drawer and full screen
p.x: The same page can open in four ways. Which one you get depends on where you open it from. Opens as What you see Examples To close it A page The page in the middle of the frame; the address in the browser changes. Anything in the sidebar The browser's Back A dialog A box over the dimmed page, with a coloured header band, an icon and a title. On a phone it fills the screen, except a question that only asks you to confirm. The Create forms, About EiN , Keyboard shortcuts The × at the top right, Esc , or a click outside the box. On a phone, Back too. The side drawer A panel at the right. On a wide screen it sits beside the page, which makes room for it; on a narrower one it covers the page. The chat, from the assistant's chat button Its top-bar button again. Where it covers the page, Back closes it too. Full screen Over everything, the top bar included. The Archive's viewer for photos, videos and recordings Back or Esc A few things to know about each: A dialog is not part of the address, so reloading the page closes it. A link inside a dialog opens its page in the frame and closes the dialog. The side drawer keeps the width you give it. Drag its left edge, or click the edge and press ← or → to make it 20 pixels wider or narrower, between 360 and 960 pixels (460 at first). This browser remembers the width. On the drawer's own page, such as Chat , the drawer steps aside, because the page shows the same thing at full size. On a phone the chat button opens the chat as a dialog instead. Full screen is part of the address ( ?fullscreen= ), so a reload, or a link you send someone, opens it again. On a wide screen an open side drawer stays beside the viewer, so you can read the chat next to a photo; see Viewing photos, videos and recordings .

Press ? anywhere outside a text field, or choose Shortcuts in the account menu, to see the Keyboard shortcuts dialog. It lists the keys that work anywhere, and a group for each part of the screen that has keys of its own, such as the viewer or the Nodes explorer, while that part is on screen. Press ? on any page to see the keys that work there. Keys What they do Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) Search, or go to a page, person or album; > for commands ? These shortcuts Alt + T Show or hide the terminal Alt + N New terminal tab Alt + R Random album (with the archive) On a Mac the list shows Alt as ⌥ . Where a dialog or the viewer covers the search box, Ctrl + K opens the same search as a dialog of its own. Every key EiN knows, by area, is in Keyboard shortcuts .

p.h: Messages and other things you will see
p.x: Messages at the foot of the screen say what has happened, often with Undo . They leave by themselves after 4 seconds, or 8 seconds when they offer an action. EiN has no list of past messages. Back to top , a round button at the lower right, appears once you have scrolled a screen's height down a page.

What you see Why What to do Disconnected in the top bar The connection to EiN dropped: your network, or EiN restarting. Wait; EiN reconnects by itself within a second or two. If it stays, ask your administrator whether EiN is running. The sign-in page appears while you were working Your sign-in ended, or an administrator disabled your account. Sign in again. Nothing here : "There is no page at … The link may be mistyped, or what it led to has moved." The address leads to no page. Go back or Go home . This page did not load Its code could not be fetched, usually because EiN was updated while the tab was open. Reload . Something broke on this page : "The rest of EiN still works." An error while drawing the page; the error text is shown under it. Reload . If it keeps happening, send the error text to your administrator. An entry you expect is not in the sidebar It is for administrators, its module is not installed, or someone hid it. See the sidebar table above, Modules and Your sidebar and top bar .

Search and the finder : everything the search box and the Search page can find. The terminal : the command line behind Alt + T . Keyboard shortcuts : every key, by area. Your sidebar and top bar : rename, hide and add entries. EiN on a phone : the menu behind the mark, swiping and adding EiN to the home screen. Your profile, favourites and trash : your own pages from the account menu. Addresses in the web interface : every page's address, for links.

EiN gives you two ways to find something: the finder in the top bar, which takes you to a page, an action or a command in a few keystrokes, and the Search page. What there is to search comes from the modules installed; this page covers what EiN itself gives, for everyone who uses EiN in a browser. With the Archive installed, Searching your pictures covers finding photos, videos, recordings and documents, and the albums, people and places they belong to.

p.h: The finder in the top bar
p.x: The box in the middle of the top bar, Search for anything , is the finder. Click it, or press Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) wherever you are, and a list opens under it. The list closes when you press Esc , click somewhere else or choose a row, and choosing a row empties the box. When something covers the box (a dialog, the viewer, or a page shown full screen), the same keys open the finder as a dialog of its own, with the prompt Search, or go to a page… . Esc , or Ctrl + K again, closes it. On a phone the box reads Search , the list takes the width of the screen, and the keyboard's search key does what Enter does. EiN on a phone covers the rest. With no module installed, the finder finds the pages in your sidebar, the actions in the top bar and EiN's commands. Each module adds its pages and actions, and the Archive adds its albums, people, locations and devices by name.

With the box empty, the list shows two groups: Go to : every page in your sidebar, with the sidebar section it is in beside it. Do : every button in the top bar, and every row of its menus named after its menu. With the Archive and the assistant installed, these include Chat , Random album , Create: Album , Create: Import media and Account: Favourites . Use the arrow keys to light a row and Enter to open it, or click it. While nothing is typed, Enter does nothing until an arrow key has lit a row.

As you type, the list changes to these groups, in this order: Group Rows A row takes you to Search Search for "<your words>" , and with the Archive installed Pictures of "<your words>" The Search page, or the Archive's Media page, searching for the words Go to and Do The pages and actions whose names hold your words That page or action The kinds the Search page finds Their things whose names match, with the kind of each beside it. With the Archive installed the group is Albums, people, locations, devices Its page The first row is lit, so Enter opens the Search page for your words, and so does the arrow button at the end of the box. To go straight to a page or a thing, light its row with the arrow keys or click it. With the Archive installed, in the Wrenfield demo, typing peggy offers Peggy Wrenfield, and typing christmas offers albums such as Christmas 1975, Christmas 1998 and Christmas in Wellington. While names are being looked up the list says Looking… ; when nothing fits it says Nothing matches. Note Words you take to the Search or Media page from the finder are searched exactly as you typed them. To have a sentence read into people, places and years (see Write what you are looking for ), press Enter once more in that page's own box.

Starting with > turns the finder into a search of EiN's commands. Click the box or press Ctrl + K . Type > followed by what the command should do, or part of its name, such as >person . Up to six commands appear under Commands , each with its one-line description. Choose one to open its entry in EiN's documentation ( Documentation in the sidebar). Choosing a command does not run it: you run commands in the terminal . With fewer than two letters after the > , the list says Type what the command should do. , and when nothing fits, No command matches. The line at the foot of the list, Type > to find a command , is there as a reminder. When the assistant module and the media service are installed, the finder looks for commands by what they are for, so a command can turn up even when its name and description use other words than yours. Without them, and while the media service is not answering, it matches your words against the commands' names and descriptions. The command reference lists every command.

Search , under Explore in the sidebar, searches the kinds of things the installed modules make searchable. With no module installed it has nothing to search: before you type it says Search for anything , and a search answers No results found . With the Archive installed it finds albums, people, locations and devices; see Find albums, people, locations and devices . Open Search in the sidebar, or choose Search for "…" in the finder. The header reads Search and Search by name, date or @mention . Type in the box, Search, or type @ to pick something by name , and press Enter . The results appear as cards, 60 at a time, with more as you scroll. A card shows the name, a cover picture and the kind. Click a card to open its page. When the modules make more than one kind searchable, narrow the results with Show : All , or one of the kinds. Order them with Sort : Relevance (the default), Name (A-Z) , Newest first or Oldest first . When nothing is found, the page says No results found . The box takes @ to pick something exactly, turns what it understood into chips you can remove one by one, and offers the Interpreted filter to show what it searched for. Which words it reads as people, places, years and kinds comes from a module: the Archive reads them, and Searching your pictures explains how. Without it, the box searches your words as they are. Every search finds only what you are allowed to see; a visitor browsing without signing in finds only what is shared with everyone ( Sharing ).

Before you type, the Search page shows Recent searches : your last eight searches on this page. Click one to run it again, its × ( Forget … ) to drop it, or Clear to drop them all. They are kept in this browser, not in your account, so another computer or phone has a list of its own. Under them come the sections the modules give the page. With the Archive installed, these are the people, locations, years and labels to start from; see Start from people, places, years and labels . With no recent search and no module to offer a section, the page says Search for anything and "Type a name, a year or a few words; @ picks something by name."

The address in your browser holds the whole search: the words, the chips, Show and Sort . So a search can be linked, and the browser's Back and Forward step through your searches. Copy the address to send a search to someone in the family, or to come back to it later. Whoever opens the link sees only what they are allowed to see. To keep a search in your sidebar, see Your sidebar and top bar .

EiN's search is one command, search , and the modules supply what it searches. A module plugs in by the names of its commands and by its manifest: What a module gives What it adds to search search-<x> commands Hits for the words of a search; search asks every one on the path and puts the hits together subject-<kind> commands What a person, location or device picked with @ has Node types marked searchable in its manifest The kinds the Search page finds and offers under Show , and the things the finder finds by name Panels for the Search page The sections shown before you search, and what a search for one label adds A reader for the box, named by CFG_SEARCH_PARSER How a sentence is read into chips A command finder, named by CFG_COMMAND_FINDER Commands found by what they are for, in the finder With no module, search has no provider to ask and the Search page no kind to find. The Archive brings the providers for albums, people, locations, devices, tracks, media and documents, and the reader for the box; the assistant brings the command finder. Writing a module shows how a module plugs in, and the settings are in the settings reference . In the terminal , search answers the same questions as the pages. Its options are in the command reference ; Search from the terminal gives examples over the Archive.

Home is the page EiN opens on, with three sections the installed modules fill: On this day , News and Events . The Statistics page shows how what EiN holds has grown, with sections modules add.
