This page is for everyone who uses EiN, and covers what EiN itself gives; with the Archive installed, Memories, news and events on Home covers what it shows there.

Choose Home at the top of the sidebar. On a computer, the EiN mark at the top left also takes you there. EiN opens on Home when you sign in, unless you were on your way to another page. The page is headed Welcome , "What is new in the archive, what is coming up, and this day in years past". Under the header: On this day runs across the top, when there is anything to show; News fills the wider column on the left; Events stands in a card on the right. On a narrow window or a phone it comes after News, so scroll down past the news to see it. Each section loads on its own, so one can appear before the others. All three show only what you may see. "Today" is the date on your own computer or phone, not the server's.

Each section gathers what every installed module has to say about it, and each entry is drawn by the module it came from. EiN itself adds no entries: Section What EiN does with the modules' entries On this day One row, newest year first, up to 8 entries; when you have more than fit, swipe the row sideways or scroll it with a trackpad. With no entry the section is not shown at all. News A timeline, newest first, up to 8 entries. Beside each is the portrait of the person whose account did it, when the account is linked to a person in the archive ( Your profile, favourites and trash ); otherwise an icon. Events A card headed Events with the number of entries beside it, in up to three groups: Today , Coming up (nearest first) and Recently (the most recent first). It looks 7 days back and 30 days ahead, and holds up to 16 entries. At the right of each Events entry it says when: "Today", "Tomorrow", "Yesterday", "in 9 days" or "3 days ago" up to 13 days away, and after that in weeks, "in 3 weeks" or "2 weeks ago". When there are more than 16 entries, the ones their module marks as milestones are kept first, then the ones nearest to today. With no module installed, Home shows the Welcome header, News says "Nothing has been added yet" and "What people add shows up here.", Events says "Nothing comes round in the next few weeks.", and On this day is not shown. A module can offer a way to begin under the empty News: the Archive offers Import media when you are signed in. With the Archive installed, On this day shows the pictures taken on today's date in earlier years, News the albums people made lately, and Events the birthdays, memorials and wedding anniversaries around today; see Memories, news and events on Home .

Choose Statistics in the sidebar, under System . Everyone can open it. The page is headed Statistics , "Archive statistics over time". It holds the sections the installed modules give it, then Nodes , which is EiN's own. With the Archive installed, the first section is Events , charts of when in the year births, weddings and deaths fall; see Life events on the Statistics page .

The Nodes section shows what has been added to EiN, year by year. Everything in EiN is a node: each file and folder, and with the Archive each photo, album, person and place, and each file EiN makes from them; see How EiN works . File storage growth runs across the full width: the size of the files added each year, counting the originals and the smaller versions EiN makes of them, with a line for "Cumulative file size by month". The total is at the top right. Then one chart for each kind of node, such as Person nodes or Album nodes , File nodes first and the others largest first: bars for the nodes created in each calendar year, a line for the "Cumulative total by month", and the total, such as "2,431 nodes". Rest the pointer on a bar to read the year's count. A node counts in the year it was created in EiN. The charts leave out the kinds that make up the system itself, such as folders, links, accounts and sessions, and they count what you may see. These charts can take a few seconds to appear on a large archive. When there is nothing to count, the section says "No node history found".

What you see Why, and what to do Home is empty No installed module fills it. Modules says which modules there are. Events is a day out Home takes today's date from your computer or phone. Check its date and time zone. A red box above the sections One section could not be loaded, and the box gives the reason. The other sections still show. Reload the page; if the box stays, tell whoever looks after EiN. Memories, news and events on Home covers what goes differently in the Archive's entries.

Home runs ordinary commands, which you can run yourself in the terminal . The Home page passes your own date to them; run in the terminal, they take today's date in UTC unless you name a day. # in EiN's terminal onthisday # what On this day shows, one line a year onthisday 12-25 -- limit 20 # another day, more years news # what News shows, with the time in UTC news -- limit 20 events # what Events shows: 7 days back, 30 days ahead events --today 2026-01-20 # around another date events --days-ahead 0 --days-past 0 # today only Each of the three gathers what every installed module offers, from the commands named onthisday-… , news-… and events-… ; with no module they print nothing. Writing a module shows how a module adds to them. The full options are in the reference for onthisday , news and events , and Commands by task lists more.

Memories, news and events on Home : what the Archive shows on Home and on the Statistics page. Sharing : who sees what. Modules : the modules that fill Home. Commands by task : the shell commands by what they do.

Whoever may change something in EiN decides who else sees it. This page is for everyone who shares what they keep in EiN: the Share dialog, the chip that says how visible something is, links for people without an account, keeping a few photos private in a shared album, how new albums start out, and why you may not see everything that is there. The Share dialog is EiN's own and works on any node. Most of what people share are albums, which come with the Archive , so the examples here are albums, and the parts that only albums have say so.

An album, and everything in it, can be seen by: its owner , usually whoever made it, who can always see and change it; the people and groups it is shared with , each with Can view or Can edit ; everyone with an account , when it is shared with them, as most albums are; visitors who are not signed in , only when the administrator lets visitors browse and the album is shared with them; anyone with its link , a link you send to someone without an account. On a standard installation a new album starts out seen by everyone with an account and changed only by you. How new albums start out has the details. Note The administrator sees and can change everything, private albums included. "Private" keeps an album from the rest of the family, not from the administrator. You do not need to know how this is stored. The Share dialog says it in words, and Permissions in depth has the exact rules underneath.

Share is offered only on things you may change: Anything in the tree : open Nodes , pick the node and choose the Sharing tab. Nodes is under System in an administrator's sidebar; anyone signed in can open it at /system/nodes . With the Archive installed, its pages offer Share as well: An album : Share in the album's header. On a phone the header's buttons are under ⋮ . A person, a location or a device : Share in its header. Sharing a person shares their page, not the photos they are in. One photo, video or recording : open it in the viewer and choose Share in the cog menu of the details panel (see Viewing photos, videos and recordings ). Several photos of an album : select them and choose Share in the selection bar; see Keep some photos private in a shared album . The chip under an album's title, and the one in the viewer's details panel, both the Archive's, open the same dialog; see The visibility chip . Opened by someone who may only look, the dialog shows who has access without letting them change it, and says "Only Helen Okafor and people who can edit it can change who it is shared with." One dialog decides who sees an album and who may change it, and makes the link for someone without an account. The dialog is headed with what it shares, such as Share “Christmas at the cottage” , and has up to four parts: Who can see it , People with access , Share with a link (albums only) and With their own sharing (when some photos keep sharing of their own).

Open the album and choose Share . Under People with access , click Add people or groups and type a name. The list offers Everyone with an account first, then groups, such as Family (group) , then people, such as Jon Wrenfield (jon) . Choose one. The new row starts at Can view . To let someone change the album too, open the menu at the right of their row and choose Can edit . To take someone away, open the same menu and choose Remove access . Choose Save . Nothing changes until you choose Save . Until then the button at the left says Cancel , and closing the dialog drops your changes. Once nothing is left to save it says Close .

p.h: Who can see it, and the two presets
p.x: The top of the dialog says in a sentence who can see the album, with the visibility chip beside the heading. The sentence follows your changes before you save, so you can see what a change will do. Two buttons fill the list for you: Button What it sets Default Everyone with an account can view it, and nobody else is listed. The owner keeps their access. Private Nobody but the owner: every person, group and visitor row is taken away. The button that matches the list is highlighted. A preset only fills the list; Save applies it. Default here always means "everyone with an account can see it". It is not the sharing your administrator chose for new albums, which can be narrower. Private does not touch a share link. An album with a link stays Public to anyone holding the link until you choose Delete link under Share with a link . On a photo that keeps its own sharing there is a third button, Like the album . It shares the photo as the album is, and lets the album's later changes reach it again. See Put photos back to the album's sharing .

The list starts with the owner, marked Owner (and "(you)" when it is you). Then comes everyone the album is shared with, each row with a picture, a name and a line under it: Row The line under it Who it is Everyone with an account The Users group Everyone who signs in, including accounts made later. A group, such as Family Group · 6 people The members of the group, as the administrator set it up. A person Their username That account only. When the list is empty, it says "Nobody else has access." Each row's menu sets what they may do: Level What the menu says What it allows Can view See it and download it Open the album and its pictures, and download them. Can edit Also add to it, change it and delete from it Everything above, and add pictures, change them, delete from the album, and change who it is shared with, links included. Remove access Takes the row away when you save. Give Can edit only to people you trust with the album: they can share it further or make it private. Groups are made by the administrator, under Settings → Groups (see Accounts and groups ). To share with part of the family only, ask for a group such as family , then share with the group rather than with each person. An administrator can rest the pointer on a group's row to see who is in it.

p.h: Visitors who are not signed in
p.x: Visitors who are not signed in is a row of its own, under the others. It is there when the administrator lets visitors browse EiN without an account, and then says "Anyone who opens EiN, without an account". Its menu has only Can view and No access : visitors never change anything. When visitors may not browse, the row is shown only on something already shared with them, and says "This EiN asks visitors to sign in, so they see it only once it lets them browse." To let one person without an account see an album, send them a link instead.

Save applies the list to the album and to everything in it, in one go. Two kinds of things inside are left as they are: photos that keep their own sharing (see Keep some photos private in a shared album ); what you may not change, or may not even see. The dialog says what happened under the list: "Saved.", followed by "2 items inside keep their own sharing." or "3 items inside were left as they were: you cannot change them." where that applies. Pictures uploaded into the album later get the album's sharing, its link included. A picture added to the album from another album keeps the sharing of the album it lives in: sharing this album does not change it, and someone who may see this album but not the other one cannot open it.

With the Archive installed, under an album's title, and in the viewer's details panel for a single file, a small coloured chip says how widely it is shared. Resting the pointer on it shows the sentence from the table, and clicking it opens the Share dialog. The chip answers one question at a glance: who besides you can see this. Chip When What it says Public , green, with a globe A share link opens it, or it is shared with visitors and visitors may browse. "Anyone with its link, or any visitor, can see it without signing in" No chip Everyone with an account can see it. "Everyone with an account can see it" (in the dialog) Restricted , orange, with a lock in a frame Some people or groups besides the owner can see it, but not everyone with an account. "Only some of the people with an account can see it" Private , red, with a lock Nobody but its owner. "Only its owner can see it" Most albums have no chip, because most are seen by everyone with an account. Visitors and people who opened a link never see the chip: they are not told who else can see something.

p.h: Share an album with a link
p.x: A link lets someone without an account see one album, without signing in. The dialog makes links for albums only, so they come with the Archive. Open the album and choose Share . Under Share with a link , next to "Send a link to someone without an account", choose Create link . The link is made at once; it does not wait for Save . Click the address, your EiN's address followed by /s/ and a code, or the copy button at its right. EiN says "Link copied to clipboard". Paste the link into a message to the person. The address starts with the address you opened EiN at. Open EiN at an address the person can reach before you copy the link: one with localhost in it works only on the machine EiN runs on, and one such as http://ein.local:8080 only on your home network. Reaching EiN from outside the home is the administrator's to set up; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Under the address, the link's row says when it stops working and how often it has been opened: When it stops working. A new link works for 30 days: "Expires in 30 days, on 24 Nov". Click that text for the Works for menu: 1 day , 1 week , 30 days , 3 months , 1 year or No end date , counted from now. The change is made at once. A link without an end says "Never expires", and one in its last day "Expires within a day". How often it was opened. "Not opened yet", "Opened once, last today", "Opened 4 times, last yesterday", "Opened 9 times, last 3 days ago", or a date. The count covers everyone who has the link; it does not say who opened it. Delete link turns the link off at once, for everyone who has it. The album gets one link in the dialog, so everyone you send it to uses the same address. While the album has a link its chip says Public . The link opens the album and everything in it that you may change, except photos that keep their own sharing: then the dialog adds "The link does not open what keeps its own sharing, listed below." Pictures uploaded into the album later are opened by the link too. Someone who may only look at the album sees that it has a link, when it expires and how often it was opened, but not the address. Without a link, they see "No link opens this album."

p.h: What the person you send it to sees
p.x: The link opens a page that says "Opening what was shared with you…". Then the album's page opens, without signing in. They see that album and what is in it, and no other page of EiN: there is no sidebar and no search box, and the EiN mark at the top leads back to the album. Any other page asks them to sign in. In the viewer they see the pictures without the details panel, and can save each one with Download in the viewer's More menu . A few things to know about links: A browser holds one link at a time. Opening a link to another album leaves the first one. To go back, open the first link again. Someone signed in stays themselves. If the person has an account and is signed in, the album opens as their own account sees it. Where visitors may browse , someone who opened a link also sees what visitors see. When a link has expired or been deleted, or the address is mistyped, the page says This link no longer works : "It may have expired, or the person who shared it has turned it off. Ask them to send you a new link." with a Sign in button for someone who has an account.

An expired link opens nothing. The dialog shows it marked Expired until EiN clears expired links, which it does every hour by default. While it is still listed, choose a new time in its Works for menu to make the same address work again, or choose Delete link and then Create link for a new address.

p.h: Keep some photos private in a shared album
p.x: With the Archive installed, you can keep a few photos of a shared album to yourself, or show them to fewer people, without moving them out of the album. Share in the selection bar gives the chosen photos sharing of their own, apart from the album's. In the album, select the photos: tick the round box in a picture's top-left corner, Ctrl -click ( ⌘ -click on a Mac) to add more, or Shift -click to add a range. On a phone, press and hold a picture. Albums has every way to select. Choose Share in the selection bar at the bottom. The dialog is headed Share 3 photos , with "In “Christmas at the cottage”" under it. Choose Their own sharing : "Only those you choose below. They keep this when the album's sharing changes, and the album's link does not open them." Under People with access , the photos start with nobody but their owner ("Each keeps its owner, who can always see and change it."). Leave it so to keep them to yourself, or add the people or groups who should still see them. Choose Save . EiN says "3 photos now keep their own sharing". Everyone else no longer sees those photos in the album at all, and the album's link does not open them. When the album's sharing changes later, they keep theirs. If you may change the album, a lock in the corner of a picture marks one that keeps its own sharing; resting the pointer on it says "Keeps its own sharing". A folder inside an album can carry the lock too. People who may only look at the album do not see it. Share in the selection bar is greyed out when the selection includes a picture that is only linked into this album from another album. Such a picture has the sharing of the album it lives in; change it there. Selecting only photos that already keep their own sharing opens the dialog on Their own sharing , with the first photo's people, so you can change who sees them.

p.h: Put photos back to the album's sharing
p.x: There are three ways: From the selection bar. Select the photos, choose Share , then Like the album : "Whoever can see “Christmas at the cottage” can see them. When the album's sharing changes, they change with it." Choose Save . EiN says "3 photos shared like the album". From the album's Share dialog. With their own sharing , with a count beside it, lists the photos that keep their own sharing: "These keep their own sharing: changes to the album's sharing, and its link, do not reach them." Each row shows the photo, its name and Private , Shared differently or Open to visitors . Share like the album on a row puts that photo back at once, and Share all like the album puts every one of them back, listed or not. The first five are listed; Show all 12 lists the rest. The list stops at 50, and "And 7 more." under it counts the others. From the viewer. Open the photo, choose Share in the cog menu, and the dialog says "It keeps its own sharing: changes to the album “Christmas at the cottage” do not reach it." Choose Like the album , then Save .

Albums come with the Archive. Create → Album asks only for a name and a description. The new album gets the sharing your new albums start with, which comes from two places, both EiN's own settings. The administrator's default sharing , under Settings → Permissions → Sharing , sets who may see and change anything created as shared, which group it is shared with, and, if they choose, an account that owns it instead of its creator. On a standard installation the group is users , so a new album is seen by everyone with an account and changed only by you. See Permissions in depth . Your own preference narrows or widens that. Choose your picture at the right of the top bar, then Profile , the Preferences tab, and How widely what you create is shared : Choice A new album starts out default As the administrator set it. This is the choice until you change it. private Seen by you alone. Its chip says Private . shared Seen by the administrator's default group. On a standard installation that is everyone with an account; with a narrower group, such as family , only its members. everyone Seen by the default group and by everyone with an account. It never includes visitors who are not signed in. Change the choice and Save change appears under it. Your profile, favourites and trash has more on preferences. The preference applies to albums you create with Create → Album , and to new albums you make when you file pictures from your staging area. There, New private album always makes one only you can open, and pictures filed into an existing album take that album's sharing; see Sorting in staging . Anything else you create, such as a person or a location, or a picture you upload into an album, takes the sharing of where it is created. Changing the preference changes no album you already have. To change one, use its Share dialog.

EiN leaves out what you may not open. A folder, file or album that is private to someone else is not listed to you at all: not in search, not in ls or find in the terminal, and with the Archive not on Albums , in News or on the map. Here EiN differs from the files on a computer, where you see every name in a folder you can open, only not what is inside. So two people can see the same album differently, and an album can look emptier to you than to its owner. The administrator sees all of it. What is hidden is still there, and that explains some surprises: Counts are your own. The number on an album's card counts only the pictures you can see, so it can differ from person to person. Changing an album's sharing leaves what you cannot see as it is. The Share dialog says "3 items inside were left as they were: you cannot change them."; in the terminal, share-set and chmod -r say "1 child the caller may not read left unchanged". Moving or renaming an album or folder takes everything in it along , including what you cannot see. So does moving it to the trash. A folder can look empty and not be. In the terminal, rmdir answers "Directory not empty" and rm "Node not empty" for a folder whose only contents are hidden from you. A name can be taken by something you cannot see. Moving something to that name fails with "Access denied for operation 'w'". Copying a folder fails if it holds anything you cannot read , with "Access denied for operation 'r'" naming the folder, rather than making a copy that is missing it. Deleting a folder you may change with rm -r deletes everything in it , including what you cannot see, as on a computer, where deleting needs only the right to change the folder. If something behaves as though it holds more than you see, ask its owner or the administrator.

There is no Share button. You may not change the album, person or file. Ask its owner to give you Can edit , or to share it for you. Someone you shared with cannot see the album. If you shared it with a group they joined recently, they sign out and in again: group changes apply at the next sign-in. If they see the album but miss some pictures, those keep their own sharing (the lock), or live in another album that is not shared with them. Share in the selection bar is greyed out. The selection includes a picture linked in from another album. Select only pictures that live in this album, or change the other album's sharing. There is no Share with a link part. Links are made for albums only, not for a person, a location, a device or a single photo. The person you sent a link to sees "This link no longer works". The link expired or was deleted, or the address was cut short when it was pasted. Look in the album's Share dialog: create a link, or give the expired one a new time, and send it again. The link does not load for them at all. The address points somewhere they cannot reach, such as localhost or your home network. Open EiN at an address they can reach and copy the link again. The person with the link sees the album as their own account sees it. They were signed in when they opened the link, and then their own access counts. If they sign out and open the link again, it opens the album for them. EiN says "The browser would not copy the link: it is selected for you to copy." Browsers allow copying only on some pages, such as those over HTTPS. The address is selected: press Ctrl + C ( ⌘ + C on a Mac). The album still says Public after you chose Private. It has a link. Choose Delete link under Share with a link . There is no Visitors who are not signed in row. Visitors may not browse this EiN. The administrator turns that on; see Accounts and groups . To show one album to someone without an account, send a link instead. New albums start out private, or shared more widely, than you expected. Check How widely what you create is shared under Profile → Preferences , and ask the administrator what the default sharing is.

The same can be done in EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal share-info '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # who has access, and through what share-link create '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # a link for 30 days share-link list # the links you made share-link remove 3f9a0c1d2e4b5a69 # turn one off, by its id album create '/archive/albums/Christmas 1998' --name 'Christmas 1998' --share private share-link create prints the end of the address, what it opens and until when; put your EiN's address in front of it: /s/q7Rk2mWx9TbN4vLc8HsJ3d opens /archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage until 2026-11-24T10:12:00.000Z The share- commands are EiN's own and work on any node; album comes with the Archive. The reference has every option: share-info , share-link , share-set and album . Permissions in depth explains chmod , chown and acl , which the dialog sets for you.

This page covers the pages that belong to your account alone: your profile, where you change your name, your preferences and your password; your favourites, which the Archive gathers on a page of their own; and your trash, where what you delete waits before it is removed for good. It is for everyone who has an account on EiN. All three open from the account menu, Favourites once the Archive is installed. Choose your picture at the right end of the top bar: Favourites, Profile and Trash are the pages of your own account. They need you to be signed in. A visitor who opens one of them is asked to sign in first, and lands on the page afterwards. Finding your way around describes the rest of the account menu.

Choose your picture, then Profile . The page's header shows your display name, your username after an @ , and the description you gave yourself. With the Archive, its picture is the cover photo of the person your account is linked to; without one it shows the first letter of your name. The profile has three tabs: Account , Preferences and Security . The tab you are on is in the page's address, so /profile?tab=preferences opens your preferences and /profile?tab=security the password form directly.

Choose your picture, then Profile . It opens on the Account tab. In Display name , "Your name as it appears to others", type your name the way you want others to see it, for example Helen Okafor . In Description , "A line about you, shown under your name", type a line about yourself, such as Peggy's daughter, in Wellington , or leave it empty. Choose Save changes . Saved appears beside the button. Save changes stays greyed out while Display name is empty: every account has a name. Your picture's tooltip and the profile's header show the new name at once. Three things about your account are not on this tab: Your username , the name after the @ . Nobody can change it once the account exists, an administrator included. Your e-mail address. Only an administrator sets it, in your account under Settings → Users ; see Accounts and groups . When your account has one, you can type it instead of your username when you sign in. The profile does not show it; user-info in the terminal does, under From the terminal . Your picture , which with the Archive comes from the person your account is linked to, below. Note Your display name, description and e-mail address are not private. Anyone who is signed in can read them, for example with user-info in the terminal.

p.h: Your picture and the person you are
p.x: EiN has no way to upload a picture for an account. With the Archive installed, your picture is the person in the archive that your account is linked to. Helen Okafor's account, for example, can be linked to her page among the People , and then: your picture in the top bar and on your profile is her cover photo; the account menu has Me above Favourites , which opens her page; News on Home shows her picture beside the albums you add; an event or note you add to an album starts with her under Written by ; staging uses her homes to tell a trip from days at home when it suggests albums; see Sorting in staging . Without a link, your picture is an image of your username's first letters, which the browser fetches from the outside service ui-avatars.com . Where the browser cannot reach the internet, the first letter of your name shows instead. There is no button to link an account to a person. An administrator makes the link in the terminal: it is a softlink named person in the account's folder under /etc/users . For the account helen and the person whose page is at /people/Helen_Okafor : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator ln -s /archive/people/Helen_Okafor /etc/users/helen/person Helen sees her picture and Me the next time her page loads. rm /etc/users/helen/person takes the link away again; removing a link never removes the person it points at.

Choose your picture, then Profile , then the Preferences tab. It says: "These apply to you alone. They are stored in your home directory and follow you to the terminal as well." Your preferences belong to your account, so they follow you to every browser and device you sign in on. Preferences are grouped in categories; the badge under each says whether the value is the default or your own. The tab is laid out like the administrator's settings page: Find a setting searches names, descriptions, modules and keys, across every category. Categories , at the left, shows one category at a time. On a phone a Category list above the settings does the same. Overrides only shows only the settings you have changed; the button gives their number in brackets once there are some. A badge under each setting says where its value comes from: Default when nobody has changed it, Your setting when you have, and From deployment when the administrator gave everyone a starting value when setting up EiN. Your own value wins over the other two. A setting a module adds also carries the module's name, such as archive . To change a setting: Change the value in its control: pick from the list, type a number, or flip the switch between On and Off . Cancel and Save change appear under the control. Choose Save change ; Cancel puts the value back as it was. The badge turns to Your setting . To undo your choice later, choose Restore inherited value under a setting marked Your setting . It removes your own value, and the setting falls back to the deployment's value or to the default. If a save fails, the reason shows in a red box under the setting.

Category Setting Default What it changes Appearance Header entrance drawn How the tiles of the coloured band at the top of a page arrive when the page opens; the choices are below. A device set to reduce motion never animates it. Appearance Header entrance time 450 How many milliseconds that entrance takes, from the first tile starting to the last one in place. 0 shows the header as it is, without an entrance. Appearance Header over a cover split How the tiles meet a page's cover photo, such as an album's or a person's: split gives the left of the header to the tiles, which dissolve into the photo along a slanted edge; lines lays only their outlines over the photo. Playback Seconds per slide 3 How long each photo is shown in a slideshow. Playback Ken Burns effect On Slowly pan and zoom each photo during a slideshow. Sharing How widely what you create is shared default Where an album you create starts out; see below. Shell Shell history length 1000 How many commands the terminal remembers between sessions, in ~/.bash_history . EiN itself gives the settings under Appearance, Sharing and Shell. The two under Playback come with the archive module, and only an EiN with the archive has them. Viewing photos, videos and recordings shows a slideshow, and the settings reference lists each with its key, such as CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS . The choices for Header entrance : Choice The tiles are drawn drawn as if by pen, and filled from the bottom up falling falling into place sliding sliding in from the right sweep swept in from left to right growing growing from the bottom edge ripple rippling out from the title puzzle snapping in like puzzle pieces wave crossed by a wave of light

p.h: How widely what you create is shared
p.x: This preference decides how an album you create starts out: one made with Create → Album , with New album “…” in Add to an album , or with New album in staging. It does not change albums that exist already; to change who sees one of those, use its Share button. Albums come with the Archive; without it, nothing you create follows this preference. Choice A new album starts out default As the administrator's default sharing says, under Settings → Permissions . Unless the administrator has changed it, everyone with an account can see the album. private Seen only by you. shared Seen by the members of the default group the administrator chose. Unless the administrator has changed it, that group is everyone with an account. everyone Seen by everyone with an account, even where the administrator's default group is a smaller one. None of them shows an album to visitors who are not signed in, unless you keep default and the administrator's default sharing lets everyone else view; otherwise you grant that yourself in the Share dialog. An administrator can see every album, whatever you choose. New private album in staging is always private, whatever you choose here. Sharing explains the default sharing and the Share dialog.

Setting Takes effect Appearance and Playback At once, in the browser tab where you saved it. Other open tabs, and your other devices, when their page loads again. How widely what you create is shared At once, for the next album you create. Shell history length In the next terminal you open.

EiN keeps your preferences in the file .config in your home folder, /home/<your username>/.config , which only you can read. Every shell you open reads it, in the web terminal and over SSH, so a preference is also a variable there: # in EiN's terminal echo $CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS 5 It prints an empty line for a setting you have never changed: defaults are not written into the file. A terminal that is open when you save a change reads it before its next command; only a command that was already running keeps the old value. The config command lists and changes your preferences: # in EiN's terminal config list --scope user # your preferences, and where each value comes from config set CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS 5 # the same as Save change config unset CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS # the same as Restore inherited value config list --scope user prints each setting and its value, followed by (user) for your own value or (environment) for the deployment's; a default has no mark: CFG_USER_HEADER_ENTRANCE drawn CFG_USER_HEADER_ENTRANCE_TIME 450 CFG_USER_HEADER_COVER split CFG_USER_KEN_BURNS true CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS 5 (user) CFG_USER_DEFAULT_SHARE default HISTSIZE 1000 config set answers CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS = 5 , and config unset answers CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS reset to 3 (default) . A value of the wrong kind is refused, for example config set: CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS: expected a number, got 'five' . The file holds one line per setting, such as export CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS='5' , and you can edit it with edit ~/.config ; nothing then checks the values you type. Configuration explains how settings work for the whole installation, and Configuration files lists the files.

Update password stays greyed out until all three fields are filled in and the two new ones match. Choose your picture, then Profile , then the Security tab. In Current password , type the password you sign in with. In New password , type the new one. In Confirm new password , type the new one again. If the two differ, the field says "Does not match the new password". Choose Update password . It can be chosen once all three fields are filled in and the two new ones match. Password updated appears beside it, and the fields empty. The eye at the right of each field shows what you typed. EiN has no rules for passwords: it takes any password that is not empty, so how strong yours is is up to you. The new password is the one you sign in with from then on, in the browser and over SSH and SFTP. A key you added for SSH keeps working; see SSH and SFTP . Changing your password does not sign out the browsers and terminals where you are signed in already. If you change it because someone else may know it, ask an administrator to choose Disable sign-in for your account and then Enable sign-in : that signs your account out everywhere. If the password is not changed, the reason shows in a red box above the fields: Message What it means What to do user passwd: authentication failed Current password is not your password. Type it again. If you have forgotten it, see the next section. user passwd: no existing password found, contact admin Your account has no password to check against. Ask an administrator to set one.

p.h: If you have forgotten your password
p.x: EiN sends no e-mail and has no link for a forgotten password. Ask an administrator to set a new one for you: they do it in your account under Settings → Users , in its Password section, with Set password . Your old password stops working at once. Sign in with the one they give you, then change it on the Security tab to one that only you know. An administrator cannot make you choose a new password at your next sign-in; EiN has no such switch. An account that an administrator made without a password, and an account marked as needing one ( mustResetPassword ), cannot sign in at all until an administrator sets a password for it. Accounts and groups covers this from the administrator's side.

Your favourites are the pictures you have marked with a heart, from any album, gathered on one page. Only someone signed in has favourites; visitors have none. The heart, the Favourites page and its row in the account menu come with the Archive ; in any EiN, star in the terminal marks a node as a favourite (see From the terminal ). A favourite is a link to the picture where it lives, kept in the folder stars in your home folder. Hearting a picture never copies or moves it, and taking it out of your favourites never deletes it. Links explains how one picture can be in many places.

In the viewer , press the heart in the bar under the picture, whose tooltip says Favourite (s) , or press s . The heart fills in. On a phone it is Favourite in ⋮ at the top right. In a grid , such as an album or the Media page, select pictures and choose Favourite in the selection bar. EiN says, for example, 12 files added to favourites , with Undo . A small heart on a tile marks a picture in your favourites. A picture marked as a favourite in a Google Photos export becomes one of your favourites when you import it; see Getting your photos in .

Choose your picture, then Favourites . The page, "The pictures you have hearted", shows them in day sections, the way an album shows its pictures. Click one to open it in the viewer, which then steps through your favourites; Start slideshow there shows them all. With nothing hearted yet, the page says No favourites yet , "Select pictures and choose Favourite, or press the heart in the lightbox.", with a button Open Media .

p.h: Take a picture out of your favourites
p.x: In the viewer, press the filled heart, Unfavourite (s) , or press s again. In a grid, select pictures that are all favourites already. The selection bar's button reads Unfavourite ; choose it, and EiN says, for example, 3 files taken out of favourites , with Undo .

When you delete something in the web interface, such as with the Archive a picture, an album or a person, it goes to your trash first. You can restore it from there for 30 days, unless your administrator chose another number; the few ways of deleting that skip the trash are listed below. Only you see your trash, apart from an administrator, who can see everyone's.

Every row but the last is on the Archive's pages; trash put works in any EiN. What you do What goes Delete in the selection bar The selected pictures that live where you are; see Albums . Move to trash under ⋮ on an album, person, location or device That album, person, location or device, with everything that lives in it. Delete in Edit event That event or note. Discard in staging The files, kept together as one entry; see Sorting in staging . Removing copies in staging's Duplicates The copies, kept together as one entry; see Duplicates . trash put in the terminal What you name, if you may change it. Each of these in the browser says what it did in a message at the foot of the screen, with Undo . Undo is the quickest way back; the Trash page is for later. What you delete goes to your trash, also when it belongs to someone else who lets you change it. If a picture disappears from an album of yours, the person who deleted it has it in their trash. While something is in the trash, it is gone for everyone: from search, ls and every other list, and with the Archive from albums and the map. It keeps what EiN worked out about it, such as faces and a transcript, and comes back with all of it when you restore it.

p.h: What is deleted for good at once
p.x: Warning These do not use the trash. What they delete is gone at once, with no Undo : Delete in the Nodes explorer, which runs rm ; rm in the terminal; deleting a file over SFTP, which takes its thumbnails and faces with it; see SSH and SFTP ; Delete for good and Empty trash on the Trash page. To delete something in the terminal that you may want back, use trash put instead of rm .

Choose your picture, then Trash . The list shows what you deleted, newest first. Each row is named by the place it came from, such as /archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg . Things deleted together, such as a group discarded in staging, are one row with a name and a count, such as Discarded from Inbox: “Boat trip” · 86 items . Select a row. The pane beside the list, or under it on a phone, shows its name, From where it came, when it was Deleted , and a preview. Hold Ctrl ( ⌘ on a Mac) while you click to add a row to the selection, or Shift to select a range. Choose Restore , or Restore 3 with three rows selected. EiN says Restored to and the path, or how many it restored. A restored thing goes back where it came from, and the links to it work again: a restored picture is back in the albums it was added to, and in your favourites if it was one. If something else has taken its name there in the meantime, it comes back beside it with a number, such as IMG_0412 (2).jpg . A row that holds several things opens with Enter , or the arrow at its left. In a row of things deleted together, you can select one of them and restore it alone. Something inside a deleted album or folder cannot come back without the rest: the pane says "Inside what was deleted; restoring puts back all of it." Restore all , in the bar at the top of the page, puts back everything in the trash at once, without asking.

On the Trash page, select one or more rows. Choose Delete for good , or press Delete . The dialog Delete for good? says, for a single item: "This item and everything derived from it is removed for good. This cannot be undone." Choose Delete for good , or Cancel . Empty trash , in the bar at the top, does the same for everything in the trash, and its dialog's button reads Empty trash . "Everything derived from it" is what EiN made from a file: its thumbnails, faces, transcript and the rest. Something in the trash still takes up its space on disk, so removing it for good frees that space.

p.h: How long things stay in the trash
p.x: Things stay for the number of days set by Days in the trash , CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS : 30 unless the administrator changed it, under Settings → System , in the category Trash . An empty Trash page gives the number: The trash is empty , "What you delete waits here for 30 days, in case you want it back." The days count from when you deleted it; for things deleted together, from the last time something was added to that row. EiN clears out what is older when it starts and every 12 hours after that, so something can stay up to half a day past its time. Once it is cleared, nothing in EiN brings it back: EiN has no backup of its own; see Your data: backup, moving and removing .

The trash command works on the same trash as the page: # in EiN's terminal trash put "/archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg" trash list trash restore 01J9Z8Q4R7XKD3V5B2N6M0PA1C trash empty --older-than 7 trash list prints one line per row: its id, when it was deleted and where it came from. 01J9Z8Q4R7XKD3V5B2N6M0PA1C 2026-10-22T09:14:03.120Z /archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg trash restore takes that id and answers Restored and the path. trash empty --older-than 7 removes for good what was deleted more than 7 days ago; trash empty with no id and no --older-than empties your whole trash, for good.

Besides config and trash above, these commands do in the terminal what this page does in the browser: Command What it does user-info <username> Shows an account's display name, numbers, e-mail address and description. user-update <username> --name=… --description=… Changes your display name and description, as Save changes does. user-passwd <username> --old-password=… Changes your password; it asks for the new one with Password: . A password typed on the command line can end up in your shell history, so the Security tab is the better way. star <path> , star -d <path> , star list Marks a node, such as a picture, as a favourite, takes the mark away, or lists your favourites. # in EiN's terminal user-info helen user-update helen --name= 'Helen Okafor' --description= "Peggy's daughter, in Wellington" star "/archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg" User: Helen Okafor UID: 1003 GID: 1003 E-mail: helen@example.com Description: Peggy's daughter, in Wellington User 'helen' updated Starred /archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg

What you see Why What to do There is no Me in the account menu, and your picture is letters The Archive is not installed, or your account is not linked to a person in the archive. Ask an administrator to link it, as under Your picture and the person you are . Update password stays greyed out A field is empty, or the two new passwords differ. Fill in all three, and type the new password the same way twice. A preference you saved does not show in another tab That tab loaded your preferences before you saved. Reload the tab. echo $CFG_USER_… prints an empty line You never changed that setting: defaults are not written into the file. config list --scope user shows every value, defaults included. There is no heart in the viewer and no Favourite button You are not signed in. The viewer and the button come with the Archive. Sign in. Something you deleted is not in your trash Someone else deleted it, and it is in their trash; or it was deleted for good; or its days ran out. Ask the person who deleted it. Nothing brings back what was deleted for good. Restoring fails with a message that ends in is gone The folder or album it came from is no longer there. Restore that album or folder first, if it is in the trash, then restore the picture.

Finding your way around : the account menu, signing in and out, and admin mode. Sharing : who sees what you create, the Share dialog and share links. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the heart and slideshows in the viewer. Albums : Delete and Remove , and moving an album to the trash. Configuration : how settings work for the whole installation. Settings : every setting with its key and default. Accounts and groups : passwords, e-mail addresses and accounts, for administrators.

You can rename, reorder and hide the entries in the sidebar and the buttons in the top bar, and add pages, buttons and menus of your own, by writing a short JSON file. This page shows how to do it for yourself and, if you are an administrator, for everyone on your EiN or for one group. There is no page in Settings for this: the files on this page are the only way. You need to be signed in and able to edit a few lines of JSON, usually in the terminal .

p.h: How the sidebar and top bar are put together
p.x: The sidebar and the top bar are laid together from four layers, read in this order: Layer File Written by Applies to The modules' entries /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json , one for each module; EiN's own is /etc/ui/nav.d/ui.json each module, when it is set up everyone Changes for everyone /etc/ui/nav.json an administrator everyone A group's changes /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.json , one for each group that has one an administrator the group's members Your changes ~/.ui/nav.json , which is /home/<your username>/.ui/nav.json you you only Each layer changes only what it names, so your file holds only what you want different. Every entry has an id, such as archive.albums for Albums . A later layer works on the earlier ones by id: Same id: change fields. Naming an id that an earlier layer gives changes only the fields you write. The entry keeps all the others. Another id: add. An id that no earlier layer gives adds an entry of your own. hide : remove. The ids listed under "hide" are left out. So your file holds only what you want different, and when a module is updated, its changes still reach everything you left alone. A few things follow from this: None of /etc/ui/nav.json , /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.json and ~/.ui/nav.json exists until someone writes it. What one layer hides stays hidden. There is no way to unhide, so you cannot bring back an entry your administrator hid. The files in /etc/ui/nav.d are links to the modules' own files, and an update replaces them. Leave them alone and put changes in /etc/ui/nav.json instead. EiN reads the navigation once, when a page loads. After you change a file, reload the page in your browser. Your terminal sessions come back after the reload.

Run ui-nav in the terminal. It prints the sidebar and the top bar as they are for you, with every entry's id: # in EiN's terminal ui-nav For someone signed in who is not an administrator, on an EiN with the archive, the assistant and the media service modules, it prints: (main) Home / ui.home Chat /chat assistant.chat Media /media archive.media Staging /staging archive.staging Explore Search /search ui.search Year /year archive.year Map /map archive.map Browse Albums /albums archive.albums People /people archive.people Locations /locations archive.locations Devices /devices archive.devices System Settings /settings ui.settings Statistics /stats ui.stats Documentation /docs ui.docs top bar Chat assistant.chat Create ui.create Import media archive.import Album archive.create-album Person archive.create-person Location archive.create-location Device archive.create-device Random album archive.random-album (alt+R) Account ui.account Favourites archive.favourites panels search.explore People /explore/people archive.explore-people search.explore Locations /explore/locations archive.explore-locations search.explore Years /explore/years archive.explore-years search.explore Labels /explore/labels archive.explore-labels nodes.tools Duplicates /duplicates?path={path} archive.duplicates stats.sections Events /stats/life-events archive.life-events home.start Import media /start/upload archive.start-upload search.label Looks like /looks-like?path={path} archive.looks-like about.services Language model /about/language-model assistant.about system.overview GPU /system/gpu ems.gpu system.tabs Media service /system/media-service ems.media-service about.services Media service /about/media-service ems.about The sidebar comes first, a section at a time. Each section starts with its heading; the first section has none, so its id shows in brackets, (main) . Under it, each entry's label, its address and its id. top bar lists the buttons with their titles and ids, and a key in brackets where one is set. A dropdown's rows are indented under it: Create is the plus, and Account is the menu under your picture. panels are parts that modules draw inside other pages; see Change the panels inside pages . An administrator also gets Nodes and Dashboard under System . The sidebar and top bar sections of Finding your way around say what each entry is. The first part of an id says where the entry comes from: ui. is EiN's own, and archive. , assistant. and ems. are the Archive 's, the assistant 's and the media service module 's, there once that module is installed. On an EiN with no modules, the sidebar holds only Home , Search , Settings , Statistics and Documentation , with Nodes and Dashboard for an administrator, and there are no panels. When something in a file cannot be used, ui-nav says so after the list, on lines that start with ui-nav: ; When something goes differently explains each one. The browser's console shows the same lines. To read every field a module gives its entries, print its file, for example cat /etc/ui/nav.d/archive.json . JSON_OUTPUT=1 ui-nav gives the result as JSON, the form the web interface reads.

Open the terminal with the Toggle Terminal (Alt+T) button in the top bar, or press Alt + T . Make the folder and open the file in the editor: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/.ui edit ~/.ui/nav.json When the file does not exist, the editor starts empty and creates the file when you save. Type or paste the JSON. The editor checks it as you type and marks a mistake with ✗. Press Ctrl + S to save, then Ctrl + Q to quit. If the JSON has a mistake, saving first asks Save with errors? (y/N) and shows the problem. Run ui-nav to check the result, then reload the page. The editor lists all of the editor's keys. You can do the same over SSH from your own computer, or put the file at /home/<your username>/.ui/nav.json with an SFTP client. A phone has no terminal button; use a computer for this.

p.h: In the Nodes explorer's code editor
p.x: The Nodes explorer opens an existing file in a code editor, but it cannot create a file. Make the file in the terminal first; after that you can edit it here: Open Nodes . Administrators have it under System in the sidebar; anyone signed in can open it at the address /system/nodes . The first time, it opens at your home folder. Names that start with a dot are hidden. Press Ctrl + H , or choose the eye button, Show names starting with a dot (Ctrl+H) . Double-click the .ui folder, then right-click nav.json and choose Open . Make your changes, then choose Save or press Ctrl + S . While a change is not saved, the editor shows unsaved , and Close asks Discard unsaved changes? with Keep editing and Discard . This editor does not check the JSON. Run ui-nav afterwards, or reload the page and look.

The examples on this page change entries the Archive and the assistant add, and lead to their pages, such as /albums and /people/Peggy_Wrenfield . The same works for any entry, EiN's own included, and for any address on your EiN. To rename Albums to Photo albums , move it up beside Home , and hide Map , write this in ~/.ui/nav.json : { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "archive.albums" , "section" : "main" , "label" : "Photo albums" , "order" : 15 } ] , "hide" : [ "archive.map" ] } Save, reload the page, and the first section reads Home , Photo albums , Chat , Media , Staging ; Explore has no Map . ui-nav shows the same: (main) Home / ui.home Photo albums /albums archive.albums Chat /chat assistant.chat Media /media archive.media Staging /staging archive.staging Explore Search /search ui.search Year /year archive.year Browse People /people archive.people ... order places an entry within its section, lowest first. The shipped entries count in tens ( Home 10, Chat 20, Media 30), so 15 lands between Home and Chat . An entry without order goes to the end of its section. section moves the entry to another section: main , explore , browse , system , or one of your own. hide takes away anything by id: an entry, a top-bar button, a panel or a whole section. A hidden section takes its entries with it. One id can name both a sidebar entry and a top-bar button: assistant.chat is the sidebar's Chat and the top bar's chat button, so hiding it removes both. Sections can be changed the same way. This gives the first section the heading Start and renames Browse : { "sections" : [ { "id" : "main" , "label" : "Start" } , { "id" : "browse" , "label" : "Collections" } ] }

p.h: Add a page of your own
p.x: An entry of your own needs an id that nothing else uses, and four fields: section , label , icon and to . This adds a section Family with two people's pages, and puts a saved search for Cornwall in Explore after Search : { "sections" : [ { "id" : "family" , "label" : "Family" , "order" : 25 } ] , "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "me.peggy" , "section" : "family" , "label" : "Grandma Peggy" , "icon" : "user" , "to" : "/people/Peggy_Wrenfield" } , { "id" : "me.ruby" , "section" : "family" , "label" : "Ruby" , "icon" : "user" , "to" : "/people/Ruby_Wrenfield" } , { "id" : "me.cornwall" , "section" : "explore" , "label" : "Cornwall" , "icon" : "beach" , "to" : "/media?q=Cornwall" , "order" : 15 } ] } With "order": 25 , Family stands between Explore (20) and Browse (30). Your entries also appear in the search box's list under Go to , like every sidebar entry. to is an address inside EiN, starting with / . The easiest way to get one is to open the page and copy what your browser's address bar shows after the host, such as /people/Peggy_Wrenfield . Filters you set on a page are part of its address, which is how /media?q=Cornwall opens Media already searching for Cornwall. Addresses in the web interface lists them all. A sidebar entry cannot lead to another website. icon is the name of any icon at tabler.io/icons , written as it is there: map-pin , beach , heart . Add -filled for the filled form, heart-filled . It can also be the full path, starting with / , of an SVG file in EiN that you may read, which is drawn in the colour of the text. id can be anything no one else uses. The shipped ones are <module>.<name> ; starting yours with me. keeps them apart. The sidebar lights the entry whose address is the page's, or the start of it, so Albums is lit on an album too. When several match, the longest address wins: on /system/nodes only Nodes is lit, not Dashboard at /system . An entry whose address has a ? in it, like the saved search above, is never lit.

p.h: Add buttons to the top bar
p.x: A top-bar button is an entry under "topbar" with an id , a title (its tooltip), an icon and an action that says what choosing it does: Action What choosing the button does { "navigate": "/albums" } Opens the address as the page. { "dialog": "/albums/new" } Opens it in a dialog over the page you are on. { "drawer": "/favourites" } Opens it in the side drawer at the right, or closes the drawer when it shows that address. The button is lit while the drawer is open, and left out on that address's own page. On a phone it opens a dialog instead. { "fullscreen": "/map" } Opens it over everything, the top bar too, until Esc or the browser's Back. { "run": "<command line>" } Runs the command line as you, as the web interface runs its commands: with JSON_OUTPUT=1 . { "run": "album-random", "navigate": "/albums/{path}" } Runs the command, then opens an address filled in from its answer. Finding your way around shows what a dialog, the side drawer and full screen look like. This adds four buttons: { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.peggy-button" , "title" : "Grandma Peggy" , "icon" : "user" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/people/Peggy_Wrenfield" } } , { "id" : "me.new-album" , "title" : "New album" , "icon" : "photo-plus" , "action" : { "dialog" : "/albums/new" } } , { "id" : "me.favourites" , "title" : "Favourites" , "icon" : "heart" , "action" : { "drawer" : "/favourites" } } , { "id" : "me.map" , "title" : "Map" , "icon" : "map" , "action" : { "fullscreen" : "/map" } } ] } They stand between Create and the terminal button, in the order you wrote them; hold the pointer over one to see its title. They also appear in the search box's list under Do . About run : The command's output is not shown anywhere. The button turns into a spinner while the command takes more than a moment. If the command fails, the page shows nothing; the browser's console has the error. With navigate as well, EiN reads the command's answer as JSON and replaces each {key} in the address with the answer's field of that name, or with nothing when there is none. The archive's Random album is made this way: album-random answers with an album's path , and the button opens /albums/{path} . Three more fields change a button: "place": "search" stands the button beside the search box, as Random album does, instead of with the others at the right. "phone": false leaves the button out on a phone. Its key, if it has one, still works. "color" colours its icon: blue , cyan , grape , green , indigo , lime , orange , pink , red , teal , violet or yellow . { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.year" , "title" : "This year" , "icon" : "calendar" , "color" : "teal" , "place" : "search" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/year" } } ] }

A top-bar entry with no action becomes a dropdown when other entries name it as their parent . Each of those is a row of the menu and needs an action of its own: { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.family-menu" , "title" : "Family" , "label" : "Family pages" , "icon" : "users" , "order" : 15 } , { "id" : "me.family-peggy" , "parent" : "me.family-menu" , "title" : "Grandma Peggy" , "icon" : "user" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/people/Peggy_Wrenfield" } } , { "id" : "me.family-ruby" , "parent" : "me.family-menu" , "title" : "Ruby" , "icon" : "user" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/people/Ruby_Wrenfield" } } ] } The dropdown's title is its button's tooltip, and its label is the heading at the top of the open menu. With "order": 15 the button stands between Chat (10) and Create (20). A row's title is its text, and order places it in the menu. Rows can go into the menus EiN has as well: "parent": "ui.create" adds a row to the Create New menu under the plus. The archive's rows are Import media (5), Album (10), Person (20), Location (30) and Device (40). "parent": "ui.account" adds a row to the menu under your picture, after Me and before Profile , where the archive puts Favourites . The menu's other rows are EiN's own and cannot be changed. { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.new-category" , "parent" : "ui.create" , "title" : "Staging category" , "icon" : "folder-plus" , "color" : "cyan" , "order" : 50 , "action" : { "dialog" : "/staging/categories/new" } } , { "id" : "me.docs" , "parent" : "ui.account" , "title" : "Documentation" , "icon" : "book" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/docs" } } ] } A dropdown with no rows left, because they were all hidden or none were given, is not shown. A row goes where its dropdown goes: hide the dropdown, or keep it from someone, and its rows go too. In the search box's list a row reads with its menu's title, as Create: Staging category .

A top-bar button or a dropdown's row can have a key that does what choosing it does, from anywhere outside a text field: { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "archive.create-album" , "shortcut" : "alt+A" } , { "id" : "me.map" , "title" : "Map" , "icon" : "map" , "shortcut" : "alt+P" , "action" : { "fullscreen" : "/map" } } , { "id" : "archive.random-album" , "shortcut" : null } ] } This gives Create › Album the key Alt + A , gives your Map button Alt + P , and takes Alt + R away from Random album . A key is modifiers and one key, joined by + . The modifiers are alt , ctrl , shift , meta , and mod , which is Ctrl , or ⌘ on a Mac. Letter case does not matter: alt+R and Alt+r are the same key. null takes a key away, which is how you remove a module's key. The key shows in the button's tooltip, such as Map (Alt+P) , beside the row in its menu, and in the Keyboard shortcuts list that ? opens, under Anywhere ; a row is listed with its menu, as Create › Album . On a Mac, Alt shows as ⌥ . A dropdown itself cannot have a key; its rows can. A key is given once. When two entries ask for the same key, the one that comes first in the top bar's order keeps it: by order , lowest first, and a dropdown's rows where their dropdown stands. A button placed beside the search box counts by its order too. EiN keeps its own keys: Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K ), ? , and Alt with T , N , M , W or an arrow key, which the terminal uses. An entry that asks for one of these as EiN writes it ( mod+K , shift+? , alt+T and so on) does not get it. Some pages have keys of their own while they are on screen, such as the photo viewer. Press ? on a page to see which keys it uses before you pick one; Keyboard shortcuts lists every key EiN knows.

Panels are parts that modules draw inside EiN's own pages, such as the Media service tab on the Dashboard or the People , Locations , Years and Labels sections of the Search page. They are in the same files under "panels" , so you can reorder, rename or hide them by id like any entry. This puts Years first on the Search page and hides Labels there: { "panels" : [ { "id" : "archive.explore-years" , "order" : 5 } ] , "hide" : [ "archive.explore-labels" ] } Each panel has a slot, the place in a page where it is drawn: Slot Where it is drawn Panels the modules ship search.explore A section of the Search page before you search archive.explore-people , -locations , -years , -labels search.label Above the Search page's results when it searches for one label archive.looks-like ( Looks like , signed in only) home.start Under News on Home while there is no news archive.start-upload ( Import media , signed in only) stats.sections A section of Statistics archive.life-events ( Events ) nodes.tools A tool in the Nodes explorer's tool pane archive.duplicates ( Duplicates ) system.tabs A tab of the Dashboard ems.media-service ( Media service ) system.overview Gauges beside the computer's own on the Dashboard 's overview ems.gpu ( GPU ) about.services A tile in About EiN assistant.about ( Language model ), ems.about ( Media service ) A panel draws a page that a module made for that place. Adding panels of your own works the same way in principle, but it is a module's work; see Writing a module .

As an administrator, signed in as admin or in admin mode , you write the same kind of file to /etc/ui/nav.json . It applies to every account and to visitors, and each person's own file is laid over it. # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator edit /etc/ui/nav.json Two fields show an entry to some people only. They work in any file, but the file for everyone is where they matter: Field The entry is shown "admin": true Only to administrators: the admin account and anyone in admin mode. In your own file, it shows the entry only while you are in admin mode. "signedIn": true Only to someone signed in, never to a visitor browsing without signing in, where Visitors may browse is on. EiN uses them itself: Nodes and Dashboard are admin ; Staging , Settings , Create and the account menu are signedIn . This file, for a family with no cameras or GPS trackers to register, hides Devices in the sidebar and in the Create menu, keeps Statistics from visitors, and gives administrators a button that reruns failed work with pipeline-heal : { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "ui.stats" , "signedIn" : true } ] , "topbar" : [ { "id" : "site.retry" , "title" : "Retry failed work" , "icon" : "refresh" , "admin" : true , "action" : { "run" : "pipeline-heal --apply" } } ] , "hide" : [ "archive.devices" , "archive.create-device" ] } Everyone gets the change the next time they load a page. People can still rename and move, in their own files, what you changed, but they cannot bring back what you hid. To change the navigation for some accounts only, write a group's file . Processing and pipelines explains what pipeline-heal reruns.

p.h: Change the navigation for a group
p.x: As an administrator you can also change the navigation for the members of one group, such as a link to a page only they use. The file is /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.json , where <group> is the group's name as group-list prints it, not its title, in the same format as the other files. This gives the members of a sailors group a page of their own in the Explore section: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator mkdir -p /etc/ui/groups/sailors edit /etc/ui/groups/sailors/nav.json { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "sailors.boats" , "section" : "explore" , "label" : "Boats" , "icon" : "sailboat" , "to" : "/search?q=sailboat" } ] } A group's file is laid over /etc/ui/nav.json and under each member's own file, so members can still rename and move what it gives. Someone in several groups with a file gets each of them, in the order of the groups' names. Groups are read at sign-in, so someone added to a group gets its file the next time they sign in. The guest group's file is for visitors browsing without signing in. If the folder's name is not a group, ui-nav warns /etc/ui/groups/<name>: no group <name> . A group's folder may also hold nav.d , with the entries of the modules kept to the group . mod setup links them there, and they count as modules' entries, under everything else, for the group's members alone. Warning hide , admin and signedIn decide only what the sidebar and top bar show. A page still opens by its address for anyone whose permissions allow it, and anyone can add an entry of their own that leads to it. To keep people away from something, set its permissions; see Permissions in depth .

A file is one JSON object with any of these keys: Key Holds sections A list of the sidebar's sections. sidebar A list of sidebar entries. topbar A list of top-bar buttons, dropdowns and dropdown rows. panels A list of panels. hide A list of ids to leave out, of any kind. Hidden in one layer means hidden in all after it. Every entry in the four lists needs an id . To change an entry, give its id and the fields to change. An entry of your own needs every field marked required below.

Field Required Value id yes main , explore , browse , system , or one of your own. label no The heading, shown in capitals; choosing it folds the section. Without one the section has no heading and cannot fold, as main . order no The section's place, lowest first: main 10, explore 20, browse 30, system 40. Without it, 1000. A section with no entries left to show is not drawn.

Field Required Value id yes The entry's id: archive.albums , or one of your own such as me.peggy . section yes The id of the section it is in. label yes The text. icon yes A Tabler icon name ( map-pin , heart-filled ), or the path of an SVG file in EiN. to yes The address it opens, inside EiN, starting with / . The entry is lit on this address and those below it, unless the address has a ? . order no Its place in the section, lowest first. Without it, 1000; entries with the same number keep the order the files give them. admin no true : shown to administrators only. signedIn no true : never shown to a visitor.

Field Required Value id yes The entry's id. EiN's dropdowns are ui.create (the plus) and ui.account (the menu under your picture). title yes A button's tooltip, a row's text; also its name in the search box's list and the Keyboard shortcuts list. icon yes As for the sidebar. action see text What choosing it does; see action . A button and a row need one. An entry with neither an action nor rows is left out, without a warning. parent no The id of the dropdown this entry is a row of: ui.create , ui.account or one of your own. label no A dropdown's heading in the open menu, such as Create New . color no The icon's colour: blue , cyan , grape , green , indigo , lime , orange , pink , red , teal , violet or yellow . order no Its place, lowest first: among the buttons ( Chat 10, Create 20, Random album 30), or in its menu for a row. Without it, 1000. place no "search" : the button stands beside the search box instead of at the right. phone no false : the button is left out on a phone; its key still works. shortcut no A key, such as alt+R or mod+shift+K ; see Give an entry a key . null takes a key away. Not on a dropdown. admin no true : shown to administrators only. signedIn no true : never shown to a visitor. The terminal button and your picture are EiN's own, always at the right end, and cannot be moved or hidden; neither can the search box.

Give one of these: Action Does { "navigate": "<address>" } Opens the address as the page. { "dialog": "<address>" } Opens it in a dialog over the page. { "drawer": "<address>" } Opens it in the side drawer, or closes the drawer when it shows it. A dialog on a phone. { "fullscreen": "<address>" } Opens it over everything until Esc or the browser's Back. { "run": "<command line>" } Runs the command line as you. Its output is not shown. { "run": "<command line>", "navigate": "<address>" } Runs it, then opens the address with each {key} replaced by that field of the command's JSON answer, URI-encoded; a missing field leaves nothing.

Field Required Value id yes The panel's id, such as archive.explore-years . slot yes Where it is drawn; see the slots in Change the panels inside pages . label yes The tab's or tool's label, or the section's heading. route yes The address drawn there. In nodes.tools and search.label , {path} is replaced by a path in the tree. icon no An icon, as for the sidebar, for the slots that show one. order no Its place among the panels of its slot. Without it, 1000. admin no true : shown to administrators only. signedIn no true : never shown to a visitor.

ui-nav prints a line for each thing it could not use, and leaves that thing out. The rest of the file still applies, except when the file is not valid JSON. Line after ui-nav: What it means What to do /home/anna/.ui/nav.json: Expected ',' or '}' after property value in JSON at position 71 (line 3 column 3) The file is not valid JSON, so none of it is used. The end says where the parser stopped. Look just before that line and column: often a missing comma, or a comma after the last item of a list. <file>: not a navigation object The file is valid JSON but not one object in { } . Put everything inside one pair of braces. <file>: sidebar is not a list sidebar , sections , topbar or panels holds something other than a list. Put the entries in [ ] , even a single one. <file>: a sidebar entry without an id An entry in that list has no id . Give it one. <file>: hide is not a list hide holds a single id. Write "hide": ["archive.map"] . me.cornwall: no icon, to An entry of your own lacks the required fields named. Add them. If you meant to change a module's entry, check the id: a misspelled id makes an entry of your own. me.peggy: no section family The section does not exist. Check the spelling, or add the section under "sections" . me.family-peggy: no top-bar entry me.family-menu The parent names no top-bar entry. Check the spelling, or add the dropdown. me.map: action is none of navigate, dialog, drawer, fullscreen or run The action has none of those keys with text after it. Check the spelling and the quotes. me.map: shortcut "alt+" is not modifiers and one key joined by + The key is not written as modifiers and one key. Write it like alt+P . me.family-menu: a dropdown has no shortcut, its rows may A key was given to a dropdown. Give keys to its rows. The dropdown is still shown. me.map: shortcut alt+A is already archive.create-album's Another entry, earlier in the top bar's order, has the key. Choose another key, or take it from the other entry with "shortcut": null . me.map: shortcut alt+T is already the shell's EiN keeps that key for itself. Choose another key. ui: archive.albums is already given by archive Two modules give the same id; the first by module name keeps it. Tell the authors of the module named first. Other things that can go differently: Nothing changes. Reload the page; EiN reads the navigation only when a page loads. Then check that the file is where EiN looks, with cat ~/.ui/nav.json . A button you added is missing, and ui-nav says nothing. It has no action and no rows; or it is a dropdown whose rows are all hidden; or it has "phone": false and you are on a phone; or it opens the side drawer and you are on that address's own page. An empty space where an icon should be. The name is not one of Tabler's. ui-icons checks names: it prints the size of each icon it has and none for a name it does not know. # in EiN's terminal ui-icons beach beech beach: 807 bytes beech: none An entry of yours is never lit. Its address has a ? in it, so it cannot match the page. A key does nothing. Keys do not work while the cursor is in a text field. Press ? to see whether the key is listed; if it is not, run ui-nav for the reason. An entry you want back was hidden by your administrator. You cannot unhide it. Ask your administrator.

Finding your way around : every part of the sidebar and the top bar. The editor : editing files in the terminal and in the Nodes explorer. Configuration files : /etc/ui/nav.json , a group's file, ~/.ui/nav.json and the other files you can edit. Writing a module : how a module gives its own entries, routes and panels.

This page covers what is different when you use EiN on a phone or a tablet: the menu behind the EiN mark, the gestures in grids and in the viewer, uploading from the phone, and putting EiN on your home screen.
