It is for everyone in the family who opens EiN away from a computer. The grids, the viewer and the uploads are the Archive 's, and the sections on them apply once it is installed.

Open the same address you use on a computer, for example http://ein.local:8080 , in your phone's browser, and sign in as you would on a computer (see Sign in ). It is the same EiN, with the same account, pictures and permissions; only the layout changes to fit the screen. The phone keeps a few choices of its own, separate from your computer's: whether the menu shows icons or names, whether it is shown, and how many pictures a grid puts in a row. They are kept in the phone's browser, not in your account.

p.h: What changes on a small screen
p.x: What you get depends on the width of the browser window, and on whether the screen is a touch screen. Screen Layout Narrower than 768 pixels: most phones held upright The phone layout this page describes. 768 to 991 pixels: tablets, and some large phones held sideways The computer's layout, with the sidebar beside the page and the terminal button. The chat's side drawer covers the page, and the browser's Back closes it. 992 pixels and wider The computer's layout, with the side drawer beside the page. On any touch screen, whatever its width, the Archive's viewer uses its touch layout and pressing and holding a picture selects it. So a tablet has the computer's frame with the phone's viewer. Home on a phone. The menu is out of sight until you tap the EiN mark or swipe right. In the phone layout: The top bar shows the EiN mark without the name, the search box (it reads Search ), then the buttons the modules add, such as the Archive's Random album , the assistant's Chat and the plus of the Create menu, and your picture. Its buttons are larger, to suit a finger. The Uploads button appears there while files are going up. The menu is hidden until you ask for it: see Open the menu . There is no terminal button. When the connection drops, a red crossed-out plug stands in the top bar in place of the Disconnected badge. The search box opens its list across the whole width of the screen, above the keyboard, and the keyboard's search key does what Enter does. Search and the finder covers what it finds. Dialogs fill the screen , with their buttons in a bar across the foot. Fields use larger text, so the phone does not zoom in while you type. A question that only asks you to confirm stays a small box. The phone's Back closes a dialog. The chat , with the assistant installed, opens as a dialog over the whole screen instead of in the side drawer; see Chatting with the assistant . The create and account menus are wider, with taller rows.

On a phone the tabs show only their icons, except the one you are on, and the header's actions are under ⋮. Actions such as Upload , Share and Edit fold into ⋮ at the header's top right, with the page's other actions. Tabs with icons show only their icons, and the tab you are on keeps its name. On a person's page, which the Archive adds, the icons stand for Info , Media , Faces , Heard in , Family and Homes . Choices such as Show and Sort become a button that shows the chosen option's icon; on some pages, such as Year , several fold into one button. Scrolled down , the header goes away, and the page's filter box and choices float at the foot of the screen beside Back to top . An empty filter box folds to a magnifier: tap it to type, and it takes the whole row while you type.

On a phone the EiN mark at the left of the top bar is the menu button; there is no separate menu icon. It does not go to Home, as it does on a computer: Home is the first entry in the menu. The menu has two forms: A column of icons at the left of the screen, which is what you get at first. Tap the mark to show it; the page moves over to make room. Tap an icon to go to its page; the column stays until you tap the mark again. The full list with names , under the headings Explore , Browse and System . Tap the button at the foot of the icon column ( Show labels ) to switch to it. It opens over the page, and closes when you choose a page; tap the mark to open it again. The button at its foot ( Collapse to icons ) switches back to the column of icons. You can also swipe: a one-finger swipe to the right across the page or the menu brings the menu out, and a swipe to the left puts it away. The swipe has to be mostly sideways and quick, and it does nothing: in the viewer or anything else shown full screen, where a sideways swipe moves between pictures; in a dialog, such as the chat; on something that moves sideways itself: the map, the time rail at the right of a long grid, a story, a slider, a text field, or a row that scrolls sideways. A swipe that starts at the very edge of the screen may be taken by the phone as its own Back gesture, so start a little way in. The phone remembers which form of the menu you chose, and whether the icon column is shown. Finding your way around lists what is in the menu.

p.h: Pinch, press and tap in a grid
p.x: With the Archive installed, a grid of pictures, such as an album or the Media page, works by touch like this: To Do this Open a picture in the viewer Tap it. Show fewer, larger pictures Spread two fingers apart on the grid, then lift them. Each pinch takes away one picture per row, down to 2. Show more, smaller pictures Pinch two fingers together, then lift them. Each pinch adds one picture per row, up to 5. Start selecting Press and hold a picture for a moment. It is ticked, and the phone gives a short buzz where its browser allows it. Add or take away a picture Once anything is selected, tap it. Select a whole day Tap the date in the day's heading. Move through a long grid Drag the time rail at the right edge, which appears once the grid holds more than 120 pictures. A phone's grid starts with 2 pictures in a row, and keeps the number you pinch to in this browser. Pinching works where pictures keep their own shapes, such as an album or the Media page in its Default layout. The Days and Months layouts of the Media page have square tiles, three and five across on a phone, and do not change with a pinch; see Media, Year and labels . Where the grid is 640 pixels wide or more, as on most tablets, it fills its rows by height instead, and a pinch does not change it. Moving your finger while you hold cancels the press, so scrolling a grid never selects a picture. Once something is selected, the bar at the foot of the screen shows how many, for example 3 selected , with all its buttons in one Actions menu and × to clear the selection. Albums covers selecting, and The selection bar what each action does. A video in a grid plays a short silent preview when it scrolls into view, as there is no pointer to rest on it.

With the Archive installed, its viewer takes a touch layout on any touch screen, and in any browser window narrower than 768 pixels. Swipe sideways between files, up for the details, and down to put them away or, with them closed, to close the viewer: the touch layout has no close button. On a phone or tablet covers its layout and gestures, and Watch the memories story the story that On this day plays on Home, which works by touch too.

With the Archive installed, bring the photos and videos on your phone into your staging area with Import media : Tap the plus in the top bar, then Import media . The dialog fills the screen. Under Into which category? , pick where the files go. The Inbox is chosen at first. To keep a phone's pictures together, choose New category and, under What it holds , Phone ; see The kinds of category . Tap Choose files . Your phone's own picker opens, with your photo library, the camera or your files, depending on the phone. Pick the files, then tap the button that counts them, for example Upload 24 . The category opens on its Files tab, and the Uploads ring in the top bar shows how far the upload is. Getting your photos in covers the dialog in full, and Sorting in staging what to do with the files once they are in. Upload also sits under ⋮ on an album you may change, on the Media page and on a staging category. On a phone its picker offers only photos, videos, recordings and GPX tracks, with the camera among the choices, so you can take a picture and upload it in one go. An album's Upload puts the files straight into that album; the Media page's puts them into your Inbox. To bring in a PDF or another kind of file from a phone, use Choose files in Import media . Choose a folder and Upload a folder need a browser that can pick a folder, which a phone's browser may not offer. Warning An upload runs in the open page. Keep EiN on screen until the upload has finished: a phone may pause a browser that is in the background or behind a locked screen, and closing or reloading the page stops the files not sent yet. The files already sent stay. For a whole camera roll, thousands of files, copying from a computer is steadier than uploading from the phone. The Import media dialog itself suggests copying over SFTP for more than about 10,000 files; see Copy files in over SFTP . On the Media page, Search with a picture can take a photo with the camera and find what looks like it; see Search with a picture .

p.h: Put EiN on your home screen
p.x: You can add EiN to your phone's home screen, where it looks and opens like an app: its icon is the EiN mark, named EiN under it; it opens on Home , using the whole screen, without the browser's address bar and buttons; the phone's status bar and the screen shown while it starts are in EiN's dark colour. Most browsers, Chrome on Android among them, install it as an app only over HTTPS: an address that begins with https:// . EiN on its own serves plain HTTP, on port 8080, so your administrator first has to put it behind an HTTPS proxy; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Over plain http:// , a phone may only add a bookmark that opens in the browser. To add it: iPhone or iPad, in Safari: open EiN, tap the share button, then Add to Home Screen , then Add . Android, in Chrome: open EiN, open the browser's ⋮ menu, choose Add to Home screen or Install app , and confirm. The names of these menu items differ between phones and browser versions. EiN itself has no install button and never asks to be installed. Opened from the home screen, EiN has no address bar and, on an iPhone, no Back button: use the menu to move between pages, swipe down to close the viewer, and the × to close a dialog. On an iPhone the home-screen EiN may keep a sign-in of its own, separate from Safari's, and ask you to sign in once more.

EiN has no offline mode. Nothing is kept on the phone for use without a connection: every page, picture and search comes from your EiN as you open it, so you need a connection to it, at home or wherever your administrator has made it reachable. When the connection drops while EiN is open, pages stop loading and EiN tries again every 2 seconds by itself. On a phone a red crossed-out plug in the top bar tells you, in place of the Disconnected badge; EiN picks up again by itself once the phone is back on the network.

p.h: What a phone does not have
p.x: The terminal. There is no terminal button on a phone. With a keyboard connected to it, Alt + T still opens it; see The terminal . Keyboard shortcuts , unless a keyboard is connected. Shortcuts in the account menu still lists them. Edit faces in the Archive's viewer while the phone is held upright; turn it sideways to draw face boxes. Keys and the column beside the stream in the Archive's staging Sort tab , and selecting several groups there; see Sorting in staging .

What you see Why What to do The address does not open on the phone The phone is not on the network EiN is on, or it does not understand a name ending in .local . Join the same network, or use the address with the machine's IP number that your administrator gives you. Away from home, see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . No Add to Home Screen or Install app , or EiN opens with the browser's address bar from the home screen EiN is reached over plain http:// . Ask your administrator for an https:// address. Swiping does not bring the menu out The swipe was too slow or too slanted, began at the screen's edge, or landed on the map, a slider, a field or a row that scrolls sideways. Tap the EiN mark instead. Pinching does not change the grid The grid has square tiles ( Days or Months ), or the screen is wide enough for the grid to fill its rows by itself. Choose the Default layout on the Media page. The upload stopped The phone paused the browser, or the page was closed or reloaded. If Uploads in the top bar lists failed files, choose Retry failed . After a reload the list is gone: choose the files that did not arrive and upload them again. An exact copy of a file already sent is recognised in staging; see Duplicates . You cannot find Upload , Share or Edit On a phone they are under ⋮ at the top right of the header. Tap ⋮. You cannot find the viewer's close button The touch layout has none. Swipe down on the picture, or use the phone's Back.

Finding your way around : the top bar, the menu and how pages, dialogs and full screen open and close. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer, its details and its gestures. Getting your photos in : every way files get into EiN. Albums : selecting pictures and the selection bar. Ports, HTTPS and remote access : HTTPS and reaching EiN from outside the home, for administrators.

The terminal is a command line inside EiN's web interface: a shell that works on the same tree of nodes that the pages show, with the same commands and the same permissions. This page is for anyone who signs in and wants to use it: how to open it, work in tabs, move around with the keyboard, find earlier commands, get help, and find the command you need.

Sign in. Visitors browsing without an account have no terminal. Choose the terminal button in the top bar (tooltip Toggle Terminal (Alt+T) ), or press Alt + T wherever you are. The terminal drops down from the top of the window over the page, half the window high, with the cursor ready at the prompt. Try a first command: # in EiN's terminal ls /archive albums devices locations people tags tracks That is an EiN with the Archive installed, which makes every folder there but tags . Without it, /archive holds only tags , and ls / shows the rest of the tree . To hide it again, press Alt + T , choose the chevron at the right end of the tab bar ( Hide terminal (Alt+T) ), or click anywhere outside it. Hiding the terminal does not stop it: the shells keep running, a command you started goes on, and the terminal is as you left it when you open it again. On a phone-sized screen the top bar has no terminal button; Alt + T still works with a keyboard attached. From your own computer you can also reach the same shell over SSH (see Use the same shell over SSH ). Administrators have one more way in: in the Nodes explorer, right-click a folder and choose Open terminal here . EiN opens a new tab and types cd to that folder for you. The terminal works on the same tree the pages show: people, albums and photos are paths you can list, read and open.

The prompt says who you are and where you are: helen@:~$ helen is your username, in green, or in red for an administrator. Between @ and : stands the host name, which is empty unless you set one, for example with export HOSTNAME=ein in your ~/.bashrc . ~ is the folder you are in. ~ stands for your home folder, /home/helen ; elsewhere you see the path, such as /archive/albums/christmas-2019 . $ becomes # when the shell acts as an administrator. Folders and files are nodes of EiN's tree: paths start at / , .. is the folder above, and cd moves you around. The tree shows what lies where.

The tab bar runs along the foot of the terminal. Each tab is a shell of its own, with its own current folder, its own variables and whatever is running in it; switching tabs does not stop the others. Add a tab : choose + ( New session (Alt+N) ) or press Alt + N . The first tab is called Session 1 , the next Session 2 , and so on. If the terminal is hidden, Alt + N adds the tab without showing it. Know which is which : once a tab's shell has reported its folder, the tab shows that path instead of its name, such as /home/helen or /archive/albums/christmas-2019 . Switch : click a tab, or press Alt + ← and Alt + → . Close a tab : choose its × , or press Alt + W while you are typing in it. Closing a tab ends its shell and everything running in it. The last tab has no × and cannot be closed. End a shell from inside : type exit , or press Ctrl + D on an empty line. The tab goes away; if it was the only one, a fresh shell takes its place.

p.h: Make the terminal taller or shorter
p.x: The terminal starts at half the window's height. Maximize (Alt+M) , the button at the right of the tab bar, makes it fill the window. Pressed again, as Restore (Alt+M) , it returns to half the window. Alt + ↓ makes it a tenth of the window taller, Alt + ↑ a tenth shorter, between a tenth and the whole window. The browser remembers the height for the next time, on that computer and in that browser.

The ? button at the right of the tab bar ( Terminal shortcuts ) lists the keys of the terminal itself. They work whether you are typing in the terminal or not, and only with Alt alone, without Ctrl , Shift or ⌘ : Keys In the ? list What happens Alt + T Toggle terminal Shows or hides the terminal Alt + N New tab Adds a tab with a new shell Alt + W Close tab Closes the tab you are typing in; never the last one Alt + M Maximize Fills the window, or returns to half the window Alt + ← Previous tab Moves to the tab on the left, from the first to the last Alt + → Next tab Moves to the tab on the right, from the last to the first Alt + ↑ Shrink height A tenth of the window shorter Alt + ↓ Grow height A tenth of the window taller The Keyboard shortcuts dialog that ? opens anywhere in EiN lists only the first two, under Anywhere . Keyboard shortcuts has every key in EiN. Note On a Mac, ⌥ with a letter types a character of its own (⌥T types †), while the terminal looks for the letter itself, so ⌥T, ⌥N, ⌥W and ⌥M may not reach it. The top-bar button and the buttons in the tab bar do the same. ⌥ with the arrow keys is not affected.

p.h: Come back to a running shell
p.x: Reload the page, or lose the connection for a moment, and the terminal comes back as you left it: the same tabs, open or hidden as before, and in each tab the same shell, in the same folder, with up to 1000 lines of what scrolled past drawn again. A command that was running carries on while the page is away. How long EiN waits. EiN keeps a shell without a page for five minutes. The administrator sets this with Terminal reconnect grace ( CFG_TERMINAL_RECONNECT_GRACE_SEC , 300 seconds; 0 ends a shell as soon as its page goes; a change applies from the next disconnect). After that the shell ends, with whatever runs in it, and the tab starts a fresh one when you come back. To keep a long job going after you leave, see The shell language . One browser tab, one set of terminals. The tabs belong to the browser tab they were opened in. EiN in a second browser tab gets terminals of its own, starting again at Session 1 , and closing a browser tab leaves its shells to end after the five minutes. Signing out ends every terminal of that sign-in and starts the tabs over, so the next person who signs in on that browser finds none of your shells. When EiN restarts , for example for an update, every shell ends. The tabs stay, and each starts a fresh shell once EiN answers again. While the connection is down , the top bar shows a red Disconnected badge, and each tab whose shell is not connected shows a red crossed-out plug in place of its terminal icon. The terminal reconnects by itself; there is nothing to press. Your command history is kept through all of this (see Find an earlier command ).

Drag files from your computer onto the terminal and let go. EiN uploads them into the folder the tab is in, the path the tab shows. The Uploads button in the top bar follows them, as for any upload, and a file whose name is taken in that folder is stored under a numbered name beside it. Where you drop decides what happens next. With the Archive installed, go to a staging category or an album first to have it take new pictures in: # in EiN's terminal cd ~/staging/files/inbox Then drop the files. Getting your photos in explains staging, albums and what happens after an upload. You need permission to write in the folder; an upload into a folder you may only read fails and is listed under Uploads .

cat on a picture or a video draws it right in the terminal, 20 lines tall, wherever the file is in the tree. Here it draws a photo in one of the Archive's albums: # in EiN's terminal cd /archive/albums/christmas-2019 && cat 20191225_155434.jpg cat -s draws it half as tall, cat -l twice as tall. export MEDIA_LINES=30 changes the height for the rest of the session (see Environment variables ). A video plays at once, with its controls under it. A recording gets a player two lines tall and starts playing. A text file is printed with colours for its language, such as JSON, YAML, bash or Markdown. Only the terminal in the browser draws pictures. Over SSH, cat prints marker lines starting __IMG: instead. Note A picture whose path holds a space or a colon, such as one in /archive/albums/Summer 2020 , is not drawn: the terminal shows its __IMG: lines instead. Open it in the web interface.

The line you type is edited with the keys of bash on Linux, in its default (emacs) mode. The ones used most: Keys What they do Tab Complete what you are typing (see Let Tab complete ) ↑ ↓ The previous and the next command from your history Ctrl + R Search your history as you type Home End , or Ctrl + A Ctrl + E Start and end of the line Ctrl + ← Ctrl + → A word left or right Ctrl + K / Ctrl + U Cut from the cursor to the end / to the start of the line Ctrl + Y Paste what you cut last Alt + . Insert the last word of the previous command (not with ⌥ on a Mac) Ctrl + C At the prompt: drop the line ( ^C is printed). While a command runs: stop it Ctrl + D On an empty line: end the shell and its tab Ctrl + L Clear the screen, as the command clear does Some keys mean something else in the browser: Alt + ← , Alt + → , Alt + ↑ and Alt + ↓ are the terminal's own keys for tabs and height; move by word with Ctrl + ← and Ctrl + → . Ctrl + R searches your history instead of reloading the page. To reload, press F5 . The browser keeps some keys for itself before the terminal sees them. In most browsers Ctrl + W closes the browser tab rather than cutting a word; use Alt + W to close a terminal tab. Ctrl + Z does not pause a running command. Start a long one in the background with & instead; The shell language covers jobs.

Press ↑ to step back through the commands you ran, ↓ to step forward again. To find one by a word in it, press Ctrl + R and type part of it. The prompt turns into the search and shows the newest command that matches: (reverse-i-search)`peg': person-info /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield Ctrl + R again finds the next older match. Enter runs the command found. Esc leaves it on the line for you to change first. Ctrl + G gives up and brings back what you had typed. bash's history commands work too: history lists what you ran, !! runs the last command again, !42 runs number 42 of the list, and ^old^new runs the last command with old replaced by new . What EiN keeps: Your history is the file ~/.bash_history . Every terminal tab and every SSH login of yours adds to it as each command runs, so a tab you open afterwards finds the commands typed in the others. A tab that is already open keeps the list it started with. A command typed with a space in front, or the same as the one before it, is not kept. It keeps the last 1000 commands. Change this under Profile → Preferences , Shell history length ( HISTSIZE ); a tab you open afterwards uses the new length. Your profile, favourites and trash shows where. Commands the web pages run for you, and commands sent with ssh host 'command' , are not kept.

Press Tab while you type a command name, a path, an option, a user or a group. When only one thing fits, EiN fills it in, with / after a folder and a space after anything else, and quotes it if it holds spaces. When several fit, it fills in as much as they share; press Tab again to list them all. The first two rows are on an EiN with the Archive installed: You type Tab gives cd /archive/al cd /archive/albums/ person-info /archive/people/Peg person-info /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield search --ki search --kind= , ready for the value user-info he user-info helen pipeline , a space, Tab twice the list of pipeline 's subcommands Completion reads each command's own description of its arguments and options, so it knows a command's options without being told. A command of a family, such as pipeline status , is completed as two words. Scripts of your own can take part; see The shell language .

Put --help (or -h ) straight after a command's name. The command does not run; it says how to use it instead: # in EiN's terminal onthisday -- help Usage: onthisday [OPTIONS] <day> What the archive has from a calendar day (MM-DD, default today) in earlier years, from every onthisday-* command on PATH Arguments: <day> day as MM-DD (default today, UTC) Options: --limit <number> entries returned across all providers (default 8) -h, --help Show this help message Returns: the entries of every onthisday-* provider, newest year first: the year, what, the node it is about, which provider, and the route that draws it. Examples: onthisday onthisday 06-21 --limit 20 A family of commands , such as config , docs , group , mod , pipeline , pool , service and user , lists its members with --help : service --help . Each member answers for itself: service status --help . The two words are another way of typing the member's name: service status runs service-status . bash's own commands , such as cd , export and history , are described by help : help cd . -h first always means help , even for a command whose own -h means something else: du -h shows the help of du . Put another option first, as in du -sh . There is no man and no pager. Long output scrolls past; scroll back with the mouse wheel or the scrollbar. The same descriptions are in Documentation in the sidebar, under Commands , for every command installed on your EiN, and on this site in the command reference .

When you know what you want done but not which command does it, ask by what it does. In the finder. Press Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) and type > followed by what the command should do, or part of its name. Up to six commands appear under Commands ; choosing one opens its description in Documentation . It does not run the command: you run it in the terminal. Search and the finder has the details. Starting with > in the finder searches EiN's commands rather than the archive. In the terminal. docs find lists the best commands, best first, each with a score, its name and its description: # in EiN's terminal docs find restart a service With the assistant module installed there is also assistant-commands find , which adds whether each command only reads or also changes something, and assistant-commands judge tells you which a whole command line would do: # in EiN's terminal assistant-commands find 'list running services' assistant-commands judge 'service restart pipeline-pruner' How well this works depends on what is installed: Installed How commands are found Core alone Your words are matched against the commands' names and descriptions; a word in the name counts double The assistant module The assistant answers for docs find and the finder, and still matches words The assistant module and the media service Commands are found by meaning, so one can turn up even when its description uses other words than yours The settings behind this are Command finder ( CFG_COMMAND_FINDER ) and Text embedder ( CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER ); the assistant module and the media service set them when they are installed.

p.h: Use the same shell over SSH
p.x: The terminal is one of several interfaces to the same shell. From your own computer you can log in over SSH with your EiN username and password, on port 2222 unless your administrator chose another: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local You get the same shell as in a terminal tab: the same prompt, your history, your ~/.bashrc , Tab completion and the same keys. Two things belong to the browser alone: pictures and videos drawn by cat , and dropping files to upload them. Over SSH, copy files with SFTP or scp instead. Whichever interface you use, the same commands run as you, with the same permissions. The web pages run these same commands for you, and so does the assistant, always as the person signed in. A command you may not run in the terminal is refused through every other interface too. SSH and SFTP covers keys, running one command at a time, and copying files.

Commands marked archive come with the Archive and exist only where it is installed, as do the /archive/albums and /archive/people paths in the examples. search , news , events and onthisday are EiN's own, but answer with what the installed modules provide, so without a module they find nothing. Commands by task has many more, grouped by what you want to do. Command What it does ls Lists what is in a folder; ls -l with details cd Moves into a folder; cd alone goes home, cd - back to where you were cat Prints a text file, or draws a picture edit Edits a text file in the terminal; see The editor cp Copies; cp -r for a folder and what is in it mv Moves or renames, and keeps the links to what it moves pointing at the new place rm Deletes for good; rm -r for anything that has children, a processed photo included trash trash put <path> moves into your trash, from which you can restore it mkdir Makes a folder; mkdir -p makes the folders above it too mkfile Makes an empty text file, what touch does elsewhere du Adds up sizes; du -chs * gives readable sizes and a total find Finds nodes under a path, as GNU find does: find /archive/people -maxdepth 1 -type person search Searches what the modules make searchable: search christmas --kind photo stat Shows a node's details: type, owner, times ln ln -s makes a softlink, one thing in a second place news What has been added lately, newest first events What falls on the days around today, such as birthdays and anniversaries onthisday What the modules have from this day in earlier years timeline archive : albums, life events, birthdays and tracks, newest first person-info archive : a person's details, relations, homes and events top Watches the system live; q quits ps , who What is running now, and who is connected; your own, or everyone's for an administrator health One line on how the system is doing, and the checks behind it docs docs find <words> finds a command by what it does whoami Prints your username Warning rm deletes at once and for good: it does not use the trash, and nothing brings the node back. Use trash put for anything you may want again; it then shows under Trash in your account menu (see Your profile, favourites and trash ). top fills the terminal with what EiN is doing and keeps it up to date. Press Alt + M first to give it the whole window. Health and the dashboard explains what it shows and all its keys. top shows on one screen what the Dashboard spreads over several tabs. Steps that belong together can be joined with && , and paths with spaces go in quotes, as in bash: # in EiN's terminal cd "/archive/albums/Summer 2020" && ls -l The shell language covers what else bash syntax can do in EiN, and how it differs from bash on Linux.

There is no terminal button. You are not signed in, or the window is phone-sized. Sign in; on a small screen press Alt + T with a keyboard, or use SSH from a computer. The terminal closed while I was clicking on the page. A click outside the terminal hides it. Its shells keep running; press Alt + T to bring it back. The top bar says Disconnected, or a tab shows a red crossed-out plug. EiN cannot be reached from the browser just now: the badge is the page's own connection, the plug that tab's shell. The terminal reconnects by itself and finds its shell again if the connection is back within five minutes. The screen was cleared and a fresh prompt waits. The shell ended: you were away longer than five minutes, EiN restarted, or you signed out. Your history is still there; ↑ and Ctrl + R find your commands. error: command 'albm' not found . No command of that name is on your path. Check the spelling with Tab , or look for it with docs find . Commands such as timeline and person-info exist only where their module is installed. service-restart: permission denied: only an administrator may run it . The command is for administrators. Through every interface it is refused the same way; ask your administrator. du -h shows help instead of sizes. -h straight after a command's name always asks for help. Write du -sh or du -ch . cat prints lines starting __IMG: instead of the picture. You are connected over SSH, or the picture's path holds a space or a colon. Open the picture in the web interface. Dropped files landed in the wrong folder. They go into the folder the tab is in, the path on the tab. cd to where they belong and drop them again, or move them with mv . The browser tab closed when I pressed Ctrl+W. The browser keeps that key for itself. Open EiN again: you get new terminals, and the old shells end after five minutes.

The shell language : the bash syntax EiN understands, scripts, jobs and JSON_OUTPUT=1 . Commands by task : which command does what, grouped by task. The editor : edit and its keys. SSH and SFTP : the same shell from your own computer, and copying files. Commands : every command, with all its options. Keyboard shortcuts : every key in EiN.

EiN's shell speaks bash: the quoting, variables, loops, functions, pipes and redirections you know from bash on Linux work the same way on EiN's tree. This page is for anyone who writes more than one command at a time: what EiN's shell does like bash, where it differs, how to keep settings in ~/.bashrc , how to write scripts of your own, how to run long jobs in the background, and how to get answers as JSON. The terminal itself, with its tabs, keys, history and Tab completion, has a page of its own: The terminal . Commands by task tells you which command does what. The examples work on the Archive 's folders, such as /archive/albums and /archive/people , which are there once it is installed. The shell itself is the same on any EiN: try them on your home folder or /etc where the Archive is not installed.

p.h: Bash, on a tree of nodes
p.x: The shell is a bash written for EiN and tested against the test suite of GNU bash 5.2. Nearly all of the language is there: What Example Pipes and lists find /archive/people -type person | wc -l , cd /archive && ls , a || b Quoting ls "/archive/albums/Summer 2020" , echo 'no $expansion here' Variables and parameters name=${file%.jpg} , ${#name} , ${name^^} , ${dir:-/archive} Command substitution count=$(ls -1 /archive/people | wc -l) Arithmetic $(( 6 * 7 )) , (( n >= 10 )) , let n++ Brace expansion echo {2019..2023} Arrays people=(Peggy Ruby Jon) , "${people[@]}" , declare -A seen Tests [[ $name == *.jpg ]] , [[ $line =~ ^([0-9]+) ]] , [ -e "$path" ] Control flow if , for , while , until , case , for (( i = 0; i < 3; i++ )) Functions count() { ls -1 "$1" | wc -l; } Redirections > out.txt , >> log.txt , 2>/dev/null , 2>&1 , < in.txt Here-documents cat > note.txt <<'EOF' … EOF , and here-strings <<< "$line" Process substitution mapfile -t names < <(find /archive/people -type person) Jobs cmd & , jobs , fg , bg , wait , kill %1 Options and traps set -euo pipefail , shopt -s globstar , trap 'echo bye' EXIT The difference is what the words name. A path is a node of EiN's tree, not a file on a disk: / is the root of the tree, ~ is your home folder /home/<you> , and globs such as *.jpg match the names of nodes. Commands are EiN's own, not programs installed on a machine. The tree shows what lies where, and Nodes and node types what a node is. # in EiN's terminal for person in /archive/people/*_Wrenfield; do echo " ${person##*/} " done Arthur_Wrenfield Erik_Wrenfield Freya_Wrenfield Jon_Wrenfield Kiri_Wrenfield Leo_Wrenfield Peggy_Wrenfield Ruby_Wrenfield Thomas_Wrenfield

p.h: What happens when you press Enter
p.x: The shell reads the line you typed. When it is not finished yet, because a quote is open, an if has no fi or a here-document has no end line, the prompt changes to > and waits for the next line. Press Ctrl + C to give up on it. The first word is then looked up in this order, the first match wins: An alias, such as ll for ls -al . A function you defined. A builtin of the shell: cd , echo , read , export , source and the others in Builtins . One of EiN's own commands, such as ls , cp or search . A command found on PATH : core's other commands, then each installed module's. echo $PATH shows the folders: /usr/bin and /usr/lib/core/bin first, then /usr/modules/<module>/bin for each module. A word with a / in it, such as ./tidy.sh or ~/bin/album-sizes , runs that node instead. type <name> says which of these a name is, and command -v <name> prints only where it is found. When nothing matches, you see: error: command 'albm' not found and the status is 127 . Commands such as person-info exist only where their module is installed; mod list shows which modules are. Ctrl + C stops the command that is running. A loop stops too, rather than going on with the next round.

p.h: How EiN's shell differs from bash on Linux
p.x: Most scripts written for bash run unchanged. These are the places where EiN behaves differently, because the tree is not a disk and the commands are not Linux programs. Every node can hold others. A file can have children of its own, as a photo in the Archive has its EXIF data and the regions of its faces, so [ -d "$path" ] is true for every node that exists. Test with [ -e "$path" ] whether a node is there, and [ -f "$path" ] whether it is a file. [ -s "$path" ] is true only for a file with content. [ -t 1 ] is always false. Plain variables reach commands. A command or script started from the shell sees all of the shell's variables, not only the exported ones. JSON_OUTPUT=1 on a line of its own therefore changes every command after it until you unset JSON_OUTPUT . Put it in front of one command to change only that one. ls in the terminal writes columns into a pipe too. In the terminal panel and an SSH login, ls lays names out in columns even when its output goes to another command. Give -1 when you count or loop over names: ls -1 /archive/albums | wc -l . find always writes one path per line. -h right after a command's name asks for help. du -h prints du 's help instead of sizes; write du -sh . A value that starts with a minus goes after an equals sign, --lng=-3.7 ; on its own -3.7 would be read as another option. There is no sh or bash command. Run a script by its path, or read it into the shell you are in with source . See Write a script . Ctrl + Z does not pause a command. Start a long one with & instead; see Run a long job in the background . Process substitution waits for the end. <(cmd) writes the command's whole output to a temporary node under /tmp before the reading command opens it, so it is not streamed. Many Unix programs are missing. tar , curl , diff , less and others have no EiN command. Commands by task lists what to use instead. Permissions are EiN's. A command you may not run is refused the same way in the shell, the web interface and over SSH. Permissions in depth explains who may do what.

Each terminal tab, and each SSH login, is one shell that lasts until you close it. A cd , an export , an alias or a function you define stays for the next command in that tab, and survives a page reload (see Come back to a running shell ). Other tabs have shells of their own and do not see it. A command sent with ssh host 'command' from your own computer gets a fresh shell that ends with the command. Join what belongs together with && in one line: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'cd /archive/albums && ls -1 | wc -l' SSH and SFTP covers logging in from your own computer.

When a terminal tab or an SSH login opens, the shell reads, in this order: /etc/bashrc , the same for everyone. It defines the aliases ll ( ls -al ), la ( ls -A ), whoami and id , and reads the settings: the modules' own, the administrator's in /etc/config , then your own in ~/.config . /etc/bashrc.d/<group> for each of your groups that has one, in the order of their names: what the administrator gives a group, such as the commands of a module kept to the group . An administrator also gets /etc/bashrc.d/admin . ~/.bashrc , your own file, if you have one. EiN reads no ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile . A command sent with ssh host 'command' reads /etc/bashrc and your groups' files but not ~/.bashrc . To make a change that lasts: Open the file in the editor: # in EiN's terminal edit ~/.bashrc Add what you want, for example: # ~/.bashrc export HOSTNAME=ein export PATH= " $HOME /bin: $PATH " alias albums= 'cd /archive/albums && ls' people () { find /archive/people -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 - type person; } Save with Ctrl + S and leave with Ctrl + Q . The editor has its other keys. Run source ~/.bashrc to use it in the tab you are in. New tabs read it when they open. A ~/.bashrc that fails does not stop the shell from opening: you get a prompt all the same. Fix the file and source it again. Some things to put there: Line What it does export HOSTNAME=ein Shows a host name in the prompt, helen@ein:~$ PS1='\u:\W\$ ' Changes the prompt; see below export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" Lets your own scripts in ~/bin run by name export MEDIA_LINES=30 Draws pictures with cat 30 lines tall export HISTSIZE=5000 Keeps more history in this shell set -o ignoreeof Ctrl + D on an empty line no longer ends the shell complete -F _my_func my-script Your own Tab completion for a command PS1 understands \u (your username), \h (the host name), \w (the folder, with ~ for your home), \W (the last part of the folder), \$ ( # when the shell acts as an administrator, $ otherwise), \t and \T (the time in 24- and 12-hour form), \n (a new line) and \e for colour codes. Unset PS1 to get EiN's coloured prompt back. Settings such as the length of your history are better changed under Profile → Preferences , which writes them to ~/.config ; see Your profile, favourites and trash . Configuration explains how the administrator's settings and yours are layered.

A script is a text file of shell commands. EiN runs any text file you have execute permission on as a bash script. Make a folder for your scripts and open a new file in it: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/bin edit ~/bin/album-sizes Write the script. Start it with #!bash , so the editor colours and checks it as bash: #!bash # How much each album holds, largest first for album in /archive/albums/*; do printf '%6d %s\n' " $(ls -1 " $album " | wc -l) " " ${album##*/} " done | sort -rn Save it, and give yourself permission to run it: # in EiN's terminal chmod 755 ~/bin/album-sizes Run it by its path: # in EiN's terminal ~/bin/album-sizes With ~/bin on your PATH (see Keep your settings in ~/.bashrc ), album-sizes alone is enough. A script run like this is a process of its own: its cd , variables and functions end with it, and exit ends the script, not your shell. $1 , $2 , $@ and $# are its arguments, and $0 is its path. source ~/bin/album-sizes (or . ~/bin/album-sizes ) runs the same lines in the shell you are in instead, so what they change stays; a sourced file needs no execute permission. Pick a name that is not already a command: a name such as ls or cp always runs EiN's own command, whatever is on your PATH . type album-sizes shows what a name runs. A file whose first line is #!ts is a TypeScript command, and EiN runs those only from a module installed under /usr/modules . Writing a module covers that.

p.h: Give a script options and help with arg
p.x: The builtin arg gives a script the options, help and Tab completion that EiN's own commands have. Declare what the script takes, then arg --export reads the arguments and sets one variable for each, named in capitals: #!bash arg --desc "Count what each album holds" arg '[<under>]' path = /archive/albums "where the albums are" arg -m --min number = 0 "leave out albums holding fewer" arg --example "album-sizes --min 50" arg -- export for album in " $UNDER " /*; do n=$( ls -1 " $album " | wc -l) if (( n >= MIN )); then printf '%6d %s\n' " $n " " ${album##*/} " ; fi done album-sizes --help then prints: Usage: /home/helen/bin/album-sizes [OPTIONS] [<under>] Count what each album holds Arguments: [<under>] where the albums are [default: /archive/albums] Options: -m, --min <number> leave out albums holding fewer [default: 0] -h, --help Show this help message Examples: album-sizes --min 50 An option the script does not declare, a missing argument, or a word where a number belongs stops the script with a message such as Unknown option: --bogus and Try '/home/helen/bin/album-sizes --help' for more information. , status 1 . Line Declares arg --desc "text" What the script does, shown by --help arg '<name>' type "text" An argument that must be given; its value is in $NAME arg '[<name>]' type = value "text" An argument that may be left out, with its default arg -s --long type "text" An option that takes a value, $LONG ; = value gives it a default arg -s --long "text" An option without a value: $LONG is 1 when given, empty if not arg --rest Leaves the arguments it does not know in $@ instead of refusing arg --example "command line" An example for --help arg --returns "text" What the script answers with, in a sentence arg --effect read or write Whether running it changes anything arg --export Reads the arguments and sets the variables; put it last The types are string , number , boolean , path , user , group and command . A - in an option's name becomes _ in its variable: --max-count is $MAX_COUNT . Because the script declares what it takes, Tab completes its options and, for a path , user or group , their values, once the script is on your PATH . A script without arg completes paths.

p.h: Run a long job in the background
p.x: End a command with & and the prompt comes back at once while it runs: # in EiN's terminal ~/bin/album-sizes > ~/album-sizes.txt & [1] bg-01JBXK4T9Q2M8N5R7V3W6Y0Z1A [1] is the job's number in this shell, and the rest is its process id, which ps lists too. When the job ends, the shell says so before the next prompt, as [1]+ Done with the command. Command What it does jobs Lists this shell's jobs and whether they still run fg %1 Waits for job 1 in the foreground; Ctrl + C stops it wait Waits for all of this shell's jobs to end kill %1 Stops job 1, everything it runs included kill <pid> Stops a process by its id from ps ; your own, or anyone's for an administrator echo $! The process id of the last job you started A background job belongs to its shell. When the shell ends (you close the tab, sign out, or stay away longer than the five minutes the terminal waits), its jobs are stopped with it.

p.h: Keep a job running after you leave
p.x: To let a job go on after its shell has ended, detach it. Start it detached with nohup : # in EiN's terminal nohup album-sizes --min 50 nohup: [1] bg-01JBXM2C6D8F0G3H5J7K9L1N4P -> /var/logs/jobs/bg-01JBXM2C6D8F0G3H5J7K9L1N4P/ Or detach a job you already started with & : detach %1 , or detach alone for the latest. EiN answers detached [1] <pid> <command> . A detached job leaves the shell's jobs list and no longer writes to the terminal. Its output goes to stdout.log and stderr.log in /var/logs/jobs/<pid>/ , beside a status.json that says whether it still runs and how it ended. detach --list lists the detached jobs, newest first, one line each with the process id, the state, when it started and the command, or no detached jobs . running means it still goes, exited gives its status in brackets, and abandoned means EiN restarted while it ran. A detached job does not survive a restart of EiN. nohup runs one command with its arguments. For several steps, or a pipe, put them in a script and detach that, or nohup source ~/sweep.sh . Stop a detached job with kill <pid> . detach and nohup are in the reference.

Put JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of a command and it answers in JSON instead of text. This is how the web interface runs every command, so the JSON holds everything the pages show. Read it with jq : # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls /archive/people | jq -r '.[]' JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l /archive/albums | jq '.[].name' ls alone answers with a list of names; ls -l with a record for each node. JSON_OUTPUT=1 <command> --help answers with the command's description of its arguments and options as JSON, a script's from its arg lines included. Text tools such as grep , sort , head , cut , wc and cat keep writing text, so they work in the same pipe. Set without a command in front, JSON_OUTPUT=1 holds for every command after it in that shell, until unset JSON_OUTPUT . jq is EiN's own, a lighter jq that knows filters such as .field , .field.nested , .[] , .[] | .name and startswith("x") , with -r for plain text and -c for one line per result. Environment variables lists JSON_OUTPUT with the other variables that change how commands behave, and docs env prints them in the terminal.

These are part of the shell itself, so they have no entry in the commands reference . help <name> prints a builtin's usage in the terminal. Builtins For cd , pwd , pushd , popd , dirs Moving around; cd alone goes home, cd - back echo , printf , read , mapfile , readarray Writing and reading lines export , unset , local , declare , typeset , readonly , let , shift Variables source , . , eval , exit , return , true , false , : Running and ending test , [ Tests jobs , fg , bg , wait , kill , disown Jobs set , shopt , trap , umask , ulimit Options and signals alias , unalias , type , command , builtin , hash , enable , help Names and lookup history , fc History; see Find an earlier command complete , compgen , compopt Tab completion getopts , arg , caller , times Scripts disown takes a job out of the list and lets it outlive the shell, as detach does. kill takes the signals HUP , INT , TERM , KILL , PIPE , TSTP and CONT by name, kill -TERM %1 .

The prompt shows > and nothing happens. The line is not finished: a quote or a bracket is open, or an if , for or here-document has no end. Type the rest, or press Ctrl + C to start again. error: command 'album-sizes' not found . The script's folder is not on your PATH . Run it by its path, ~/bin/album-sizes , or add export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" to ~/.bashrc and source ~/.bashrc . Running a script by its path is refused. You have no execute permission on it. Run chmod 755 <script> , or read it in with source <script> . error: <name>: a #!ts command runs only from a module in /usr/modules . A #!ts file runs only from an installed module. Write the script in bash, or make it part of a module. A count from ls | wc -l is too small. ls wrote its names in columns. Use ls -1 . Every command answers in JSON. JSON_OUTPUT=1 was set on its own line, or in ~/.bashrc . Run unset JSON_OUTPUT . An alias or function from ~/.bashrc is missing. It is read when a tab opens: run source ~/.bashrc in tabs that were open before you changed it. A command sent with ssh host 'command' does not read ~/.bashrc . A background job stopped when I closed the tab. Jobs end with their shell. Start it with nohup , or detach it before you leave. nohup: <command>: nothing left to detach — it had already finished . The command ended, or failed to start, before nohup could detach it. Run it without nohup to see what it says. detach: no such job: %2 . This shell has no such job, or it has ended. jobs lists the ones there are.

The terminal : opening it, tabs, keys, history and Tab completion. Commands by task : which command does what. The editor : edit , for ~/.bashrc and scripts. SSH and SFTP : the same shell from your own computer. Commands reference : every command with all its options. Environment variables : the variables every shell has. Writing a module : commands that come with a module.

This page is for power users and administrators who know what they want to do and need the command for it. Each table row gives a task, a command line that does it, and a link to that command's full entry in the reference .

Every command runs as you, with your permissions, in the terminal or over SSH . The examples use the demo archive's invented Wrenfield family: the album /archive/albums/christmas-2019 , the person /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield , the account helen . Albums and people come with the Archive , so those paths are there once it is installed. administrators only marks a command that anyone else is refused before it starts, with <name>: permission denied: only an administrator may run it . A member of the sudo group can type admin to act as the administrator in that terminal. Accounts and groups explains who that is. This page has core's commands. The modules' commands come with their modules , and their tasks are on Archive commands by task and Assistant commands by task ; the media service 's are on its page. Without the module, the shell answers error: command '<name>' not found . mod list shows what is installed. A command of a family can be typed as two words: mod install is mod-install , and pipeline status is pipeline-status . The families are config , docs , group , mod , pipeline , pool , service , share and user , and with the archive also person and device . <family> --help , such as mod --help , lists its subcommands; typing mod alone answers mod: missing subcommand . <command> --help prints a command's arguments, options and examples without running it. JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of a command makes it answer in JSON; The shell language covers that and the rest of the syntax. cd , pwd , jobs , kill and the other bash builtins have no reference entry. They are described in The shell language .

The tree works like a file system: paths start at / , .. is the parent, and cd moves you around. Any node can have children, so cd into a photo works and ls shows what EiN learnt about it, such as exif , position , thumbnails and regions . The tree says what lives where. search looks through what EiN knows about your content. It asks each installed module's search, so what it finds comes from the modules: with no module it finds nothing, and with the Archive the words, what the pictures show, the people in them, dates and places; Archive commands by task has those searches. find walks the tree by name and type, as GNU find does. Search and the finder covers searching in the web interface. In EiN a pid is a name, such as sleep- followed by a unique id, not a number. Ctrl + Z does not suspend a command; start it with & instead.

Task Command Reference How much work is waiting, per kind, and how fast it goes pool stat pool-stat The jobs of a pool that failed pool list /var/pools/media --state failed pool-list Try resting kinds of work again, administrators only pool wake pool-wake Return failed jobs of a kind to the pool, administrators only pool retry /var/pools/media --kind faces pool-retry Pipelines at a glance pipeline overview pipeline-overview The pipeline definitions pipeline list pipeline-list Failed pipeline runs, newest first pipeline instances -s failed pipeline-instances One run's steps and what each did pipeline status <id> pipeline-status Run a failed run's failed steps again, administrators only pipeline restart <id> pipeline-restart Run a run again from the current definition, administrators only pipeline rerun <id> pipeline-rerun Rerun failed work that waited long enough, administrators only pipeline heal (says what it would do), pipeline heal --apply pipeline-heal Process one file with a pipeline, forcing it, administrators only pipeline start media-transcribe <file> --var FORCE=-f pipeline-start The next entries of a queue, without taking them queue-peek /var/queues/archive-bridge queue-peek Entries a queue set aside after failing queue-dead /var/queues/archive-bridge queue-dead The services and how often each restarted service list , service list --detail service-list One service's state and where its log is service status cpu service-status Restart, stop or start a service, administrators only service restart cpu , service stop cpu , service start cpu service-restart , service-stop , service-start Warning cat on a queue takes the entries it prints out of the queue. Use queue-peek to look.

There is no logs command. The system log and each service's output are log nodes, read with dmesg , tail and cat . Task Command Reference The system log dmesg -n 50 dmesg The last ten problems dmesg --level warn -n 10 dmesg Follow the system log as it grows tail -f /var/logs/system tail A service's own output tail -f /var/logs/services/cpu/stdout.log , and stderr.log beside it tail Who changed, moved or removed what, administrators only audit --user anna --since 2026-10-01 /archive/albums audit The system log starts empty at every start of EiN, and a service's two log files start empty at every start of that service.

ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id are for administrators and members of the group ssh . Reaching other machines covers them, with the host key prompts and ~/.ssh/config . Task Command Reference Make a key pair in ~/.ssh ssh-keygen ssh-keygen Put your public key on another machine ssh-copy-id anna@nas.local ssh-copy-id Log in to another machine, or run one command there ssh anna@nas.local , ssh nas.local 'df -h' ssh Copy files in from another machine scp -r anna@nas.local:photos/1968 /home/anna/staging/files/inbox/ scp List what is mounted mount mount Mount a folder of another machine (administrators) mount --save /mnt/nas sftp "host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos" mount Connecting to EiN from your own computer is described in SSH and SFTP .

These work on text files, logs and the output of other commands, as their GNU namesakes do. Run <command> --help for the options each has. Task Command Reference Pick fields from JSON JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l /archive/albums | jq -r '.[].name' jq Find lines matching a pattern grep -i -c christmas ~/notes.md grep Replace text in a stream sed 's/Wrenfeld/Wrenfield/g' ~/notes.md sed Work with columns awk -F'\t' '{ print $1 }' , cut -f1 awk , cut Sort, count and remove repeats sort , uniq -c , wc -l sort , uniq , wc Run a command for each line of input ls /archive/people | xargs -I {} info /archive/people/{} xargs Change or delete characters tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' tr Dates, numbers, waiting date -I , seq 1 10 , sleep 5 date , seq , sleep Parts of a path basename <path> , dirname <path> , abspath <path> basename , dirname , abspath The environment of your shell env , docs env env , docs-env

p.h: Unix commands EiN does not have
p.x: EiN's commands are its own, so some familiar names are missing. Use these instead. You may type Use instead touch mkfile vi , nano edit less , more , man the terminal's scrollback, <command> --help , and the reference realpath abspath which type <name> or command -v <name> passwd , useradd , usermod user-passwd , user-create , user-update ; for groups, group-add-member chgrp chown :<group> <path> sudo , su admin or user-elevate , for members of sudo getfacl , setfacl acl tar , rsync , curl , wget , diff , tee none in EiN; unzip unpacks zip files, and scp copies over SSH There is also no sh or bash command: a script is run by its path, or with source . The shell language explains scripts.

p.h: When a command is refused or missing
p.x: What you see Why What to do error: command '<name>' not found No command of that name is on your PATH : a typing error, or a module that is not installed Check the name with docs find <words> ; see mod list <name>: permission denied: only an administrator may run it The command is for administrators Ask an administrator, or type admin if you are in the sudo group <name>: permission denied, you must be a member of group 'ssh' ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id need the ssh group An administrator adds you with group-add-member ssh <you> ; sign in again <name>: sign in first You are not signed in, and visitors may not browse login <username> rm: cannot remove '<path>': Node not empty The node has children rm -r <path> deletes it with them; trash put <path> keeps it recoverable edit: not a terminal edit needs a terminal, which ssh host 'command' does not give Log in with ssh first, or use the terminal panel <name>: no terminal to answer on; add --force The command would ask a question, and ssh host 'command' or a script has no one to answer Give the answer as the option it names, or run it in the terminal panel mount: permission denied, only admin is allowed to mount Mounting is for administrators Ask an administrator For anything else, Troubleshooting goes through problems by area, and the reference has every command with all its options.

EiN has two places to change a text file: edit in the terminal, which colours the text and checks JSON, YAML and bash as you type, and the code editor on the Nodes page of the web interface. This page is for anyone who edits a script, a note or a configuration file in EiN.

edit runs in a terminal: the terminal panel in the browser, or an SSH login from your own computer. Open the terminal with the terminal button in the top bar, or Alt + T . Type edit and the path of the file, and press Enter : # in EiN's terminal edit ~/notes.md The editor fills the terminal. Change the text, press Ctrl + S to save and Ctrl + Q to leave. The shell's screen comes back as you left it. A path is read from the directory you are in, so edit tidy.sh opens tidy.sh there. Tab completes paths after edit as it does after any command. What the editor shows, here on a nav.json with a missing comma: 1 { ✗2 "hide": ["archive.map" "archive.devices"] 3 } ~ ~ nav.json ✗ 2:26 expected ',' or ']' after array element JSON ✗ L 1:1 ^S Save ^Q Quit ^F Find ^G Line ^Z Undo ^Y Redo ^K Cut ^U Paste The text , with line numbers at the left. The cursor's line number is in the text's own colour, the others grey. Rows after the end of the file show ~ . The status bar , the second row from the bottom. At the left: the file's name, [New] for a file not saved yet, [Modified] while there are unsaved changes, then a message or the syntax error described under Checks as you type . At the right: the language, a check mark or cross where the language is checked, and the cursor's position as L line:column . The bottom row lists the main keys, ^S meaning Ctrl + S . While the editor asks you something, such as Find: , the question takes this row.

Give edit a path that does not exist yet. The editor opens empty with [New] in the status bar. Nothing is created until you save; leaving without saving leaves nothing behind. The first save creates the file in the folder the path names, and decides its type: from the name's extension: notes.md becomes Markdown, nav.json JSON, tidy.sh a shell script; for a name without a known extension, from a first line starting with #! : #!bash makes a script, #!/usr/bin/env python3 a Python file; otherwise plain text. Typing a #!bash line into a new file colours and checks it as bash at once, unless its name already has one of the extensions under Colours and line wrapping . The folder must exist. To start a file in a folder that is not there yet, make the folder first: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/.ui && edit ~/.ui/nav.json A script you write with edit needs execute permission before it runs as a command: chmod 755 tidy.sh . The shell language covers scripts.

p.h: When edit will not open a file
p.x: edit prints one line and goes back to the prompt: Message Why What to do edit: missing file operand You gave no path. Name the file: edit notes.md . edit: not a terminal The command did not run in a terminal: one command sent with ssh … 'edit notes.md' , or a script started without one. The assistant never runs edit . Use the terminal panel, or sign in over SSH with a shell of your own ( ssh -p 2222 anna@ein.local ) and run edit there. edit: /home/anna/staging: not a file (directory) The path is a folder, or another kind of node such as an album or a person. The type is in brackets. Name a file. ls -l shows what a folder holds. edit: /home/anna/beach.jpg: not a text file (mimetype: image/jpeg) The file is a picture, a video, a PDF or another file that is not text. Nothing to edit here. With the Archive, a picture opens in its viewer. edit: /home/anna/old.txt: not UTF-8 text The file is text in another encoding, such as Latin-1, or holds bytes that are not text. Convert it to UTF-8 on your own computer and upload it again. edit: /etc/keys: Access denied … You may not read the file. Ask its owner or an administrator. Permissions in depth explains who may read what. The full entry for the command is edit in the reference.

Press Ctrl + S . The status bar says Saved and [Modified] goes away. If the text has a syntax error, the editor asks first, on the bottom row, with the first error after the question: Save with errors? (y/N) ✗ 2:26 expected ',' or ']' after array element Press y to save anyway. n , Enter or any other letter leaves the file as it was and the status bar says Not saved ; Esc takes the question away. To leave, press Ctrl + Q . With nothing unsaved the editor closes at once. Otherwise it asks: Save changes? (y/n, Esc cancels) y saves and leaves. If the text has an error, Save with errors? (y/N) comes first. n leaves without saving. Esc or Ctrl + C goes back to the text. Ctrl + C does not leave the editor: on its own it only shows ^Q quits . Tip If your browser or terminal program keeps Ctrl + S or Ctrl + Q for itself, Ctrl + O saves and Ctrl + X quits. Saving keeps the file's line endings: a file written with Windows line endings (CRLF) keeps them, and a file that ended without a final newline still does. A new file ends with a newline.

The status bar shows Not saved: and the reason in red, and your text stays in the editor. The usual reasons are a folder that does not exist and a file you may read but not change ( Access denied ). In the terminal panel you can put it right without losing the text: Press Alt + N for a new terminal tab. Make the folder there with mkdir -p , or ask for access to the file. Go back to the editor's tab, by clicking it or with Alt + ← , and press Ctrl + S again. Over SSH, open a second SSH login for the same purpose. edit does not notice when someone else changes the file while you have it open: saving writes your text over theirs.

Keys What they do Ctrl + S or Ctrl + O Save. With a syntax error in the text, asks first. Ctrl + Q or Ctrl + X Leave. With unsaved changes, asks first. Ctrl + F Find. The question starts with the last search; Enter goes to the next match. Ctrl + G Go to a line, or to line:column . Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Y Undo / redo. Ctrl + K Cut the cursor's line. Lines cut one after another collect into one cut. Ctrl + U Paste what was cut, at the cursor. ← → One character left or right, on to the next or previous line at a line's end. ↑ ↓ One row up or down, keeping to the column you started from. Ctrl + ← Ctrl + → , Alt + ← Alt + → One word left or right. In the terminal panel only the Ctrl keys reach the editor. Home or Ctrl + A To the first character of the line that is not a space; pressed again, to the very start. On a wrapped row, to the start of that row. End or Ctrl + E To the end of the line. On a wrapped row, to the end of that row. Ctrl + Home / Ctrl + End To the start / end of the file. PgUp / PgDn A screen up / down. Enter A new line, indented as the line it came from. Tab Indent. See Indentation . Backspace / Delete Delete the character before / after the cursor. At the start or end of a line, join it with the line before or after. Esc or Ctrl + C Cancel a question: find, go to a line, save with errors, save changes. Ctrl + C with no question open Shows ^Q quits . On a Mac, too, the keys are Ctrl , not ⌘ .

p.h: Find text and go to a line
p.x: Press Ctrl + F . The bottom row shows Find: , with your last search already typed. Type what you are looking for and press Enter . The cursor moves to the next match after it. Case does not matter. When the search runs past the end of the file it goes on from the top and the status bar says Search wrapped ; with no match at all it says Not found . To go on to the next match, press Ctrl + F and Enter again. Ctrl + G shows Go to line[:column]: . Type 40 for line 40, or 40:12 for its twelfth column, and press Enter . A number past the end goes to the last line; anything that is not a number shows Not a line number .

Ctrl + Z undoes up to 200 steps, and Ctrl + Y redoes them. A word typed in one go is one step, and so is a run of deletions or a paste; a pause of half a second starts a new step. With nothing left, the status bar says Nothing to undo or Nothing to redo . Ctrl + K and Ctrl + U use the editor's own clipboard, not your computer's: press Ctrl + K three times to cut three lines, move, and press Ctrl + U to put them back there. Text pasted from your computer goes in exactly as it is, without being indented again, and undoes in one step.

Enter starts the new line with the indent of the one before. A line left holding only spaces is emptied. Tab inserts one step of the file's own indent: a tab, when the file indents mostly with tabs, and always in a Makefile; otherwise as many spaces as the smallest indent of two or more spaces the file has, at most 8; two spaces in a file with no indent yet. Shift + Tab does nothing; take an indent away with Backspace . Tabs in the text reach the next stop of four columns, and other control characters as ^ and a letter.

edit works out the language of a file in this order, and colours the text by it: the name: its extension, or the names Makefile and GNUmakefile ; the file's type, as EiN recorded it when the file came in; a first line starting with #! , when the type says no more than that the file is text. Language Files Checked as you type JSON .json Yes JSONC .jsonc : JSON in which comments are allowed Yes YAML .yaml , .yml Yes bash .sh , .bash ; a shell-script type; a #! line naming bash, sh or any other interpreter not below Yes Markdown .md , .markdown Its code blocks TypeScript .ts , .mts , .tsx ; #!ts or #!deno No JavaScript .js , .mjs , .cjs , .jsx ; #!node or #!js No Python .py ; #!python or #!python3 , also through #!/usr/bin/env No XML .xml , .html , .htm , .svg No CSS .css No Makefile Makefile , GNUmakefile , .mk No Others .scss ; .ini , .conf and .toml (as ini); .sql ; .diff , .patch ; .go ; .rs (rust); .lua No The status bar names the language at its right; a file that matches none is text . A file without an extension, such as ~/.bashrc , is plain text unless its first line starts with #! . In a Markdown file, each fenced code block is coloured in the language its fence names. A text longer than 262,144 characters (256 K) is shown without colours. Plain text and Markdown wrap at the edge of the window, at the last space that fits; a row that continues a line has no line number in front of it, and ↑ and ↓ move by rows on the screen. Code does not wrap: a long line scrolls sideways to keep the cursor in view, and Home brings the indent back into view. cat colours a text file in the terminal the same way, without opening it.

edit checks a JSON, JSONC, YAML or bash file after each change. In a Markdown file it checks every fenced code block whose fence names one of those languages: json , jsonc or json5 , yaml or yml , and bash , sh , shell , zsh or console , fenced with ``` or ~~~ . An error in a block is shown at its line in the whole document. Hide the map for everyone: ```json { "hide": ["archive.map"] } ``` An error shows in three places: A red ✗ in front of the line number of the line it is on. The character where the parser stopped, underlined in red. When the error is at the end of the line, a red block stands after its last character. The status bar : at the left, ✗ , the line and column, and what is wrong, such as ✗ 2:26 expected ',' or ']' after array element , followed by (+2 more) when there are more. It shows the error on the cursor's line when there is one, otherwise the first. At the right, the language with ✓ when the text is correct, ✗ when it has an error, and … while a check is still to come. Fix the error and the marks go away as you type. An empty JSON file is not an error: it is one you are starting. For bash the messages are those of EiN's shell, among them unexpected token 'fi' , unexpected end of file , and here-document not closed (wanted 'EOF') for a here-document that is never ended. A check that takes longer than 50 milliseconds waits until you stop typing for half a second, and the status bar shows … meanwhile, so a long file stays quick to type in. A text longer than 1,000,000 characters is not checked. Saving always checks the text as it is at that moment. The checks say whether a file can be read, not whether it does what you mean. For the file of your sidebar, ui-nav also checks the fields in it; see Your sidebar and top bar .

p.h: Edit in the terminal panel and over SSH
p.x: In the terminal panel: Alt + M gives the terminal the full height of the window, and the editor redraws to fill it. The editor also follows any other change of size. Alt + ← and Alt + → switch between terminal tabs, and Alt + ↑ and Alt + ↓ change the panel's height, so they never reach the editor. Move by word with Ctrl + ← and Ctrl + → . Hiding the panel, with Alt + T or a click outside it, leaves the editor open in its tab, unsaved changes and all. Warning Closing the editor's terminal tab, with its × or Alt + W , ends the editor without saving and without asking. So does closing an SSH connection. Over SSH, edit needs the shell you get by signing in: ssh -p 2222 anna@ein.local , then edit notes.md . A command sent along on the ssh line, even with ssh -t , runs without a terminal and stops with edit: not a terminal . SSH and SFTP has the rest.

p.h: Edit a file in the web interface
p.x: The Nodes page has a code editor for those who would rather stay in the browser. Nodes is under System in an administrator's sidebar. Other people do not have it in their sidebar, but anyone signed in can open it at /system/nodes (for example http://ein.local:8080/system/nodes ), and sees there what they may read. The Nodes page browses the whole tree. Right-click a text file here and choose Open to edit it. Open Nodes . It starts in your home folder, /home/<you> . Go to the folder that holds the file. Names that start with a dot, such as .bashrc , .config and .ui , are hidden: press Ctrl + H , or the eye button at the end of the address bar ("Show names starting with a dot (Ctrl+H)"), to show them. Right-click the file and choose Open . Double-clicking or Enter goes into the file instead, to the nodes it holds. The code editor opens in a dialog, titled with the file's name and with its path under it. Beside the title, badges name the language (such as JSON , SHELL or TEXT ), say READ-ONLY when you may not change the file, and UNSAVED once you have changed it. Make your change and choose Save , or press Ctrl + S ( ⌘ + S on a Mac). Save is greyed until there is something to save. Choose Close when you are done. If you close with unsaved changes, the dialog asks "Discard unsaved changes?": Keep editing takes you back, Discard closes without saving. Esc closes the dialog only when there is nothing unsaved. Raw , at the left under the editor, opens the file itself in a new browser tab. The code editor has line numbers, Ctrl + F to find, Ctrl + Z to undo and Tab to indent. It colours JSON, JavaScript, TypeScript, YAML, Markdown, HTML, CSS, XML and shell scripts, by the file's type first and then its extension. What Open does depends on the file: a text file opens in the code editor, a picture, video or recording in the viewer that the Archive adds, and any other file in a new browser tab. The Preview in the tool pane beside the list shows the first 64 KB of a text file without opening it. Where the code editor stops: What you see or want What to do "Too large to edit here (N KB). Open the raw file instead." The file is larger than 2 MB. Use the link to read it, or edit in the terminal to change it. A new file The Nodes page makes folders ( New directory ) but not files. Start the file with edit , or upload it. A check of your JSON or YAML The code editor colours but does not check. Open the file with edit to see errors as you type. A red box under the editor: "could not write …" The file was not saved: usually you may read it but not change it. Your text is still in the editor; copy it before you discard it.

edit in the terminal Code editor on the Nodes page Where Terminal panel, SSH login Browser, Nodes page New files Yes, on the first save No Checks JSON, YAML and bash Yes, as you type, and before saving No Colours By name, type or #! line By type, then name Largest file Any; no checks over 1,000,000 characters 2 MB Keys Its own , Ctrl on a Mac too A browser editor's, ⌘ on a Mac Files people often edit are ~/.bashrc ( The shell language ), ~/.ui/nav.json ( Your sidebar and top bar ) and the files listed in Configuration files . Every key in EiN is gathered in Keyboard shortcuts .

EiN runs its own SSH server, so you can reach it from your own computer: log in to the same shell as the terminal in the web interface, run one command from a script, and copy files in and out with SFTP, scp or a graphical file manager. This page is for anyone with an EiN account who wants to work from their own machine; going the other way, from EiN out to a NAS or another server, is on Reaching other machines .

What Example Where it comes from The host ein.local The name or address of the machine EiN runs on, the same one you open in the browser. The SSH port 2222 2222 unless your administrator chose another. Your account helen Your EiN username. Your e-mail address works too, where your account has one. Your secret your password The password you sign in to the web interface with, or a key once you have added one. SSH and SFTP share the one port. With the standard install it is set by EIN_SSH_PORT in .env on the machine EiN runs on; Ports, HTTPS and remote access explains how to change it and how to reach EiN from outside your home network. The setting CFG_SSH_PORT ( SSH port in Settings ) is the port EiN listens on inside its container, and takes effect the next time EiN starts. With the standard install leave it at 2222 : that is the port EIN_SSH_PORT is passed on to. The examples below use Helen Okafor's account helen on ein.local , port 2222 . Use your own.

On your own computer, open a terminal (on Windows, PowerShell has ssh built in) and run: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local The first time, ssh shows the key EiN's server identifies itself with and asks whether to trust it: The authenticity of host '[ein.local]:2222 ([192.168.1.20]:2222)' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:… Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? Type yes . Your computer remembers the key and does not ask again. To be sure it is your EiN answering, ask your administrator to compare the fingerprint; they see it in EiN's terminal with ssh-keygen -l -f /etc/ssh_host_key.pub . Enter your EiN password. You land in your home folder, /home/helen , at the same prompt as in a terminal tab.
