Everything on The terminal holds here too: your history, your ~/.bashrc , Tab completion and the same keys, and every command on Commands by task . The editor works as well ( The editor ). Two things belong to the browser alone: the pictures, videos and recordings cat shows, which over SSH print lines starting __IMG: , __VID: or __AUD: instead, and dropping files to upload them. To log out, type exit . Closing the window or losing the connection ends the shell too, and stops whatever command was running in it. Tip If your username is an e-mail address, give it with -l so the two @ do not get mixed up: ssh -p 2222 -l helen@example.com ein.local .

With a key you are no longer asked for your password. If you have no key yet, make one on your own computer with ssh-keygen and accept the defaults. Give EiN the public half of your key, once: # on your own computer ssh-copy-id -s -p 2222 helen@ein.local It asks for your EiN password this one time. The -s matters: it makes ssh-copy-id copy the key over SFTP. Without it, ssh-copy-id sends a script of Unix shell commands, which EiN's shell does not run. Log in as before. ssh and sftp now use the key and do not ask for the password. The key lives in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys in your EiN home, one key per line, as on any Linux server. You can add and remove lines there yourself. EiN reads lines starting with a key type such as ssh-ed25519 , ssh-rsa or ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 , and skips empty lines and lines starting with # . A line with options in front of the key ( command="…" , from="…" , no-pty and the like) is skipped entirely. EiN trusts the file only while nobody but you can change it, since anyone who could write to it could sign in as you. Your home, ~/.ssh and authorized_keys must each be owned by you (or the administrator), writable by neither group nor others nor by anyone else through an access list, and none of them may be a link. ssh-copy-id -s sets the modes for you.

Where ssh-copy-id is missing, as on Windows, add the key from EiN's terminal. Copy the contents of your public key file ( id_ed25519.pub in the .ssh folder of your home on your own computer), then: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/.ssh chmod 700 ~/.ssh echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA… helen@laptop' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys The two chmod lines are what make EiN trust the file. If key sign-in still asks for a password, check the modes with ls -la ~/.ssh : the folder should show rwx------ and the file rw------- .

p.h: Run one command at a time
p.x: Give ssh a command after the host and it runs just that one, prints the answer and exits with the command's exit status. That is what a script on your own computer wants: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'ls /archive/albums' ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l /archive/albums/cornwall-1968' | jq . The examples on this page use the Archive 's albums, which are there once it is installed; any folder you may read works the same way. With JSON_OUTPUT=1 commands answer in JSON instead of text (see Environment variables ). Each command gets a shell of its own, so cd does not carry over to the next ssh . Chain steps that belong together in one line: 'cd /archive/albums && ls' . The command runs without a terminal, so edit and anything else that needs one stops; log in with a shell for those. A command that would ask a question, such as a password or "Remove module?", stops instead with <name>: no terminal to answer on , followed by the option that gives the answer: mod remove --force , user-passwd --new-password , user-elevate --password . Commands sent this way are not added to your history. Errors arrive on the same stream as the output, so 2>/dev/null on your side does not separate them. Use the exit status to tell success from failure.

Any SFTP client works: the sftp command, a graphical client such as FileZilla or Cyberduck, or your file manager's "connect to server". Give it the protocol SFTP, the host, the port and your username, with your password or key. # on your own computer sftp -P 2222 helen@ein.local Note the capital -P for the port in sftp and scp , where ssh takes a lowercase -p . You start in your home folder. Then move around and copy as on any server: sftp> cd /archive/albums/cornwall-1968 sftp> get beach.jpg sftp> put harbour.jpg sftp> bye scp works the same way, one command at a time: # on your own computer scp -P 2222 harbour.jpg helen@ein.local:/home/helen/ scp -P 2222 -r helen@ein.local:/archive/albums/cornwall-1968 . scp from OpenSSH 9.0 and later copies over SFTP, which EiN serves. An older scp uses a different protocol that EiN does not speak; with OpenSSH 8.7 or 8.8 add -s , and with anything older use sftp . What you may see and change is decided by the same permissions as in the web interface: a folder you cannot open in the browser cannot be opened over SFTP either.

p.h: Bring in a large batch of photos
p.x: With the Archive installed, an export or a scanned box of tens of thousands of files is better copied over SFTP into your staging area than uploaded in the browser, and a photo copied into an album is taken in as an upload is. Copy files in over SFTP gives the folder to copy into and how to keep folder names for the grouping, and Zips what happens to a zip you copy in.

p.h: What the tree looks like over SFTP
p.x: EiN's tree holds more than an ordinary file system can show, so a few things look different. What belongs to a photo. A file can hold nodes of its own: with the Archive, a photo keeps its EXIF data, the faces found in it and its thumbnails. Those live in a hidden folder named after the photo with _ added: what belongs to beach.jpg is in beach.jpg_ . It is not listed, so copying an album with scp -r or get -r copies the photos without it. You can still go in by typing its name ( cd beach.jpg_ ), look around and download at any depth. Nothing in it can be changed over SFTP, and removing the photo removes it too. Modification times. A file's modification time is when its content last changed, not when EiN last added something about it. Backup tools therefore see a photo as unchanged while its faces or description are being worked out. put -p , scp -p and cp -p on a mount keep the time they set. Sizes. A file can be emptied by setting its size to 0. Any other change of size without writing the content is refused. Links. Softlinks, such as your favourites, or with the Archive an album's cover, a picture added to an album and a person tagged in a photo, appear as symbolic links, and following one takes you to what it points to. A recursive copy therefore copies the link, not what lies behind it. ln -s in sftp makes a new link, and removing a link removes only the link, never what it points to. Links explains what they are for. Warning Removing a file over SFTP deletes it for good, with everything that belongs to it. It does not go to your trash, as deleting in the web interface does. Removing a folder works only once it is empty.

With sshfs on Linux or macOS you can mount EiN's tree as a folder on your own computer and use any program on it: # on your own computer mkdir -p ~/ein sshfs -p 2222 -o transform_symlinks helen@ein.local:/ ~/ein -o transform_symlinks matters: a link's target is a path in EiN, such as /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield , and the option makes it point inside the mount rather than to the same path on your computer. fusermount -u ~/ein (on macOS umount ~/ein ) unmounts it. rsync works against such a mount. Over SSH directly, rsync helen@ein.local:… does not, because it needs an rsync program on EiN's side, and EiN's shell has none.

Every account with a password can sign in over SSH and SFTP; no group membership is needed. Being in the group ssh is about reaching other machines from EiN, not about reaching EiN (see Reaching other machines ). An account still waiting for a password, such as one imported without one, cannot sign in over SSH, with a key or with a password, nor anywhere else, until the administrator sets one for it. A disabled account cannot sign in at all, and disabling an account, or deleting it, ends the SSH and SFTP connections it already has open. Accounts and groups covers both. After five wrong passwords from one address, that address is refused for a while, starting at a second and doubling with each further failure up to 15 minutes; failures are forgotten an hour after the last one. Your ssh shows the same Permission denied as for a wrong password, so wait before trying again. EiN's SSH server offers logins, single commands and SFTP. It does not forward ports, X11 or your SSH agent.

What you see Why What to do Connection refused or a time-out Wrong port or host, or EiN is not running, or the port is not reachable from where you are. Check the port with your administrator; from outside your home network see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Permission denied (publickey,password) with the right password The account still waits for a password, is disabled, or your address is held back after failed attempts. Ask your administrator to set a password or enable the account, or wait and try again. The key is not used and you are asked for the password authorized_keys is missing, the key line has options in front, or the modes let others write. Check with ls -la ~/.ssh in EiN's terminal and fix with chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! EiN's server key is not the one your computer remembers, as after EiN was installed again from scratch. Ask your administrator whether that happened. If so, forget the old key with ssh-keygen -R "[ein.local]:2222" and connect again. ssh-copy-id fails without -s Without -s it runs Unix shell commands on EiN's side. Run it with -s . scp fails right away An scp older than OpenSSH 9.0 uses a protocol EiN does not speak. Add -s (OpenSSH 8.7 or 8.8), or use sftp . edit: not a terminal The command was sent along on the ssh line, without a shell. Log in with ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local and run it there. A copied folder lacks faces, EXIF and thumbnails What belongs to a photo is in its hidden _ folder, which recursive copies skip. Go into beach.jpg_ by name to fetch it; the photos themselves are complete. Writing in a folder is refused You may not change that folder, or it lies inside a photo's _ folder. See Permissions in depth , or copy into your home or staging area instead.

From EiN's shell you can log in to another machine, run a command there, copy files in and out, and put your key on it, with ssh , scp , ssh-copy-id and ssh-keygen . An administrator can also mount a folder of another machine into the tree over SFTP. This page is for members of the group ssh and for the administrator who lets them in. Everything here goes out from EiN to another machine. To come in to EiN from your own computer, see SSH and SFTP .

Membership of the group ssh , or the administrator account. ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id refuse everyone else: ssh: permission denied, you must be a member of group 'ssh' ssh-keygen works for everyone, since it only touches your own ~/.ssh . An account on the other machine , and that machine running an SSH server. A network path from the machine EiN runs on. The connection starts there, not on the computer your browser runs on. A host you can reach from your laptop is not always one EiN can reach. The commands work the way OpenSSH's do, and read and write the same files, but those files live in your home folder in EiN's tree ( /home/<you>/.ssh ), not on the machine EiN runs on. You can look at them with ls -la ~/.ssh and open them with edit .

The group ssh is made when EiN starts for the first time, with the title SSH users . It is empty until the administrator adds people. Open Settings → Groups and choose SSH users . The page says what the group is for: "Its members may use ssh, scp and ssh-copy-id to reach other machines." Under Members , tick the people who may use them. Ask them to sign out and in again. As the section says, changes apply the next time each person signs in. The same from the terminal, as the administrator: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator group-add-member ssh helen Take someone out again by unticking them, or with group-remove-member ssh helen . Accounts and groups covers groups in general. Warning A member of ssh can copy anything they may read in EiN to any machine they can log in to, and run commands on those machines from the machine EiN runs on. Add only people you would give that.

# in EiN's terminal ssh anna@nas.local The first time, ssh does not know the machine and asks: The authenticity of host 'nas.local' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:Xb7k2Qy9mWv0Tz4hJc1pLr8sNe5uGa3dFo6iKq2YwBM. Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? Compare the fingerprint with the one the other machine shows for its own key (on a Linux machine, ssh-keygen -l -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub there). Type yes , or paste the fingerprint, to go on; anything else is asked again, and no stops. The key is then written to ~/.ssh/known_hosts : Warning: Permanently added 'nas.local' (ED25519) to the list of known hosts. Next, ssh offers your keys. When none is accepted it asks for the password: anna@nas.local's password: You are then in the other machine's shell, in the same terminal tab. Everything you type goes to it, Ctrl + C included, and full-screen programs such as top or an editor draw as they would anywhere. Resizing the panel resizes the remote terminal. To leave, type exit or press Ctrl + D . If the other side stops answering, type ~ and . at the start of a line (after Enter ): that cuts the connection, and ssh prints Connection to anna@nas.local closed. Who you log in as: You type Remote user ssh anna@nas.local anna ssh -l anna nas.local anna ssh nas.local a User from ~/.ssh/config , else your EiN username The port is 22 unless you give another with -p : ssh -p 2222 backup.example.com . A host followed by :port is not understood; use -p . An IPv6 address may be bracketed: ssh anna@[fe80::1] .

p.h: Run one command on another machine
p.x: Put the command after the host. Everything after the host goes to the other machine, flags included: # in EiN's terminal ssh nas.local 'df -h' ssh anna@nas.local ls -la photos The output comes back to your terminal, and ssh ends with the remote command's exit status, so it works in scripts and with && . When the connection itself fails, the status is 255 . A single command runs without a terminal on the other side. Add -t for one that needs a terminal, such as top ; -tt asks for one even when ssh itself runs without a terminal. -T never asks for one. Input is passed along, so pipes work in both directions: # in EiN's terminal cat ~/notes.md | ssh anna@nas.local 'cat > notes-from-ein.md' ssh anna@nas.local 'cat photos/list.txt' | wc -l A plain ssh nas.local without a terminal (in a script, or with input from a pipe) warns Pseudo-terminal will not be allocated because stdin is not a terminal. and runs the remote shell on your input. -q leaves out that warning and the Connection to … closed. line.

p.h: Log in with a key instead of a password
p.x: A key saves you typing the password, and is required for a mount . Make a key pair: # in EiN's terminal ssh-keygen Generating public/private ed25519 key pair. Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase): Enter same passphrase again: Your identification has been saved in /home/helen/.ssh/id_ed25519 Your public key has been saved in /home/helen/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub The key fingerprint is: SHA256:4fJq0Vw2nRb8tYc6LmZ1xKd9sPe3uHa7gTo5iNy2QwE helen@ein A passphrase protects the private key; ssh and scp then ask for it when they use the key. Leave it empty for a key that scripts and mounts can use without anyone at the keyboard. Put the public key on the other machine: # in EiN's terminal ssh-copy-id anna@nas.local ssh-copy-id: INFO: Source of key(s) to be installed: "/home/helen/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub" anna@nas.local's password: Number of key(s) added: 1 Now try logging into the machine, with: "ssh 'anna@nas.local'" and check to make sure that only the key(s) you wanted were added. It logs in once with the password, adds the key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys there (making the folder and file when they are missing), and adds nothing when the key is already in the file. Run ssh anna@nas.local . It logs in without asking for the password. When you do not name a key, ssh and scp offer every key they find of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 , ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa and ~/.ssh/id_rsa , in that order; ssh-copy-id installs the first public key it finds of the same three. Name another with -i . Task Command An RSA key, for an old server ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "backup key" A key in a file of its own ssh-keygen -f ~/.ssh/nas -N '' Show a key's fingerprint ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Print the public key of a private key file ssh-keygen -y -f ~/.ssh/nas Show what ssh-copy-id would add ssh-copy-id -n anna@nas.local Install a named key on another port ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/nas.pub -p 2222 anna@backup.example.com Key types are ed25519 (the default), ecdsa (256, 384 or 521 bits) and rsa (3072 bits unless you give at least 2048 with -b ). The comment is <your username>@ein unless you give one with -C . A key named with -f goes into a folder that must exist already: plain ssh-keygen , or accepting a first host key, makes ~/.ssh for you. When the file exists, ssh-keygen asks Overwrite (y/n)? ; without a terminal it stops instead. See ssh-keygen and ssh-copy-id for every option.

scp copies between EiN's tree and one other machine. A path is remote when it has host: before any / , as in OpenSSH: anna@nas.local:photos/1968 . A remote path without a leading / starts in the remote user's home folder; anna@nas.local: alone is that home folder. Copy in from another machine: # in EiN's terminal scp anna@nas.local:photos/sailboat.jpg /home/helen/staging/files/inbox/ scp -r anna@nas.local:photos/1968 /home/helen/staging/files/inbox/ scp "anna@nas.local:photos/*.jpg" /home/helen/staging/files/inbox/ Quote a remote pattern so EiN's shell leaves it alone; the other machine's files are matched against it ( * , ? and […] , and a name starting with a dot only by a pattern that starts with one). When nothing matches, scp says No match . A file copied in is recorded the way an upload is: its size, checksum and type are worked out, and the installed modules' pipelines take it in from there. The examples copy into a staging folder, which the Archive gives you: with it installed, that is a way to bring a machine's photos into the archive; see Sorting in staging . Copy out to another machine: # in EiN's terminal scp -r /archive/albums/christmas-2019 anna@nas.local:backup/ Copying a folder out carries its files and folders only. What EiN keeps beside a photo (its thumbnails, the metadata read from it, its links to people and places) stays behind. Option What it does -r Copy folders and everything in them. Without it a folder is refused with not a regular file . -p Keep modes and modification times. -q No progress meter. The meter shows only in a terminal. -B Never ask for a password or passphrase. -P The port (capital P, unlike ssh ). -i , -F , -o A key, a config file, an option: as for ssh . scp ends with 0 when every file was copied and 1 when any failed; each failure is printed with the path. It does not copy between two remote machines ( copying between two remote hosts is not supported; copy into EiN first ), nor between two EiN paths (use cp ). All remote sources in one command must be on the same machine. See scp .

Settings you would otherwise type every time go in ~/.ssh/config , in OpenSSH's format: # ~/.ssh/config in your EiN home Host nas HostName 192.168.1.20 User anna IdentityFile ~/.ssh/nas Host backup HostName backup.example.com Port 2222 StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new Then ssh nas , scp -r nas:photos/1968 . and ssh-copy-id nas use them. Open the file with edit ~/.ssh/config . EiN acts on these keywords, from the file or from -o Keyword=value on the command line: Keyword What it sets HostName The machine to reach, when the name you type is an alias. Port The port. User The remote user. IdentityFile The key to use. ~/ is your EiN home. StrictHostKeyChecking What to do about an unknown host key: see the next section. BatchMode yes : never ask for anything. ConnectTimeout Seconds to connect and log in (15 unless set). ServerAliveInterval Seconds between keepalives (none unless set). PasswordAuthentication no : do not fall back to a password. As in OpenSSH, the first value found for a keyword wins, so put the specific Host blocks before a Host * block. Match with all , host , originalhost , user and localuser works, and so does Include . Other keywords in the file are skipped without a word; on the command line, -o with a keyword not in the table stops with unsupported option . -F <file> reads another file instead, and -F none reads none.

~/.ssh/known_hosts holds the key of each machine you have accepted, filed under its name, or under [name]:port for a port other than 22. Each EiN account has its own. What happens with a machine whose key is not in the file is up to StrictHostKeyChecking : Value Unknown host Changed key ask (default) Asks you; refuses when there is no terminal Refuses yes Refuses Refuses accept-new Adds the key without asking Refuses no Adds the key without asking Warns, then connects In a script, -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new saves the first question while still catching a key that changes later. When a machine's key has changed, ssh stops with a warning that starts WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! , prints the new fingerprint and the line numbers of the old entry, and ends with Host key verification failed. Either someone is between you and the machine, or the machine was reinstalled and has a new key. When you know it is the second, forget the old key and connect again to accept the new one: # in EiN's terminal ssh-keygen -R nas.local ssh-keygen -R '[backup.example.com]:2222' known_hosts lines written by OpenSSH work as they are, hashed names and @revoked included. @cert-authority lines are skipped: EiN does not check host certificates.

p.h: Mount a folder of another machine
p.x: The administrator can mount a folder of another machine into the tree over SFTP. Its files then show under the mount point and stay on the other machine. As the administrator, make a key without a passphrase and put it on the other machine. A mount logs in with a key only, since it reconnects on its own when nobody is there to type a password. If ~/.ssh does not exist yet, run ssh-keygen once without -f first, or mkdir ~/.ssh : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator ssh-keygen -f ~/.ssh/nas -N '' ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/nas.pub anna@nas.local Make the mount point, which must exist, and mount the folder on it: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mkdir -p /mnt/nas mount --save /mnt/nas sftp "host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos,key=/home/admin/.ssh/nas" mounted sftp at '/mnt/nas' (saved in /etc/fstab) The first mount from a terminal asks about an unknown host key as ssh does. --save writes the mount to /etc/fstab , so it is made again every time EiN starts. Run ls /mnt/nas to see the files, and mount alone to list every mount. Option What it is host The machine. Required. port The port; 22 unless set. user The remote user; the administrator's EiN username unless set. path The remote folder to mount. A relative one starts in the remote user's home. key The key file in EiN's tree. Without it, the default keys in ~/.ssh are tried. hostkey The host key's fingerprint ( SHA256:… ) to accept, instead of known_hosts . uid , gid The EiN user and group that own every file in the mount; the administrator's unless set. readonly Nothing in the mount can be changed from EiN. Options are key=value pairs separated by commas; values cannot hold a comma or = . How a mount behaves: Ownership comes from the mount, permissions from the other machine. Every file belongs to the mount's uid and gid , whoever owns it there; the permission bits are the other machine's. To let a group read the files, give the mount that gid and make the files group-readable there. Nothing is processed. The mount is a mirror: EiN makes no thumbnails, reads no dates and finds no faces in it. With the Archive installed, copy photos into staging to bring them into the archive. It reconnects on its own. When the other machine goes away, commands on the mount fail with the reason and the time of the next attempt ( next attempt in 8s ); the wait grows to at most a minute between attempts. At start-up it does not wait. EiN mounts the saved entries without waiting for the other machine, and connects once it answers. It asks nobody about host keys then, so a host must already be in known_hosts or be pinned with hostkey= . Pinning the fingerprint is the safer choice for a saved mount. To take a mount away, and out of /etc/fstab : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator unmount --save /mnt/nas mount -a makes every /etc/fstab entry that is not mounted yet. Only the administrator can mount and unmount; everyone can list mounts with mount . See mount and unmount .

The commands cover logging in, running commands, copying and keys. There is no port forwarding ( -L , -R , -D ), no agent and no agent forwarding, no jump hosts, and no sftp or rsync command; use scp , or a mount. ssh refuses flags it does not have with unknown option .

Message What it means and what to do permission denied, you must be a member of group 'ssh' Ask the administrator to add you to SSH users , then sign out and in. Could not resolve hostname nas.local: Name or service not known The machine EiN runs on does not know that name. Names ending in .local may not resolve where EiN runs; use the IP address, or set it as HostName in ~/.ssh/config . connect to host nas.local port 22: Connection refused Nothing listens on that port: the SSH server is off, or on another port ( -p ). connect to host nas.local port 22: Connection timed out No answer within 15 seconds: the machine is off, or a firewall is between it and EiN. anna@nas.local: Permission denied. The keys were refused and the password was wrong or not asked for. In a script there is nobody to ask, so only keys are tried: install one with ssh-copy-id . No ED25519 host key is known for nas.local … Connect once from an interactive shell to accept it. The host is unknown and there was nobody to ask (a script, BatchMode , or StrictHostKeyChecking yes ). Connect once from the terminal, or use -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new . WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! See Host keys . Warning: Identity file /home/helen/.ssh/nas not accessible: No such file or directory. The key named with -i or IdentityFile is not there. Check the path with ls ~/.ssh . Load key "/home/helen/.ssh/id_rsa": encrypted, and no one to ask for its passphrase A key with a passphrase and no .pub beside it, used where nobody can type it. Use a key without a passphrase for scripts and mounts. ssh-copy-id: no public key found in ~/.ssh; make one with ssh-keygen Run ssh-keygen first. ssh-copy-id: WARNING: All keys were skipped because they already exist on the remote system. Nothing to do: the key is installed. -f adds it again. mount: permission denied, only admin is allowed to mount Mounting is for the administrator.

SSH and SFTP : reaching EiN from your own computer. The terminal : where these commands run. Commands by task : the other commands, grouped by what they do. Accounts and groups : groups and how membership works. Ports, HTTPS and remote access : the network around the machine EiN runs on. Files and storage : where file contents are kept.

This page is for whoever installs and runs EiN on a machine: every option and variable the installer takes, what its checks measure, podman and Docker, what runs where once EiN is up, and how to run it day to day. Install EiN is the short path; read it first if you have not installed EiN yet.

The install is two scripts, run one after the other: Script Where it is What it does install.sh einhq.eu/install.sh , from the einhq.github.io repository Checks the machine. When nothing is missing, clones ein/deploy into ~/ein , or updates it there with git pull --ff-only , and runs ~/ein/setup.sh with your options. setup.sh ~/ein/setup.sh , from ein/deploy Brings ~/ein up to date from ein/deploy, writes ~/ein/.env the first time, downloads the images (or, from another source, fetches the sources into ~/ein/src and builds them), starts them with compose and waits for EiN to answer. Run again, it updates. Both run as your own user and need no root. Every option you give the installer after bash -s -- is passed on to setup.sh unchanged; the installer reads only --ems , --no-ems , --llm , --no-llm and --module itself, to choose which checks to run, and --source , to fetch ein/deploy from there. # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- --ems --module archive The installer's code runs from a function called on its last line, so a download cut short runs nothing.

These are setup.sh 's options, and so the installer's too. ~/ein/setup.sh --help lists them. Option What it does --ems Adds the media service, which the Archive needs: every media tool and model, in an image of about 30 GB. Sets EIN_EMS=1 in .env . See The media service . --no-ems Takes the media service out again: its container stops and is removed. Sets EIN_EMS=0 . Its data stays. --llm Adds the language model the Assistant answers with, Qwen3.5-4B in llama.cpp. Sets EIN_LLM=1 . --no-llm Takes the language model out again. Sets EIN_LLM=0 . The downloaded model stays in the data folder. --module <name> Adds a module's name to EIN_MODULES in .env , such as archive or assistant . EiN installs it at its start, with the modules it needs. Give it once for each module. A name is lower case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. --only <service> Updates one service, ein , ems , db or llm : downloads its newest image, or builds it from another source, and restarts it alone, leaving the others running ( db restarts EiN with it). It updates an installation, so it needs .env , and takes no other option. --source <address> Fetches the sources from this organisation instead of https://github.com/einhq , such as http://forge.example:3000/ein on a Forgejo or a Gitea. Sets EIN_SOURCE . See Where the sources come from . --db-dir <folder> Keeps the database in this folder, an absolute path, instead of the volume ein_db in the container engine's storage, such as on a faster disk. Sets EIN_DB_DIR . The folder must be empty or hold a database. -h , --help Prints the help and stops. An option other than --only is kept in .env once given, so a run without it keeps it: ~/ein/setup.sh alone runs with the options you chose before. Anything else stops setup.sh with setup.sh: unknown option <option> (--help lists them) . With no module installed, EiN is core alone: the tree, the shell, accounts and the frame of the web interface. --module only adds names; there is no option that takes one out. To stop EiN installing a module at its start, remove its name from EIN_MODULES in ~/ein/.env . Modules explains installing, updating and removing modules, which EiN does itself, not setup.sh .

Variables go in front of the command they are for. For the installer that is in front of bash , not in front of curl , which only downloads it: # on the machine that will run EiN curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | EIN_DATA=/srv/ein-data EIN_ENGINE=docker bash -s -- --ems Variable Read by Default What it does EIN_HOME install.sh ~/ein The folder EiN is installed in. Later, run setup.sh from there. EIN_DATA both, the first time ~/ein/data The folder for your files: originals, renditions, scratch space, the language model and the installed modules. Read only when .env is written; later runs keep the folder .env names. EIN_CHECK install.sh unset 1 runs the checks for the options given and stops, installing nothing. EIN_ENGINE setup.sh , the first time podman when installed, else Docker docker uses Docker even when podman is installed. Kept in .env , and later runs use that engine; given with the other engine later, it stops setup.sh . EIN_SOURCE_KEY both unset The token that reads --source 's repositories when they are private. Kept in .env with the source; a --source on another host without one drops it. EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT setup.sh , the first time 8080 , 2222 The ports on the machine for the web interface and for SSH and SFTP. Read only when .env is written. EIN_DATA is made into an absolute path when .env is written, so a relative folder is taken from where setup.sh runs, which is ~/ein .

--source names an organisation on GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea, not a repository: it must hold deploy , core , db , and ems and llm when you use those options, under those names. The installer fetches ein/deploy from there, and setup.sh keeps the address in .env as EIN_SOURCE , so later runs fetch from there too. EiN's, the database's and the media service's images are downloaded ready-made only from https://github.com/einhq , which publishes them; from any other organisation setup.sh builds them on the machine from its core , db and ems , since the published images have none of its own commits, and the media service's build takes about an hour. On GitHub the modules do not come from there: EiN looks for them in the places the setting CFG_MODULE_SOURCES names, https://github.com/einhq unless you change it. On a Forgejo or a Gitea, setup.sh sets CFG_MODULE_SOURCES in .env to the same organisation, and CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY to its token, so EiN installs its modules from there too.

The installer checks the machine before it touches anything. Each check prints one line: ok , low (the install goes on) or missing (nothing is installed). The thresholds depend on whether --ems is among the options, or EIN_EMS=1 is already in ~/ein/.env from an earlier install and --no-ems is not given; the same goes for --llm . Check ok low missing system Linux on x86-64 anything else; the installer stops at once podman podman installed and rootless podman run as root, or podman info fails neither podman nor Docker installed docker Docker installed, when podman is not compose podman compose version or docker compose version runs; under podman, with podman-compose, or with docker-compose and podman's socket answering it does not, or docker-compose under podman finds no socket network podman's older network backend, CNI, with its dnsname plugin; the line appears only under CNI CNI without dnsname : the containers cannot find each other by name git , curl , openssl installed not installed processor 2 physical cores; with --ems , 6 with --ems , 4 or 5 fewer than 2; with --ems , fewer than 4 memory 4 GB; with --ems , 30 GB with --ems , 15 to 29 GB less than 4 GB; with --ems , less than 15 GB disk 10 GB free; with --ems , 100 GB less graphics an NVIDIA card with driver 610 or newer no NVIDIA card, nvidia-smi cannot reach the driver, or an older driver card memory 15000 MB or more; the line is left out then less container GPU nvidia-container-toolkit 1.18 or newer, with its spec in /var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml no toolkit, an older one, no spec, or a spec made by hand in /etc/cdi ; podman before 5 with a spec it rejects; Docker before 28.2 archive the Archive module named, by --module archive or in .env , without the media service; the line appears only then The three before archive appear only with --ems or --llm , and none of them can stop the install: without a usable card the media service and the model run on the processor. With several cards, the line names the one with the most memory. The graphics card explains what each low line asks of you. A few details of how the checks count: Cores are physical cores, counted with lscpu across every socket, not threads. When lscpu gives nothing, the thread count stands in. Memory is the machine's total, rounded to whole GB. That is why the full threshold is 30 GB: a machine sold with 32 GB reports a little less. Disk is measured where your files go: on a later run the data folder .env names, which setup.sh keeps to, else EIN_DATA . When that folder does not exist yet, the check measures the nearest folder above it that does, and says so: (not made yet; measured on /home/anna) . The container engine is checked podman first. With both installed, the report shows podman's lines even when you set EIN_ENGINE=docker or .env keeps Docker: only setup.sh reads EIN_ENGINE . The images, a download's or build's scratch files and the database (unless you gave --db-dir ) live in the container engine's own storage, not in EIN_DATA . For rootless podman that is usually ~/.local/share/containers , for Docker /var/lib/docker . When that is another disk than your data folder, it needs room too: the disk check does not measure it. To run only the checks: # on the machine that will run EiN curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | EIN_CHECK=1 bash -s -- --ems --llm

You can do what the installer does yourself, for example to read setup.sh before it runs or to put EiN in another folder. This skips the machine checks. Clone ein/deploy into the folder EiN should live in: # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user git clone https://github.com/einhq/deploy.git ~/ein Run setup.sh from it with your options, and any variables in front: # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user EIN_DATA=/srv/ein-data ~/ein/setup.sh --ems --llm --module archive --module assistant setup.sh changes to its own folder first, so you can run it from anywhere. Each later run brings the folder up to date itself, with git pull --ff-only from the source, and runs the new setup.sh when that changed it; the installer with EIN_HOME set to the folder does the same.

EiN runs under either. At the install, setup.sh takes podman when the podman command exists, Docker when only docker does, and Docker when EIN_ENGINE=docker is set. It keeps the engine in .env as EIN_ENGINE , and every later run uses it, whichever else is installed. It then needs podman compose or docker compose to run, or stops with setup.sh: 'podman compose' does not run: install podman-compose (or docker-compose) for podman, or the compose plugin for Docker . The compose files are plain Compose Spec, so both read them alike. What differs: Rootless podman Docker Who runs the containers your user the Docker daemon; your user needs access to it, usually by being in the docker group, which nothing checks Who owns what EiN writes in EIN_DATA your user root, unless Docker itself runs rootless Where images and the database are ~/.local/share/containers , usually /var/lib/docker , usually The graphics card through the CDI spec; podman before 5 needs a fix first, see The graphics card through the CDI spec, from Docker Engine 28.2 After the machine restarts podman-restart.service starts the containers, once setup.sh or you have turned it on; see Start EiN when the machine boots Docker starts the containers again with its daemon, unless you stopped them A download's or build's scratch files setup.sh puts them in a tmp folder in podman's storage, as /tmp is often too small for the media service in Docker's own storage All data folders are mounted with z , which labels them for sharing between containers under SELinux and is ignored where SELinux is not on.

Each engine has its own images, containers and volumes, and so its own database. Install with one and keep to it. setup.sh keeps the engine it installed with in .env as EIN_ENGINE , and every later run uses it, whichever else is installed. Run with an EIN_ENGINE that names the other one, it stops before building anything: setup.sh: EiN here runs under docker (EIN_ENGINE in .env); under podman it would be a second, empty EiN beside it. Run ./setup.sh without EIN_ENGINE=podman An installation whose .env has no EIN_ENGINE line yet gets one at its next run, for the engine that run picks: podman when it is installed, unless EIN_ENGINE=docker is given. On a machine with both, run that first update of an installation made under Docker as EIN_ENGINE=docker ./setup.sh . Otherwise it is built again under podman, with podman's own empty database volume, and .env then keeps podman. While Docker's containers hold ports 8080 and 2222, setup.sh moves podman's EiN to the next free ports and writes them into .env ; with Docker's stopped, it takes 8080 and 2222. Either way an empty EiN starts on your data folder, with no account but admin and its first password. If that has happened, remove podman's containers, put EIN_ENGINE=docker in .env , put EIN_HTTP_PORT and EIN_SSH_PORT back if setup.sh moved them, and run setup.sh again: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose down ./setup.sh podman compose down keeps podman's volumes. The empty database volume it made is ein_db in podman's storage; remove it with podman volume rm ein_db once you are sure your EiN runs under Docker, as removing it under the engine your EiN actually uses deletes its database.

compose runs EiN as the project ein , from the files in ~/ein . Each service is a container of its own, and only ein is reached from other machines. Only EiN is reached from outside; the database, the media service and the language model answer EiN alone. Service Image Reached at Memory limit When ein ghcr.io/einhq/core , ready-made with the web interface; built from the core sources as localhost/ein-core from any other source ports 8080 (web) and 2222 (SSH and SFTP) on the machine EIN_MEMORY , 6g always db ghcr.io/einhq/db , PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB, pgvector and PostGIS, ready-made; built from the db sources as localhost/ein-db from any other source db:5432 , on the compose network only none always ems ghcr.io/einhq/ems , ready-made with every model; built from the ems sources as localhost/ein-ems from any other source ems:8181 , on the compose network only EMS_MEMORY , 16g with --ems llm llama.cpp's server, downloaded ready-made from ghcr.io llm:8190 , on the compose network only LLM_MEMORY , 10g with --llm Every service restarts by itself if it stops on its own: compose.yaml gives each restart: unless-stopped , and under podman compose.override.yaml makes it always , the policy podman starts again at boot. EiN starts once the database answers a query, and waits up to 60 seconds to stop cleanly, as does the media service. How EiN works says what each part is for; The media service , which the Archive needs, and The language model , which the Assistant uses, cover the two optional ones.

Path What it is From setup.sh the install and update script ein/deploy compose.yaml EiN and its database: what every install runs ein/deploy compose.ems.yaml the media service ein/deploy compose.llm.yaml the language model ein/deploy .env your options, settings and the passwords made at the install made by setup.sh compose.override.yaml the options in .env as services made by setup.sh src/ the sources: llm with its option, and core , db and ems from any source but GitHub's einhq , which are built made by setup.sh data/ the data folder, when EIN_DATA was left at its default made by setup.sh Leave the files from ein/deploy as they are: the installer and every run of setup.sh update the folder with git pull --ff-only , which stops when a file you changed is in its way. What you want to change goes in .env , which git ignores.

setup.sh makes these folders in EIN_DATA on every run. Both EiN and the media service mount the first four at the same paths, so a path EiN hands the media service is the path it opens. Folder Mounted at What it holds files /files ; read-only for the media service your originals old /old ; read-only for the media service older originals files-volatile /files-volatile thumbnails and other renditions, which EiN can make again files-tmp /files-tmp scratch space llm /models in the language model the model, downloaded at its first start, with --llm modules /modules-installed in EiN the installed modules, so they stay when EiN is updated or its container made again The database is not in the data folder. It is the volume ein_db in the container engine's storage, or the folder you gave --db-dir , which setup.sh gives to the database's own user before the database starts. Your data explains what to back up and why the database and the data folder belong together.

setup.sh writes ~/ein/.env the first time it runs, readable by your user only. It is three things at once: compose reads it for the values in the compose files, EiN and the media service get every line of it as their environment, and setup.sh keeps your options in it. A fresh one looks like this: # ~/ein/.env, as setup.sh writes it (without the comments it writes) COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME =ein EIN_ENGINE =podman EIN_EMS = 0 EIN_LLM = 0 EIN_GPU = 1 EIN_MODULES = "" EIN_DATA =/home/anna/ein/data POSTGRES_PASSWORD = 5 c0d2e7a91f84b36a0e9c4d17b2f6385e1a9c07d4b2e8f13 EMS_KEY =a83f19c26d0e47b5928c1f6e3d7a04b9c5e2f18d6a3b7c90 TZ =Europe/Stockholm INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD = 5 e0c9a2f71b3d846 EIN_BIND = 0.0 . 0.0 EIN_HTTP_PORT = 8080 EIN_SSH_PORT = 2222 # CFG_LLM_URL=https://api.openai.com # CFG_LLM_KEY= # CFG_LLM_PROVIDER=OpenAI # CFG_LLM_MODEL= EIN_SOURCE =https://github.com/einhq EIN_SOURCE_KEY = EIN_DB_DIR= setup.sh then sets the options you gave in their own lines: EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM , EIN_MODULES , EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY and EIN_DB_DIR . With a Forgejo or a Gitea as the source it adds CFG_MODULE_SOURCES , and CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY with a token. When a port is taken, it changes EIN_HTTP_PORT or EIN_SSH_PORT . Line What it is COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME ein , the compose project's name, which names its containers, network and volumes EIN_ENGINE podman or docker , the engine setup.sh picked at the install and keeps to; see Keep to one engine EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM 1 when the media service or the language model is installed; --ems , --no-ems , --llm and --no-llm set them EIN_GPU 1 when the first run found an NVIDIA card that nvidia-smi reaches, with a CDI spec in /var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml or /etc/cdi . Set only then; see The graphics card for a card added later EIN_MODULES the modules EiN installs at its start when they are missing, separated by spaces EIN_DATA the data folder POSTGRES_PASSWORD the database's password, random, made here EMS_KEY the key EiN and the media service share, random, made here TZ the machine's time zone, from timedatectl , /etc/timezone or UTC INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD the admin account's first password, random, made here. EiN takes it at its first start, and changing it later does nothing; setup.sh prints it at the end of every run until you delete the line, which you do once you have changed the password EIN_BIND the address the ports listen on: 0.0.0.0 for every address of the machine, 127.0.0.1 for the machine alone EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT the ports on the machine for the web interface and for SSH and SFTP; setup.sh moves one to the next free port when something else uses it while EiN is stopped CFG_LLM_… the Assistant's settings for a hosted language model instead of --llm ; see The language model EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY where the sources are cloned from, and the token that reads them when they are private; --source sets them, and one on another host empties the token unless EIN_SOURCE_KEY gives a new one EIN_DB_DIR the database's folder; empty keeps it in the volume ein_db . --db-dir sets it The database's password and the media service's key are kept nowhere else. Without them the database cannot be reached, so copy .env with every backup. Configuration files has every file EiN reads.

Every compose command reads compose.override.yaml beside compose.yaml by itself, so a plain podman compose up -d starts the same services setup.sh does. setup.sh writes it from .env and the container engine on every run; do not edit it, as the next run writes over it. Under podman, with the media service, the model and a card, it reads: # ~/ein/compose.override.yaml # Written by setup.sh from the options in .env and the container engine; edit those and run # setup.sh again. services: db: restart: always ein: environment: CFG_LLM_CARD: card restart: always ems: extends: { file: compose.ems.yaml , service: ems } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always llm: extends: { file: compose.llm.yaml , service: llm } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always Under Docker the restart: always lines are left out. CFG_LLM_CARD , the Assistant's setting, tells EiN whether the model runs on the card ( card ) or the processor ( cpu ).

To change Do this Add or remove the media service or the language model ~/ein/setup.sh --ems , --no-ems , --llm or --no-llm . This is also an update: see Updating . Add a module EiN installs at its start ~/ein/setup.sh --module <name> , or install it at once in Settings → Modules ; see Modules . A setting of EiN or a module ( CFG_… ) or of the media service ( EMS_… ) Add the line to ~/ein/.env , then run podman compose up -d in ~/ein . Most settings can instead be changed while EiN runs; see Configuration . The ports, or keep EiN to the machine Change EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT or EIN_BIND in .env , then podman compose up -d ; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . A container's memory limit Add EIN_MEMORY=8g , EMS_MEMORY=20g or LLM_MEMORY=12g to .env , then podman compose up -d ; see Performance and sizing . The language model's model or image LLM_GGUF_REPO , LLM_GGUF_FILE , LLM_IMAGE and LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB in .env ; see The language model . The data folder EIN_DATA in .env names it, but changing the line does not move your files; see Your data . When a change does not take, podman compose up -d --force-recreate makes every container again. With Docker, write docker compose for podman compose . Under podman-compose, a container that podman compose up -d makes again has no swap limit, which setup.sh gives each one: the media service's idle models then go to swap, and a search waits for them. ~/ein/setup.sh makes the containers again with it. Some of EiN's environment is set by compose.yaml and wins over a line in .env : POSTGRES_URL , CFG_HTTP_PORT and CFG_SSH_PORT (always 8080 and 2222 inside the container), the ems module's CFG_EMS_URL and CFG_EMS_KEY (from EMS_KEY ), and the folder paths. For the media service, EMS_PORT , EMS_KEY and EMS_ROOTS are set the same way.

Run compose from ~/ein , where it finds the project and its .env : # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose ps # what runs, and whether db and ems are healthy podman compose logs -f ein # follow EiN's log; ems, llm or db for the others podman compose restart ein # restart EiN alone podman compose stop # stop everything, keeping the containers podman compose start # start them again podman compose down # stop everything and remove the containers podman compose up -d # make the containers and start them With Docker, write docker compose instead. down keeps the database and the data folder; the containers are made again by the next up -d . It does remove the log, and with it a random admin password a new EiN printed there; the first password setup.sh made stays in .env as INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD . Warning podman compose down -v also deletes the volumes, and the volume ein_db is your database: every name, album, person, setting and account. Never add -v unless you mean to start from nothing. EiN is down while it restarts, and a restart takes longer when there is a module to install. Services and logs covers EiN's own logs and services, the ones inside the container, and Health and the dashboard what to watch.

p.h: Start EiN when the machine boots
p.x: Under Docker the containers come back with the Docker daemon, which starts with the machine on most systems, as long as you did not stop them yourself. When the daemon is not set to start at boot, setup.sh says so and lists sudo systemctl enable docker . Under podman, compose.override.yaml gives every service restart: always , the policy podman's own podman-restart.service starts at boot. Under rootless podman that is a service of your user's, which runs at boot only when your user lingers, that is, when its services run without you being signed in. At the end of every run, setup.sh turns on both where your user may, and says so: Enabled podman-restart.service, which starts EiN's containers at boot Enabled lingering for anna, so podman-restart.service runs at boot without a login EiN starts again when the machine does. What it may not do, it lists instead. Lingering often needs an administrator: EiN does not start again when the machine does until this has run: sudo loginctl enable-linger anna Until then, start it after a reboot with: cd /home/anna/ein && podman compose up -d Run what it lists once. After the next restart of the machine, podman compose ps in ~/ein shows the containers up.

Running the installer or ~/ein/setup.sh again is the update: ~/ein itself and the newest images of everything installed, downloaded and started again, every container made again from the new images, and a service you left out stopped and removed. ~/ein/setup.sh --only ein (or ems , db , llm ) updates one service and leaves the others running. Updating explains what it touches and what it keeps. There is no uninstall script. Your data says how to move EiN to another machine and how to remove it with its data.

The commands are written for podman; with Docker, write docker compose . Install EiN covers the messages of a first install, and Troubleshooting everything after. What you see What to do fatal: destination path '/home/anna/ein' already exists and is not an empty directory. ~/ein exists but is not a clone of ein/deploy. Move it away, or install elsewhere with EIN_HOME . git pull stops with a message about local changes, and nothing is installed, or setup.sh: /home/anna/ein could not be brought up to date from …: git status there says why A file from ein/deploy in ~/ein was changed. See what with git -C ~/ein status , put back the original with git -C ~/ein checkout -- <file> , and move the change into .env . setup.sh: EiN here runs under docker (EIN_ENGINE in .env); under podman it would be a second, empty EiN beside it. … EIN_ENGINE was given for the other engine. Run ./setup.sh without it; see Keep to one engine . setup.sh: EiN here runs under docker, which is not installed The engine .env keeps is gone from the machine. Install it again, or, to move to the other engine, see Keep to one engine : the database stays with the old one. setup.sh: neither podman nor Docker is installed Install one, with its compose. setup.sh: --module takes a module's name, such as archive: <name> A module is given by its name, such as archive , in lower case. A repository address goes to mod install in EiN's terminal instead. setup.sh: --module needs a name, such as archive --module was the last word of the command. Give the name after it. The download or the build stops with no space left on the device The container engine's storage is full, not necessarily your data folder. podman system df shows what takes the room there. podman compose up says a port is already in use Something else listens on the port .env names, perhaps an EiN under the other engine (see Keep to one engine ). Stop it, or choose other ports in .env . setup.sh moves EiN to the next free port by itself, but only while EiN is stopped. setup.sh: 'podman compose' runs docker-compose here, which needs podman's socket: … Turn on podman's socket for your user with systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket , or install podman-compose , and run setup.sh again. setup.sh: podman's networks here give no names, which EiN needs to find its database: … podman uses its older network backend, CNI, without the dnsname plugin. Install the package the message names and run setup.sh again. setup.sh: the database of an earlier install is here, the volume ein_db, and its password was in the .env that is gone. … .env is missing but the database is not. Put the old .env back, or, to start from nothing, remove the database with podman volume rm ein_db . setup.sh: EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/ in 10 minutes: podman compose logs ein Read the log it names. podman compose ps shows whether db became healthy; EiN does not start before it. EiN is up, but a new CFG_ line in .env has no effect Run podman compose up -d --force-recreate to make EiN's container again with it, and check that compose.yaml does not set the same variable itself (see Change the installation afterwards ). The Archive module needs the media service, which is not installed here: ./setup.sh --ems adds it. at the end The Archive is in EIN_MODULES but EIN_EMS is not 1 . Without the media service its photos, videos and documents are not analysed. Run ~/ein/setup.sh --ems . After an update, a module is still the old version setup.sh does not update modules. Use Update in Settings → Modules ; see Modules .

This page is for whoever runs EiN: which ports it listens on and how to change them, how to put it behind an HTTPS proxy, and how to reach it from outside your home safely. It assumes an installation made with the installer, in ~/ein ; Installing in detail explains that folder.

EiN publishes two ports, on every address of the machine it runs on: Port What answers Protocol 8080 the web interface, its files and its WebSocket plain HTTP 2222 the SSH and SFTP server SSH These are the ports setup.sh picks. When another program on the machine already listens on one, it takes the next free port instead, writes it to .env and says so ("Port 8080 is taken on this machine: EiN uses 8081 instead"). Nothing else is reachable from outside. The database, and the media service and the language model when they are installed, answer only EiN, on the containers' own network: no port of theirs is published on the machine. EiN itself serves plain HTTP only. It has no certificate and no HTTPS port of its own. On your home network that is fine; for anything else, an HTTPS proxy goes in front of it, as described in Put EiN behind HTTPS .

p.h: Change the ports or the address
p.x: Which ports the machine publishes, and on which address, are three lines in ~/ein/.env , written at the install: # in ~/ein/.env EIN_BIND = 0.0 . 0.0 EIN_HTTP_PORT = 8080 EIN_SSH_PORT = 2222 Line What it decides EIN_BIND The address of the machine the two ports are published on. 0.0.0.0 is every address; 127.0.0.1 keeps them to the machine itself. EIN_HTTP_PORT The port of the machine that reaches the web interface. EIN_SSH_PORT The port of the machine that reaches SSH and SFTP. To change one: Open ~/ein/.env in an editor and change the value. Apply it: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d # or: docker compose up -d Running ./setup.sh applies it too, and also updates EiN. Open EiN at the new address, such as http://ein.local:8443/ after EIN_HTTP_PORT=8443 . Inside its container EiN always listens on 8080 and 2222; these lines only change what the machine maps to them. Warning Leave the settings HTTP port and SSH port ( CFG_HTTP_PORT , CFG_SSH_PORT ) on Settings → System , in the Network group, as they are. They set the ports EiN listens on inside its container, and the machine forwards only 8080 and 2222 to it: a change there makes the web interface or SSH unreachable at the next start. Change .env instead. A few things to know: Ports below 1024 , such as 80 or 443, cannot be published by rootless podman unless the machine allows it (the kernel setting net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start ). Use a port above 1024, or let an HTTPS proxy take 443. EIN_BIND takes one address. With an address other than 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 , such as the machine's LAN address, EiN runs normally, but setup.sh waits for it at 127.0.0.1 , does not find it, and ends with "EiN did not answer" after ten minutes. The built-in guide shows SSH commands with port 2222 even when EIN_SSH_PORT maps another port, since that is the port EiN listens on. Tell your family the port you chose.

p.h: Open the ports in the firewall
p.x: When another computer on the network cannot open EiN while the machine itself can, the machine's firewall is the usual cause. Open the two ports there: # on the machine EiN runs on, with ufw (Ubuntu, Debian) sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp # on the machine EiN runs on, with firewalld (Fedora, RHEL) sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp --add-port=2222/tcp sudo firewall-cmd --reload Use your own port numbers if you changed them. Behind an HTTPS proxy on the same machine, open the proxy's port (443) instead, and not 8080. Note Docker opens the ports it publishes in the machine's packet filter itself, past rules set with ufw. A closed port in ufw does not keep EiN's ports off the network under Docker; EIN_BIND=127.0.0.1 does.

An HTTPS proxy is a web server that holds the certificate, answers browsers over HTTPS, and passes each request on to EiN over plain HTTP. You need one when: EiN is reached from outside your home, so that passwords and pictures do not cross the internet unencrypted; a phone should add EiN to its home screen as an app, which needs an address beginning with https:// (see EiN on a phone ); you want the browser's clipboard to work everywhere: over plain HTTP, copying a share link falls back to selecting the text.

p.h: What EiN needs from the proxy
p.x: Any proxy works, such as Caddy, nginx or Traefik, when it does the following: Requirement Why Serves EiN at the root of its own host name The interface asks for /file/… , /s/… and /__shell from the root. EiN cannot be served under a path such as https://example.org/ein/ . Passes WebSocket connections The whole interface talks to EiN over a WebSocket at /__shell , not only the terminal. Without it, pages do not load their contents. Sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https (or Forwarded: proto=https ) EiN then marks its sign-in cookie Secure , so the browser sends it only over HTTPS. Over plain HTTP the cookie is not marked, so the same EiN keeps working on the home network. Has no limit on the size of a request A file is uploaded in one request, whole: a long video is several gigabytes. Allows long requests and idle connections Uploads and downloads of large files take time, and the WebSocket can be quiet for minutes. When the proxy closes it, the interface reconnects after two seconds. The proxy keeps the Host header as the browser sent it; EiN uses whatever address the browser shows.

Caddy gets a certificate from Let's Encrypt by itself and does everything in the table without further settings. For a host name that points at your home, such as ein.wrenfield.example : # /etc/caddy/Caddyfile, on the machine EiN runs on ein.wrenfield.example { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 } Then reload Caddy ( sudo systemctl reload caddy ). For the certificate, Caddy must be reachable on ports 80 and 443 from the internet under that name. For HTTPS on the home network only, such as for ein.local , Caddy can sign its own certificate with tls internal . Browsers warn about it until Caddy's root certificate is installed on each device: # /etc/caddy/Caddyfile, on the machine EiN runs on ein.local { tls internal reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 }

nginx needs the WebSocket, the size limit and the timeouts set explicitly. With a certificate you have already obtained, for example with certbot: # /etc/nginx/conf.d/ein.conf, on the machine EiN runs on map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' close; } server { listen 443 ssl; server_name ein.wrenfield.example; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/ein.wrenfield.example/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/ein.wrenfield.example/privkey.pem; client_max_body_size 0; proxy_request_buffering off; proxy_buffering off; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_read_timeout 1h; proxy_send_timeout 1h; } } Check it with sudo nginx -t and reload with sudo systemctl reload nginx .

p.h: Keep EiN's own port to the machine
p.x: With the proxy on the same machine, nothing else needs to reach port 8080. Close it to the network: In ~/ein/.env , set EIN_BIND=127.0.0.1 . Apply it with podman compose up -d (or docker compose up -d ) in ~/ein . Open https://ein.wrenfield.example/ and sign in. This closes port 2222 to the network as well, since EIN_BIND applies to both. To keep SSH and SFTP reachable from other machines, leave EIN_BIND=0.0.0.0 and close 8080 in the firewall instead (under Docker, see the note in Open the ports in the firewall ). To check that the proxy passes everything, sign in, open a few pages, upload a file, and open the terminal with Alt + T (see The terminal ): each of these uses a different part of the table above.

p.h: Reach EiN from outside your home
p.x: There are three ways, from the least exposed to the most: Way What you set up Who can reach EiN A VPN, such as WireGuard or Tailscale The VPN on the machine and on each device. EiN needs no change: devices open its usual address over the VPN. Only devices on the VPN. An SSH tunnel through the machine The machine's own SSH server (not EiN's), reachable from outside. On the laptop: ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 you@your-home , then open http://localhost:8080/ . Only people with an account on the machine. A public HTTPS proxy A host name pointing at your home, ports 80 and 443 forwarded by your router to the proxy, and the proxy in front of EiN as above. Anyone on the internet can reach the sign-in page. EiN's own SSH server does not forward ports, so the tunnel goes through the machine's SSH server, not through port 2222. Only the public proxy makes share links work for people outside the family: a share link begins with the address the person who made it had open, so it reaches whoever can reach that address. Make links while EiN is open at its public address, not at http://ein.local:8080 .

p.h: Before you open EiN to the internet
p.x: Change the admin password if you have not: Install EiN shows how. Give every account a password of its own; Accounts and groups covers them. Leave visitors out. The setting Visitors may browse ( CFG_GUEST_BROWSING , under Settings → System ) is off after an install. Keep it off: on, anyone who reaches EiN can browse what is shared with visitors without signing in. Publish HTTPS only. Forward only the proxy's ports, never 8080, which is plain HTTP. Decide about SSH. Port 2222 is not needed for the web interface. Leave it closed to the internet and use SSH and SFTP over the VPN, or forward it on your router and have people sign in with keys; see SSH and SFTP .

p.h: How EiN slows down password guessing
p.x: EiN counts failed sign-ins, in the web interface and over SSH alike, per client address and per account: After five failures from one address, that address is refused without its password being checked, with "too many failed sign-ins; try again in" and the number of seconds. The wait starts at a second and doubles with each further failure, up to 15 minutes. After five failures at one account, each attempt at it waits, up to 10 seconds, but the account is never locked: someone guessing a password cannot lock its owner out. A failed attempt is answered no sooner than a second after it was made. Failures are forgotten an hour after the last one. Repeated failures are logged as "repeated failed sign-ins", with the address or account; Services and logs shows where to read them. EiN believes X-Forwarded-For and Forwarded only from a proxy whose connections reach it from the loopback address. When the proxy's connections reach EiN from another address, as can happen with the container's network in between, EiN sees every visitor as the proxy: who in EiN's terminal then shows the proxy's address for every web connection, and failures from one visitor hold back everyone who comes through the proxy. Run who once after setting up the proxy to see which you have. # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator who

p.h: SSH and SFTP from another network
p.x: SSH does not go through an HTTPS proxy. To reach EiN's SSH server from outside, forward a TCP port on your router to the machine's EIN_SSH_PORT , or connect over a VPN. Then connect with the host name and the port: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.wrenfield.example sftp -P 2222 helen@ein.wrenfield.example The server's host key is made at EiN's first start and kept in the tree as /etc/ssh_host_key , with its public half in /etc/ssh_host_key.pub , so it stays the same across updates and new containers. A client warns about a changed host key only when EiN was installed afresh. SSH and SFTP covers keys, clients and file managers.

What you see What to do EiN opens on the machine itself but not from another computer Open the ports in the machine's firewall, and check that EIN_BIND is 0.0.0.0 . Try the machine's IP address instead of a name ending in .local . compose up fails because the address or port is already in use Another program has the port. Choose another EIN_HTTP_PORT or EIN_SSH_PORT in .env , or stop that program. Behind the proxy, the page frame loads but stays empty, and the terminal does not connect The proxy does not pass WebSocket connections. Add the Upgrade and Connection headers (nginx) or check the proxy's WebSocket support. Uploads of large files fail behind the proxy, often with 413 The proxy limits the size of a request. In nginx, set client_max_body_size 0; . The terminal or the interface reconnects every minute behind the proxy The proxy closes idle connections. Raise its read timeout, such as proxy_read_timeout 1h; in nginx. Signing in works, but the next page asks you to sign in again The browser uses plain http:// while something in front of EiN sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https , so the cookie is marked Secure and the browser does not send it back. Open the https:// address, or have the proxy send the scheme the browser used. Signing in says "too many failed sign-ins" Wait the seconds it names. When it keeps happening to everyone behind your proxy, EiN sees all of them as one address: see How EiN slows down password guessing . After a change to HTTP port or SSH port on Settings → System , the web interface or SSH does not answer Reset the setting through the one that still answers: on the System tab, or with config unset CFG_HTTP_PORT (or CFG_SSH_PORT ) in EiN's terminal or over SSH. Then restart EiN with podman compose restart ein in ~/ein . A share link does not open for the person you sent it to It begins with the address you had open. Open EiN at its public address and make the link again; see Sharing . setup.sh ends with "EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:… " When EIN_BIND is an address other than 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 , this is expected and EiN is running: open it at that address. Otherwise read podman compose logs ein ; see Troubleshooting .

Installing in detail : the ~/ein folder, .env and setup.sh . Configuration : settings, .env and where each is kept. SSH and SFTP : signing in with keys, file managers and scp . EiN on a phone : what HTTPS gives a phone. Sharing : share links and who can open them. Settings : the reference entries for the ports and every other setting. Troubleshooting : when EiN does not start or answer at all.

This page is for the administrator who runs EiN: where its settings live, how to change them on the Settings page, in the terminal or in the installation's .env , which value wins when several are set, and what a change restarts. Every setting itself, with its default, is listed on Settings .

EiN has a single table of settings. Each one is an environment variable, such as CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS , with a plain name, a description, a kind of value and a default. Core declares some, and each module declares its own when it is installed, so the table grows and shrinks with the modules. Each setting belongs to one of two scopes: Scope Who changes it Where Named System An administrator, for everyone Settings → System , or config set CFG_… Personal Each person, for themselves Profile → Preferences , or config set CFG_USER_… , and HISTSIZE This page is about the system settings. Personal ones, such as Shell history length , or Seconds per slide with the Archive installed, are described in Your profile, favourites and trash . Apart from the settings, the installation has its own environment in .env , in the folder EiN was installed in ( ~/ein with the installer). It holds what is fixed before EiN starts: where your files are, which ports the machine publishes, the database password. It can also give a setting its starting value. Set a value in the deployment explains how the two meet.

p.h: Change a setting on the Settings page
p.x: Sign in as an administrator. Accounts and groups explains who that is. Choose Settings in the sidebar, under System . The page opens on the System tab. Pick a category in the Categories list on the left, or type in Find a setting to search names, descriptions, modules and keys across every category. Change the value in the setting's field. Save change and Cancel appear under it. Choose Save change . A line under the setting says what was restarted, for example "Restarted trash-purger.", or why nothing could be. Settings are browsed by category, and each says where its value comes from and which module it belongs to. Each setting is saved on its own; there is no button that saves the page. The other tabs of Settings hold accounts, groups and modules: Accounts and groups covers Users , Groups and Permissions , and Modules covers Modules . The Permissions tab shows some of the same settings as System , such as the default sharing, and a change made on either shows on both. The control depends on the kind of value: a switch shows On or Off , a choice is a list, a number has arrows, a person or a group is picked by name, and a permission mode is a choice of None, View or Edit for the owner, the group and everyone else. On a narrow screen the categories are a Category list above the settings instead.

p.h: Read where a value comes from
p.x: Under each setting's description, a badge says where the value in force comes from. A second badge names the module the setting belongs to, and settings that restart a service say which, as in "Restarts trash-purger". Badge What it means Default Nobody has set it: the setting's own default is in force. From deployment The installation's environment sets it, usually .env . From module , such as From archive An installed module chose the value, such as the Archive naming its search parser. Set here An administrator saved it on this page or with config set . Not set A key to another service that nobody has given. Default , From deployment and From module can all be overridden: save a value and the badge becomes Set here . A setting that is set here shows Restore inherited value instead of Save change . Choose it to remove your value, and the setting falls back to what it would be without it: the module's choice, the deployment's value or the default, in that order. Overrides only limits the page to the settings set here, with their number on the button. It is the quickest way to see what has been changed on this installation. When nothing matches a search, Clear filters empties the search and turns Overrides only off. Some settings mean something when they are empty. For those, the description ends with what an empty value does, such as "Currently: the person who creates it.", and an empty text field says what it means, such as "Empty means no model".

p.h: Give a key to another service
p.x: A few settings are keys that EiN sends to another service: the access tokens for private module sources, and, with the modules that bring them, the media service's key and a hosted language model's key. Their names end in _KEY , and they are kept apart from every other setting: Nobody can read a key back, administrators included. The field is empty, with "Not set" or "Set — type a new one to replace it" in it, and the badge says whether the key comes from the deployment or was set here. To replace a key, type the new one and choose Save change . The field empties again once it is saved. A key is in no shell's environment, and EiN sends it only to the address set for its service. If a shell gives that address another value for one command, the request goes without the key. Warning With the ems module installed, the media service's key, CFG_EMS_KEY , must be one the media service accepts. The installer gives both sides the same key from .env . A different key saved here leaves EiN unable to reach the media service; Restore inherited value brings back the deployment's. The media service explains the keys.

A setting that names the services that read it when they start restarts them when you save it, so the change takes effect without restarting EiN. The setting's card lists those services before you save, and the line under it confirms what was restarted afterwards. A setting that names no service restarts nothing. Work already running is not lost: it is picked up again when the service is back. Only services that are running are restarted. A service you stopped stays stopped, and reads the new value when you start it. Services and logs shows how. If a restart fails, the value is still saved, and a red message says "Could not restart" with the service's name and the reason. The service keeps running on the old value until it starts again. The ports, HTTP port and SSH port , restart nothing: restarting the web server from a web page would drop the connection you are using. They take effect the next time EiN starts, and the page says so. Worker backlog rotation (ms) is read by each pipeline worker as it starts, so the services that run one must be restarted by hand. Settings that are policy, such as the default sharing or Visitors may browse , are read each time they are applied, so they take effect at once and restart nothing. Some settings that name no service are read by the commands a pipeline runs, in the environment of the service that runs them, such as the Archive's Face match threshold . Nothing restarts for them: the service's shell reads the settings again before its next command, so they take effect from the next step it runs, such as the next picture it looks for faces in. A step already running finishes with the value it started with. Warning With the installer's setup, EiN listens on 8080 and 2222 inside its container, and the machine publishes those two. Changing HTTP port or SSH port on the Settings page moves EiN off them at its next start, and the web interface or SSH becomes unreachable. Change the published ports in .env instead, as Ports, HTTPS and remote access describes. A terminal that is open when a setting changes reads the settings again before its next command, so echo shows the new value. A command already running keeps the value it started with.

The config command does everything the Settings page does. Everyone signed in can list and read settings, and change their own; only an administrator can change a system setting. # in EiN's terminal config list # every setting, with where its value comes from config list --scope system # the system settings only; --scope user for your own config get CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS # the value in force config set CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 14 config unset CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS config list prints a setting per line: its name, a tab, its value, and in brackets where the value comes from.
