A default has no mark. A key shows (set) in place of its value, or nothing when it is not set. On an EiN with the Archive, the Assistant and the ems module installed, it starts like this: CFG_EMS_KEY (set) (environment) CFG_HTTP_PORT 8080 (environment) CFG_COMMAND_FINDER assistant-commands (module assistant) CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL llm-chat (module assistant) CFG_SEARCH_PARSER archive-parse (module archive) CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER ems-text-embed (module ems) CFG_SESSION_REAP_INTERVAL 3600 CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 14 (system) The marks match the badges on the Settings page: (system) is Set here , (environment) is From deployment , (module archive) is From archive , and (user) is a person's own value. config set answers with the new value and what it restarted, and config unset with the value it falls back to and where that comes from: $ config set CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 14 CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS = 14 Restarted: trash-purger $ config unset CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS reset to 30 (default) Restarted: trash-purger For a port, the answer ends with the note that it takes effect the next time the server starts. For a key, config set answers only CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY set , without the value. The command line you typed is kept in your shell history like any other; start it with a space to leave it out. A value of the wrong kind is refused before anything is written: Kind What config set accepts Refused, for example number digits, with an optional minus and decimals config set: CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS: expected a number, got 'four' on or off true or false expected 'true' or 'false', got 'yes' choice one of the setting's choices expected one of en, sv, got 'english' permission mode an octal mode such as 0750 expected an octal mode such as 0750, got 'rwxr-x---' person or group a name of letters, digits, . , _ and - 'Anna Andersson' is not a valid user name text or key anything An empty value is refused too, with value must not be empty , except for the settings where empty means something. To return a setting to its inherited value, use config unset , not an empty config set . Other refusals: config set: unknown setting 'CFG_TRASH_DAYS' : no installed part of EiN declares that name. config list shows the names there are; a module's settings exist only while the module is installed. config set: 'CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS' is a system setting and needs administrator rights : you are signed in as someone else. Accounts and groups explains how a member of the sudo group becomes the administrator in a terminal with admin . A value with spaces, such as two module sources, is best quoted: config set CFG_MODULE_SOURCES 'https://github.com/einhq https://forge.example:3000/family' . With JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front, config list , config get , config set and config unset answer in JSON: config list and config get with each setting's label, description, value and source, config set and config unset with the value and what was restarted. Core commands has the full entries.

p.h: Set a value in the deployment
p.x: .env is EiN's environment. Every CFG_… line in it reaches EiN when its container starts, and appears on the Settings page as From deployment . Use it for a value that belongs with the installation rather than with the running system, such as a hosted language model's address and key. On the machine EiN runs on, open .env in the folder EiN was installed in. Add or change the line: # ~/ein/.env, on the machine EiN runs on CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS = 14 Apply it. This makes EiN's container again with the new environment: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d # or: docker compose up -d Under podman-compose, a container made again this way has no swap limit, which setup.sh gives each one; ./setup.sh makes the containers again with it. Reload the Settings page. The setting shows the value with From deployment . Running ./setup.sh applies .env too, but it also downloads the newest images: it is an update. Updating explains it. A value in .env does not always win: A value set here wins over it. If the setting shows Set here , the line in .env has no visible effect. Choose Restore inherited value , or run config unset , to let it through. A module's choice wins over it. An installed module may name commands for the Search settings: the Archive names CFG_SEARCH_PARSER , the Assistant CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL and CFG_COMMAND_FINDER , and the ems module CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER . To use another one, set it on the Settings page. Some settings are fixed by the installation's compose.yaml , which wins over .env : CFG_HTTP_PORT , CFG_SSH_PORT , and the ems module's CFG_EMS_URL and CFG_EMS_KEY . A line for them in .env changes nothing. The published ports are EIN_HTTP_PORT and EIN_SSH_PORT instead, and the media service's key is EMS_KEY , which goes to both sides. The Assistant's CFG_LLM_URL is read from .env and defaults to the language model the installer adds. An empty line sets nothing. CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL= in .env is the same as leaving the line out. The rest of .env is not settings but the installation's own variables: EIN_DATA , EIN_BIND , EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT , EIN_MODULES , EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM , EIN_GPU , EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY , EIN_DB_DIR , EIN_ENGINE , COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME , TZ and the passwords. Installing in detail explains each, and Environment variables lists every variable EiN reads besides its settings. With the media service installed, its settings are EMS_… lines in the same file; The media service describes them. Note .env holds the database password and the media service's key, and nothing else keeps them. Keep a copy of it with your backups; Your data: backup, moving and removing says what else to keep.

A setting can be given a value in up to four places. The narrowest wins: Order Layer File in EiN's tree Badge 1, wins A person's own value, for personal settings ~/.config Your setting 2 The administrator's value /etc/config Set here 3 A module's choice /etc/config.d/<module> From module 4 The deployment's environment /etc/environment From deployment 5 The setting's default none Default A personal setting comes from ~/.config , the deployment or its default: neither a module nor /etc/config sets it. A system setting is never read from anyone's ~/.config . The highest layer that sets a value wins, and each scope skips the layers that are not its own. Every shell in EiN, the services' shells included, sources these files at its start, /etc/environment first and ~/.config last, so each is exported over the one before. That is why every setting is an ordinary environment variable in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal echo $CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS cat /etc/config The files are ordinary shell files in EiN's tree, kept in the database, so they survive a restart. Each line is an assignment such as export CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS='14' : /etc/environment is written again at every start, from the CFG_… variables EiN's container was started with. A value the deployment stops passing is gone from it. It never holds a key. /etc/config.d/<module> is a module's etc/config , linked there when the module is set up and gone when it is removed. /etc/config is what Save change and config set write for a system setting. Everyone can read it. /etc/keys holds the keys saved here. Only the administrator can read it, and no shell sources it. A key from the deployment stays in EiN's own process and is never written to a file. Configuration files lists these and EiN's other files.

p.h: Edit the settings file by hand
p.x: An administrator can open /etc/config in the editor, edit /etc/config , and add, change or remove export lines. Two things differ from the Settings page: Nothing checks the values. A number written as four reaches the service that reads it as it is. Nothing is restarted. Policy settings apply at once, and settings read by the commands a pipeline runs from the next step; a setting a service reads at its start applies when that service restarts, from Services and logs or the next time EiN starts. A line for a name no part of EiN declares is exported into every shell but shows nowhere. Prefer the Settings page or config set for anything listed there.

p.h: When a change does not take effect
p.x: The value in .env does not show. The setting is Set here or chosen by a module, both of which win; or it is one of the values compose.yaml fixes; or EiN's container was not made again. See Set a value in the deployment . The page says the value is saved, but the service behaves as before. Look for a red "Could not restart" message under the setting, or check the service on Services and logs . A stopped service reads the value when it starts. The terminal shows the old value. A command that was already running when you saved keeps the value it started with; the next command reads the new one. A port change did nothing. Ports take effect when EiN starts again, and with the installer's setup they should be changed in .env , not here. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . A module's settings are missing. They exist only while the module is installed and working; check it on Settings → Modules , as Modules describes. Something else is wrong. Troubleshooting goes through the common problems.

Settings : every setting, with its default, kind and what it restarts. Environment variables : the variables EiN reads that are not settings. Your profile, favourites and trash : personal preferences. Accounts and groups : the Users , Groups and Permissions tabs, and the default sharing. Modules : the Modules tab, module sources and their tokens. Processing and pipelines and Performance and sizing : what the Processing settings do in practice. The media service and The language model : their addresses and keys.

Modules decide what your EiN is for: the Archive, the assistant and the client for the media service are each a module. This page is for the administrator: which modules there are and what they need, how to install, update and remove them on Settings → Modules or in the terminal, how to keep one to some groups, how to see whether each one works, and what to do when one does not.

EiN without modules is the tree, the shell, accounts and the frame of the web interface. Every page for photos, people and places, the chat, and the work done on what you upload comes from a module. How EiN works explains what a module is made of. Each module has a section of its own in this documentation, under Modules ; skip the sections of modules you have not installed. The published modules are the repositories named module-<name> in the einhq organisation on GitHub: Module What it gives you What it needs archive The Archive: albums, media, people and the family tree, locations, devices and tracks, staging, and the search that finds things among them The ems module, installed along with it, and the media service to do its work assistant Chat : the assistant that answers questions by running EiN's commands for you A language model , either the installer's --llm or a hosted one ems EiN's side of the media service: the client the Archive reaches it through, its health and the graphics card's readings on the Dashboard The media service A module needs only what its manifest names as dependencies; EiN installs those with it. A service that runs beside EiN, such as the media service or the language model, is no module: the installer adds it (see Installing in detail ). Installing archive without the media service gives no error, only a reminder from the installer and setup.sh when EIN_MODULES names it, but nothing you upload gets thumbnails, dates, faces or searchable text until the media service is there.

Open Settings in the sidebar and choose the Modules tab. Everyone who is signed in has this tab; for anyone but an administrator it is the only one, and it shows the modules without the buttons that change them. Each installed module, whether it works, and everything it brings, in one place. The list at the left holds every installed module with its description. A module that works shows its version at the right; one that does not shows a badge instead and is listed first: Badge What it means Active Set up since EiN started: its commands are on the path, its services are registered and its pages are built. Setup failed EiN tried to set it up and refused or failed; the module's panel says why. Not set up Installed, but not set up since EiN started: its commands are not on the path and its services are not running. Type in the filter box to narrow the list by name or description. Show only active modules , at the foot of the list, leaves out the ones that do not work; your browser remembers the switch. Choose a module to open its panel. At the top it shows the module's name, its version and the core API it is written for ( version 0.1.0 · core API ^0.6.0 ), where it is installed ( /usr/modules/archive ), when it was set up, and its state. Reference and guide opens the module's own page in Documentation , with its pages in this guide and every command, setting and node type it brings. Below are tabs, each with a count; About and Dependencies are always there, and another tab the module has nothing for is left out: Tab What it shows About The introduction from the module's guide, or "It has no guide." Dependencies The modules it needs ( It needs ) and the modules that need it ( Needs it ), with the versions accepted, the version installed and each one's state, or Not installed Services Its background services, their state now and how long they have been up. They are started and stopped on the Dashboard 's services tab. Pages The addresses of the pages it adds; one without a parameter is a link to the page Commands Its commands; each opens to its help Settings Its settings with their values, each marked personal or system ; a row opens to the setting's description and, if you may change it, its control Node types The kinds of node it defines, with how many of each exist A module's system settings are the same ones the System tab lists, and its personal ones are those on Profile → Preferences ; they save the same way: Configuration explains where a value comes from and what a change restarts. The About EiN dialog, in the menu under your picture, also lists the installed modules, with a setup failed badge on any that did not set up. In the terminal, mod list gives the same list: # in EiN's terminal mod list archive (0.1.0) assistant (0.1.0) ems (0.1.0) A module that does not work has [setup failed] or [not set up] after its version. mod list --long adds each one's description, the problems its setup ran into, its path, the repository and commit it was installed from, and its commands and services. mod info archive shows one module's manifest: its version, core API, the modules it requires and whether they are installed, what it exports, and the modules that use it.

You need to be an administrator: signed in as admin , or in admin mode . EiN needs to reach GitHub, or whichever forge holds the module. Open Settings → Modules . Choose the Published modules button beside the filter box, the box with an arrow. The panel at the right lists the published modules, each with its version, its description and its repository. Choose Install on the module you want. EiN asks who the module is for. Keep Everyone , or choose Only some groups and the groups (see Keep a module to some groups ), then choose Install and the module's name. The published modules and what is installed of each; on this EiN all three came with the deployment, so none offers Install. EiN fetches the module, checks it, installs any module it needs that is missing, sets them all up and starts their services. Under the module it then says "Installed", or, when it brought dependencies along, for example "Installed, with ems". Its entries in the sidebar and its pages appear without reloading the page. Each published module carries a badge for what is installed of it: Badge What it means none Not installed; the button reads Install . Installed Installed from this repository, at the commit its default branch has now. Update available Installed from this repository, and its default branch has moved on; the button reads Update . Hold the pointer over the badge to see both commits. Installed from elsewhere A module of this name is installed from another repository. The deployment's The module comes with the deployment itself (see Modules the deployment provides ) and cannot be installed over. A module written for a different core API says "Needs core API ^0.6.0, which this EiN does not provide." (with its own range), and its button is greyed out. Refresh asks the sources again. In the terminal, mod search lists the same, and mod install installs: # in EiN's terminal mod search archive 0.1.0 EiN module: the family archive, with people, media, places and staging https://github.com/einhq/module-archive assistant 0.1.0 [installed] EiN module: the chat that answers questions about the archive https://github.com/einhq/module-assistant ems 0.1.0 EiN module: the client for EMS, the media service https://github.com/einhq/module-ems Words after mod search narrow the list to modules whose name or description holds them all. # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install archive Fetching https://github.com/einhq/module-archive at main (5e1c07a42)... archive needs ems ^0.1.0, which is not installed Fetching https://github.com/einhq/module-ems at main (b83d2f610)... Installed ems 0.1.0 from https://github.com/einhq/module-ems at b83d2f610 Installed archive 0.1.0 from https://github.com/einhq/module-archive at 5e1c07a42 Setting up module 'ems'... A line follows for each step of each setup, ending in Module 'archive' setup complete and the services it started. mod install takes several modules at once, and each can be named in three ways: You write What is installed archive module-archive from the first module source that has it, at its default branch https://github.com/einhq/module-archive That repository, at its default branch archive@v0.1.0 , …/module-archive@<commit> That branch or tag, or a commit by its id, whole or its first seven characters or more, which EiN records whole The reference lists its options.

The installer's --module option names a module for EiN to install at its start, with the modules it needs: # on the machine EiN runs on ~/ein/setup.sh --module assistant setup.sh adds the name to EIN_MODULES in ~/ein/.env and, as on every run, fetches the newest sources, builds and starts EiN again, which installs every module named there that is missing. One installed already is left as it is, at whatever version, without asking GitHub, so a restart never updates a module. If EiN cannot download one at its start, its log says some of INSTALL_MODULES could not be installed; continuing boot and EiN starts without it; install it from Settings → Modules once EiN is up. Installing in detail has the other options.

Updating EiN with setup.sh does not update its modules. Update them here instead. On Settings → Modules , open Published modules and choose Update on a module marked Update available . Or open the module's panel. A module installed from its repository has a section Installed from its repository , saying which repository and commit it came from and when, with Update and Remove . Update there fetches the newest commit of the branch it was installed from, or the same tag again for one installed at a tag. One installed at a commit stays there, and its panel offers no Update . It answers Updated , or Up to date when there was nothing newer. In the terminal, mod install archive updates an installed module. The same commit again is left alone: archive is installed at 5e1c07a42 (main) already . An update installs what the new version needs and is missing. It is refused when an installed module depends on this one and does not accept the new version; the message names them, for example letters needs archive ^0.1.0, and this is archive 0.2.0: --force installs it all the same . mod install --force updates anyway, and also fetches again a commit that is installed already. After the update EiN sets the module up again and restarts its services. Every module that depends on it, directly or through another, is set up again too, and its running services restarted, so nothing keeps running the code that was replaced. The new version takes the old one's place in a single step: the module's folder always holds one whole version. To pin a module to a version, install it at a tag, such as mod install archive@v0.1.0 where its repository has that tag, or at a commit, such as mod install archive@463a92f . Its panel's Update then keeps it at the tag, and a module installed at a commit has no Update there. The published modules always compare with the default branch, so they may offer Update for it, which installs the default branch, as mod install archive without a ref does.

p.h: Keep a module to some groups
p.x: A module is everyone's until you keep it to some groups. Then only the members of those groups, and administrators, have it: its commands, its entries in the sidebar and the top bar, its pages, its personal settings, and the module itself on Settings → Modules and on the Docs page's reference. For everyone else it is as if it were not installed. On Settings → Modules , open the module. Its section Available to says who has it. Choose the groups in the box and choose Save ; empty the box to make it everyone's again. When you install a module there, Install asks first who it is for: Everyone , or Only some groups with the groups to choose. The modules it needs and brings along stay everyone's, and an Update asks nothing and keeps whom the module was for. In the terminal, mod groups says who a module is for and changes it, and mod install --groups installs a module for some groups from the start: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod groups assistant family mod groups assistant family # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod groups assistant --everyone mod install -- groups family,friends assistant mod groups names groups as group-list prints them, and refuses one there is not: mod groups: no group famly . Someone outside the groups who types one of the module's commands gets command not found , and one who names it by its path is refused: /usr/modules/assistant/bin/assistant-ask: permission denied: module assistant is kept to groups you are not in . The module's services and pipelines go on working for the whole archive, as they run as the administrator. Groups are read when someone signs in, so a person added to a group gets its modules the next time they sign in. A terminal open already picks up a change to who a module is for at its next command. When a module that is everyone's needs the one you keep to groups, mod groups and the panel warn that what it runs of that module fails for anyone outside them, for example mod groups: archive depends on ems and is everyone's: what it runs of ems fails for anyone outside family . Keep both to the same groups, or neither. Behind this, the groups are in /etc/modules/<module>.groups , one name per line. Setting the module up puts its commands on the path in /etc/bashrc.d/<group> for each group and for admin , instead of in /etc/bashrc , and its sidebar entries in /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.d/<module>.json instead of in /etc/ui/nav.d . Removing the module forgets its groups. Configuration files lists these files.

Open Settings → Modules and choose the module. In Installed from its repository , choose Remove . EiN says what goes: "Removing assistant stops its services and takes its commands, pages and files away. What it made in the archive stays." When other modules need it, it adds which ones and that they will not work without it. Choose Remove assistant to go ahead, or Cancel . In the terminal, mod remove asks first, and --force skips the question: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod remove assistant Remove module 'assistant' (0.1.0)? (y/N) y Where no one can answer, as in ssh host 'mod remove assistant' or a script, it does not ask: it stops with mod-remove: no terminal to answer on; add --force , and removes nothing. Removing stops and unregisters the module's services, takes its commands off the path, retires its pipelines, its sidebar entries and its documentation, rebuilds the pages and deletes its folder. Some things stay, so that installing it again finds them as they were: What it made in the tree: albums, people, labels and the folders under /archive that hold them. Values set for its settings. They no longer appear on the System tab, but come back with the module. The database indexes it asked for. EiN does not stop you removing a module that others need. Those modules then fail to set up at the next start, with requires module 'ems' (^0.1.0), which is not installed ; install it again to bring them back. Warning A module named in EIN_MODULES in ~/ein/.env comes back at EiN's next start, because EiN installs every module named there that is missing. To keep it removed, delete its name from that line as well.

Module sources , CFG_MODULE_SOURCES , lists where published modules are looked for: organisations on GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea, as their addresses separated by spaces. It is https://github.com/einhq by default. Each repository named module-<name> in a source is a module; mod install <name> takes the first source that has it, and a module's dependencies come from its own organisation first. Change it on Settings → System , in its Modules group, or in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator config set CFG_MODULE_SOURCES "https://github.com/einhq https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield" A source that is not public needs an access token. Tokens for module sources , CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY , takes one per host, as host=token separated by spaces, such as forge.example:3000=… . Like every key, nobody can read it back once set, and EiN sends each token only to its own host. The settings reference has both. A source that does not answer is named above the published modules, as " https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield did not answer" with the reason, and the other sources are still listed. A module that is in no source can still be installed from its repository's address: mod install https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield/module-recipes , or the From a repository box at the top of the Published modules panel, whose Install asks who the module is for as on a published one. EiN fetches modules over plain HTTPS, so the forge must answer git's HTTP protocol and serve an archive of a commit, as GitHub, Forgejo and Gitea do. Writing a module is for making one of your own.

A module installed from its repository is kept in a folder of its own outside EiN's container, so it stays when EiN is updated or its container is made again. With the standard installation that folder is modules/ in the data folder, ~/ein/data/modules unless you chose another EIN_DATA . Inside EiN it is /var/lib/modules , and each module is linked as /usr/modules/<name> . Each module's .install.json records the repository, the branch or tag, the commit and when it was installed. At every start EiN links each module in the folder and sets them all up, in the order of their dependencies. A module whose setup fails is logged and the others carry on.

A deployment can also mount a folder of module checkouts of its own, named by DEV_MODULES_PATH (see Environment variables ). The standard installation does not; it is for running EiN from its source. A module the deployment provides runs from there: the published modules mark it The deployment's , mod install refuses it with 'archive' is one of the deployment's modules (…), which runs instead , and it has no Update or Remove in its panel. mod remove takes away only its link, which the next start puts back. It is updated with the deployment.

p.h: When a module does not work
p.x: Open Settings → Modules : a module that does not work is at the top of the list with its badge. Setup failed. Its panel shows "Its setup failed" with each problem, as mod list --long does. The usual ones: Problem What to do archive: requires module 'ems' (^0.1.0), which is not installed Install the missing module: mod install ems , or Install in Published modules . archive: requires 'ems' ^0.2.0, but 0.1.0 is installed Update the module it needs. archive: needs @ein/client ^0.7.0, this core provides 0.6.0 The module is written for another version of EiN, often after EiN was updated. Update the module; if no published version fits yet, it waits for one. After fixing the cause, set the module up again with mod setup archive , or every module with mod setup --all , which is what EiN runs at each start. Restarting EiN does the same. Not set up. EiN has not set the module up since it started, for example because it was put in place without setup. mod setup <name> sets it up. Active, but something is missing. Check its Services tab: a service that shows failed or disabled can be started again on the Dashboard 's services tab, and Services and logs explains how to read its log. A module installed from the terminal shows its pages in a browser tab that was already open once that page is reloaded. Install or update refused. The message says why, in words like these: Message What it means no module source has 'recipes': … None of the module sources has module-recipes , or none answered; the reasons follow. https://github.com/einhq/module-archive has no branch, tag or commit 'v9' The ref after @ does not exist. … has no mod.json at its top: not a module The repository is not a module. /usr/modules/archive is a module mod install did not put there; mod remove archive first Something else holds the name. no module sources to find 'archive' in: CFG_MODULE_SOURCES is empty; name its repository instead Module sources is empty. Troubleshooting covers problems beyond modules.

Every command here runs in EiN's terminal or over SSH. Those that change something are for administrators only. Command What it does mod list [--long] The installed modules and whether each works mod info <name> One module's manifest, what it requires and what uses it mod search [words] The published modules of the module sources, and what is installed of them mod install <module>... Install or update modules with what they need, and set them up mod groups <name> [group...] Who a module is for, or keep it to groups; --everyone makes it everyone's mod remove [--force] <name> Stop and remove a module mod setup <name> , mod setup --all Set up one module, or every module in the order of their dependencies The core commands reference has each one's options, and Updating covers updating EiN itself.

This page is for the administrator who gives people accounts in EiN and puts them in groups. It covers the Users , Groups and Permissions tabs of Settings , the built-in accounts and groups, how to let a second person administer, and the same work in the terminal. What a group may see and change is decided by the sharing of each folder, and with the Archive of each album, not here. Sharing shows how to share with a group, and Permissions in depth explains owners, groups and modes.

Choose Settings under System in the sidebar. The Users , Groups and Permissions tabs are there only while you act as the administrator; anyone else sees Modules alone. On Users and Groups , nothing opens over the page. The list is on the left; pick an entry and its panel opens beside it, where each change is made as you make it. The button beside the list's filter makes a new entry: New user on Users, New group on Groups. On a wide screen the list and the panel fill the window side by side and each scrolls on its own. On a phone or in a narrow window they take turns: the panel has All users or All groups above it, and the browser's Back button returns to the list too. The open entry is part of the address, such as /settings?tab=users&user=helen , so you can bookmark an account or send the link to another administrator.

p.h: The accounts and groups EiN starts with
p.x: EiN makes these at its first start, and none can be deleted. The two accounts are marked Administrator and Guest in their panels, and each of the groups Built in . Account Title What it is admin Administrator The administrator. It cannot be disabled or deleted. Its first password is INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD in ~/ein/.env , which setup.sh prints at the end of each run until you delete that line; First steps shows how to change it. guest Guest Who a visitor browses as when Visitors may browse is on. It has no password, cannot be given one, and its groups give it nothing. Group Title What it is for admin Administrators The admin account's own group, as root 's is on Linux. Being in it does not make anyone an administrator and gives no write to the system's own folders and settings. users Users Every account that signs in belongs to it, without being added. Sharing with users shares with everyone who has an account. ssh SSH users Its members may use ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id to reach other machines from EiN. See Reaching other machines . sudo Administrators on request Its members may act as the administrator for one sign-in, after entering their own password again. See Let a second person administer . guest Guests The guest account's own group. What this group may see, visitors may see. Besides these, every account made on the Users tab or with user-create gets a group of its own, named like the account: Helen Okafor's account helen has the group helen . These are its personal group.

Open Settings → Users and choose the New user button beside the filter. Type the person's Name , such as Helen Okafor. E-mail is optional. With one, the person can sign in with it instead of the username. No two accounts can have the same address, and EiN sends no e-mail to it. Check Username . It is suggested from the name ( helen ) until you type one. It is lower case, holds only letters, digits and . _ - , starts with a letter or _ , and cannot be changed later. It cannot be the name of an existing account or group. Type a Password and Repeat it, or leave both empty to set the password later. An account without a password cannot sign in. Under Groups , Users is ticked and greyed: everyone who signs in is in it. The groups set as the default for new users are ticked already (see What new accounts start with ). Tick or untick the others. Choose Create user . EiN says "Created helen." and opens the new account. The account has a home folder, /home/helen , which holds the person's own things, such as their preferences and, with the Archive installed, what they upload to staging, and a personal group helen . While something is missing, Create user says why under it: "Choose a username", "Already taken", "Repeat the password" or "The passwords do not match". If the account was made but its password could not be set, the account opens with the reason in its Password section; set the password there. Each account opens in a panel beside the list, where every change is made in place

Pick the account in the list. Its panel shows its picture, display name, username and uid, and badges for its state: Administrator , Guest , Disabled , Needs a password or Signed in now . Below are four sections, each saved on its own.

Display name , E-mail and Description , saved with Save profile . The display name is how the account is named to others; the person can change their own name and description too, on their profile (see Your profile ). Only an administrator sets the e-mail address. Empty the field and save to remove it. The account's picture is not set here: with the Archive installed, it is the cover photo of the person in the archive that the account is linked to. Your picture and the person you are shows how to make that link in the terminal.

A box per group: tick to put the person in, untick to take them out. Each box saves as you click it. Some boxes are ticked and greyed, with the reason beside them: everyone who signs in : the users group. primary group , or their own group, primary : the account's primary group, which it leaves only when its primary group is changed. Other people's personal groups are listed only while this account is in one. Primary group is the group that files the person creates belong to, unless they are created as shared. It starts as the personal group. You can pick any shared group instead. Note Group changes apply the next time the person signs in. Until then they keep the groups they signed in with, and the section says so when they are signed in now. To make a change apply at once, sign them out everywhere with Disable sign-in and then Enable sign-in .

Type a New password , Repeat it, and choose Set password . Password set appears beside it. Their current password stops working at once, in the browser and over SSH and SFTP, but browsers and terminals where they are signed in stay signed in. EiN has no rules for passwords: it takes any password that is not empty. It has no "forgot password" by e-mail and cannot make someone choose a new password at their next sign-in. When someone has forgotten theirs, set a new one here and ask them to change it on their profile's Security tab (see Change your password ). An account marked mustResetPassword has no usable password. It shows Needs a password , and cannot sign in by any means, an SSH key included, until you set one here; setting it clears the mark.

Signed in now lists where the person is signed in: In the browser , Over SSH or In a terminal , each with the address it comes from and since when. Disable sign-in signs them out everywhere at once, ends what they have running, and keeps them out of the browser, SSH and SFTP alike. Nothing they own is changed. The button then reads Enable sign-in , which lets them sign in again with their password. A disabled account is hidden from the Users list until you switch on Show disabled users at the foot of the list, which is there only while some account is disabled. The admin account has neither button: "The administrator can't be disabled or deleted." The guest account's panel shows only what it is for.

Open the account and choose Delete account… under Sign-in and removal . Read what will happen. Deleting the account removes its home folder and everything in it: the person's preferences, their staging with the Archive, and anything else they kept there. Pick who takes over everything they own elsewhere, such as folders and files, and with the Archive albums and pictures. The administrator is picked to start with. Choose Delete followed by the username, such as Delete helen . EiN ends the person's sessions, says how many items passed to whom, and returns to the list. Their personal group goes too, unless someone else is in it; then it stays, and EiN says so. Warning There is no undo, and deleted home folders do not go to the trash. If you only want to keep someone out, use Disable sign-in instead. EiN has no backup command; see Your data before you delete an account whose home folder holds anything you want to keep, such as pictures still unsorted in the Archive's staging.

A group is a set of accounts to share with. If everyone with an account is family, the built-in users group covers them and you need no other. Make a group when only some accounts should see something, such as a family group when friends also have accounts. Open Settings → Groups and choose the New group button beside the filter. Type a Name , such as family . It is how commands and settings name the group, follows the same rules as a username, and cannot be changed later. Type a Title , such as Family, and a Description if you like. The title is what people see where things are shared with the group. Tick the Members . This is optional; you can add anyone later, here or on their own page. Choose Create group . EiN says "Created family." and opens it. The Groups list shows each group's title and name, and up to four of its members' faces with a count of the rest. users reads Everyone . Personal groups are hidden until you switch on Show personal groups at the foot of the list, which is there only when there are some. In a group's panel: Profile changes its Title and Description , saved with Save profile . Members has a box per account: tick to add, untick to remove. Someone whose primary group it is stays ticked and greyed; the panel links to their page, where their primary group is changed. An account that no longer exists but is still linked shows as no longer an account , ready to untick. users has no list, since everyone who signs in is in it. Built-in groups say what they are for at the top, and "Built-in groups can't be deleted." Built-in groups say what they are for; the Users group shows Everyone instead of faces

Open the group and choose Delete group… under Delete . Pick the group that takes over what this one owns. Administrators is picked to start with. Choose Delete followed by the group's name, such as Delete family . Nobody loses their account. Accounts whose primary group it was go back to their own groups, and grants that named the group on folders, or on albums with the Archive, are dropped, so its members lose what they could see only through it.

The Permissions tab has four cards. Each says in a sentence what its saved values come to, and each setting on it is saved on its own with Save change , as on the System tab. A value changed here is marked Set here , and Restore inherited value clears it again. Card Setting What it decides Default New users Groups ( CFG_DEFAULT_USER_GROUPS ) The groups ticked on the New user form, besides the account's own. Empty means none. users Visitors Visitors may browse ( CFG_GUEST_BROWSING ) Whether someone who has not signed in browses as guest , seeing what is shared with visitors, instead of being asked to sign in. off Sharing Owner , Group , Permissions Who owns anything created as shared, such as a new album with the Archive, which group it is shared with, and what the owner, the group and everyone else may do with it. creator, users , 0750 Sign-in sessions Browser sign-in ( CFG_SESSION_MAX_AGE_SEC ) How long a browser stays signed in after its last visit. 1 day Sign-in sessions Idle session ( CFG_SESSION_EXPIRES_SEC ) How long a session lasts unused. A change applies to new sign-ins. 12 hours Leave Visitors may browse off for a family's own archive. With it off, someone who is not signed in can only sign in or open a share link. Sharing explains what visitors see when it is on. The Sharing card's settings are CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_OWNER , CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP and CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_MODE . They apply to what is created after you change them; First steps suggests values for common households, and How new albums start out shows how each person can narrow them. Each card says in plain words what new accounts, visitors and new albums get

Being in the admin group does not make anyone an administrator. To let someone you trust act as the administrator, or to keep an everyday account for yourself, put that account in Administrators on request ( sudo ): Open their account in Settings → Users . Under Groups , tick Administrators on request . Ask them to reload the page. Membership of sudo counts at once, without signing in again. They then have Administer… in the account menu under their picture. It asks for their own password again: "Enter your password again to act as the administrator until you sign out or leave admin mode." After Administer , the page reloads with the administrator's tabs and pages, an orange ring and a shield on their picture, and Leave admin mode in the account menu in place of Administer… . A wrong password answers "That is not your password." In a terminal, admin does the same for that terminal alone, and admin --off ends it. user-elevate --session acts for the whole sign-in, every page and terminal of it. Taking someone out of sudo ends their admin mode at once, in every page and terminal. Such a person can also set a new password for admin if it is lost, so keep at least one account you trust in sudo .

p.h: Signing in and why it fails
p.x: People sign in with their username or their e-mail address, in the browser under Username or e-mail , and over SSH and SFTP (see SSH and SFTP ). Their groups are read at that moment. A wrong password, an unknown username and an account without a password all fail the same way, so the answer does not tell anyone which accounts exist. Only with the right password does EiN say that an account is disabled. After five failed attempts from one address, that address is held back for a while that doubles with each further failure, up to 15 minutes, and the answer says how many seconds to wait. Failed attempts at one account only slow it down; they never lock its owner out. Failures are forgotten an hour after the last one.

Every change on these tabs is a command, and the tabs run the same commands. They are for the administrator, apart from reading lists and changing your own name and password. # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator user-create helen --title= 'Helen Okafor' --email=helen@example.com -- groups = users ,family user-passwd helen # asks for the new password after Password: user-update helen --name= 'Helen Okafor' --description= 'Scans the family letters' user-set-primary-group helen family user-disable helen # signs her out everywhere and keeps her out user-enable helen user-delete helen --to=peggy # what she owned passes to peggy group-create family --title=Family group-add-member family helen group-remove-member family helen group-update family --description= 'The Wrenfield household' group-delete family --to= users # --force when it is someone's primary group To see who there is and who is signed in: # in EiN's terminal user-list # every account, with uid and title; --inactive for the disabled ones user-info helen user-groups helen group-list --members # every group, and who is linked into it who # who is signed in, from where, and what they run user-create without --groups uses CFG_DEFAULT_USER_GROUPS ; --groups= with nothing after it adds the account to no group but its own. user-delete and group-delete without --to hand what was owned to admin . Commands by task and the core command reference list every option.

What you see What it means What to do Needs a password on an account It has no password, or is marked mustResetPassword until it is given one. Set one under Password . Someone does not see a folder or album shared with a group you just put them in Group changes apply at the next sign-in. Ask them to sign out and in, or choose Disable sign-in and Enable sign-in . Create user says "Already taken" An account or a group has that name. Each account's personal group is named like it. Choose another username. "Another account has this address" under E-mail Two accounts cannot share an address. Use another address, or remove it from the other account. user create: '<name>' is the name of a built-in group The names users and ssh belong to built-in groups. Choose another username. group delete: cannot delete the built-in group '<name>' Built-in groups stay. Nothing to do. user passwd: the guest account cannot have a password guest never signs in. Turn Visitors may browse on or off instead. <name>: permission denied: only an administrator may run it The command is the administrator's. Choose Administer… , or type admin in that terminal, if you are in sudo . The admin password is lost Nothing else keeps it. A member of sudo sets a new one with user-passwd admin .

First steps : accounts for a family, in order Sharing : sharing albums with groups, people and links Permissions in depth : owners, groups, modes and grants Your profile, favourites and trash : what each person changes themselves SSH and SFTP : signing in from other machines with a password or key Configuration : every other system setting

Every node in EiN has an owner, a group, mode bits and, when it needs one, an access list. This page is for administrators, and for anyone who wants to see what the Share dialog writes: how EiN decides who may read, change and pass through a node, what a new node starts with, and how to read and change it all from the terminal. The Share dialog sets all of this without numbers, and Sharing explains it for everyone in the family. Accounts and groups themselves are made on Accounts and groups . The examples use albums such as /archive/albums/Summer 1987 , which exist with the Archive installed. The commands and rules are core's, and work the same on any node, such as a folder under /home .

p.h: The four parts of a node's access
p.x: Like a file on Linux, every node carries: Part What it is Shown as Owner One account, by its uid. Usually whoever created the node. helen Group One group, by its gid. Usually the group of the folder it was created in. users Mode Read, write and execute, once for the owner, once for the group and once for everyone else. rwxr-x--- , or 0750 Access list Further users and groups, each with its own read, write and execute. Optional. group:family:rwx What the three letters allow on a node: Bit On a node On a folder, album or anything with children r read See its bytes and attributes. See what it holds; listing takes r and x . w write Change it, its attributes, its mode and its access list. Add to it and remove from it (with x ). x execute — Pass through it to what lies below. Any node can hold children here, so the folder column applies to folders and files alike, and with the Archive to albums, people and locations: a photo holds its thumbnails and metadata as children.

EiN asks, in this order, and stops at the first yes: Are you an administrator? Then yes, always. Is this a write, and are you not signed in? Then no, whatever the bits say. Are you the owner, and do the owner's bits allow it? Is the node's group one of your groups, and do the group's bits allow it? Do everyone else's bits allow it? Does an entry in the access list name you or one of your groups, and allow it? Every step can only grant. Unlike Linux, being the owner does not shut you out of what the other bits give: a node at 0074 still lets its owner read it. The access list adds people and never takes anyone away; there is no entry that denies. Note Write on a node is enough to change its mode and its access list. That is why Can edit in the Share dialog also lets someone change who a node is shared with. Changing the owner is the exception; see Change the owner and the group .

Who uid Groups What is special The administrator, admin 0 admin ( 0 ), users Passes every check. An account, such as helen its own its own group, users , and every group it is a member of — A member of sudo who chose Administer… its own as above Passes every check until the sign-in ends or they leave admin mode. The guest, guest 1001 guest ( 1001 ) Never writes. Whoever opens EiN without signing in. A share link one of its own, from 1073741824 up none Never writes; its entries stop granting when the link expires. A few rules follow from how groups are read: Every signed-in person is in users (gid 1002 ). Sharing with users , which the dialog calls Everyone with an account , shares with all of them. A member is someone with a membership link. group-add-member family jon puts a link named jon to /etc/users/jon in /etc/groups/family/users . Anything else placed there makes nobody a member. Groups are read when someone signs in. A person added to or taken out of a group keeps the groups they signed in with until they sign in again. Membership of sudo is the exception: it counts at once, and taking someone out of sudo ends their admin mode at once. Being in the admin group makes nobody an administrator. It is the administrator's own group, as root's is on Linux, and gives no write to the system's folders. To let someone act as the administrator when they need to, add them to sudo ; see Accounts and groups . To see who you are: # in EiN's terminal user-whoami user-groups helen

Open Nodes under System in the sidebar. Go to the node. The Mode , Owner and Group columns show its access; a lock in place of the arrow means you may not list what it holds. Choose Properties in the node's context menu, or press Alt + Enter . The Nodes page shows every node's mode, owner and group, and the properties dialog changes them. The properties dialog has three tabs: General shows the node's Mode as a number and as a grid of Owner , Group and Other against r , w and x , with Owner and Group pickers. Apply saves them, and stays off when you may not change the node. Attributes lists the node's attributes. Sharing is the Share dialog's own body: owner, grants, visitors and links in words.

# in EiN's terminal ls -l '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # mode, owner and group of what it holds stat '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the node itself: type, mode, owner, times acl '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # owner, group, bits and access list share-info '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the Share dialog's view, as YAML In ls -l a + after the mode, as in rwxr-x---+ , says the node has an access list. acl prints the bits and the list in the shape getfacl uses: # node: /archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage # owner: helen (1003) # group: users (1002) user::rwx group::r-x other::--- group:family:rwx user:jon:r-x link:1073741825:r-x A link: line is a share link's entry, by its uid; share-link list <path> says which link it is. share-info also lists the photos below a folder that keep their own sharing, its links, and, for an administrator, everyone who has access and through what.

chmod takes a mode as four octal digits or as symbolic clauses: # in EiN's terminal chmod 0750 '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' chmod g+w '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o-rwx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' chmod -r o-rw /archive # the whole subtree; each node keeps its other bits Form Meaning 0750 , 750 Set all nine bits. The same mode on every node of a recursive change. u , g , o , a Owner, group, everyone else, all three. No letter means all three. + , - , = Add these bits, take them away, or set exactly these. r , w , x The bits. Clauses are joined with commas. A symbolic mode is worked out from each node's own mode, as coreutils' chmod -R does, so chmod -r o-rw clears only those bits and leaves every node's other bits as they were. EiN has no setuid, setgid or sticky bit and no X . -r applies the change to the whole subtree (see What a recursive change does ); -L changes a softlink itself rather than what it points to.

p.h: Change the owner and the group
p.x: # in EiN's terminal chown jon '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # owner only (administrator) chown jon:family '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # owner and group (administrator) chown :family '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # group only chown -r :family '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # group of the whole subtree The owner and group are written user:group (or user.group ), by name or by number, and either half may be left out. The rules are Linux's: Only an administrator gives a node to another user. Anyone else is refused with Access denied for operation 'change uid' . Anyone else may move a node only into a group they are in , and needs write on it. Another group is refused with Access denied for operation 'change gid' . Without these rules someone could make what they wrote look like someone else's, or file it in a group they do not belong to. The owners of accounts, groups and sign-in sessions are the administrator's alone to change.

p.h: Grant more people with an access list
p.x: The mode names one group. An access list adds as many users and groups as you need, each with its own bits: # in EiN's terminal acl -m g:family:rwx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the family group may edit acl -m u:jon:rx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # Jon may view acl -x u:jon '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # take Jon's entry away acl -b '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # remove every user and group entry acl -r -m g:family:rx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the whole subtree An entry is u:<user>:<bits> or g:<group>:<bits> ( user: and group: work too), by name or number. -m replaces an entry for the same user or group rather than adding a second. Can view in the Share dialog is rx and Can edit is rwx . -b leaves share links' entries in place: share-link gives and takes those. share-set --drop-links removes them too. Each node in a recursive change edits its own list, as setfacl -R does, so an entry a folder inside already has beyond the edit stays.

p.h: Set it all at once with share-set
p.x: share-set changes the mode, the owner, the group and the access list together, in one walk of the subtree, and is what the Share dialog runs when you click Save . Unlike chmod -r , it is recursive unless you say otherwise: # in EiN's terminal share-set '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' --mode 0750 -b -m g:family:rwx -m u:jon:rx share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --group family --mode g+rx share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --default-owner # the configured default owner and group share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --reference '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --mode 0700 -b --drop-links --pin updated 214, kept own access 3, skipped 0, failed 0 Option What it does --mode The mode, octal or symbolic. --owner The owner, by name or uid. Administrators only. --group The group, by name or gid: one you are in, unless you are an administrator. --default-owner The configured default owner and group (see The default sharing ), applied by the server to every node you may write. --reference <path> Share the node as another one is: its group, mode and access list. The owner stays. -m , -x , -b Edit the access list, as acl does. --drop-links Remove share links' entries too, so no link opens the nodes. --pin , --unpin Hold the node against changes from further up, or let them reach it again. --pinned-below Change the pinned nodes below each path named, in place of the path itself. --no-recursive Change only the node named. --strict Exit non-zero when any node below could not be changed. share-set exits 0 when only some nodes below refused, and reports them in its counts and on standard error; it fails only when every path it was given refused. Every option is in the reference .

A pinned node keeps its access when a change comes from further up. A recursive change always writes the node it was aimed at, but passes over a pinned node and everything below it. With the Archive, this is what Share in an album's selection bar does when you give chosen photos sharing of their own, and how one photo stays private in a shared album; see Keep some photos private in a shared album . # in EiN's terminal share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --pin share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --reference '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --unpin share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --pinned-below --reference '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --unpin The pin is written on that node only. share-info on the album lists the pinned nodes below it, and a share link made on the album does not open them. The last line shares every pinned node in the album as the album is, which is what Share all like the album in the Share dialog runs.

chmod -r , chown -r , acl -r and share-set walk the subtree the same way: It reads the whole subtree first and writes the folder you named last. A change can take away the access the walk needs to get through, so nothing is written until everything has been found, and the folder's own access, which share-info reports, is never ahead of what is below it. Pinned nodes and everything below them are passed over , and counted as "kept own access". Softlinks are changed as links , never followed to their targets, so a link in an album to a photo elsewhere does not change that photo. It stops at mount points. What another store mounts inside the subtree is left alone. A node is changed once , however many places it hangs in. A node that refuses is counted, not fatal , as chmod -R behaves over files someone else owns. What you may not read is not listed to you, so it counts against its folder without names. Ctrl + C stops between batches , with the folder you named as it was. A plain chmod of a large folder rewrites the stored reach of everything below it (see A folder governs what is under it ), so expect it to take a while on an album of thousands of photos.

p.h: What a new node starts with
p.x: When a node is created and nothing names its access: Part What it gets Owner Whoever created it. Group Its parent's group, as a setgid directory does on Linux. Mode Everything for the owner; read and pass-through for the group, plus write where the group could write the parent; for everyone else, only the read and pass-through the parent gives them. Others' write is never inherited. Access list Its parent's, as a Linux default ACL carries down. So, with the Archive, a family album's new uploads, and the thumbnails, faces and metadata processing adds under them, take the album's group and grants whoever created them: a person or group granted an album sees what is added to it later. What is made under /home/<user> stays in that user's group, and the system tree under / stays 0755 . Moving a node with mv keeps its own access, as on Linux. Copying with cp is a create in the destination: the copy takes the destination's group and keeps its source's mode, less group write where the new parent gives none and less everyone else's write.

The default sharing is an owner, a group and a mode for what is created as shared, which an administrator sets under Settings → Permissions , on the Sharing card. Default in the Share dialog and share-set --default-owner apply it to a node. With the Archive installed, a new album, made in the web interface or with album create , and what staging publishes start with it. The Sharing card sets what every new album starts with, and says in a sentence what that comes to. Setting On the card Default CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_OWNER Owner empty: whoever creates it CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP Group users CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_MODE Permissions : None , View or Edit for owner, group and everyone else 0750 With the defaults, a new album is therefore owned by its creator, seen by everyone with an account and changed only by its owner. Each person narrows or widens that for what they create with How widely what you create is shared on their profile ( CFG_USER_DEFAULT_SHARE ); see Your profile . With the defaults, Default in the Share dialog lets everyone with an account see a node. The same settings in the terminal, in the octal form: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator config set CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP family config set CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_MODE 0750 Configuration explains where settings are kept.

p.h: A folder governs what is under it
p.x: Reaching a node by its path takes execute on every folder along the way, from / down. EiN applies the same rule wherever it finds a node without walking a path: search and links, and with the Archive the Media feed, the map, a person's faces and duplicates. A node shows up only when you may read it and at least one of its paths is open to you all the way down. With the Archive, this is what keeps staging private. /home/<user>/staging is 0700 , so the uploads inside it stay out of everyone else's search and map, whatever their own modes say. A node linked in two places is reachable through either. A hard link ( ln without -s ) into an open folder makes it visible there even when its other path is closed. A softlink is not a path. It points somewhere; whoever follows it still needs the access along the target's own path. What is in someone's trash is never offered by a search , to anyone, the administrator included, though counts may still include it until the trash is emptied. EiN keeps on each node who can get there, and works it out again below every node whose parents or access change, so group membership and link expiry are judged as you read and changing them rewrites nothing. If you suspect the stored answer is wrong, an administrator can check a sample of nodes against a walk of their paths: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator reach-check reach-check --sample=10000 2000 nodes judged for 9 callers: 0 disagree Any line under it names a node, a path and a uid for which the stored answer and the walk differ, and the uids or gids the stored answers name that no account, group or link holds.

p.h: The other bits are the system's
p.x: The bits for everyone else give every visitor and every account the parts of EiN they all need to run: / , /etc , the commands, the web interface, the modules' files. Content does not use them to share: Path Owner and group Mode Why /archive admin , users 0771 Everyone may pass through; nobody but the group reads it. /archive/tags admin , users 0771 The same. /home/<user> the account, its own group 0751 Others may pass through to what the owner grants, and read nothing else. /home/<user>/staging the account 0700 With the Archive. Nobody else, not even through search. /etc/users/<name> admin 0755 The account itself; only the administrator changes it. /etc/users/<name>/.password admin 0600 Its user can neither read nor replace it. /etc/groups/<group>/users its creator, the group 0750 Members may see who else is in the group, not add anyone. /var/links/<id> admin 0600 A share link's record, holding its token. Content reaches every account through the users group, and visitors who are not signed in through an access-list entry for the guest group, g:guest:rx , which the Share dialog shows as Visitors who are not signed in . When you open the Share dialog on something whose everyone-else bits still read it, the dialog shows them as Everyone with an account , and Save moves them there and clears the bits. To clear what older content still gives everyone else: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator chmod -r o-rw /archive

Someone who opens EiN without signing in acts as the guest. Whether they see anything depends on Visitors may browse under Settings → Permissions ( CFG_GUEST_BROWSING , off unless set): Off : the guest gets the sign-in page and nothing else. In the terminal they may run only login , logout , user-whoami , share-link , config and config-list ; anything else answers sign in first . On : the guest sees what is granted to the guest group, and what the other bits give. The guest never writes, whatever a mode or an access list says, its own /home/guest included. A share link is a principal of its own: a uid nobody else holds, in no group. Making a link adds an entry rx for it on the node and on everything below it that its creator may change, passing over pinned nodes. Whoever opens the link reads what it opens and nothing an earlier link opened, never writes, and loses the access when the link expires. Turning a link off takes its entry off every node, wherever the node has moved since. Someone already signed in who opens a link stays themselves. How to make and send one is on Sharing .

The administrator, uid 0 , passes every check, as root does on Linux: other people's homes and private albums included. A member of the sudo group passes them too while their sign-in is elevated, which they start with Administer… in the account menu (or admin in a terminal) and end with Leave admin mode (or admin --off ). A terminal acting as the administrator ends its prompt in # . Accounts and groups covers who may do this. Commands that only an administrator may run refuse everyone else before they start: user-create: permission denied: only an administrator may run it Only an administrator creates or hard-links an account, group or session node, and nobody, the administrator included, changes an account's uid or a group's gid once it exists, since ownership and access lists name the number. When an account or group is deleted, its number is taken off every node first: what it owned goes to the account named with --to (the administrator by default), and every access-list entry naming it is dropped, so whoever is given that number later inherits nothing.

p.h: Over SSH, SFTP and the web
p.x: The same rules apply wherever you come in: the web interface, EiN's terminal, SSH and SFTP all sign in as the same account and see only what it may. Downloading a file over the web takes read on it. See SSH and SFTP . A folder mounted from another machine with mount … sftp is different: every node in it is owned by the mount's owner and group (the administrator who mounted it, by default), and its bits are the ones the SFTP server reports.

A command says Access denied for operation 'w' on node: … . The letter is what was missing: r , w or x . The node named is the one that refused, which may be the folder above what you asked for: creating, removing or moving a node takes w and x on its folder, and moving it also takes w on the node itself. Check with acl on the node and on its folder. Someone added to a group still cannot see what is shared with it. Groups are read at sign-in. Ask them to sign out and in again. A folder's mode changed but a file inside did not. The file is pinned, or you may not write it. The counts after share-set ( kept own access , failed ) and the lines on standard error say which. share-info on the folder lists the pinned nodes; share-set <path> --unpin lets changes reach a node again. A file is open to someone but they cannot find it in search, or on the Archive's map. A folder on every path to it is closed to them. Give them pass-through on that folder, or link the file into a folder they can reach. chown says Access denied for operation 'change gid' . You are not in the group you named. An administrator can make the change, or add you to the group. share-info says sign in to see who has access . You have not signed in, or you came in through a share link. Who has access names people and groups, so it is shown only to someone signed in. A visitor sees the sign-in page instead of what was shared with visitors. Visitors may browse is off. Turn it on under Settings → Permissions , or send them a share link , which works either way.

Sharing : the Share dialog, the visibility chip and share links. Accounts and groups : making accounts and groups, membership, sudo . Configuration : where the default sharing and other settings are kept. The tree and Links : where nodes live, and hard and soft links. Core commands : every option of chmod , chown , acl , share-set , share-info and reach-check .

This page is for the administrator who keeps EiN running: how to tell at a glance whether it is well and keeping up, what each part of the System dashboard shows, how to ask the same questions in the terminal or from another computer, and what to do when the answer is not Healthy .

Choose Dashboard under System in the sidebar. The sidebar shows it only to administrators; the page is at /system , and someone who is not an administrator and opens that address reads the same figures without the controls to start and stop services. The badge above the title answers the first question: is anything wrong The page, System dashboard , has up to three badges above its title and four tabs below it, five with the ems module installed: Badge What it says Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person How things stand. Hover it for the sentence behind it, such as 1,240 jobs waiting, the slowest kind done in 25m00s . offline The browser has lost its connection to EiN and is reconnecting; the figures are from the last update. warming up The sampler that records CPU, memory and disk has not written anything yet. The charts fill in within a minute of a start. Tab What it holds Overview The checks that are not fine, the machine's CPU and memory, the work done, storage and the instance Work Every pipeline and every kind of job: what is waiting, how fast it goes, when it will be done Media service With the ems module: the media service's own state; see The media service Services Which services run, with start, stop and restart for the administrator Log The last problems logged, and the system log as it is written The tab you choose goes into the address ( /system?tab=work ), so a link opens the same view. The pipeline figures update whenever the pipelines change; every other card asks EiN for its own figures every 10 seconds, and only while its tab is open. The badges and the alarm above the tabs are kept current on every tab. Nothing is fetched while the browser tab is hidden, and the numbers refresh as soon as you come back.

The badge is the first line of the health command. It is decided in this order: a failed check first, then whether anything is waiting, then whether the waiting work moves. Verdict When What to do Healthy No check failed and nothing is waiting. Nothing. Catching up Work is waiting, and some kind of it was done, or some pipeline instance finished, in the last hour. Wait. After an import this can last hours; it turns to Healthy when the work is done. Stuck Work is waiting, and none of it was done and no instance finished in the last hour. Look at the checks on Overview and the Kinds of work table on Work ; see below. Needs a person At least one check failed. Read the failed check on Overview : each one says what is wrong and, often, the command that fixes it. Warnings never change the verdict on their own. An install that has the ems module but no media service, or the Assistant but no language model, reads Healthy with a warning about each, and the same warnings show for a while after every start while the services load their models. An EiN with no modules has neither check. A busy service only makes work wait; a person is asked for only when work fails through every retry and heal, or a check fails.

On Overview , a card above the tiles lists every check that is not fine, failed ones first, each with its reason; a red edge marks a failed check, a yellow one a warning. When every check is fine the card is not there. health in the terminal lists them all, the fine ones too. These are the checks core makes about EiN's own work, with or without modules: Check State Reason, as it reads What to do intake ok 12 matched triggers waiting to start pipeline work Nothing: new work about to start. kind <name> ok 340 left, 120/h eta 2.8h , or 340 waiting, the oldest for 4m10s Nothing: a kind of job that is being done, or has just arrived. kind <name> warn 340 waiting for EMS, which could not run it yet; next try in 1m30s With the Archive: the media service could not take the jobs; they are tried again on their own. See The media service if it lasts. kind <name> warn 340 waiting, the oldest for 2h05m, none done in the last hour The worker for this kind is not getting through it. Check the Services tab and the Log tab. kind <name> fail 340 waiting, and no worker offers this kind, the oldest for 12m30s See Work that nothing will run . failed work warn 3 failed instances, run again on their own after 1 h, 6 h and 24 h Nothing yet: failed work is run again on its own. failed work fail 2 instances failed again after three more runs and need a person (pipeline-instances --status failed) List them with pipeline-instances -s failed and see Processing and pipelines . input ok 5 steps met input nothing can process, and will not be run again Nothing: a damaged or unreadable file. Running it again would give the same result. quiet steps warn 1 running step silent for 30m00s or more: media-transcode/transcode A step has written nothing for a long while. It keeps running; nothing stops a step for taking long. queue <name> fail 4 entries dropped after their delivery attempts (queue-dead /var/queues/archive-bridge: --retry or --drop) Look at them with queue-dead <path> , then put them back with --retry or delete them with --drop . How long a step may stay silent before it counts as quiet is the setting CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS , 30 minutes by default. Modules add checks of their own, through the services they run. Each is there only with its module installed, and asked only while its service runs: Check From What it says ems and ems … the ems module's ems-link service ( ems-status --checks ) Whether the media service answers, its model worker, each degradation and the card; the table is in The media service . Only ems gpu can fail. llm and llm model the Assistant's llm-link service ( llm-status --checks ) Whether the language model answers, whose it is and where it runs, and whether its model has been tried with the assistant. See The language model . the service's name any service whose check does not answer its check did not answer , as a warning. When a check names a hosted language model, its reason says so plainly, for example …: questions, and what the assistant reads to answer them, leave this host .

Under the checks, Overview shows the machine and the work in five parts. CPU and Memory tiles: the share of all the machine's processor cores in use, with the number of cores, the load and EiN's own share, and EiN's container's memory against its limit, each with a small chart of the last six hours. A tile turns amber at 75% and red at 90%. GPU and VRAM tiles, beside them, with the ems module installed and a media service that has a graphics card: how busy the card is and its temperature, and its memory in use. They come from the ems module and are not there without it, without a card or without the media service; see The graphics card . Work : Completed per hour , the pipeline instances finished in the last hour, with the count for the last 24 hours and a chart of them; the total number of instances; and Instances by state , a bar of Queued , Running , Failed , Completed and Cancelled . Storage : each storage tier, its path, a bar of used and free space, % used , how much it grows per day and, when it grows, full in ~N days , in red when that is under 14 days. Tiers that share one disk say so, with the device in brackets: their free space is the same space, counted once. The database's size is in the corner. Files and storage explains the tiers. A line at the bottom naming the instance: host , uptime , deno and database . It tells you which EiN you are looking at when you run more than one. The storage projection is measured over the last seven days. A tier that is not growing has no "full in" figure, and a tier filling up fast is the one thing on this tab that needs action before it becomes a problem: Your data covers moving the archive to a bigger disk.

Work shows what the pipelines are doing; Processing and pipelines explains pipelines, how to rerun, cancel and retry work, and what each one does. One row per pipeline: Out and ETA say whether a backlog is shrinking and when it will be gone The pipeline table has one row per defined pipeline, even one that has never run, with Workload , Waiting , Queued , Running , Failed , Completed and Cancelled . In is the work arriving for it per hour, Out what it finished in the last hour, and ETA the waiting work divided by Out ; no rate when nothing finished recently, — when nothing waits. When queue entries were dropped after their delivery attempts, a red N dropped stands above the table. Choose a row to see that pipeline's instances. Kinds of work lists each kind of job in the work pools that has something left or was done lately: Left , Running , In , Out , ETA and Oldest waiting .
