A red no worker badge marks a kind nothing runs; with the Archive, a yellow waiting for EMS badge marks a kind resting because the media service could not run it, with the next try in its tooltip. Ongoing lists the instances running now, with how long each has run. Steps that have written nothing for the quiet time are listed above it in a yellow box.

When jobs of some kind are ready and no running worker offers that kind for more than five minutes, a red box, Work that nothing will run , stands above the tabs on every tab, and the kind <name> check fails. The box names the pool, how many jobs are ready and for how long, and the pipelines that queue that kind. When it names pipelines, the worker that should run the kind is not running. Open Services and start the stopped one, or read the Log tab for why it stopped. When it says that no defined pipeline queues the kind any more, the jobs are left over from a pipeline that was removed or renamed. Cancel them with the command the box gives: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pool cancel /var/pools/media --kind gpu-describe

The ems module adds this tab, and it is there only while that module is installed. It shows the media service's version, its models, what it runs now and what is on the graphics card; The media service describes it.

Services lists the services inside EiN, the ones that are not running first. Each row has the service's name, its own status line or description, how long it has been up, how many times it has restarted ( ×3 ), and its state: running , starting , stopping , stopped , failed or disabled . The heading counts them, 21 healthy , or in red 2 down ; with the Archive installed, its stopped models-second , off while CFG_MODEL_SECOND_SLOTS is 0 , counts as down. A service that has restarted many times, or is down while enabled, is the row to look at An administrator has Restart and Stop on a running service and Start on a stopped one. A disabled service has no buttons; enable it from the terminal first. Services and logs explains each service and the commands behind these buttons.

Log has two cards. Recent problems shows the last 10 lines logged at WARN or ERROR, newest first, or Nothing logged at WARN or above . Live log follows the system log, /var/logs/system , as it is written: choose DEBUG , INFO , WARN or ERROR to show that level and above, pause it, or clear it. While you read further up, new lines do not scroll the view away. Recent problems answers whether anything went wrong while you were not watching With the Archive, a warning such as pooled step could not run yet, kind resting means the media service was not ready for a job; the job is tried again on its own. Services and logs covers the logs and dmesg .

Every figure on the dashboard comes from an ordinary command, and you can run the same commands in EiN's terminal or over SSH. health gives the verdict and every check: # in EiN's terminal health On an EiN with the Archive and the ems module, it reads like this: catching up: 1,240 jobs waiting, the slowest kind done in 2h48m warn kind transcribe 40 waiting for EMS, which could not run it yet; next try in 1m30s ok ems EMS 3f2a91c answering, up 2.1h ok intake 12 matched triggers waiting to start pipeline work ok kind faces 1,188 left, 420/h eta 2.8h What you want to know Command The verdict and the checks health CPU, memory and event-loop lag, with history host-metrics Free space per tier, when it fills, the database's size df Which instance, its versions and uptime system-info Each pool and kind of job: left, rates, oldest waiting pool-stat Every pipeline's counts and rates pipeline-overview The meters services add, such as the card's memory gauges The services and their status lines service-list --detail The last problems in the log dmesg --level warn -n 10 What is running now, and who is connected ps , who host-metrics also shows the event loop's lag, lag p99 1.2 ms max 8.4 ms , which the dashboard does not: how long ready work waits for EiN's process. High lag with low CPU is the case where everything feels slow and nothing looks busy; Performance and sizing covers it. Put JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of any of them for the answer as JSON. The verdict is then one of healthy , catching-up , stuck and needs-person : # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 health | jq -r .verdict

top draws on one screen what the dashboard spreads over its tabs: a CPU graph and the load, memory, the event loop and the services' gauges, the disks, the verdict with every check that is not fine and the work done in the last hour, the running commands, the sessions, the services and the latest problems. It redraws every 2 seconds. # in EiN's terminal top top fits the whole dashboard into one terminal, and works over SSH In the terminal panel, press Alt + M first to give it the whole window ( The terminal ). Key What it does q or Ctrl + C Quit ↑ ↓ , k j Scroll the list of commands PgUp PgDn , Home End Scroll a page, or to the top or bottom s Sort the commands: newest, oldest, by user or by command + and - Update less or more often, in steps from 0.5 to 60 seconds p Pause, so a list can be read; again to go on Space Update now top -d 5 starts at 5 seconds between updates. top -n 1 writes one frame and stops, which is what you want in a script or over ssh without a terminal.

EiN sends no e-mail and raises no alert outside itself: the dashboard and health are where problems show. To look without opening the web interface, send health over SSH: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local health health always ends with exit status 0, whatever the verdict, so a script that watches EiN has to read the verdict. The first word of the text is enough, or the JSON: # on your own computer, for example from cron verdict=$(ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'JSON_OUTPUT=1 health' | jq -r .verdict) [ " $verdict " = needs-person ] && echo "EiN needs a person" | mail -s "EiN" helen@example.com SSH and SFTP explains signing in with a key so a script needs no password.

The metrics-sampler service records the machine's and the work's figures, one log per series under /var/logs/metrics , and the dashboard, top and the commands above read them back. The charts therefore survive a reload of the page and a restart of EiN. Series What it holds How often Kept cpu Processor time used by the machine and by EiN's container 15 seconds 7 days memory Memory in use against the container's limit 15 seconds 7 days runtime Event-loop lag 15 seconds 7 days pools Jobs per pool, by state 15 seconds 7 days pipelines Instances completed per pipeline 1 minute 30 days disk Free and total space per storage tier 15 minutes 90 days nodes How many nodes of each type 15 minutes 365 days With the ems module installed, it adds a gpu series, sampled every 15 seconds by its gpu-sampler service, for the GPU and VRAM tiles. Memory is EiN's container's own, read from its cgroup. CPU is read both ways: the whole machine's, since the media service and the language model, when installed, load it from containers of their own, and EiN's container's share of it. How the tree has grown over the years is not on the dashboard: Statistics , under System , shows it, and anyone can open it ( Home and statistics ).

What you see Why What to do warming up stays, the tiles are empty, host-metrics says no metrics sampled yet — is metrics-sampler running? The metrics-sampler service is not running. Start it on the Services tab, or service start metrics-sampler , and read the Log tab for why it stopped. Storage says No tier data sampled yet , df says no disk sample yet — is metrics-sampler running? The disk is sampled every 15 minutes; right after a start there is no sample yet. Wait 15 minutes. If it stays, check metrics-sampler as above. offline next to the verdict The browser lost its connection to EiN, for example while EiN restarts. Wait; it reconnects by itself. If it stays, reload the page and see Troubleshooting . Stuck , with waiting for EMS on the kinds With the Archive: the media service is down, restarting or busy loading models. See The media service . The work goes on by itself once it answers. Stuck , with none done in the last hour on a kind The worker for that kind is stopped or hangs. Look on Services for a stopped or often restarted worker, and on Log for its errors. Services and logs . Needs a person , kind <name> failed Nothing runs that kind of job. Work that nothing will run . Needs a person , ems gpu failed With the ems module: the media service is meant to have a graphics card and sees none. The graphics card . Needs a person , failed work or queue <name> failed Work failed for good, or queue entries were dropped. Follow the command in the check's reason, and see Processing and pipelines . full in ~N days in red A storage tier will be full within two weeks at its present rate. Free space, or move the archive to a bigger disk: Your data . The CPU or memory tile is red for long The machine's processors, or EiN's container's memory, are 90% or more in use. Performance and sizing . Dashboard is not in the sidebar You are not an administrator. Ask an administrator, or open /system to read the figures; health works for everyone.

This page is for the administrator. It covers core's pipeline engine: how pipelines, steps, pools and workers run, how to watch them on the Dashboard and in the terminal, what to do when work fails or stops moving, how to run work again on purpose, and the settings the engine has. Core brings the engine and no pipelines of its own, so an EiN without modules runs none, and the Work tab of the Dashboard stays empty. Pipelines come with modules: of the published ones, the Archive brings them all, with the workers that run them. Processing pictures covers the Archive's pipelines, workers and settings. The examples on this page name the Archive's pipelines, such as media-faces , which exist only with the Archive installed.

A pipeline waits for one kind of change and then runs its steps, each a command, on the node that changed. Changes and pipelines explains the idea; this page is about running it. Work is done in three places: The pipeline engine (the pipeline-engine service) matches changes to pipelines, creates an instance for each pipeline and node, and runs the short steps itself. Pool workers run the long steps. A step that names a pool and a kind of job goes as a job into that pool, under /var/pools/ , and a worker takes it when it has room. A worker is a service that runs pipeline-worker , which takes the kinds it names from one pool, as many at once as its capacity allows. Core runs no workers of its own; a module that brings pipelines brings their workers. Background services of the modules turn changes into the events their pipelines wait for, and may announce work again on their own. Every pipeline runs at most once per node at a time: a file announced ten times while it waits is worked on once. Waiting work is kept in nodes, so nothing is lost when EiN restarts. pipeline-list prints every pipeline that is defined, with its trigger.

p.h: Watch the work on the Dashboard
p.x: Sign in as an administrator and choose Dashboard in the sidebar, under System . Read the badge above the title System dashboard : Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person . Health and the dashboard explains each word and the Overview tab. Choose the Work tab. One row per pipeline says how much is left, how fast it goes, and when it will be done; the pipelines here are the Archive's. The table has a row for every defined pipeline, also one that has never run, and a total row All pipelines at the foot. The bar draws the same counts as the columns. Column What it counts Waiting Nodes the pipeline has matched but not yet started on: no instance yet Queued Instances that are started and waiting for a worker or for an earlier step Running Instances with a step running this moment Failed Instances that failed Completed Instances that finished, counting those pruned since. Taken once a minute, so it can be a minute old Cancelled Instances stopped on purpose In Jobs that arrived per hour, over the last hour Out Instances completed in the last hour, the rate the ETA divides by ETA When what is waiting will be done at that rate; no rate when nothing completed recently Hover over the lightning sign beside a pipeline's name to see what starts it. Choose a row to open the pipeline's page. Below the table, Kinds of work lists what the pools hold, a row per kind of job: Left , Running , In , Out , ETA and Oldest waiting . This is where the slow steps are. A kind may carry a badge: waiting for EMS : a step of this kind could not run yet, because a service it needs was busy, loading a model, restarting or unreachable; for the Archive's steps that service is the media service. The jobs are not failed. The kind rests for 30 seconds, then twice as long each time it is refused again, up to 10 minutes; hover over the badge for the next try. no worker : no running worker takes this kind, so the jobs will never run. Ongoing lists the instances with a step running, with the target file and how long it has run. A step that has written nothing for 30 minutes is listed above it as quiet, with "Still running; nothing stops a step for taking long." No step is stopped for taking long; a quiet step is for you to look at, not a fault in itself. Two warnings can appear above the tabs or the table: Work that nothing will run names each kind that has jobs and no worker, and the pipelines that queue it. See Work that nothing will run . N dropped , above the table, counts events that failed every delivery attempt. See Dropped events .

p.h: Watch the work in the terminal
p.x: Everything on the Work tab comes from ordinary commands, which you can run in the terminal or over SSH: # in EiN's terminal health # the verdict in one line, and each check that decides it pipeline-overview # instances by pipeline, unfinished steps, queues, completions in the last hour pool-stat # each pool and kind: what is left, how fast, workers and what they take pipeline-instances -s failed # the failed instances, newest first top # all of it live, with CPU, memory and services; q quits pipeline-instances lists 100 at a time and prints (more: --after …) when there are more; pass that to --after for the next page. Give it pipeline names to narrow it: pipeline-instances -s failed media-faces media-ocr .

p.h: Look at one pipeline and its instances
p.x: A pipeline's page, opened from the Work table, shows its description, its Trigger , its Steps and its Priority , and below them its Instances : Status , Target , Started and Duration . The tabs All , Running , Completed , Failed and Cancelled narrow the list, and Load more fetches the next page. Choose an instance to open it. Its page shows the status, the target node and the steps: Step , Status , Depends on , Command and Duration . A step's status is one of these: Status What it means pending Waits for the steps it depends on queued Waits for a free place in the engine waiting Waits in a pool for a worker; the pool and kind are shown beside it, and "retrying" if it ran before running Runs now; "last output … ago" says when it last wrote anything completed Finished failed Failed on its last attempt skipped Not run: its condition said no, or the instance was cancelled Choose a step to see its Exit code , its Attempts , its pool and its condition, and for a failed step the Error it wrote. In the terminal, pipeline-status prints the same: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-status media-faces/< id > An instance is named after the node it works on, so one file has the same id in every pipeline that ran on it. Give the id as <pipeline>/<id> , as pipeline-instances and the pages show it; a bare id that more than one pipeline uses is refused with the pipelines it could mean.

A failed step is tried again up to its limit of attempts, three unless the pipeline says otherwise, before the instance fails. Two kinds of failure are treated differently: A service the step needs could not do it yet. The step goes back to wait with its attempt given back, and its kind rests, as waiting for EMS shows. Nothing fails however long the service is away. The Archive's steps fail this way while the media service is busy or away. The file itself cannot be processed , such as bytes no decoder can open. The step fails at once, whatever attempts are left, and the file is not tried again. health counts these under input and treats them as settled. A step tells the two apart by its exit code; Changes and pipelines lists them.

p.h: Failed work is run again on its own
p.x: The pipeline-pruner service runs pipeline-heal --apply every hour ( CFG_PIPELINE_PRUNE_INTERVAL , 3600 seconds). It runs each failed instance again 1 hour after it failed, then 6 hours after the next failure, then 24 hours after that. An instance that fails all three times is marked as needing a person and left alone, and health then reads Needs a person . Instances that failed on their input, and instances of pipelines no longer defined, are never run again. pipeline-heal without --apply only says what it would do: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-heal would rerun 3, would mark 0 for a person; 12 waiting, 1 failed on their input When you know the cause has passed, for example after the media service was fixed, run them all now. --now skips the waits, and the run does not count as one of the three: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-heal --apply --now Your sidebar and top bar shows how to give administrators a button that runs pipeline-heal --apply .

List the failed instances: pipeline-instances -s failed , or the Failed tab of the pipeline's page. Open one and choose the failed step to read its Error . Fix the cause: start the service the step needs, free disk space, or replace the file. Run the instance again with Rerun on its page, or with pipeline-rerun : # in EiN's terminal pipeline-rerun media-faces/< id > To act on many at once, tick them on the pipeline's page and choose Rerun . To On the pages In the terminal Run an instance afresh from the pipeline's current steps Rerun pipeline-rerun <pipeline>/<id> … Run only the failed steps again none pipeline-restart <pipeline>/<id> Run one failed or skipped step again Retry on the step pipeline-step-restart <pipeline>/<id> <step> Stop a running instance Cancel pipeline-cancel <pipeline>/<id> Delete instances, cancelling running ones first Remove pipeline-remove <pipeline>/<id> … Only an administrator sees these buttons, and only an administrator can run these commands.

A kind with jobs and no worker never moves. Work that nothing will run on the Dashboard and health (as a failed check kind <name> ) both say so. The usual cause is that the worker service is stopped: Open the Services tab of the Dashboard , or run service-list , and look at the workers; with the Archive installed, they are cpu and models . Start the one that is stopped, or read its log if it keeps stopping. Services and logs shows how. When no defined pipeline queues the kind any more, the jobs are left over from a pipeline that was removed. The warning then gives the command that cancels them, with the pool's path, such as the Archive's /var/pools/media : # in EiN's terminal pool-cancel /var/pools/media --kind <kind>

An event that fails ten delivery attempts, for example because its node no longer exists, is set aside rather than tried forever. The Work table then shows N dropped , and health fails its queue … check until you deal with them. The engine's own queue is /var/queues/pipeline-engine ; a module that turns changes into events has a queue of its own, such as the Archive's /var/queues/archive-bridge : # in EiN's terminal queue-dead /var/queues/pipeline-engine # list what was set aside queue-dead --retry /var/queues/pipeline-engine # put them back in line queue-dead --drop /var/queues/pipeline-engine # delete them --id limits --retry or --drop to one entry.

When waiting for EMS stays on a kind, the service its steps need is the place to look; for the Archive's steps it is the media service, and The media service shows how to check it. Once it answers again, the kind tries on its own at its next try. To try at once: # in EiN's terminal pool-wake # every resting kind pool-wake transcribe # one kind

pipeline-start runs one pipeline on one node: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-start media-faces /archive/albums/christmas-2019/IMG_2041.jpg pipeline-start --var FORCE=-f media-transcode /archive/albums/christmas-2019/MVI_0412.mp4 It starts the run at once, in the normal lane, and skips the checks a trigger makes. --var sets a variable the pipeline declares; the second line makes the Archive's media-transcode redo a video that already has its renditions. A pipeline that reads its starting event has nothing to read when started by hand, and pipeline-start warns about it. A module may bring commands of its own for redoing its work over many files; the Archive's are regenerate and media-scan , described in Processing pictures .

An event can put the work it starts in the bulk lane, below all other work, so that what people do in the meantime is processed first. Bulk work is put behind, never stopped: it runs whenever nothing else that could run is waiting. With the Archive installed, the work on a large import runs there; Processing pictures says which. pipeline-rerun and pipeline-start always run in the normal lane; pipeline-heal keeps the lane an instance had.

These settings are in the Processing category of Settings → System , or set with config set . Saving one restarts the service that reads it, when it is read by a service, and work in progress is picked up again; CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS restarts nothing and counts from the next look. Configuration explains how. Setting Default What it decides CFG_PIPELINE_MAX_CONCURRENT 4 Steps the engine itself runs at once CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS 1800000 How long a running step may be silent before it is listed as quiet CFG_PIPELINE_PRUNE_INTERVAL 3600 Seconds between the pruner's rounds, which also run pipeline-heal The engine has more settings, for how many triggers and instances it holds; their defaults suit a machine of any size, and Settings lists them all. The Processing category also holds the settings modules bring, such as how much work the Archive's workers run at once; Processing pictures covers those. Performance and sizing says what to set on a small or a large machine.

Instances are nodes under /var/pipelines/instances/<pipeline>/ . Every hour the pipeline-pruner service deletes pool jobs that finished more than 24 hours ago, runs pipeline-heal --apply , and then keeps the 2000 most recently completed instances of each pipeline and deletes the rest. It leaves failed and running instances alone. A pipeline that is no longer defined, because its module was removed or it was renamed, loses all its instances once its definition has been gone for 10 minutes. To delete by hand, use Prune on a pipeline's page, which removes its finished instances, or only those of the tab you are on, or pipeline-prune : # in EiN's terminal pipeline-prune -s failed media-faces # the failed instances of one pipeline pipeline-prune --older-than 30d # completed more than 30 days ago, every pipeline

A module's pipelines are defined when it is set up and removed when it is removed; Modules covers both. Removing a pipeline cancels its running instances. To write a pipeline of your own, see Writing a module .

Changes and pipelines : how a change becomes finished work. Processing pictures : the Archive's pipelines, workers and settings. Health and the dashboard : the four words and the Overview tab. Performance and sizing : what to set on your machine. Services and logs : starting, stopping and reading the workers. Troubleshooting : when work does not get done. Core commands : every pipeline- and pool- command.

This page is for whoever runs EiN: the services that run inside EiN and keep it working, how to see and restart them on the dashboard and in the terminal, and where EiN, its services and its containers write what they do. The containers themselves, and how to start and stop them with compose, are on Installing in detail .

Inside the ein container, EiN runs a set of long-running jobs it calls services: the web server, the SSH server, the pipeline engine, small loops that tidy up on a timer, and the services modules bring, such as the Archive's workers that process your media. Each service is a shell script, start.sh , that EiN runs in a shell of its own as the administrator. A service is not a container: the database ( db ), and the media service ( ems ) and the language model ( llm ) when they are installed, are containers beside EiN. The ems module and the Assistant watch the last two through services of their own, ems-link and llm-link . Core brings nine services, the first nine below, and they are all an EiN without modules runs. Each module brings its own, listed after core's with the module they come from. With the Archive , the ems module it brings along ( The media service ) and the Assistant installed, there are 21: Service From What it does http-server core Serves the web UI and the WebSocket API ssh-server core Serves the EiN shell and SFTP over SSH pipeline-engine core Matches events against pipeline triggers and runs the resulting steps pipeline-pruner core Runs failed pipeline work again after a growing wait, and keeps the pipeline instances and the pools bounded relations-guard core Removes links that would dangle after a node is deleted metrics-sampler core Samples host, storage and workload counters into /var/logs/metrics , which the dashboard draws session-reaper core Removes expired sessions, and turns off expired share links; hourly tmp-sweeper core Removes files left in /tmp once they are older than CFG_TMP_RETENTION_HOURS ; hourly trash-purger core Removes trashed files for good once they are older than CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS ; twice a day archive-bridge archive Turns changes in the tree into the media and location facts that pipelines trigger on cpu archive Worker for CPU-bound media jobs: transcodes, derivatives, fingerprints models archive Worker for the model-bound media steps: faces, picture and text vectors, text in pictures, transcripts, voices models-second archive A second worker for the same steps, in the reverse order; it ends at once, stopped, while CFG_MODEL_SECOND_SLOTS is 0 media-heal archive Closes media gaps nothing announced, such as a pipeline never run on a file or work a crash lost, once the engine has caught up album-metadata archive Keeps each album's photo stacks, time span and cover current label-models archive Keeps the models behind label suggestions trained person-covers archive Gives every named person without a cover the crop of one of their own faces staging-organizer archive Runs the staging organizer when something waits for it, and matches the groups due a match ems-link ems Watches the media service and reports what it holds gpu-sampler ems Samples the media service's graphics card for the dashboard llm-link assistant Watches the assistant's language model and reports whose it is and where it runs Every time EiN starts, it registers and enables core's services and those of every module that is set up, then starts every enabled service as the last step of its start. A module's services are added when it is installed and removed with it; see Modules .

p.h: See the services on the dashboard
p.x: Open Dashboard under System in the sidebar. The dashboard is the administrator's; see Health and the dashboard for its other tabs. Choose the Services tab. One row per service, with the ones that need attention sorted to the top The card lists every service, one row each, and asks again every 10 seconds while the tab is open: The service's name, and under it its description. A service that reports on itself shows that line instead, and its description when you hover it: with their modules installed, ems-link shows what the media service holds, or not answering , and llm-link shows where the language model runs. How long it has been up, such as up 8h 50m . Hover it for the time it started. × and a number when EiN has restarted it since it was last started by hand. Hover it for "Restarted 2 time(s)". A badge: running , starting , stopping , stopped , failed , or disabled for a service that is switched off. The heading counts them: 21 healthy , or in red 1 down when an enabled service is not running. With the Archive installed, its stopped models-second is counted as down while CFG_MODEL_SECOND_SLOTS is 0 . Rows are sorted by what needs attention: failed services first, then other enabled services that are not running, then services that have restarted, then the rest by name. Settings → Modules also shows a module's services and whether each runs, on the module's Services tab; the controls are here on the dashboard.

p.h: Restart, stop and start a service
p.x: On the Services tab, as the administrator or in admin mode , each row has buttons at its right: Service is Buttons running Restart (the circling arrows) and Stop (the square) stopped or failed Start (the triangle) starting or stopping a spinner; wait for it to settle disabled a dash; its tooltip says "Disabled — enable it from the shell to run it" The row shows a spinner while the action runs and is read again as soon as it is done. If the action fails, a red line above the table names it and the reason, such as stop cpu: … . In the terminal the same actions are commands, which only an administrator may run: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator service-restart metrics-sampler service-stop trash-purger service-start trash-purger service-start-all # every enabled service that is not running service restart metrics-sampler , with a space, is the same command. Each answers with one line, such as Restarted service 'metrics-sampler' . What happens when you stop a service: EiN sends the command the script is running a stop signal and waits for the script to end: 5 seconds by default, and up to 16 minutes for pipeline-engine , which lets the steps it runs finish. A script that has not ended by then is closed. Work the service would do waits. A worker that is stopped, such as one of the Archive's media workers, leaves its jobs in the pool, and they run when it starts again; see Processing and pipelines . A stopped service stays stopped until you start it, or until EiN itself starts again, which starts every enabled service. With their modules installed, ems-link and llm-link add the media service's and the language model's checks to health . While one is stopped, its checks are missing from the dashboard's verdict rather than failing. Warning Stopping http-server takes the web interface away, the page you stopped it from included, and stopping ssh-server closes SSH and SFTP. Start them again from the other one ( service-start http-server over SSH), or restart EiN's container: podman compose restart ein in ~/ein . Restarting http-server from the dashboard drops the page's connection for a moment. Saving a setting on the Settings page restarts the services that read it by itself; Configuration lists what restarts what.

p.h: When EiN restarts a service by itself
p.x: Every service that ships with EiN restarts when its script fails: when it ends with an exit code other than 0, EiN starts it again a second later, and the × count on its row goes up. A service that has been restarted three times within a minute and fails again is not started again; it stays failed until you start it. A script that ends with 0 is stopped , and is not started again. The count belongs to the run you started: Restart , or service-restart , starts it at 0 again.

p.h: Look at services in the terminal
p.x: service-list lists every service; anyone may run it. # in EiN's terminal service-list --detail On an EiN with the Archive and the ems module, it starts: NAME STATUS ENABLED RESTARTS DESCRIPTION -------------------- ----------- -------- -------- ----------- album-metadata running yes 0 Keeps each album's photo stacks, denormalized time span and cover current archive-bridge running yes 0 Turns VFS mutations into the media and location domain facts pipelines trigger on cpu running yes 0 Worker for CPU-bound media jobs — transcodes, derivatives, fingerprints ems-link running yes 0 Watches the media service and reports what it holds not answering … --detail asks each running service that reports on itself for its line, printed under its row; it is the line the dashboard shows. Without --detail the list is quicker. With JSON_OUTPUT=1 it is JSON, with each service's start time. service-status shows one service, and where its output goes, here the ems module's ems-link : # in EiN's terminal service-status ems-link Service: ems-link Status: running Enabled: yes Description: Watches the media service and reports what it holds Started: 2026-10-25T06:12:40.512Z Restarts: 0 Output: /var/logs/services/ems-link/stdout.log Errors: /var/logs/services/ems-link/stderr.log Last exit code appears once the script has ended. top shows the running services in a panel of its own, beside the machine's figures; Health and the dashboard covers it.

EiN writes to four places. Three are logs in the tree, which you read in EiN's terminal; the fourth is the container's own log, which you read on the machine. Log What is in it How long it is kept /var/logs/system EiN's own messages: each line with a time, a level, the part of EiN that wrote it and the message Emptied each time EiN starts /var/logs/services/<name>/stdout.log What a service's script prints Emptied each time the service starts /var/logs/services/<name>/stderr.log What a service's script prints as errors Emptied each time the service starts The ein container's log The same messages as /var/logs/system , with the details behind them, such as an error's stack, and what EiN prints while it starts Until the container is removed or made again, by podman compose down or by an up -d after a change A service's own output goes only to its pair of logs under /var/logs/services , never to the container's log. Two other folders hold logs of other kinds: /var/logs/metrics , the figures the dashboard draws, and /var/logs/jobs/<pid> , the output of a command started with nohup or kept running with detach .

p.h: Read the system log on the dashboard
p.x: Open Dashboard under System and choose the Log tab. Recent problems answers whether anything went wrong; the live log shows what EiN is doing now Recent problems lists the last ten lines at WARN or ERROR, newest first, with the time, the part of EiN and the message. It is read again every 10 seconds. With none, it says "Nothing logged at WARN or above". Live log shows /var/logs/system as it is written: the last 200 lines when you open it, then every new line as it arrives, up to 500 kept. It follows the newest line while you are at the bottom, and stays put when you scroll up to read. The controls at the right of Live log : Control What it does DEBUG , INFO , WARN , ERROR Shows lines at that level and above; INFO is chosen when the tab opens Pause Stops adding lines. The stream stays open and the lines that arrive meanwhile are dropped; Resume goes on Clear Empties the panel. The log itself is unchanged A yellow connecting badge means the page is reaching the stream; a blue paused badge that it is paused.

p.h: Read the logs in the terminal
p.x: dmesg prints the system log, oldest line first: # in EiN's terminal dmesg -n 50 # the last 50 lines dmesg --level warn -n 10 # the last 10 problems, as Recent problems shows them dmesg --level error # every error since EiN started 2026-10-25 21:34:13 WARN pool-worker pooled step could not run yet, kind resting 2026-10-25 21:35:02 INFO service-registry Service 'label-models' started --level filters before -n counts, so --level warn -n 10 is the last ten problems, not the problems among the last ten lines. The levels are debug , info , warn and error . Pipe it on as with any command: dmesg | grep ssh-server . For a service's output, use tail , which prints each line as the service wrote it. The examples are the ems module's ems-link and the Archive's models : # in EiN's terminal tail -n 50 /var/logs/services/ems-link/stdout.log tail -f /var/logs/services/models/stderr.log # keep following; Ctrl+C ends it ems-link: watching http://ems:8181 ems-link: down — not answering tail -f /var/logs/system follows the system log in the terminal the way the Live log does.

The container's log is on the machine EiN runs on, and compose shows it: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose logs -- tail 200 ein # the last 200 lines podman compose logs -f ein # follow; Ctrl+C ends it podman compose logs db # the database: ems or llm for the others, when installed With Docker, write docker compose . Each line reads [2026-10-25 21:35:02] [INFO ] [service-registry] Service 'label-models' started , followed by any details the message carries. This is the log to read when EiN does not start, since the tree's logs are not there until it has, and when a line in the system log needs its details: the system log keeps the message only. It also holds the admin password a new EiN prints once, Admin password set to: … , which is gone once the container is made again, as after podman compose down . The database, and the media service and the language model when installed, write only to their containers' logs. The media service covers reading its log.

How much EiN logs is set by two variables in ~/ein/.env , read when the container starts: Variable Default What it does LOG_LEVEL INFO The lowest level EiN logs: DEBUG , INFO , WARN or ERROR LOG_MODULES none A level for one part of EiN over LOG_LEVEL , by the name the log shows, such as ssh-server:DEBUG,pipeline-engine:WARN A line below the level is written nowhere: not to the system log, not to the container's log. The DEBUG button on the Live log shows DEBUG lines only once EiN writes them. Add the line to ~/ein/.env : # in ~/ein/.env LOG_MODULES =ssh-server:DEBUG Apply it, which restarts EiN: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d Take the line out again when you have what you need; DEBUG fills the logs quickly. Environment variables lists the other variables of the deployment.

p.h: Add a service of your own
p.x: A service is a folder in the tree with a start.sh , and optionally a config.json . EiN runs start.sh in its own shell, the same shell language as the terminal, as the administrator, with SERVICE_NAME and SERVICE_PATH set. This one writes the free space to its log every hour: Make the folder and the script: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mkdir -p /home/admin/services/disk-report edit /home/admin/services/disk-report/start.sh # /home/admin/services/disk-report/start.sh while true ; do df sleep 3600 done Give it a description, and have it started again when it fails, in /home/admin/services/disk-report/config.json : { "description" : "Writes the free space to its log every hour" , "restartPolicy" : "on-failure" } Register it, enable it and start it: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator service-add disk-report /home/admin/services/disk-report service-enable disk-report service-start disk-report It is on the dashboard from then on, and EiN starts it whenever it starts. Its output is in /var/logs/services/disk-report/stdout.log . The keys config.json takes: Key Default What it does description none The line under the service's name restartPolicy never on-failure starts it again when it ends with an exit code other than 0, always whenever it ends, never not at all maxRestarts 3 Restarts allowed within restartWindow before EiN leaves it failed restartWindow 60000 That window, in milliseconds stopTimeout 5000 Milliseconds a stop waits for the script to end before closing it env none Variables set for the script, as an object of names and values workClass none background makes its database work give way to people's, as EiN's own workers do statusCommand none A command whose first line of output is shown under the service's name, in place of its description checkCommand none A command answering checks for health , as JSON gaugeCommand none A command answering gauges for top and the dashboard, as JSON To take a service away, stop it, disable it and remove it: service-stop disk-report , service-disable disk-report , service-remove disk-report . Removing it removes only the registration, not the folder. A module's services are declared in the module itself; Writing a module covers them.

A service is failed, with ×3 beside it. It was restarted three times within a minute and failed again. Its stderr.log holds the output of the last attempt only, since each start empties it, so read it first: tail -n 50 /var/logs/services/<name>/stderr.log . dmesg | grep "<name>" shows EiN's lines about it, such as Service 'cpu' exited with code 1 and Service 'cpu' exceeded max restarts (3) within window ; the container's log has the details behind them. Start it again with Start once you have fixed the cause. service start: 'x' is not enabled . The service is switched off; the dashboard shows it as disabled . Run service-enable x , then service-start x . Disabling one of core's or a module's services lasts only until EiN starts again, which enables them all. service stop: service 'x' is not running or service 'x' is already running . The service was already in that state; the dashboard row may be up to 10 seconds old. service remove: 'x' is running, stop it first or 'x' is enabled, disable it first . Stop it and disable it, then remove it. service-restart: permission denied: only an administrator may run it . Sign in as admin , or use admin mode ( admin in the terminal). The dashboard shows the buttons only to the administrator. A restart of pipeline-engine takes minutes. It waits for the steps it runs to finish, for up to 16 minutes, and its row shows a spinner meanwhile. ems-link says not answering . With the ems module installed, this means the media service's container is down or still starting; ems-link only reports it. The media service has what to do. The system log starts only a little while ago. It is emptied each time EiN starts. Older lines, as far back as the container's life, are in the container's log: podman compose logs ein . The Live log says "Waiting for the stream" or shows connecting . The page has lost its connection to EiN, for example while http-server restarts. It reconnects by itself; reload the page if it does not. The web interface is gone after stopping http-server . Start it over SSH with service-start http-server , or restart the container with podman compose restart ein . Troubleshooting covers problems that are not a service's own.

This page is for the administrator who runs EiN on their own machine: what each part of EiN uses of the processor, memory and disk, how big a machine to give it, how to set the containers' memory limits, and which settings decide how much processing runs at once. The graphics card has a page of its own, The graphics card . EiN without modules needs little. Most of what this page sizes and tunes comes with modules: the media service, which the Archive needs, and the language model, which the Assistant answers with, are containers of their own, and the settings that pace media processing belong to the Archive. How big a machine they need is kept here, on this page alone.

EiN runs as two containers, ein and db , and up to four with the media service and the language model. Each has its own appetite, and three of them have a memory limit that compose sets from ~/ein/.env . Container What uses the machine Memory limit Processor ein The web interface, every shell and SSH session, the pipelines that decide what to do with each file, and the modules' services EIN_MEMORY , default 6g not limited db PostgreSQL: every node, link, setting and the search index none; 1 GB of shared memory not limited ems The media service, with --ems , for the Archive: thumbnails, video encoding, fingerprints, and the models for faces, voices, transcripts, text and vectors EMS_MEMORY , default 16g not limited llm The language model, with --llm , for the Assistant: about 5.6 GB of model, on the card or in memory LLM_MEMORY , default 10g not limited Nothing limits how many cores a container uses. With the Archive, the heavy work is in the media service: most of the Archive's pipeline steps are calls into it, and EiN mostly decides what to ask for and stores the answers. A machine running EiN Core alone, without the media service, does little beyond serving the interface and the shell.

The installer checks the machine against the first two rows of these figures before it installs anything ( What the checks measure ); the language model's row is advice it does not check: What you install Processor Memory Free disk EiN Core 2 cores 4 GB 10 GB, plus your files With the media service ( --ems ), for the Archive 4 cores; 6 or more recommended 16 GB; 32 GB recommended about 100 GB, plus your files With the language model as well ( --llm ), for the Assistant as above about 5.6 GB more, unless the model is on the card as above Cores are physical cores, not threads. With both installed, the default limits of the three containers that have one add up to 32 GB (6 + 16 + 10). On 16 GB the installer calls the memory enough with the language model left out or hosted, so leave it out or use a hosted one, as The language model describes. What the figures mean in practice: More cores let more of the Archive's media work run side by side, once you raise the settings in Let more work run at once . The defaults are set for a small machine and use few cores. More memory matters for the media service, which holds several models at once, and for long videos, which are decoded on the processor without a card. A graphics card changes how fast the models run, not what they find. On a card a recording's transcript takes about a minute; without one it takes about twice the length of the recording. The graphics card has the details. Disk holds your originals once, plus the thumbnails and other renditions EiN makes of each, plus the images and the database in the container engine's storage. Watch disk space shows how to see how fast it grows.

A memory limit is a ceiling, not a reservation: a container uses what it needs up to its limit, and the rest of the machine's memory stays free for the others. Change a limit in ~/ein/.env : Open ~/ein/.env in an editor and add or change the line for the container: # in ~/ein/.env EIN_MEMORY = 8 g EMS_MEMORY = 20 g LLM_MEMORY = 12 g The value is a number with a unit, g for gigabytes or m for megabytes. Leave out a line to keep its default. EMS_MEMORY and LLM_MEMORY matter only while the media service or the language model is installed. Make the containers again with the new limits: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d compose makes again the containers whose settings changed. EiN is down while it restarts. With Docker, write docker compose . Under podman-compose, a container that podman compose up -d makes again has no swap limit, so it may swap as much again as its memory limit; ./setup.sh makes the containers again with the swap limit. Check the new limit. In EiN's terminal, top shows EiN's memory against its limit in its Memory panel, for example 367 MB of 6.0 GB . top shows EiN's memory against its container's limit, so you see how close it comes. How to choose the limits: Keep the limits together below the machine's memory , with a few GB to spare for the database, which has no limit, and for the system itself. A container that grows is then stopped at its own limit, and the kernel does not have to pick a process to stop somewhere else on the machine. EIN_MEMORY : EiN itself, its shells and its pipelines. Raise it from the default of 6 GB if top shows EiN close to its limit during an import. EMS_MEMORY : the media service holds the models it is using and decodes videos. A video decoded on the processor is planned within a budget of 4000 MB ( EMS_CPU_ENCODE_MAX_MB ) and split into parts when it would need more, so keep the limit well above that. Its main model process restarts itself when it passes 60% of the limit, so the rest is left for the decoding and the tools. LLM_MEMORY : the model and its working memory. The default fits the default model; The language model explains which other models the container can run.

p.h: When a container reaches its limit
p.x: When a container needs more than its limit, the kernel stops one of its processes. Each container restarts by itself if its main process stops, and the work it had in hand is picked up again: a pipeline step that was interrupted runs again, as long as it has attempts left. To see whether that happened, read the kernel's log on the machine: # on the machine EiN runs on sudo dmesg | grep -i 'out of memory' A line that names Memory cgroup out of memory is a container that reached its limit. Raise that container's limit, or lower the work that runs at once ( Let more work run at once describes the settings, which work in both directions). The media service's model processes log a warning of their own when the models alone do not fit under their ceiling, ending in "Raise CFG_MODEL_MAX_RSS if this is the real footprint." For the media service, set it as EMS_MODEL_MAX_RSS in ~/ein/.env , such as EMS_MODEL_MAX_RSS=12g , or raise EMS_MEMORY , which raises the ceiling with it.

This section and the next two apply with the Archive installed. New files go through its pipelines, and the pipelines' heavy steps go to two workers inside EiN, which decide how much runs at once. Both are services of the Archive module, and both are paced by the Archive's settings in Settings → System , category Processing . Worker Runs Paced by cpu Unpacking zips, reading metadata, thumbnails and posters, fingerprints, duplicates, matching faces to people, staging's dating and grouping, video and audio encoding CPU budget for media work ( CFG_CPU_SLOTS , default 2 ) models Faces, picture vectors, text in pictures, text vectors, transcripts, voices and shots: each a request to the media service's models Model requests in flight ( CFG_MODEL_SLOTS , default 2 ) The CPU budget is shared by cost: most jobs take 1 of it, and a video's encoding takes 2. With the default budget of 2, an encoding runs alone, while two smaller jobs can run together. Matching faces to people has a higher priority than encoding, so a queue of videos does not hold up people appearing in the interface. Processing pictures lists every setting of the two workers. The models worker takes turns between its kinds of work. It stays on one kind for up to Model backlog rotation (ms) ( CFG_MODEL_KIND_QUANTUM_MS , an hour) while others are waiting, so that faces, which keep coming during an import, do not hold back the transcripts. The media service has its own limits on how much it runs at once, set in ~/ein/.env : Variable Default What it bounds EMS_LIMIT_MODELS 8 Model requests running at once EMS_LIMIT_TOOLS 4 Tool work at once: reading metadata, thumbnails, fingerprints EMS_LIMIT_ENCODES 2 Whole-file work at once: video encoding, storyboards, finding shots EMS_QUEUE_DEPTH 64 Requests that may wait for a place; past it the media service answers that it is busy, and EiN tries again later EMS_INTERACTIVE_RESERVE 1 Extra places for models and tools, kept for a person waiting, such as a search, so that processing never makes them wait behind it EiN's settings decide how much it asks for; the media service's decide how much it does. Asking for more than the media service runs at once only moves the wait into its queue.

p.h: Let more work run at once
p.x: With the Archive, on a machine with more cores than the minimum, raise the CPU budget so that more thumbnails, fingerprints and encodings run side by side: Sign in as an administrator and choose Settings in the sidebar, under System . Choose the category Processing . Set CPU budget for media work to the number of jobs you want at once, for example 4 on a machine with 6 cores, and choose Save change . The line under it says "Restarted cpu." If you set the budget above 4, raise CPU worker slots ( CFG_CPU_WORKERS ) to the same number. It caps how many jobs can be in flight whatever the budget. Watch the result on the Dashboard , on its Work tab, as described in Watch it keep up . Most of these jobs are work for the media service, so with a budget above 4, raise EMS_LIMIT_TOOLS in ~/ein/.env to match and run podman compose up -d . Warning Keep CPU budget for media work at 2 or more. A video's encoding takes 2 of the budget, and with 1 no video is ever encoded. With a graphics card that has room to spare, or many cores for the models, raise Model requests in flight the same way; it restarts the models service. Keep it at or below EMS_LIMIT_MODELS . More requests at once do not always finish sooner: the media service runs the requests for one model one after another, so the gain comes from different kinds of work overlapping. From the terminal, the same changes are: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator config set CFG_CPU_SLOTS 4 config set CFG_MODEL_SLOTS 4 config unset CFG_CPU_SLOTS # back to the default The other settings in Processing are core's and tune the pipeline engine itself: how many steps, queue entries and triggers it handles at once, and how often it cleans up. Their defaults suit any machine EiN runs on, and Processing and pipelines explains what they do. Every one is listed on Settings .

p.h: Keep the interface quick during heavy work
p.x: While the media service works through the Archive's import, people still search and browse. Several things keep their requests ahead of the processing without any setting: The media service answers searches from a model process of its own, on the processor, while the processing runs in another at a lower priority ( EMS_WORKER_NICE , default 10 ). When the card has been free of processing for 10 minutes ( EMS_CARD_QUIET_AFTER , 600 seconds), searches move to the card. A search uses at most a few cores ( EMS_QUERY_WORKER_THREADS , the machine's cores less two, at most 4), so it does not wait on threads the processing holds. EMS_INTERACTIVE_RESERVE keeps a place free for a person waiting. If the interface still feels slow on a small machine during an import, lower CPU budget for media work back towards 2 and Model requests in flight towards 1 until the import is done. The work waits in its queue and costs nothing there.

Your originals take the space they take. On top of them, with the Archive, EiN keeps, in the data folder's files-volatile , the thumbnails, posters, storyboards and the AV1 versions of videos it makes for the browser, which it can make again if they are lost. In EiN's terminal, df shows each storage tier's free space, how fast it grows a day, and when it will be full at that rate, with the size of the database: # in EiN's terminal df The same figures are on the Dashboard , and top 's Disk panel shows them live. Files and storage explains the tiers. The container engine keeps the images, the build's scratch files and the database in its own storage, usually ~/.local/share/containers for rootless podman and /var/lib/docker for Docker, which may be another disk than your data folder. Each update builds new images, and setup.sh removes the ones they replaced once the new EiN answers; a build's intermediate stages and other images without a name stay. To see what the images take, and to remove the unnamed ones no container uses: # on the machine EiN runs on podman system df podman image prune With Docker, write docker for podman . podman image prune removes only images without a name that no container uses; the database is a volume and is never touched by it. Never add --volumes to a prune: ein_db is your database.

Whether the machine is big enough shows in whether it keeps up with the work: Where What it tells you The Dashboard 's badge Healthy : nothing is waiting. Catching up : work is waiting and some of it, or a pipeline instance, finished in the last hour. Stuck : work is waiting and none finished in the last hour. Needs a person : a check failed The Dashboard 's Work tab Each kind of work, what is left of it, how fast it goes, and when it will be done top The processor, EiN's memory and the event loop's lag, the disks, and the work, live host-metrics EiN's processor and memory use now and over the last 6 hours ( --window in minutes) pool-stat The backlog, rates and policy of each kind of work in the queues gauges What the running services report beside the machine's figures, such as the card's memory ems-status With the ems module: the media service's models, what it is running, its queues and the memory of its model processes Catching up after an import is normal; the time it takes depends on the machine and on how much there is. A machine that is too small shows as a Work tab whose time to completion keeps growing while new files come in, or as containers stopped at their memory limits. Health and the dashboard explains the badge, the checks and the tabs.

The Dashboard reads Stuck. Nothing has finished in the last hour. Read the checks under the badge on the Overview tab: they name the kind of work that is not moving and why, with the Archive often the media service not answering. Troubleshooting goes through the causes. Videos in the Archive never get their browser version. Check that CPU budget for media work is 2 or more, and on the Work tab whether transcode is waiting. Without a graphics card, a long video takes many minutes to encode. A container restarts on its own. Look for Memory cgroup out of memory in the kernel log as in When a container reaches its limit , and raise that container's limit. The whole machine slows down or stops responding during an import. The containers together are using more memory than the machine has. Lower the limits so that they fit the machine, or leave out the language model, and lower the processing settings while the import runs. Searches are slow while an Archive import runs. Lower Model requests in flight and CPU budget for media work for the duration of the import, as in Keep the interface quick during heavy work . The disk fills up. Run df in EiN's terminal to see which tier grows, and podman system df on the machine to see what the container engine's storage takes. EiN has no command that moves the data folder; Your data: backup, moving and removing explains how.
