Applies to new detections; a box below it is not stored unless someone tags it by hand. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.7 Kind number From the module Archive

Minimum face size (px) . The shorter side a face box must have, in pixels of the displayed photo, to be kept as a face. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 24 Kind number From the module Archive

Size to start a new person from a face (px) . The shorter side, in pixels, a face that matches nobody must have before it starts a new, unnamed person. Small faces stay unknown rather than seeding people from blur. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 48 Kind number From the module Archive

Archive language . The language the archive is kept in: the order names are sorted in, the words it offers as labels, and how it describes how two people are related. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default en Choices en , sv Kind select

Media service address . Where EMS answers. Every model and media-tool request goes there; the models themselves are configured on the EMS side. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default http://127.0.0.1:8181 Kind string Restarts models , cpu , ems-link , metrics-sampler From the module Media service

Media service check interval (seconds) . How often the ems-link service asks whether EMS answers, and logs when that changes. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 60 Kind number Restarts ems-link From the module Media service

Media service key . The bearer key EMS expects (one of the lines in its keys file), sent only to the media service address above. Unset when EMS runs without keys. No shell sees it, and nothing shows it once it is set. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default none: a key is set by you, and never shown again Kind a key: never readable, in no shell Restarts ems-link From the module Media service

Media service restart patience (seconds) . How long a batch request keeps retrying a refused connection before the step fails. EMS restarts refuse connections for tens of seconds; this is what keeps the steps in flight across one from failing for good. Interactive requests never wait. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 90 Kind number Restarts models , cpu From the module Media service

Module sources . Where published modules are looked for: organisations on GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea, as their addresses separated by spaces, such as https://github.com/einhq . Each repository named module- in them is a module. A module installed by name comes from the first source that has it, and a module's dependencies from its own organisation first. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default https://github.com/einhq Kind string

Tokens for module sources . Access tokens for module sources that are not public, as host=token separated by spaces, such as forge.example:3000=… github.com=…. Each token is sent to its own host only. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default none: a key is set by you, and never shown again Kind a key: never readable, in no shell

HTTP port . The port the web interface listens on. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 8080 Kind number Takes effect Takes effect the next time the server starts — restarting it from here would drop this connection.
SSH port . The port the SSH and SFTP server listens on. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 2222 Kind number Takes effect Takes effect the next time the server starts.
Ken Burns effect . Slowly pan and zoom each photo during a slideshow. Who it is for Each person (Profile → Preferences) Default true Kind boolean From the module Archive
Seconds per slide . How long each photo is shown in a slideshow. Who it is for Each person (Profile → Preferences) Default 3 Kind number From the module Archive

CPU budget for media work . How much CPU-bound media work runs at once. Each job declares what it costs, so one video transcode can exclude a face assignment on a small box. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 2 Kind number Restarts cpu From the module Archive

CPU slots for downstream media . Soft reservation for non-ingest CPU work. Ingest borrows unused slots, but ready downstream jobs get them first so a continuous ingest backlog cannot starve the rest of the pipeline. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 1 Kind number Restarts cpu From the module Archive

CPU worker slots . Upper bound on concurrent CPU media jobs. The budget above is the real limit; this only caps how many can be in flight. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 4 Kind number Restarts cpu From the module Archive

Entry pipeline reservation (%) . Share of trigger claims that first try pipelines declaring options.entryPoint. Empty reserved claims fall back to the ordinary fair rotation. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0 Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine

Gap check interval (seconds) . How often the background check looks for media missing something a pipeline should have given it, when nothing else is waiting to be processed. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 900 Kind number Restarts media-heal From the module Archive

Keep transcripts current . Videos and recordings transcribed with other speech-recognition settings than the media service runs now are transcribed again in the background, behind new media. Set to "off" to leave existing transcripts alone. On a large library a change of settings means hours of background work. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty Kind string From the module Archive

Model backlog rotation (ms) . How long the models worker stays on one backlog (faces, picture vectors, text in pictures, text vectors, transcripts, voices) before rotating to the next when work remains on more than one. Faces outrank the other backlogs and a crawl finds new ones continuously, so without this they would starve the rest outright. Each rotation costs the media service a minute or two of loading models and of slots waiting for the last long step of the old backlog, so an hour puts throughput before the wait of the other backlogs; a backlog with no work hands its turn on at once either way. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 3600000 Kind number Restarts models From the module Archive

Model requests in flight . How many model-bound media steps (faces, picture vectors, text in pictures, text vectors, transcripts, voices) EiN keeps in flight against the media service at once. Whether each runs on the GPU or the CPU is the media service's decision; size this against its own model limit, since more slots than it runs at once only move the wait into its queue. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 2 Kind number Restarts models From the module Archive
Pipeline cleanup interval (seconds) . How often finished pipeline instances are pruned. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 3600 Kind number Restarts pipeline-pruner

Pipeline instances held open . How many pipeline instances the engine holds open at once, including those waiting on a worker pool. Every stuck sweep re-advances each open instance, so raise it together with the sweep interval. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 5000 Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine

Pipeline steps in parallel . How many inline pipeline steps the engine runs at once. Steps that are GPU- or CPU-heavy go to a worker pool instead and are bounded separately. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 4 Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine
Queue consume concurrency . How many queue entries the engine consumes in parallel. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 4 Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine

Quiet step warning (ms) . How long a running pipeline step may go without writing any output before the pipeline overview flags it. A flagged step keeps running: no step is ever stopped for taking long. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 1800000 Kind number

Rest after a full gap check (seconds) . How long the background gap check waits after it has been through the whole archive before it starts over. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 21600 Kind number Restarts media-heal From the module Archive

Second models worker's slots . Slots of a second worker for the model-bound media steps, which goes through the same backlogs in the reverse order, so the media service runs a second model family beside the first worker's. 0 leaves it off. Size both workers' slots together against the media service's model limit, and mind its card: two families' models must fit there, or one runs on the CPU. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0 Kind number Restarts models-second From the module Archive

Steps held in flight . How many dispatched steps the engine holds in memory before it stops claiming triggers. Work beyond it waits in the pool, where it costs nothing. Empty means 25 times the pipeline steps in parallel. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means 25 × pipeline steps in parallel Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine

Stuck sweep interval (ms) . How often, at most, the engine re-advances its open instances to repair any that stopped without finishing, and how long it backs off while admission is full. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 60000 Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine

Trigger concurrency . How many pipeline triggers the engine evaluates at once against incoming VFS events. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 4 Kind number Restarts pipeline-engine

Worker backlog rotation (ms) . How long a pipeline worker that serves several kinds of job stays on one before rotating to the next when work remains on both. 0 always takes the highest-priority kind. Applies to workers whose service does not set its own rotation. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0 Kind number Takes effect Read by each pipeline worker when it starts: restart the services that run one.

Command finder . The command that finds shell commands by what they are for, in the documentation's command search. Empty matches the words against command names and descriptions. The assistant sets itself here when it is installed. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means a match on names and descriptions Kind string

Language model command . The command that asks a language model, for reading what a person writes as they write it — the search box's parser reads people, locations and words with it. Empty asks no model. The assistant sets itself here when it is installed. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means no model Kind string

Search parser . The command that reads what is typed into the search box as filters — people, locations, years, kinds. Empty searches the words as they are. Archive sets its parser here when it is installed. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means the words as they are Kind string

Text embedder . The command that turns texts into vectors, for finding by meaning — the command finder ranks commands with it. Empty finds by words alone. The media service sets itself here when it is installed. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means by words alone Kind string

Session cleanup interval (seconds) . How often expired sessions and stranded terminals are collected, and expired share links turned off. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 3600 Kind number Restarts session-reaper

Session cookie lifetime . How long a browser keeps its session cookie. Refreshed on every navigation, so this bounds idleness rather than total session age. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 86400 Kind number

Session expiry . How long after its last activity a session is collected by the reaper. A session keeps the value it was created with; one holding an open terminal is never collected, whatever this says. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 43200 Kind number

Terminal reconnect grace . How long an interactive terminal survives without a browser connection, allowing reloads and short network interruptions to reattach. A change applies from the next disconnect. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 300 Kind number

How widely what you create is shared . Where anything you create as shared starts out: private, shared with its group, or with everyone who has an account. "Default" follows the system setting. Who it is for Each person (Profile → Preferences) Default default Choices default , private , shared , everyone Kind select
Shell history length . How many commands the terminal remembers between sessions. Who it is for Each person (Profile → Preferences) Default 1000 Kind number

Hours in /tmp . How long a file left in /tmp, such as a picture sent to search with, is kept before it is removed. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 24 Kind number Restarts tmp-sweeper

Silence that splits speech (ms) . How long a pause must be before transcription treats it as the end of a stretch of speech. Empty uses the media service's own setting. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means the media service decides Kind number From the module Media service

Transcription language . The language spoken in recordings, as a code such as sv or en, sent with every transcription. Empty lets the media service detect it, or use its own default. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means the media service decides Kind string From the module Media service

Word timings . 1 asks transcription for the time of every word, 0 for timings per segment only. Empty uses the media service's own setting. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means the media service decides Choices 1 , 0 Kind select From the module Media service
Days in the trash . How long a trashed file stays restorable before it is removed for good. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 30 Kind number Restarts trash-purger

Default group . The group anything created as shared belongs to. This is the grant that lets the rest of the household see it. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default users Kind group

Default groups for new users . The groups a new account joins besides its own, as a comma-separated list of names. The New user form starts with them ticked, and user-create takes them unless --groups names others. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default users Kind string

Default owner . Who owns anything created as shared. Leave empty to let whoever creates it own it. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default empty, which means the person who creates it Kind user

Default permissions . Who may see and who may change anything created as shared: its owner, its group and everyone else, each with no access, view or edit. Everyone else is visitors who are not signed in, where they may browse, and anyone with an account outside the group. Kept as an octal mode, as in 0750. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0750 Kind mode

Visitors may browse . Whether someone who has not signed in may browse the archive as the guest, seeing what is shared with visitors, rather than being asked to sign in. Off, the guest can only sign in or open a share link, in the web interface and through the API alike. Only on does the assistant's language model answer them. Off for a family's own archive; on for a public demo. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default false Kind boolean

Lip-sync vote weight . How much it counts, as a similarity, that a person's face is seen speaking in step with the voice. Only voices someone named or locked are weighed against it. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.9 Kind number From the module Archive

Minimum lip-sync score . How clearly a face must be seen speaking in step with a voice before that counts as a vote at all. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.6 Kind number From the module Archive

Speech to start a new person (seconds) . How long a voice that matches nobody must have spoken in a recording, in all, before it starts a new, unnamed person. Voices heard for less stay unknown. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 10 Kind number From the module Archive

Voice likeness to the person . How similar a voice must be to the average of a person's voices before it joins them. Stops a person drifting from one speaker to the next through a chain of loosely similar voices. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.7 Kind number From the module Archive

Voice likeness to the person seen speaking . How similar a voice must be to the average of a person's voices before a face seen speaking with it may join them. Lower than the plain likeness bar, since the face is evidence too; it stops the camera operator's voice going to whoever is in frame. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.5 Kind number From the module Archive

Voice match threshold . How similar a voice in a recording must be to a known voice before it is attached to that person. Higher is stricter and produces fewer wrong matches but more unknown speakers. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.55 Kind number From the module Archive

Voice neighbour similarity . How similar a known voice must be to count as a vote for its person. Voices less alike than this are ignored when deciding who is speaking. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 0.5 Kind number From the module Archive

Voice neighbours compared . How many of the most similar known voices are compared with each unknown one. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 24 Kind number From the module Archive

Voice winner margin . How far the leading person's votes must outweigh the runner-up's before a voice is attached. 1.2 means 20% more; higher leaves close calls unknown. Who it is for Everyone (an administrator sets it) Default 1.2 Kind number From the module Archive
The variables EiN reads or sets, apart from its settings ( CFG_… ), which are on Settings . In the shell, docs env lists them with their values there.

Read once, from EiN's own environment, when it starts: .env in an installation made with the installer. No shell has them, and none is shown back, since POSTGRES_URL carries the database's password. Variable Default What it is POSTGRES_URL postgres://ein:ein@127.0.0.1:5432/ein The PostgreSQL database holding the whole tree. POSTGRES_POOL_MAX 20 Database connections the process may hold at once. Parallel work queues on this long before PostgreSQL itself is the limit. POSTGRES_POOL_RESERVED 4 Of those, connections background work may never take, so an interactive command never waits behind a crawl. 0 is first come, first served. POSTGRES_LISTEN_POOL_MAX 4 Connections kept apart for change notifications, which hold theirs for good. FILE_ROOT_PATH ./files Host directory where file content is stored. VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH FILE_ROOT_PATH Host directory for content that can be made again — thumbnails, crops, transcodes — so it can live on a faster or cheaper disk. FILE_TMP_PATH /tmp Host directory for temporary files while content is written. DOCS_PATH ./guide Host directory mounted as the guide at /usr/docs/guide: the documentation at einhq.eu, as the image bundles it or a checkout of the site. Without one the Docs page links to einhq.eu. In a shell the same name is the tree path /usr/docs. DEV_MODULES_PATH ./modules The deployment's modules: a folder of module checkouts mounted read-only at /tmp/dev-modules and linked into /usr/modules. A name here wins over an installed module of the same name. In a shell the same name is that tree path. MODULE_INSTALL_PATH ./modules-installed Host directory mod install puts modules in, mounted read-write at /var/lib/modules. A folder of the host mounted into the container keeps the installed modules when the container is replaced. INSTALL_MODULES Modules boot installs with mod install when they are not installed: names or repository addresses, separated by spaces. One installed already is left as it is; mod install and the settings page update it. INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD The admin account's first password, set at the first start of a new instance. Without it that start sets a random one and prints it to the log once. Changing it later does nothing; the account's password is changed in Settings or with user-passwd . INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD The admin account's first password, set at the first start of a new instance; without it that start sets a random one and prints it to the log once. Changing it later does nothing: the account's password is changed in Settings or with user-passwd . TZ the host's zone Time zone for log lines, "today", and which year a date late on New Year's Eve belongs to. LOG_LEVEL INFO How much the process logs: DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR. LOG_MODULES Per-component log levels over LOG_LEVEL, such as ssh-server:DEBUG,pipeline:WARN. EXTERNAL_COMMANDS_CONFIG external-commands.json File listing the host programs shell commands may run. COMMAND_LOOKUP_TTL_MS 5000 How long a command name found on PATH is remembered before it is looked up again. DEBUG_LOCKS Set to 1 to record who holds each lock and warn about one held for more than five seconds.

Where the tree keeps each kind of thing, exported for every shell, so cd $LOGS_PATH works wherever the folder lives. Variable Default What it is ARCHIVE_PATH The archive: everything people put in and look at. TAGS_PATH Labels, one directory per label holding links to what carries it. HOMES_PATH One home directory per user, owned by the user. ETC_PATH System configuration: settings, groups, services, boot scripts. USERS_PATH The accounts: one user node per account, the administrator's. GROUPS_PATH Groups. SERVICES_PATH Service definitions. INIT_FILES_PATH Files installed into the tree at boot. INIT_PATH Boot scripts. VAR_PATH What the system writes as it runs. LOGS_PATH Logs and metrics. SESSIONS_PATH Open sessions. LINKS_PATH Share links: one node per link that opens an album without signing in. QUEUES_PATH Queues. PIPELINE_QUEUE_PATH The queue the pipeline engine works from. POOLS_PATH Job pools. PIPELINES_PATH Pipeline definitions and running instances. WWW_PATH Web pages served over HTTP. MOD_INSTALL_PATH The modules mod install installed, each linked into /usr/modules. USR_PATH Code and read-only payload. BIN_PATH Built-in commands. LIB_PATH Core's other files: its shell commands, its services and the web interface. MOD_PATH Installed modules. DOCS_PATH This documentation. TEMP_PATH Temporary nodes. DEV_MODULES_PATH The deployment's modules, mounted read-only. VAR_DIRS The directories under /var, as names separated by spaces, for boot scripts to loop over.

What EiN exports for every shell at its start besides the folders: the built-in accounts and the host folders its storage is on. Variable Default What it is INSTANCE_MODE What this process was started as: primary, or test. ADMIN_USERNAME The built-in administrator account. ADMIN_GROUPNAME Its group. ADMIN_UID Its user id. ADMIN_GID Its group's id. GUEST_USERNAME The account a visitor who has not signed in acts as. GUEST_GROUPNAME Its group. GUEST_UID Its user id. GUEST_GID Its group's id. USERS_GROUPNAME The group every account belongs to: what "everyone" means when sharing. USERS_GID Its id. EIN_PATH_EXPORTS The layout variables as export lines, written into /etc/layout at boot. EIN_FILE_ROOT_PATH Where file content is stored on the host, as FILE_ROOT_PATH gave it: what the dashboard reports disk use for. EIN_VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH The same for content that can be made again. EIN_FILE_TMP_PATH The same for temporary files. EXTERNAL_FILE_ROOT_PATH FILE_ROOT_PATH as boot received it, for the init scripts. EXTERNAL_VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH as boot received it. EXTERNAL_FILE_TMP_PATH FILE_TMP_PATH as boot received it. EXTERNAL_DOCS_PATH DOCS_PATH as boot received it: what is mounted at /usr/docs/guide. EXTERNAL_DEV_MODULES_PATH DEV_MODULES_PATH as boot received it. EXTERNAL_MODULE_INSTALL_PATH MODULE_INSTALL_PATH as boot received it.

Set by the server that opened the shell: the web interface, the terminal panel or SSH. Variable Default What it is USER Your user name. HOME Your home directory, holding your settings (.config) and shell history. PATH Where commands are looked up, first directory first: core's commands, then each installed module's bin directory. TMPDIR Where commands put temporary nodes. PWD The directory you are in. OLDPWD The directory you were in before, where cd - goes. UID Your user id. GID Your primary group's id. SID The session this shell belongs to. PID The running command's own id, its name and a unique suffix. TTY_NAME The terminal this shell is attached to, when it has one. TERM The terminal type an interactive shell reports to programs. HOSTNAME The host name shown in the prompt. COOKIE_NAME The browser cookie that carries a web session.

Nobody sets these for you. Export one in a shell, or put it in front of a command, to change how commands behave there: JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls . Variable Default What it is JSON_OUTPUT Set to 1 and commands answer in JSON instead of text. The web interface runs every command this way. MEDIA_LINES 20 How many text lines tall cat draws a picture in a terminal. SEARCH_TRACE Set to 1 and search reports how long each of its sources took. CFG_PASSWORD_HASH_LOGN 16 The scrypt work factor for new password hashes, as a power of two. Lowered by the test tier, where the passwords protect nothing; leave it unset anywhere else. NOMINATIM_SEARCH_URL https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search Where geocoding asks Nominatim for an address, as geocode-location and location-region do. Point it at your own server to avoid the public one's rate limit. From the archive module.

Set for each step of a pipeline by the change that started it. Variable Default What it is NODE_PATH The node the event is about. EVENT_TYPE What happened, as a dotted name such as media.metadata.extracted. EVENT_ID The event's id. EVENT_SOURCE What raised the event, such as archive-bridge. EVENT_DATA The event's details as JSON. Each field is also its own variable: mimetype becomes EVENT_MIMETYPE, deviceSerial EVENT_DEVICE_SERIAL.
Every node has a type, which decides what it holds and how it behaves. These are the 24 types of an EiN with all its modules. Nodes and node types explains what a node is.

What the archive is made of: what people add, and what EiN works out about it. Type What it is Lives under Module album Album A collection of photos and videos that behaves as a directory. It holds its files, and links the ones added to it from elsewhere. It remembers its cover, the time span of its media, and the stacks of similar photos taken in a row. /archive/albums Archive album-profile Album profile A summary of a library album's members — their times, days, places, people and a few pictures that stand for how it looks — kept beside it as its .profile child, which staging matches suggested groups against. Archive device Device A camera, phone or tracker, matched by make, model and serial number. Knows its time zone, so photos without one get their capture time right. /archive/devices Archive exif EXIF The metadata read from a media file — camera, capture time, exposure, position — kept as a child of the file. Archive file File Stored bytes with a name, a mimetype, a size and a checksum: a photo, a video, a document, an event text. Media files carry what was read from them (capture time, orientation, faces) and hold their derived pieces — thumbnails, captions, EXIF — as children. Core location Location A location under /archive/locations: its name, the address it was written down with and how that was geocoded, the people who lived there and the photos linked to it. Where it is on the map is its child named position, a point, circle or outline. /archive/locations Archive media-region Region A box on a photo, kept under the photo's regions/ directory: a face the detector found, a box someone drew, or a tag imported from the old archive. It carries who is in it. A region that shows a usable face has the face's vector as a child named embedding, and only those take part in face recognition. Archive person Person Someone in the archive, with names, dates of birth and death, and contact details. Parents, children and partners are links between people; the photos they appear in are found by their faces. /archive/people Archive position Position A point on the map with an optional radius or outline. A photo, a location or an event keeps where it is as a child named position. Core track Track The route a device recorded, kept as the device's child named track: timestamped GPS points, live or from imported GPX files, summarised by their extent and time span. Core

How the tree is arranged: folders, links, and what holds other nodes. Type What it is Lives under Module directory Directory A folder that holds other nodes. The archive roots — albums, people, locations, devices and labels — are directories. Core group Group A set of users, under /etc/groups. A node's group, and any group in its ACL, decides who besides the owner may read or change it. Core softlink Softlink A pointer to another node by path, followed transparently. Album covers, pictures added to an album, labels and the relations between people and locations are all softlinks. Core user User An account that can sign in, under /home. Owns nodes, belongs to groups, and keeps its settings and shell history in its home directory. Core

How EiN runs: its commands, logs, queues and the other parts of the system that are nodes too. Type What it is Lives under Module command Command A built-in shell command, carrying its own description, arguments and flags. Commands a module adds are files in the module's bin directory instead. Core embedding Embedding A numeric fingerprint of an image, a face or a text, kept for similarity search: what finds photos by what they show and faces of the same person. Core log Log An append-only record of lines kept for a retention period, such as the system log under /var/logs. Core null Null /dev/null: reading it gives nothing and what is written to it is thrown away, for output nobody wants. Core pool Pool Background jobs waiting for a worker with the right resources, under /var/pools. pool stat shows what is waiting. Core queue Queue A durable first-in, first-out buffer; reading an entry removes it. The pipeline engine takes its work from one. Core router Router A live broadcast channel: what is written reaches every current reader and nothing is kept. /dev/events is one. Core session Session A signed-in connection — a browser, an SSH login, a service — under /var/sessions. Removed when it ends. Core share-link Share link A link that opens an album, and what it holds, to whoever has it, without signing in; under /var/links, with when it expires and how often it was opened. share-link makes, lists and turns them off. Core tty Terminal An interactive terminal belonging to a session, with its size and working directory. Core

Every file that configures EiN, where it lives, what writes it and what reads it: the installation's files on the machine EiN runs on, and the files in EiN's own tree. This page is for administrators, and for anyone who wants to know which file a setting or a habit of the shell comes from. There are two places to look: On the machine EiN runs on , in the folder EiN was installed in ( ~/ein with the installer): .env , the compose files and setup.sh . They decide what runs and with which environment, and change only when you edit them or run setup.sh . In EiN's tree , under /etc and in each home: ordinary files kept in the database, which you read with cat and change with edit in EiN's terminal. They survive a restart and an update like the rest of the tree. How the settings in these files combine, and how to change a setting without touching a file, is on Configuration . Every setting is listed on Settings , and every other variable on Environment variables .

The installer fetches the deployment into ~/ein and runs setup.sh there. After the first run the folder holds: Path Made by What it is .env setup.sh , the first run The settings and passwords of this installation, and the environment of EiN and the media service. Yours to edit. compose.yaml the deployment EiN and its database, the base of every installation. compose.ems.yaml the deployment The media service, which the Archive needs, added with --ems . compose.llm.yaml the deployment The language model the Assistant uses, added with --llm . compose.override.yaml setup.sh , every run The options chosen in .env , as compose services. Written again on every run; do not edit it. setup.sh the deployment Brings this folder up to date, fetches the sources, writes .env and compose.override.yaml , pulls the images or builds them from your own source, and starts them. src/ setup.sh The sources it fetches: ems and llm when those options are on, and core and db from any source but GitHub's einhq , which it builds with ems . data/ setup.sh Your files, unless EIN_DATA named another folder at the install. See The data folder . The files from the deployment are replaced when setup.sh brings the folder up to date at the start of every run, so changes belong in .env , not in compose.yaml . setup.sh --help lists its options, and Installing in detail explains each. The database is not in the folder: it is the container engine's volume ein_db , or the folder setup.sh --db-dir named. Your data: backup, moving and removing says how to keep it.

.env is read in two ways. Compose reads it to fill in compose.yaml , and EiN's and the media service's containers get every line of it as their environment. setup.sh writes it once, with mode 0600 , and from then on changes only the lines its options set: EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM , EIN_MODULES , EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY and EIN_DB_DIR , and adds EIN_ENGINE to a .env written before it had that line. It also moves EIN_HTTP_PORT or EIN_SSH_PORT to the next free port when another program holds it, and with a Forgejo or Gitea source keeps CFG_MODULE_SOURCES and CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY in step with EIN_SOURCE . The file the installer writes looks like this, with your own values: # ~/ein/.env, on the machine EiN runs on COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME =ein EIN_ENGINE =podman EIN_EMS = 0 EIN_LLM = 0 EIN_GPU = 0 EIN_MODULES = "" EIN_DATA =/home/helen/ein/data POSTGRES_PASSWORD =… EMS_KEY =… TZ =Europe/London INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD =… EIN_BIND = 0.0 . 0.0 EIN_HTTP_PORT = 8080 EIN_SSH_PORT = 2222 # CFG_LLM_URL=https://api.openai.com # CFG_LLM_KEY= # CFG_LLM_PROVIDER=OpenAI # CFG_LLM_MODEL= EIN_SOURCE =https://github.com/einhq EIN_SOURCE_KEY = EIN_DB_DIR= Line What it does Explained on COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME ein , the name of the containers, network and volumes. EIN_ENGINE podman or docker , the engine setup.sh picked at the install and keeps to. Installing in detail EIN_EMS 1 runs the media service. --ems and --no-ems set it. The media service EIN_LLM 1 runs the language model. --llm and --no-llm set it. The language model EIN_GPU 1 gives the graphics card to the media service and the language model. The first run sets it when it finds a card with its CDI file. The graphics card EIN_MODULES The modules EiN installs at its start when they are missing, separated by spaces. --module adds a name. Modules EIN_DATA The data folder, as an absolute path. Installing in detail POSTGRES_PASSWORD The database's password, made at the install. EMS_KEY The media service's key, made at the install. Both EiN and the media service get it. The media service TZ The time zone, taken from the machine at the install. Environment variables INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD The admin account's first password, made at the install. EiN takes it at its first start only; setup.sh prints it at the end of every run until you delete the line, once you have changed the password. Install EiN EIN_BIND The address the ports are published on. 127.0.0.1 keeps them to the machine. Ports, HTTPS and remote access EIN_HTTP_PORT The machine's port for the web interface. Ports, HTTPS and remote access EIN_SSH_PORT The machine's port for SSH and SFTP. Ports, HTTPS and remote access CFG_LLM_… The Assistant's settings for a hosted language model in place of --llm , commented out until you use it. The language model EIN_SOURCE The organisation the sources are cloned from. --source sets it. Installing in detail EIN_SOURCE_KEY The token that reads the source's repositories when they are private. A --source on another host empties it, unless EIN_SOURCE_KEY in the environment gives a new one. Installing in detail EIN_DB_DIR The database's folder; empty keeps it in the engine's volume ein_db . --db-dir sets it. Installing in detail Lines you can add: Line Read by What it does CFG_… EiN Gives a setting its value, shown as From deployment . See the exceptions below. EMS_… the media service Configures the media service. EIN_MEMORY , EMS_MEMORY , LLM_MEMORY compose The most memory each container may use: 6g , 16g and 10g unless set. LLM_GGUF_REPO , LLM_GGUF_FILE , LLM_IMAGE , LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB compose The language model's file, image and share of the card. Four settings are fixed by compose.yaml , which wins over .env : CFG_HTTP_PORT ( 8080 ), CFG_SSH_PORT ( 2222 ), and the ems module's CFG_EMS_URL ( http://ems:8181 ) and CFG_EMS_KEY (the value of EMS_KEY ). A line for them in .env changes nothing. The Assistant's CFG_LLM_URL is read from .env and is http://llm:8190 when the line is missing. With --llm , compose.override.yaml also sets CFG_LLM_CARD to card or cpu after EIN_GPU . To apply a change to .env : # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d # or: docker compose up -d Under podman-compose, a container that podman compose up -d makes again has no swap limit, which setup.sh gives each one: the media service's idle models then go to swap, and a search waits for them. Running ./setup.sh makes the containers again with it, and applies .env too, but also fetches and builds the newest sources; Updating explains it. After a change to EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM or EIN_GPU , run setup.sh , since only it writes them into compose.override.yaml . Warning .env holds the database password and the media service's key, and no other file keeps them. Keep a copy of it with your backups.

setup.sh writes this file from .env on every run, and every compose reads it beside compose.yaml on its own, so podman compose up -d starts the same services as setup.sh does. Under podman, with the media service, the language model and a card, it reads: # Written by setup.sh from the options in .env and the container engine; edit those and run # setup.sh again. services: db: restart: always ein: environment: CFG_LLM_CARD: card restart: always ems: extends: { file: compose.ems.yaml , service: ems } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always llm: extends: { file: compose.llm.yaml , service: llm } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always Under podman every service gets restart: always , the policy podman starts again at boot; under Docker those lines are left out. A change made by hand is gone at the next run of setup.sh .

EIN_DATA is the folder for what is yours outside the database. setup.sh makes its subfolders, and the containers mount them: Folder Mounted in EiN at What it holds files /files The originals. old /old Older originals. files-volatile /files-volatile Renditions EiN can make again: thumbnails, crops, transcodes. files-tmp /files-tmp Scratch space while content is written. modules /modules-installed The modules EiN installed, which it sees in its tree at /var/lib/modules . llm not in EiN; the language model's /models The downloaded model. The media service, when installed, mounts the same four file folders at the same paths, the originals read-only. Files and storage explains how the tree's files map to these folders.

These files are nodes in the tree, so they live in the database and survive a restart, an update and a new container. Read them in EiN's terminal with cat , and change them with edit or the code editor on the Nodes page, as far as your rights allow. Path Written by Read by Mode /etc/bashrc core at the first start, then the administrator every shell, when it opens 0644 /etc/bashrc.d/<group> the administrator, mod setup the group's members' shells, when they open 0644 /etc/layout boot, at every start /etc/bashrc /etc/environment boot, at every start /etc/bashrc 0644 /etc/config.d/<module> mod setup , as a link to the module's file /etc/bashrc /etc/config Settings → System , config set /etc/bashrc 0644 /etc/keys Settings → System , config set , for keys EiN itself, never a shell 0600 ~/.config Profile → Preferences , config set /etc/bashrc 0600 ~/.bashrc you your terminal and SSH logins ~/.bash_history your shell your shell /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json mod setup , as a link to the module's file the sidebar and top bar /etc/ui/nav.json the administrator the sidebar and top bar /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.json the administrator the group's members' sidebar and top bar /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.d/<module>.json mod setup , as a link to the module's file, for a module kept to the group the group's members' sidebar and top bar /etc/modules/<module>.groups mod groups , mod install --groups , Settings → Modules mod setup and the shell, for who has the module 0644 ~/.ui/nav.json you your sidebar and top bar /etc/fstab mount --save , unmount --save boot, with mount -a 0600 /etc/ssh_host_key , .pub the SSH server, at the first start the SSH server 0700 ~/.ssh/… you, ssh-keygen , ssh the SSH server, ssh , scp , mount 0700 /etc/users/ , /etc/groups/ the account and group commands every sign-in and access check /etc/services/ service add , service enable , mod setup service start-all at boot /etc/files/ , /etc/init/ boot boot /etc/assistant-prompt.md mod setup , once; then the administrator the Assistant, when installed /etc/assistant.d/<module>/ mod setup , as a link to the module's folder the Assistant, when installed A blank mode is the default the folder gives a new file. ~ is your home, /home/<your username> .

Five files hold the values of settings, each an ordinary shell file of export lines: # /etc/config export CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS= '14' export CFG_MODULE_SOURCES= 'https://github.com/einhq https://forge.example:3000/family' File Holds /etc/environment The CFG_… variables EiN's container was started with, written whole at every start. A value the deployment stops passing is gone from it. A key is never written here. /etc/config.d/<module> A module's own choice of values: a link to the module's etc/config , made by mod setup and removed with the module. The Archive's names CFG_SEARCH_PARSER , the assistant's CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL and CFG_COMMAND_FINDER , the media service's CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER . /etc/config The administrator's values for system settings. Made by the first config set ; until then it does not exist. ~/.config One person's values for personal settings, the CFG_USER_… ones and HISTSIZE . Made by the first config set of that person. /etc/keys The keys to other services saved on the Settings page or with config set : CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY , and with their modules CFG_EMS_KEY and CFG_LLM_KEY . Owned by admin , and sourced by no shell. A key from .env is never written to any file. /etc/bashrc sources the first four in that order, so the last one wins: a person's own value, then the administrator's, then a module's, then the deployment's. How the layers combine shows the whole order with the badges of the Settings page. config set rewrites a line in place and keeps the rest of the file as it was. When you edit /etc/config or ~/.config by hand, nothing checks your values and nothing is restarted; Edit the settings file by hand says what that means.

/etc/bashrc is sourced by every shell EiN opens: a terminal tab, an SSH login, a command sent over SSH, a service, a pipeline step. It is copied from core's own file at the first start, and from then on it is the administrator's: an update does not replace it. With the Archive installed it reads, in this order: #!bash alias la= 'ls -A' alias ll= 'ls -al' alias whoami = 'user whoami' alias id = 'user id' export HISTSIZE=1000 # Configuration layers: the deployment's first, then the modules', the system's, and personal last, # so a personal setting wins. 10_config.sh adds these to an existing /etc/bashrc, which boot # never replaces. case ": $PATH :" in *:/usr/modules/archive/bin:*) ;; *) export PATH= " $PATH :/usr/modules/archive/bin" ;; esac [ -r /etc/layout ] && source /etc/layout [ -r /etc/environment ] && source /etc/environment for f in /etc/config.d/*; do [ -r " $f " ] && source " $f " ; done [ -r /etc/config ] && source /etc/config [ -n " $HOME " ] && [ -r " $HOME /.config" ] && source " $HOME /.config" Each other module with a bin/ folder, such as the ems module, has a PATH line of its own beside the Archive's. Boot and mod setup keep some lines in it, whatever else you change: mod setup adds a PATH line for each module that has a bin/ folder, once. Boot adds the line that sources /etc/layout , once. At every start, boot moves the four lines that source the settings files to the end, so they come after anything you add. /etc/layout exports where each folder of the tree is, such as ETC_PATH and LOGS_PATH , and where the data folders are on the machine ( EIN_FILE_ROOT_PATH , EIN_VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH , EIN_FILE_TMP_PATH ). Boot writes it whole at every start; leave it alone. Folders in the tree lists the variables. A change to /etc/bashrc reaches every shell before its next command, an open terminal tab included; a command already running keeps what it started with. Put aliases and settings of your own in ~/.bashrc instead, which is yours alone.

File What it is ~/.bashrc Your own aliases, functions and variables, read after /etc/bashrc by a terminal tab and an SSH login, not by a command sent with ssh host 'command' . A line that fails does not stop the shell from opening. ~/.bash_history Your command history, the file HISTFILE names. HISTSIZE sets how many commands are kept. ~/.config Your personal settings; see The settings files . EiN reads no ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile . Keep your settings in ~/.bashrc shows what to put in it.

The sidebar and the top bar are put together from four layers of JSON, each changing only what it names: File Who writes it Who it is for /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json each module, linked by mod setup ; EiN's own is /etc/ui/nav.d/ui.json everyone /etc/ui/nav.json an administrator everyone /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.json an administrator the group's members ~/.ui/nav.json you you only A module kept to some groups has its file linked in /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.d/<module>.json for each of them and for admin instead, read for the group's members alongside /etc/ui/nav.d . The files in /etc/ui/nav.d are links to the modules' files, and an update replaces them; put changes in /etc/ui/nav.json , a group's /etc/ui/groups/<group>/nav.json or ~/.ui/nav.json , which exist only once someone writes them. Your sidebar and top bar describes the format and its fields.

/etc/fstab lists the mounts EiN makes again at every start, one per line: the mount point, the type and the options, separated by spaces. A field with a space in it is in double quotes, and a line starting with # is a comment. /mnt/nas sftp host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos,key=/home/admin/.ssh/nas mount --save adds or replaces the line for its mount point, and unmount --save removes it, keeping every other line and comment. The file is made with mode 0600 , since it names other machines and their users. When it is missing, boot mounts nothing. Mount a folder of another machine explains the options.

File What it is /etc/ssh_host_key , /etc/ssh_host_key.pub The SSH server's host key, an ed25519 pair made at the first start. Kept in the tree, so it stays the same across updates and new containers. ~/.ssh/authorized_keys The public keys that may sign in as you over SSH and SFTP, one a line. SSH and SFTP explains the modes it needs. ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 , id_ecdsa , id_rsa Your own keys, for ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id to other machines, made with ssh-keygen . ~/.ssh/config Settings per machine for ssh and scp , in OpenSSH's format. ~/.ssh/known_hosts The host keys of the machines you have accepted. Lines written by OpenSSH work as they are. ~/.ssh is made with mode 0700 the first time a command needs it. Reaching other machines covers the client files.

These are kept by commands, not edited as text: /etc/users/<name> is an account, with its password in .password and, with the Archive, a link to the person it is. /etc/groups/<group> is a group, with links to its members in users . Accounts and groups and the user and group commands change them; Permissions in depth gives their modes. /etc/services/available/<name> is a link to a service's folder, which holds its start.sh , and /etc/services/enabled/<name> marks it to start at boot. A module's service that is a single script gets a folder of its own in /etc/service-scripts/<name> . Each service writes its output to /var/logs/services/<name>/stdout.log and stderr.log . Services and logs explains the service commands.

/etc/files is the folder of boot scripts that ships with EiN, mounted read-only, and /etc/init holds a link to each script boot runs, in name order. They are EiN's own; to change what happens at start-up, use the settings, /etc/fstab or a service instead.

With the Assistant installed: File What it is /etc/assistant-prompt.md The instructions the language model is given at the start of every chat. Copied from the assistant module once and never replaced, so you can edit it. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/prompt.md What a module tells the model about its part. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/tools The commands the module offers the model as tools, one a line; # starts a comment. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/examples Questions the chat suggests asking, one a line. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/cards.json The cards an answer may carry under it, drawn from the module's own pages. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/eval.json The questions agent-eval asks to test the assistant. Each /etc/assistant.d/<module> is a link to the module's etc/assistant.d , so an update of the module replaces it; only /etc/assistant-prompt.md is yours to change. Because an update does not replace that file either, a new version of the assistant's own instructions does not reach an installation where it already exists. Teaching the assistant describes these files for module authors.

When a module is set up, at every start and after mod install , mod setup puts the module's files in place: From the module In the tree How etc/config /etc/config.d/<module> Linked, and removed with the module. etc/<name>.d /etc/<name>.d/<module> Linked, and removed with the module. ui/nav.json /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json Linked, and removed with the module. any other etc/ file /etc/<file> Copied once. A file already there is left as it is. bin/ a PATH line in /etc/bashrc Added once. services/ /etc/services/available , enabled Registered and enabled. The linked files always show the module's current version. A copied file is yours after the first setup, which is why mod setup prints etc/<file> already exists, skipping for it later. The module manifest and Writing a module describe a module's folders.

The files in EiN's tree are in the database, so a backup of the database keeps them all: /etc/config , /etc/fstab , the host key, everyone's ~/.ssh and ~/.bashrc . On the machine, keep .env and the data folder besides. Your data: backup, moving and removing says how. EiN has no command that exports its configuration files on their own; copy one with cat or over SFTP when you want it apart.

p.h: When a file does not do what you expect
p.x: What you see Why, and what to do A CFG_… line in .env has no effect The setting is set on the Settings page or chosen by a module, both of which win; it is one of the four compose.yaml fixes; or the container was not made again with podman compose up -d . A change to compose.override.yaml is gone setup.sh writes it on every run. Change the options in .env , or with setup.sh , instead. A change to /etc/config , ~/.config or /etc/bashrc does not show in the terminal A command that was already running keeps the environment it started with; the next command reads the change. A service's own loop keeps it too until the service restarts. A service still uses the old value after a hand edit A hand edit restarts nothing. Restart the service from Services and logs , or save the setting on the Settings page, which does. could not write … when you save You may read the file but not change it. /etc is the administrator's; a member of the sudo group becomes the administrator with admin , as Accounts and groups explains. A line you added to /etc/environment or /etc/layout is gone Boot writes both files whole at every start. Put the value in /etc/config , or the CFG_… line in .env . A saved mount is not there after a start Run cat /etc/fstab to check its line and mount -a to try again. An SFTP mount whose host key is neither in known_hosts nor pinned with hostkey= is not connected at start-up.

Configuration : the Settings page, config set and how the layers combine. Settings and Environment variables : every setting and variable. Installing in detail : setup.sh , its options and variables. The editor : edit , for the files in the tree. Your sidebar and top bar : the navigation files. Reaching other machines and SSH and SFTP : the SSH files and /etc/fstab .
Every key EiN's web interface knows, by the part of the screen it works in. Each section links the page that explains that part in full; this page is for looking a key up.

p.h: See the keys where you are
p.x: Press ? anywhere outside a text field, or choose Shortcuts in the account menu. The Keyboard shortcuts dialog opens, listing the keys that work anywhere under Anywhere , and a group for each part of the screen that has keys of its own while that part is on screen: Pictures for a grid of pictures and Nodes , and with the Archive installed Lightbox , Video and Audio for the viewer, Staging and Memories . Press ? again or Esc to close it. The ? dialog lists only the keys of what is on screen now. Some pages also show their keys at the foot of the page while you work, such as the Archive's Sort tab in staging; each key there is a button too. How to read the keys on this page: Ctrl in a shortcut marked "( ⌘ on a Mac)" is ⌘ on a Mac. The Keyboard shortcuts dialog shows the key your computer has. Alt is ⌥ on a Mac. The terminal's command line and the editor in the terminal use Ctrl on a Mac too, never ⌘ . A letter key works without Shift unless the table says Shift . Core's keys come first on this page. The keys a module brings are grouped under the module after them, Archive and Assistant ; they work only with that module installed. Keys typed into a text field are the field's. A page's single-letter keys, ? and the top bar's keys do nothing while you type in a box; Ctrl + K and the terminal's Alt keys work there too.

Keys What they do Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) Opens the finder: search, or go to a page or, with the Archive, a person or album; type > for commands. In its dialog form, pressed again, closes it. ? Opens or closes the Keyboard shortcuts dialog. Alt + T Shows or hides the terminal. Alt + N Adds a terminal tab. Esc Closes a dialog, or a page shown full screen, such as the viewer. Where a dialog or the viewer covers the search box, Ctrl + K opens the finder as a dialog of its own. Finding your way around shows the dialog, and Search and the finder the finder.

A top-bar button or a row of one of its menus can have a key, from a module or from your own navigation file. Alt + R for the Archive's Random album is the only one a published module ships with. Each such key is listed under Anywhere in the Keyboard shortcuts dialog and shown in the button's tooltip, such as Random album (Alt+R) . Your sidebar and top bar shows how to give an entry a key, change one, or take one away. These keys are EiN's own and no top-bar entry can take them: Ctrl + K , ? , and Alt with T , N , M , W , ← , → , ↑ or ↓ .

In the finder ( Search and the finder ): Keys What they do ↑ ↓ Light the row above or below. Enter Opens the lit row. With words typed, the first row, the search, is lit from the start. Esc Closes the list. In the search box of the Search page, and of the Archive's Media page: Keys What they do Enter Runs the search. ↑ ↓ in the @ list Light a thing to pick, such as a person, place or album. Enter or Tab in the list Picks the lit row, which becomes a chip. Esc in the list Closes the list without picking.

Wherever pictures stand in a grid: search results, and with the Archive an album, Media or a person's pictures. Albums describes selecting in full. Keys What they do Shift +click Selects everything from the last picture picked to this one. Ctrl +click ( ⌘ +click on a Mac) Adds a picture to the selection, or takes it out. Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Selects every picture the page has loaded. Esc Clears the selection. With the viewer open, closes the viewer instead. Enter or Space Opens the picture that has the keyboard's focus.

While a folder listing of the Nodes explorer has the keyboard. The tree says what the nodes are. Keys What they do ↑ ↓ Move the selection to the row above or below. Shift + ↑ Shift + ↓ Extend the selection. Ctrl + ↑ Ctrl + ↓ Move without selecting, to pick rows one by one. → / ← Open / close the row's folder in place. In the icons view the arrows move by the tiles on screen instead. Space Opens or closes the row's folder in place. Enter Go into the row. Alt + Enter Properties Backspace Up a level. F2 Rename. Enter keeps the new name, Esc gives it up. Delete Delete, after asking. Only where you may write. F5 Reload the listing. Ctrl + H ( ⌘ + H on a Mac) Show or hide names that start with a dot. Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Select every row shown, open folders included. Ctrl + C ( ⌘ + C on a Mac) Copy. Ctrl + X ( ⌘ + X on a Mac) Cut. Only where you may write. Ctrl + V ( ⌘ + V on a Mac) Paste into the folder shown. Only where you may write. Tab With two panes, moves the keyboard to the other pane. In the address bar above a listing, Enter goes to the path typed and Esc puts back the path you were at. The explorer's code editor saves with Ctrl + S ( ⌘ + S on a Mac); Esc closes it only when nothing is unsaved. The editor covers it.

On the Trash page ( Your profile, favourites and trash ): Keys What they do ↑ ↓ Move the selection. Ctrl +click ( ⌘ +click on a Mac) Add a row to the selection. Shift +click Select a range. Enter Opens or closes a row that holds several things. Delete Delete for good , after asking. F5 Reload the list.

The terminal's own keys work whether you are typing in it or not, with Alt alone, without Ctrl , Shift or ⌘ . The terminal explains them. Keys What they do Alt + T Show or hide the terminal Alt + N New tab Alt + W Close the tab you are typing in; never the last one Alt + M Fill the window, or go back to half of it Alt + ← / Alt + → Previous / next tab Alt + ↑ / Alt + ↓ A tenth of the window shorter / taller Note On a Mac, ⌥ with a letter types a character of its own (⌥T types †), so ⌥T, ⌥N, ⌥W and ⌥M may not reach the terminal. Use the terminal button in the top bar and the buttons in the tab bar instead. ⌥ with an arrow key works. The command line is edited with bash's keys: Tab completes, ↑ and ↓ walk your history, Ctrl + R searches it (and does not reload the page; F5 does), Ctrl + C stops a command and Ctrl + D on an empty line ends the shell. Edit the command line has the full list. Ctrl + Z does not pause a command. In an ssh session to another machine, ~ then . at the start of a line cuts the connection; see Reaching other machines .

edit opens a file in the terminal. Its keys are Ctrl on a Mac too. The editor has every key. Keys What they do Ctrl + S or Ctrl + O Save Ctrl + Q or Ctrl + X Leave; asks first if anything is unsaved Ctrl + F Find Ctrl + G Go to a line, or line:column Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Y Undo / redo Ctrl + K / Ctrl + U Cut the line / paste what was cut Esc or Ctrl + C Cancel a question
These keys work with the Archive installed.
Alt + R opens an album at random, as Random album in the top bar does. It is a top-bar key, so it can be changed or taken away; see Keys for top-bar buttons .

The time scrubber at the right of a long list ( Scroll through time ), on the albums page, in a media timeline and in staging, takes keys once you move to it with Tab : ↑ and ↓ step to the time before or after, Home and End go to the first and the last.

While a photo, video or recording is open. Viewing photos, videos and recordings explains each. Keys What they do ← / → Previous / next file, also during a slideshow. i Shows or hides the details panel. Not for a visitor who came by a share link. f Shows or hides the face boxes with their names. t Shows or hides the text in the picture, when it has some. s Adds the file to your favourites, or takes it out. + or = Zooms in a step (photos and videos, not during a slideshow). - Zooms out a step. 0 Fits the whole picture again. Esc Closes what lies over the picture first: the enlarged map, the text dialog, drawing a face box. Then stops a slideshow. Then closes the viewer. In the Who is this? box of an unnamed face, Enter names it. In the Text in the picture dialog, Ctrl + Enter ( ⌘ + Enter on a Mac) saves. While a dialog lies over the viewer, the viewer's keys rest. Videos and recordings Keys What they do Space or k Plays or pauses (videos and recordings). j / l Back / forward 10 seconds (videos and recordings). Shift + ← / Shift + → Previous / next chapter, when the video has chapters. m Mutes or unmutes. c Turns subtitles on or off, when the file has a transcript. p Turns picture-in-picture on or off, where the browser has it. Move to the timeline, or a recording's waveform, with Tab to use these: Keys What they do ← ↓ / → ↑ Back / forward 5 seconds. Page Down / Page Up Previous / next chapter, or a tenth of the file back / forward without chapters. Home / End The start / the end. On the volume slider, after Tab : ← ↓ and → ↑ change the volume by 5 percent, Page Down and Page Up by 20 percent, Home silences it and End turns it full up. A click on the timeline or the slider leaves the keyboard where it was, so ← and → still step between files.

On Home , while On this day plays as a story ( Memories, news and events on Home ): Keys What they do → Next picture; after a year's last, the next year; after the last, closes. ← Previous picture. Space Pauses or plays. Esc Closes the story.

People and faces explains each place. Where Keys What they do Unidentified people Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Ticks every loaded card. Esc Clears what is ticked. Reviewing an unidentified person Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Picks every face and recording shown. Shift +click Picks a range. Esc Closes an open photo first, then clears what is picked, then closes the review. Enter in the name box Names the person. Split a person Esc Closes an open photo first, then the dialog. A person's faces The keys of pictures in a grid .

On a computer, the line at the foot of the stream shows the keys for where you are; hide folds it to a Keys chip. The keys do nothing while you type in a field or a dialog is open, and there are none on a phone. Sorting in staging explains what each does to a group. On a group: Keys What they do J / K Next / previous group Shift + J / Shift + K , or Shift + ↓ / Shift + ↑ Select on to the next / previous group Enter The proposal N New album from the group P New private album A Add to album… B Into the target, or Choose a target… when there is none Shift + B Choose the target 1 2 3 Into that candidate album , / . Highlight the candidate above / below R Not the highlighted candidate C Compare with the highlighted album, or narrow the column again X Discard L Later, or back to its lane Z Undo E Rename T Set the time of every picture, or of the selected ones M / Shift + M Merge into the group above / merge the group below in [ / ] Previous / next day or month of the group ← → ↑ ↓ Step through the pictures O Open the first picture On a picture (after an arrow key), on a day or month (after [ or ] ), or with pictures selected: Keys What they do Space Select the picture, or the day's pictures O Open the picture S Split the group before them; in a lane, make them a new group < / > Move them to the group above / below G Move them to a group… Enter N P A B X Act on the day or the selected pictures only Esc Back to the group, or clear the selection With a selection that reaches past the open group, Enter asks to accept the proposals of every group in it, N , P , A , B and X act on the whole selection, L puts the groups aside, and Esc clears it. < , > , [ and ] work on any keyboard layout, also where you type them with AltGr or Option. With a mouse, drag across the stream to select the pictures and groups the box touches. Esc while dragging drops the box and puts the selection back as it was. In the dialogs these keys open: Add to an album and Choose the target : with nothing typed, 1 , 2 and so on pick the suggested album of that number. Move to a group : ↑ and ↓ light a group, Enter takes it. Renaming a group: Enter keeps the name, Esc gives it up.

On the Duplicates tab and in its compare dialog ( Duplicates ): Where Keys What they do Duplicates tab J / K Mark the next / previous set Enter Remove the marked set's copies C Compare the marked set Z Undo the last removal of this visit Comparing a set ← / → Move between the files K Keep the file in focus instead (staged files only) Enter Remove the others X Not duplicates (look-alikes only) Esc Close without changing anything
These keys work with the Assistant installed.

In the chat box ( Chatting with the assistant ), Enter sends the question and Shift + Enter starts a new line. The side drawer the chat opens in can be made wider or narrower from the keyboard: move to its edge ( Resize side panel ) with Tab , then ← makes it 20 pixels wider and → 20 pixels narrower.

The focus is in a text field. Click an empty part of the page, or press Esc in a search box to leave it, and press the key again. The key belongs to something else on screen. A dialog over the page takes the keyboard: the viewer's keys rest while a dialog lies over it, and staging's keys rest while a dialog is open. Press ? to see which groups are active. The browser or the computer keeps the key. Some browsers keep Ctrl + W , Ctrl + Q or Ctrl + S for themselves; the editor in the terminal also takes Ctrl + O and Ctrl + X . A top-bar key you set is missing. A key two entries ask for goes to the first in the top bar's order, and EiN's own keys are never given away. Your sidebar and top bar helps find out why. On a phone or tablet there is no keyboard to press; the keys need a computer. EiN on a phone covers the gestures instead.
Finding your way around Viewing photos, videos and recordings Sorting in staging The terminal The editor Your sidebar and top bar

Every page of EiN's web interface has an address of its own, and most of what a page shows, such as the tab, the filters, the year or the part of the map, is written into that address. This page lists the addresses and their parameters, so you can bookmark a view, send someone a link to it, or type one in. It is for anyone who uses EiN in a browser, and for administrators who link to EiN from elsewhere.

An address is the place EiN is reached at, then a path, then sometimes a query: http://ein.local:8080/people/helen-okafor?tab=faces └──── where EiN is ──┘└────── path ──────┘└─ query ─┘ The path says which page: /people/helen-okafor is Helen Okafor's page, one of the Archive's. The query, after ? , says how the page looks: tab=faces opens it on Faces . Several parameters are joined with & . A part that holds a path in the tree, such as an album's, is URL-encoded: / becomes %2F and a space %20 . EiN writes these addresses itself when you move around; you only meet the encoding when you type one by hand. Copy the address from the browser's address bar to share or bookmark what you see. Someone who opens it sees the same page, as far as their own permissions let them. The pages come from EiN itself and from its modules . Core's addresses come first on this page; after them each module's addresses and parameters are grouped under it: the Archive , the Assistant and the media service . A module that is not installed brings none of its addresses, and opening one shows Nothing here .

p.h: Pages, dialogs, the side panel and full screen
p.x: The same address can be shown four ways. Which one depends on how you open it, not on the address: Shown as How you get there Is it in the address bar? A page The sidebar, a link, or typing the address Yes, as the path A dialog over the page Entries of the top bar's Create New menu, About EiN in the account menu No The side panel beside the page The top bar's Chat button No Full screen A picture, video or recording opened from a grid, a memory on the home page Yes, as ?fullscreen= Modules give the entries: with the Archive, Create New → Person opens /people/new in a dialog, and typing /people/new into the address bar opens the same form as a page. In the same way, with the Assistant, /chat is the side panel from the top bar and a full page from the sidebar. On a phone, what would open in the side panel opens in a dialog instead. Finding your way around shows each of these. Full screen is the one kind that lives in the address. When you open a picture from one of the Archive's albums, the address keeps the album and adds the picture: /albums/%2Farchive%2Falbums%2FMalpas%201979?fullscreen=%2Fmedia%2F%252Farchive%252F… Back closes the picture and leaves you on the album, and a reload or a shared link opens the album with the picture over it. Opened by its own address, /media/<path> , the picture is the page.

Address What it shows Who can open it / Home Everyone who can browse /login The sign-in page Everyone /s/<token> Where a share link lands, see Share links Everyone /search Search , see Search and the finder Everyone who can browse /stats Statistics Everyone who can browse /docs Documentation , see Links into the documentation Everyone who can browse /profile Profile : your account, preferences and security Signed in /settings Settings Signed in /trash Your Trash Signed in /about About EiN ; from the account menu it opens in a dialog Signed in /system Dashboard , see Health and the dashboard In the sidebar for administrators /system/nodes Nodes , the node explorer In the sidebar for administrators /system/pipelines/<pipeline> One pipeline and its recent runs, for example /system/pipelines/media-faces Reached from the Dashboard /system/pipelines/<pipeline>/<id> One run of a pipeline Reached from the pipeline's page "Everyone who can browse" means signed-in users, and also visitors who have not signed in when the administrator turns on CFG_GUEST_BROWSING . A page marked "Signed in" always asks a visitor to sign in first. What each person then sees on a page follows the permissions on the nodes behind it; see Permissions in depth .
A parameter that is missing, or holds a value the page does not know, is ignored: the page opens as it would without it. You never get an error for a mistyped parameter.

Pages with tabs keep the open tab in tab . An address without tab opens the first one. Page Values of tab (default first) /profile account ( Account ), preferences ( Preferences ), security ( Security ) /settings system ( System ), users ( Users ), groups ( Groups ), permissions ( Permissions ), modules ( Modules ) /system overview ( Overview ), work ( Work ), ems.media-service ( Media service , with the ems module), services ( Services ), log ( Log ) A module's pages keep their tabs the same way; their values are under the module below. On Settings , the first four tabs are for administrators. Anyone else who asks for one of them gets Modules , and an administrator who names no tab gets System .

Search keeps its whole search in the address, so a search can be linked to and survives a reload; the Archive's Media page takes the same parameters. The parameters are named after the flags of the search command. Parameter What it holds Example q The words searched for q=sailing kind Kinds, separated by commas: photo , video , audio , document , person , location , album , device , track kind=photo,video tag Labels, separated by commas tag=beach subject A person, location or device that must be in it, as <kind>:<name> or a path; repeat it for several, all of which must be there subject=person:helen-okafor subject-name Every subject of a kind whose name matches the words, as <kind>:<words> ; repeatable subject-name=person:Wrenfield from , to The first and last year, both included from=1975&to=1985 bbox A rectangle on the map: north, south, east, west bbox=50.3,50.2,-5.0,-5.1 circle A circle on the map: latitude, longitude, radius in metres circle=50.263,-5.051,2000 poly A polygon: at least three latitude,longitude pairs separated by ; poly=50.3,-5.1;50.3,-5.0;50.2,-5.0 under Only what one album or folder holds, by path under=/archive/albums/Malpas 1979 like Pictures that look like this one, by path like=/archive/…/IMG_0412.jpg sort score , time (oldest first), -time (newest first) or name sort=-time The kinds person , location , album and device , and a subject , find something only with the Archive installed. With it, for example, every picture and video of Helen Okafor from the 1980s, newest first: /media?kind=photo,video&subject=person:helen-okafor&from=1980&to=1989&sort=-time Only one of bbox , circle and poly applies. Search with no parameters shows its landing page rather than searching for everything.

Page Parameter What it does /settings?tab=modules module The module open, for example module=archive /settings?tab=modules section Its part: dependencies , services , pages , commands , settings or types ( About when left out) /settings?tab=modules published=1 The modules published for installing /settings?tab=users user The account open, by username /settings?tab=groups group The group open, by name /settings?tab=users , ?tab=groups new=1 The form for a new account or group /system/nodes path The path open in the explorer, for example path=/archive /docs find The words in the documentation's search box /login next Where to go after signing in

The Documentation section has its own addresses. The reference pages are drawn from the installation you are on, so they list exactly what it has. Address What it shows /docs The guide's overview /docs/<path> One guide page, by its URL-encoded path under /usr/docs/guide /docs/commands Every command, see also Commands /docs/settings Every setting with its current value, see also Settings /docs/environment The environment variables, see also Environment variables /docs/node-types The node types, see also Node types /docs/modules What is installed /docs/modules/<name> One installed module, for example /docs/modules/archive The reference pages have an anchor for every entry, which scrolls to it and marks it for a moment: Entry Address A command /docs/commands#cmd-<name> , for example /docs/commands#cmd-share-link A setting /docs/settings#set-<KEY> , for example /docs/settings#set-CFG_GUEST_BROWSING A node type /docs/node-types#type-<type>

A visitor who opens a page they must sign in for is sent to the sign-in page, with the address they asked for in next : /login?next=%2Fpeople%2Fhelen-okafor%3Ftab%3Dfaces After signing in they land on that page. next only leads to a page on the same EiN; anything else leads to Home . Someone already signed in who opens /login goes straight on to next , or to Home .

A share link has the form /s/<token> , for example http://ein.local:8080/s/ followed by a long string of letters and digits. You make one with Share in the interface, see Sharing , or with share-link create in the terminal. Opening it shows Opening what was shared with you… and then the page of what was shared, such as the album's address. Where visitors may not browse, the visitor stays on what the link opens: other pages ask them to sign in. A link that has expired or been turned off shows This link no longer works with a Sign in button.

Besides the pages, EiN's web server answers a few addresses that programs use rather than people. You meet them in links to files, in scripts, and in a reverse proxy's configuration ( Ports, HTTPS and remote access ). Address Method What it does /file/<path> GET , HEAD The bytes of a file in the tree, read with the permissions of whoever asks /file/<path> PUT Stores the body at exactly that path, creating or replacing the file /file/<directory>/?name=<name> POST Stores an upload under a name nothing in the directory has yet: name , else name (2) , name (3) and so on /archive POST Collects a selection of files for a download as one zip /archive/<token> GET Downloads that zip /log/<path> POST Adds JSON entries to a log node /track/<path> POST Adds GPS points to a track node, see Devices and GPS tracks /__shell The connection the web interface talks to EiN over; a proxy must pass it on as a WebSocket Any other path that is not a file of the web interface returns the interface itself, which then shows the page or Nothing here . A visitor who is not signed in where visitors may not browse gets sign in first from /file/ and /archive/ .

These addresses exist with the Archive installed. Addresses with <name> take the name of the node in the tree. A person's or a place's is its name in lower case with hyphens: Helen Okafor is /people/helen-okafor . A device's keeps its capitals and has _ for spaces, such as /devices/Canon_EOS_5D_Mark_III . Addresses with <path> take the node's whole path, URL-encoded.

Address What it shows /media Media : every picture, video, recording and document, see Media, Year and labels /media/<path> One file in the viewer, see Viewing photos, videos and recordings /year Year /timeline Opens /year , keeping the query /map Map , see Locations and the map /albums Albums , see Albums /albums/<path> One album, for example /albums/%2Farchive%2Falbums%2FMalpas%201979 /people People , see People and faces /people/<name> One person, for example /people/peggy-wrenfield /people/unknown The people EiN has seen or heard but nobody has named /family A family tree of chosen people, see Family tree, events and homes /locations Locations /locations/<name> One location /devices Devices , see Devices and GPS tracks /devices/<name> One device /favourites Your Favourites ; signed in only, see Your profile, favourites and trash /duplicates?path=<path> The copies of a node, see Duplicates

These are the forms of the top bar's Create New menu. They open in a dialog from the menu and as a page by their address. All of them need you to be signed in.
