EiN checks every finding each hour, and the set changes or goes away "you cannot write the kept one, which would gain from the copies" You may not change the library photo, and a copy holds something it would gain. Remove is greyed out Ask someone who may change that photo, or, if what the copy holds does not matter, discard it on the Files tab (its Folder view lists copies too) "it changed: look again" The set changed after the page read it Open the tab again "look-alikes are for you to look at: Remove all leaves them" Remove all skips this set Look at it and use Remove , Keep this one or Not duplicates The message "Left as it is: …" after Remove The set changed before the removal ran, so nothing was removed. This also happens after Keep this one on the only staged photo beside a library photo, since nothing else is left to remove Look at the set again. To keep both pictures, use Not duplicates A copy you expected is not listed It is in someone else's staging area, in an album you cannot open, or not prepared yet Look-alikes appear once the file is prepared; see Getting your photos in

The Duplicates tab compares new files with the library. It does not look for copies among photos that are already in the library, and EiN has no page that does this for family members. An administrator can look for them with the Duplicates tool on the Nodes page, or with duplicates and merge-duplicates in the shell. The web uploader sends every file, even one the library already has, and EiN then sets the copy aside without processing it. You do not need to check for copies before you upload.

Everything the tab does is a staging subcommand you can run yourself in EiN's terminal : # in EiN's terminal staging duplicates inbox --counts # copies and look-alikes in the inbox, by kind staging duplicates inbox --exact -- where library # the sets of copies of library photos staging dedupe inbox --apply --exact -- where library --dry-run # what Remove all would do staging separate <file> <other> # these files are not duplicates staging dedupe must be run by the owner of the staging area, since the copies go to their trash. Every flag is in the staging reference , and the administrator's side of staging is on Staging and importing for administrators .

Every picture in EiN gets a date when anything can tell it one, and a place when it was taken with GPS or someone gives it one. This page is for family members who fix when and where pictures were taken: where EiN finds both, how to correct them, and what happens to scans and to pictures nobody has dated.

p.h: Where you see a picture's date and place
p.x: Open a picture in the viewer. On a computer the date and the place sit in the bar under the picture; on a phone the date is centred over the top of the picture and the bar at the foot keeps the place. The date is written as precisely as it is known: "Saturday, 16 June 1956, 14:03:11" for a full time, "1975" for a picture known only to a year, "August 1968" for one known to a month. A picture with no date shows none. Point at the date for a tooltip. It names where the date came from (the time source), any note someone left with it, and the time in your own time zone when the picture was taken in another ("… your time"). The place is the name of the location the picture is linked to, else its street address, else its city and country. The details panel ( Details (i) , or i ; on a phone, swipe up) shows more. Its place section has the location's name as a link, the street address and a small map with Enlarge map . The Details fold at its foot holds Taken at (the date exactly as stored, with its time zone), Taken at (UTC) and Time source . Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers the rest of the panel. In an album the pictures are laid out in sections by day. One known only to a year sits under a heading with only the year; one with no date comes after the dated ones, under Undated . A person's, location's or device's Media tab lists undated pictures after the rest too. The Media feed lists pictures by date, so it leaves out a picture that has none.

EiN looks at up to five sources for a picture's date and takes the first one that has it. The Time source says in words which one it was. The first source on the ladder that has a date decides; a scan waits until a person gives it one Order Source Time source reads What it is 1 Set by hand entered by hand A date someone gave with Set time or file-set-time . It always wins, and it may be as vague as a year. 2 A sidecar or Google Photos from Google Photos or a sidecar A date a photo editor or scanning program wrote into an XMP sidecar, or a date someone changed in Google Photos before exporting. 3 GPS from GPS The GPS receiver's clock, the one source that knows the exact moment. 4 The camera's clock from the camera clock The date and time the camera or phone wrote into the file, or a video's recording time. 5 The file name from the file name A date the name spells, such as IMG_20190601_123456.jpg , for files from a staging category whose names count as dates. When none of them has a date, the picture is undated. EiN never dates a picture by when it was uploaded or when the file was last changed. A sidecar is a small file beside a picture that says things about it: the JSON Google Photos writes for each photo of a Takeout export, or the .xmp file a photo editor writes. EiN pairs sidecars with their pictures as they arrive in staging, in every kind of category but Messaging and Screenshots. Getting your photos in and Supported files say which names it understands. A few rules decide the close cases: A GPS time far from the camera's clock is ignored. More than 26 hours apart, the GPS time is taken for an old position the receiver kept reporting, and the camera's clock dates the picture. Google Photos' time counts as a person's date only when it differs. More than 26 hours from the camera's clock (or, for a picture without one, from when it was uploaded to Google), it is a date someone set there, and it comes second on the ladder. Closer than that, it is Google's reading of the camera's clock: the picture keeps the camera's time, Google's time tells EiN which time zone the clock was in, and Time source reads "from Google Photos or a sidecar". A GPS time still comes first then, and a camera that recorded its own time zone keeps "from the camera clock". File names count only where a staging category says so , and only the names a phone, a messenger, a screenshot tool or a desktop uploader writes. A name that dates a picture before 1995 is not believed, and a scanner's running number such as IMG_20190601_0001.jpg is no date. A scanner's clock never dates a picture once the scanner is registered as a device with Scanner or digitizer turned on (see Devices and GPS tracks ). A GPS time in the file still counts.

p.h: Date scans of old prints and slides
p.x: A scanner writes the day of the scan into the file, and a scanning app on a phone adds where the scan was made. Neither says when the picture was taken. When files arrive in a staging category of the kind Scans , EiN marks them as scans and sets aside the scanner's clock, the GPS time and position, the file name, and a Google Photos time that agrees with them. A scan is dated only by a date a person gives it: with Set time , with file-set-time , in an XMP sidecar, or by changing it in Google Photos. Until then it is undated, rather than dated to the day it was scanned. Time source on a scan adds "a scan: its scanner’s clocks are not when it was taken". The mark goes with the file when it is filed into an album, so the scan stays undated there until someone dates it. To bring in a box of scans: Open the Create menu (the plus in the top bar) and choose Import media . Under Into which category? , choose your Scans category, or New category with What it holds set to Scans and a name under Called , such as "Box 3". Press Choose files or Choose a folder , then Upload , which shows the number of files. Scans that already arrived in the Inbox can be moved: on the Inbox's Files tab, open the folder's ⋯ menu, choose Move to category… , pick the Scans category and press Move here . EiN dates the moved files again by the scans' rules, in the background. Sorting in staging explains categories and the Files tab. Note A scan uploaded straight into an album, or copied into one over SFTP, is not marked: no staging category's rules apply there. For those, register the scanner as a device with Scanner or digitizer turned on. Saving that setting re-dates the files already linked to it and says "Removed scanner dates from N linked files." Helen Okafor scanned the family's slides of "Cornwall, summer 1968" in March 2012. Uploaded into a Scans category, they wait undated until she gives them a date. Uploaded straight into an album from an unregistered scanner, they would all show March 2012. In a Scans category the Sort tab keeps the scans in runs, by folder and file name, under To sort , dated or not. Once most of a run has dates set by hand, its name gains their years, and a run splits where two neighbouring scans were given different years.

Each staging category has two time rules, which come with its kind ( What it holds ): whether its files are scans, and whether a date in a file name counts. What it holds Treated as scans File names count as dates Inbox no yes Google Photos export no no Scans yes no Phone no yes Camera no no Messaging no yes Screenshots no yes Other no no Files that move into a category with other rules are dated again by that category's rules, in the background. A move within a category, or between two with the same rules, changes nothing. Category settings has no switch for the two rules. Changing What it holds there resets them, together with the category's other settings, to those of the kind you chose. In the terminal, staging category <name> --digitized on|off and staging category <name> --filename-dates on|off change one rule and date the category's files again before they answer. A date set by hand outranks both rules.

p.h: Give pictures that need a date a date
p.x: Staging shows what has no date. A category's card on the Staging overview, and the strip above the category's tabs, has a bar whose Needs a date part counts the pictures read without a date. On the category's Sort tab, the Needs a date lane holds groups of undated pictures, named like "Undated · Peggy's shoebox", and groups of pictures dated only to a year or a month, named like "1987 · Peggy's shoebox". In a Scans category the scans stay in their runs under To sort instead, as described above. Open Staging , then the category, then its Sort tab. Choose Needs a date in the row of lanes above the groups. The row appears when more than one lane has groups, each lane with its number of groups. Open a group: click it, or move to it with J and K . Press T , or open the group's ⋯ menu and choose Set the time… . To date only some of its pictures, select them first; T then sets the time of those. In the Set time dialog, set Start time and the order (see the next section), then press Set time on N files . A picture dated only to a year or a month keeps that date unless you click its row first (see the next section), so a group named like "1987 · Peggy's shoebox" needs a click on each row you want to date. EiN confirms with "The time is set on N photos of “ ”". Within a few minutes the organizer puts the pictures into groups by the dates you gave them: an event, a trip, or a year's Everyday lane. On a phone there are no keys; tap the group and use its ⋯ menu. You can also file a Needs a date group as it is, undated, with New album… , Add to album… or the other decisions of the Sort tab. Its proposal is the category's album when the category has one; otherwise there is none. Pictures already in the library have no lane. An album lists its undated pictures last, under Undated : select them there and use Set time . In the terminal , search --undated lists everything undated in the library that you may see.

p.h: Set the time of several pictures at once
p.x: Set time is in the selection bar that appears when you select pictures: on an album page, the Media page, a person's, location's or device's Media tab, and the Files tab in staging. On a narrow screen it is under Actions . It is offered only when you may change every selected picture. In staging's Sort tab, T opens the same dialog. The dialog is titled Set time , with the number of files under it. Order decides which picture comes first: Current time (the default; earliest first, undated last), Name (by file name, IMG_2 before IMG_10 ) or Manual . Drag a row by the grip at its left to reorder; dragging switches to Manual . Start time is the time the first row gets. It starts at the earliest date in the batch, or at today's date and time when none of the pictures has one. Each row shows the picture, its name, its current date or "No date", and after the arrow the time it will get. The times are worked out from the top: The first row gets Start time . Each following row gets the time of the row before it plus the gap between their current times. Where either of the two has no date, or your order puts a later picture before an earlier one, the gap is one minute. Pictures taken in the same second stay in the same second. Changing a row's time pins it: that row keeps your time and the rows after it follow on from it. The round arrow at the end of a pinned row ("Unpin — follow the row above again") lets it follow the row above again. A picture known only to a year or a month keeps its date. Its row reads " — unchanged", with the tooltip "Keeping this date as it is. Give it a time to replace it.", and the rows after it follow the last row that took a time. Click it to give it a full time instead. Press Set time on N files . Each picture's date becomes one entered by hand, with the time of day included, also for a picture that was known only to the day. Albums holding the pictures update their date range. Warning The dialog shows and writes times in your browser's time zone. For a picture taken in another time zone, such as on a trip abroad, the time after the arrow can differ by some hours from its current date before you change anything. Compare the rows before you press Set time on N files . Some ways to use it: The camera's clock was wrong , an hour behind after a trip or never set at all: select that camera's pictures, keep Current time , and set Start time to the right time of the first picture. The others move by the same amount and keep their spacing. Scans of an album, in page order : select them, choose Name , and set Start time to the day. They spread a minute apart in scan order, so they stay in that order everywhere. Undated pictures where you know the time of some : set Start time , then change the rows whose time you know. The rows between follow on from them. One picture : select only that one.

p.h: Give a picture a vague date
p.x: A date can be as vague as it really is: a year ("1975"), a month ("August 1968") or a day. EiN keeps it that way and never adds a day or an hour nobody knew. The Set time dialog writes full times only, so a vague date is given in the terminal with file-set-time . Open the picture in the viewer and open the details panel. Open the Details fold at its foot and click the path under Path . A terminal tab opens, standing in the picture itself, so . names the picture. Type file-set-time , the picture and the date: # in EiN's terminal, opened from Path file-set-time . 1968-08 EiN answers with the date the picture has and where it came from: /archive/albums/Cornwall, summer 1968/scan0004.jpg: 1968-08 (manual) The date can be 1968 , 1968-08 , 1968-08-14 , 1968-08-14T15:30 or 1968-08-14T15:30:00 , and the last two may end in a time zone, +01:00 or Z . The year must lie between 1826 and next year; anything else is refused with "file-set-time: not a capture time: ". More forms, run in the folder that holds the pictures ( cd .. from the picture): # in EiN's terminal, in the album's folder file-set-time scan0004.jpg 1968-08 scan0005.jpg 1968-08 --note "Peggy remembers the August heatwave" for f in scan00*.jpg; do file-set-time " $f " 1968; done file-set-time --clear scan0004.jpg Several pictures go in one call as pairs of picture and date. If one date is wrong or one picture is missing, nothing is written. --note keeps a reason with the date. It shows beside the time source, in the date's tooltip and under Time source . --clear takes away a date set by hand, and its note. The picture falls back to the next source on the ladder, or to no date. The web interface has no button for this.

A picture is shown at the time on the clock the photographer was reading. A photograph taken at noon in Wellington reads 12:00, whoever looks at it; when your own time zone differs, the date's tooltip adds the same moment in yours ("… your time"). EiN works out the time zone of a picture from: the time zone the camera recorded in the file, as many phones do; the difference between the GPS time and the camera's clock, rounded to whole hours; the difference between Google Photos' time and the camera's clock, for a picture from a Takeout; the Timezone of the registered device that took it, which knows the summer time of the year the picture was taken in. A picture none of these places carries no time zone. It is shown at the camera's time without a "your time" line, and EiN reads it in the archive's own time zone, which is the time zone of the machine EiN runs on ( TZ , under Environment variables ). When a camera's pictures come out hours off: The camera's clock was set to another zone , for one bought abroad or kept on home time during a trip: give the camera's device the Timezone its clock was set to. For a registered camera, open its page, press Edit and set Timezone ; saving re-dates the pictures linked to it and says "Re-dated N linked files." Register an unregistered one from the Devices page with its Timezone , then press Link existing media on its page, which links its pictures and updates their dates. Devices and GPS tracks has the details. A phone's videos are off by exactly its time zone : turn on Video times in UTC for that phone. Phones keep their videos' recording time in UTC. The clock was wrong by some amount : use Set time as described above. A time from the Set time dialog carries no time zone and is read in the archive's time zone, so a picture from a trip abroad that you re-time loses its "your time" line. In the terminal you can give the zone with the time: # in EiN's terminal, in the album's folder file-set-time DSCF0412.JPG 1996-02-03T14:30+13:00

p.h: Where a picture's place comes from
p.x: A picture gets its place from the first of these that has one: A place set by hand, with Set location , in Edit file or with file-set-position . It replaces anything the file carries, and EiN reading the file again never puts the GPS position back over it. The GPS position in the file. The place in its sidecar: an XMP sidecar's, or a Google Photos Takeout's. A scan's own GPS position is where it was scanned, so EiN ignores it, and a Takeout's place for a scan too, unless someone set that place in Google Photos. Street addresses. EiN looks up each picture's position once in OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service, which turns coordinates into a street address. Only the coordinates are sent, never the picture. The address shows in the place section of the details panel, and in the viewer's bar when the picture is linked to no location. It can arrive a while after the picture: Nominatim answers one question a second, and a lookup that fails is asked again later. Locations. When a picture gets a position, EiN links it to the location whose shape contains the point, the nearest one when several do. A shape is a circle or a polygon drawn for the location, or the circle a location gets from its address or from its pictures. A location that is only a point, because coordinates were typed or clicked when it was created, contains nothing, so no picture joins it by itself. When a location's shape changes, the library's pictures inside it are linked to it and those left outside are let go. The link gives the picture the location's name in the viewer and puts it on the location's Media tab. A link someone made by hand, or one brought in from an older archive, is never replaced. Locations and the map shows how to draw a location's shape. A device's GPS track is drawn beside the pictures on the map and on an album's Map tab. EiN does not use it to give pictures a position.

Select the pictures in a grid: an album, the Media page, your favourites, a person's, location's or device's Media tab, the pictures behind a pile on the map, or the Files tab in staging. Press Set location in the selection bar. It is offered only when you may change every selected picture. The dialog asks "Where was this taken?", or "Where were these taken?" for several. Choose the place in one of two ways: Under A known location ("Pick one, or click the map"), pick a location. The list holds the locations that have a place on the map, and picking one moves the point to it. Under On the map ("Click where it was taken, or type the coordinates."), click the map, or type Latitude and Longitude . Press Set location . EiN confirms with "Location set on N files". The hint at the foot of the dialog says what happens: "This replaces whatever position the files carry, for the map and for searching by location." Picking a known location gives the pictures that location's point. They are linked to the location, and show its name, when the point lies inside its circle or polygon.

p.h: Change or clear the place of one picture
p.x: Open the picture in the viewer and open the details panel. Click the cog at the top of the panel and choose Edit . The Edit file dialog opens, with Description and the labels on one side and the place on the other, starting at the picture's point. To move the point, pick under A known location , click the map under On the map , or type Latitude and Longitude . The hint reads "The new location replaces the position the file carries, for the map and for searching by location." To take the place away, press Clear location . The hint reads "The file will have no location, for the map or for searching by location." Press Save . The cog menu has Edit when you may change the picture. Clear location removes the point, whether the GPS or a person put it there, and the picture's link to a location, however it was made. EiN reads a file's GPS position when it takes the file in, so the picture stays without a place. To clear several pictures at once, use file-set-position with --clear in the terminal.

The terminal does the same work with commands, and some of it only there: Task Command Give pictures a date, as vague as it is file-set-time <file> <date> [<file> <date> …] [--note <text>] Take away a date set by hand file-set-time --clear <file>… List what is undated in the library search --undated Set the place of pictures file-set-position <file>… --lat=<n> --lng=<n> Clear the place of pictures file-set-position <file>… --clear Link a picture to a location by hand ln -s -f /archive/locations/<location> '<file>/location' Look up a picture's street address again, as an administrator geocode-position -f '<file>/position' Date a staging category's files again by its rules staging retime [<category>] Change a category's time rules staging category <name> --digitized on|off or --filename-dates on|off Write a negative coordinate with = , as in --lng=-5.066 : on its own, -5.066 would be read as an option. # in EiN's terminal, in the album's folder file-set-position P1000412.JPG P1000413.JPG --lat=50.153 --lng=-5.066 Set location 50.153,-5.066 on /archive/albums/Peggy's Falmouth/P1000412.JPG Set location 50.153,-5.066 on /archive/albums/Peggy's Falmouth/P1000413.JPG

A scan shows the day it was scanned. It did not arrive in a Scans category, and its scanner is not registered as one. Give it its date with Set time , which outranks the scanner's clock; move its folder into a Scans category while it is still in staging; or register the scanner with Scanner or digitizer . A picture has a date you did not expect. Look at Time source under Details . "from the file name" means its category reads dates from names; "from the camera clock" with a wrong year means the camera's clock was wrong. All pictures from one camera are some hours off. Set the device's Timezone , or for a phone's videos turn on Video times in UTC , as described under Time zones . Set time is not in the selection bar. You may not change every selected picture: select only pictures you may change, or ask whoever owns the others. Your favourites and the pictures behind a pile on the map do not offer Set time at all; select the pictures in their album instead. The times after the arrow in Set time are hours off before you change anything. The pictures were taken in another time zone than your browser's; see the warning under Set the time of several pictures at once . The street address still names the old street after you moved the point. EiN looks up an address once per picture and does not look again when the point moves. An administrator can look it up again in the terminal with geocode-position -f '<file>/position' . A picture is on the map but has no street address. The lookup has not run yet, or the machine EiN runs on cannot reach nominatim.openstreetmap.org . It is asked again later. The picture is not linked to the location you picked. That location is a single point, which contains nothing. Draw a circle or a polygon for it, as Locations and the map describes, and the pictures inside join it. The picture still names its old location after you moved it. Its link was made by hand, and EiN never replaces such a link. In Edit file , press Clear location and Save , then open Edit file again and set the point. file-set-time answers "not a capture time". Write the date as YYYY , YYYY-MM , YYYY-MM-DD , YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS , with a year from 1826 to next year.

An album gathers the photos, videos and recordings of one occasion: a summer, a trip, a birthday. This page is for everyone who browses and organises the family's pictures. It covers finding an album, making one, filling it, changing it, and acting on the pictures in it.

Choose Albums in the sidebar, under Browse . The page lists every album you may see, with their number under the title, for example 29 albums . Each card shows the album's cover, its name, its dates and how many items it holds. Each card shows: the album's cover, with the number of items it holds in the corner; its name; its dates, from the first picture to the last, or the span someone set (see Change an album's name, description and dates ); its labels, if it has any. Rest the pointer on a card to read the album's description. A card with a photo icon instead of a picture belongs to an album with nothing to show yet, such as one that holds only documents. To narrow the list, type in Filter albums… . It matches the album's name as you type. Case and accents do not matter, and every word must appear, in any order: wellington christmas finds "Christmas in Wellington". The × in the box clears it. When nothing matches, the page says No albums found matching "<what you typed>" . Sort orders the cards. EiN remembers your choice in this browser. Choice Order Newest first (the default) The albums with the latest dates first Oldest first The albums with the earliest dates first Name (A-Z) Alphabetical by name Most items The albums holding the most pictures first Sorted by date, the page has a rail at its right edge, Scroll through time , that marks the years with albums; drag along it to jump through them. The list holds the albums people made. The albums that staging suggests for your uploads stay in your staging area until you file them, so they are not here. On an archive with no albums yet, the page says No albums yet and, if you are signed in, offers New album .

Random album , the button with two crossing arrows beside the search box in the top bar, opens an album picked at random. Alt + R does the same from anywhere outside a text field. It picks among the albums people made that you may open, never a staging suggestion. To find one particular album, start typing its name in the search box at the top ( Ctrl + K , or ⌘ + K on a Mac). Search and the finder covers that, and the Search page, which also finds albums by what their pictures show.

You need to be signed in. Choose Create , the plus in the top bar, then Album . On an empty Albums page, New album does the same. Create Album opens. In Name , type what the album is called, for example Sailing in the archipelago . If you like, write a Description . It takes Markdown, so you can use headings, lists and links. Choose Create . EiN makes the album and opens it, empty. Add pictures to it as Add pictures to an album describes. The name is also the album's folder in the tree, /archive/albums/<name> , so two albums cannot share a name. If one is taken, the dialog shows an error in red and makes nothing. You can also make an album while adding pictures to it: in Add to an album , type a name no album has and choose New album “ ” . And when you sort your uploads in staging, filing a group into an album of its own makes one. An album you create starts out shared the way your albums are by default. An administrator sets that for everyone, and you can change it for yourself with How widely what you create is shared under Profile → Preferences . Sharing explains both, and how to share one album differently with Share .

An album opens on its pictures, one section for each day they were taken. The header holds, from the top: links to the previous and next album, when the album is part of a series; the album's dates; its name, over its cover; its description; a chip that says how widely it is shared (visitors do not see it; Sharing explains the colours); its labels. Choosing one searches for everything that carries it. If you may change the album, the header also has Upload , Share and Edit , and under ⋮ the items Add event and Move to trash . On a phone they are all under ⋮ . If you may only look at the album, none of them is there. With the default sharing, everyone with an account sees every album and only its owner changes it, so on someone else's album you usually have none of these buttons. Below the header are three tabs: Media , where the album opens, Map and Info . The tab you choose goes into the page's address ( ?tab=map , ?tab=info ), so a link can open the album on it.

Show narrows the grid to one kind: All , Images , Video , Audio or Documents . It offers only the kinds the album holds, and is not there at all when the album holds one kind. Sort puts the pictures Oldest first (the default) or Newest first . EiN remembers the choice in this browser, for every album. Folders inside the album come first, as square cards (see Folders inside an album ). The pictures follow in sections, one for each day they were taken. The heading of a day gives its date and how many pictures it has. An album with pictures from more than 240 different days is shown by month instead, and one with more than 240 months by year. Pictures with no date at all are gathered under Undated . What the tiles show: a video or a recording shows its length; a video plays a short silent preview when the pointer rests on it, or on a touch screen when it scrolls into view; a stack of similar photos shows how many it holds (see Stacks of similar photos ); a heart marks a picture in your favourites; a lock marks a picture that keeps its own sharing; you see it if you may change the album. Notes added with Add event appear among the days (see Add a note to a day ). Once the album holds more than 120 pictures and notes, a Scroll through time rail at the right lets you jump through its days. Choose a picture to open it in the viewer. The viewer walks the album in the order the grid shows, and after the last picture it goes on to the first. Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers it.

The Map tab puts the album's pictures where they were taken, with the routes recorded while it lasted. The Map tab shows the album's pictures that have a position, and the routes any GPS device recorded during the album's dates. The map opens fitted to both. A picture on its own is drawn as its thumbnail; choose it to open it in the viewer. Pictures close together form a pile with a count. Choose it to list them in N photos here . Choosing never zooms. Zoom with the mouse wheel or a pinch; the map has no zoom buttons. The layers button in the corner switches between Map , Dark map and Satellite . The routes come from the album's whole span, so widening its dates in Edit album brings in the journey there and back. When nothing has a position and no route was recorded, the tab says Nothing in this album has a position, and no device recorded a route while it was taken. Dates and places of pictures shows how to give pictures a place, and Devices and GPS tracks how a route gets in.

The Info tab sums up who and what is in the album, each with a link. Section What it shows Album Name , When (its dates), Holds (for example "31 photos · 6 videos") and On the map : All of them , or how many of how many About The description People The people in its pictures, most often first Places The locations its pictures are linked to Devices The cameras and phones that took them Photographers The people who took them Labels The labels its pictures carry, with how many carry each Each name opens its page. In People , Places and Devices , the number beside a name searches the album for the pictures that have it; in Labels , a label searches the album for that label. People , Places , Devices and Photographers show their first 10, then Show all N and Show fewer ; Labels shows them all. When nobody is tagged and nothing is linked to a place or a device, the tab says so.
There are two ways: upload files from your computer or phone straight into the album, or add pictures that are already in EiN.

You can do this if you may change the album. Open the album. Choose Upload and pick the files. Or drag files from your computer and drop them anywhere on the page: while you drag, the page says Drop files to upload and, under it, Into and the album's name. Follow the upload under the Uploads button, which appears in the top bar once files are going up. It shows each upload's progress, with Cancel while files are going up, Retry failed when some failed, and Clear . The files go straight into the album; they skip staging . They are shared as the album is: whoever can see the album can see them. A file whose name the album already has is stored under a numbered name beside it; nothing is replaced. Upload takes files, not folders, and the files of a folder you drop go into the album without their folder. On a phone, the picker offers your photos, videos, recordings and GPX files, and the camera. When the upload ends, the album shows the files. Each one shows a placeholder until EiN has made its thumbnail, and goes to its day once its date has been read, which can take a few minutes after a large upload. Getting your photos in explains what happens to each file and why it takes a while. Tip For a card full of pictures you have not sorted, use Create → Import media instead. Those files wait in your private staging area, where EiN suggests albums for them and nobody else sees them until you file them. Getting your photos in compares the ways in. A suggested album from staging takes no uploads.

p.h: Add pictures that are already in EiN
p.x: Select the pictures, in any grid: an album, the Media page, a person's page, a search. Select pictures shows how. Choose Add to album in the selection bar. In the viewer, the same is in the cog menu. Add to an album opens. In Find an album, or name a new one , type part of the album's name, then choose it from the list. The list holds the albums you may change. An album whose whole name you type but cannot change is listed greyed out, marked View only . To put the pictures in an album that does not exist yet, type its name and choose New album “ ” . EiN says what it did, for example 12 added to Christmas in Wellington , adding 3 already there when some were in it before, and offers Undo . The pictures are not copied. Each stays where it lives, and the album gets a link to it, so one picture can be in several albums at once. A date, a place, a name on a face or a label given to it shows in every album it is in. The one exception is a file from your staging area: it moves into the album, and the message adds N moved out of staging .

p.h: Change an album's name, description and dates
p.x: Choose Edit in the album's header. Edit album opens. Field What it does Name What the album is called everywhere. Required. Description Text about the album, in Markdown. It shows under the title and on the Info tab. Labels The album's own labels. Pick one in use or type one; a space starts the next label. Starts and Ends The album's span, as YYYY-MM-DD . See below. Previous album and Next album Its neighbours in a series. Type part of an album's name to find one, or clear the field for none. Choose Save . EiN says Album saved . Renaming changes the name on every page. The album's folder in the tree keeps its first name, so links to the album, and to the pictures in it, keep working. The span. An album's dates are those of its first and last picture. Starts and Ends let you reach out past them, to cover the journey there and back: the dates show on the card and over the title, the Albums page sorts by them, and the Map tab draws the routes recorded within them. You cannot move them inside the pictures: Starts stops at the first picture's day and Ends at the last one's. The line under the fields says what the pictures span, for example "The media run from 2025-08-04 to 2025-08-10. Reach out past them to cover the journey there and back." To let the span follow the pictures again, clear the field or set it back to the pictures' own day. An album whose pictures have no dates has only the span you set; the line then reads "Nothing in the album is dated yet; the span is what you set here." A series. Albums of one summer after another, or the parts of a long journey, can lead from one to the next. Pick the album before this one in Previous album , or the one after it in Next album ; the album you pick links back to this one by itself. The header then shows a small pill for each neighbour, with an arrow, its cover and its name, above the dates. Rest the pointer on it to see a larger cover, and choose it to go there.

The cover is the picture on the album's card and behind its title. Open the album and select one picture. It can be one that lives in the album or one added to it from elsewhere. Choose Set as cover in the selection bar. The header changes to the picture at once. Set as cover is in the bar only if you may change the album, and it works with exactly one picture selected; with more it is greyed out. A person's page has the same button for the person's picture. An album without a cover of its own is given one by EiN: one of its own pictures, picked at random, a photo before a video or a recording. A cover you choose is never replaced. If the cover picture is deleted, the album shows another of its pictures in its place.

When someone takes several shots of the same moment, EiN folds them into a stack in the album: one tile, the stack's front photo, with a count in its corner. The other photos are still in the album; the stack only hides them from the grid. No file moves. Photos are stacked when they follow one another, look alike, and were taken at most 10 seconds apart. An administrator can change both limits under Settings → System , in the Albums group: Stack similarity ( CFG_ALBUM_STACK_THRESHOLD , 0.75) and Stack time gap (seconds) ( CFG_ALBUM_STACK_MAX_GAP_SECONDS , 10). A stack belongs to one album. The same photos can be a stack in one album and separate in another. To look through a stack, open its tile. The details panel of the viewer has a section headed with the count, for example 5 stacked photos , and a thumbnail of each photo, the front marked Front . Choose a thumbnail to see that photo. If you may change the album and every photo in the stack, the section has these buttons: Button What it does Make front Makes the photo you are looking at the one the grid shows. Keep separate Takes this photo out of stacks in this album. The section then reads Kept separate . Allow stacking On a photo kept separate: lets it be stacked again. To stack photos yourself, select two or more in the album and choose Stack in the selection bar. If one of them is already in a stack, the others join it and its front stays the front. Selecting a stack's tile selects its front photo only, so Download , Delete and the other actions of the bar act on that one photo.

An album can hold folders, for example one for each day of a long trip. They show as square cards above the pictures, with the folder's name and how many entries it holds. If you may change the album, a lock on a card marks a folder that keeps its own sharing. Choose a card to open the folder. It opens like an album page of its own, with the same tabs. The album's grid shows only the pictures at the album's own level: open a folder to see what is in it. An album that holds only folders says No media here — open a folder above. The web interface shows folders but has no button that makes one. They come from an import, from copying folders over SFTP , or from mkdir in the terminal . Once a folder is there, open it and choose Upload to upload into it. The selection bar's Stack , Set as cover and Share are offered in the album itself, not in its folders.

p.h: Add a note to a day
p.x: A note tells what happened on a day of the album: who arrived, where you sailed, why it rained. In the album's header, choose ⋮ , then Add event . Add event opens. Date is filled in with the first day of the album's pictures that has no note yet; change it as you like, as YYYY-MM-DD . Write the note in Description . Written by is you, when your account is linked to a person; choose someone else if they wrote it. Choose Add event . The note appears among the pictures, at its day, signed with the writer's name. If you may change it, a pencil on the note ( Edit event ) opens it again, with Delete to send it to the trash; EiN says Event moved to the trash and offers Undo .

You select pictures to act on several at once: download them, add them to another album, give them a date or a place, delete them. Choosing a day's heading selects all of that day; the bar at the foot acts on the selection. To Do this Select one picture Point at it and tick the checkbox in its corner. On a touch screen, press and hold it; the phone gives a short buzz. Add or take away one picture Ctrl +click it ( ⌘ +click on a Mac). Once anything is selected, a plain click or tap does the same. Select a run Shift +click: everything from the last picture you picked to this one, across days too. Select a whole day Choose the date in the day's heading. Its count then reads, for example, 24 / 24 . Choose it again to deselect the day. Select everything Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac). Clear the selection Esc , or the × at the right end of the selection bar. While anything is selected, every picture shows its checkbox, and a plain click selects instead of opening. Ctrl + A takes the pictures the page has loaded; in a long album, scroll to its end first to take them all. With the viewer open, Esc closes the viewer and leaves the selection alone. A picture that has the keyboard's focus opens with Enter or Space . ? lists these keys with the others; see Keyboard shortcuts .

As soon as one picture is selected, a bar floats at the foot of the page with the count, for example 24 selected , and buttons for what you can do. On a narrow screen the buttons fold into one Actions menu. Which buttons you see depends on the page and on what you may change. On an album page, in order: Button What it does Shown Favourite / Unfavourite Adds the pictures to your favourites, or takes them out when every one is there already. EiN says, for example, 12 files added to favourites , with Undo . Your profile, favourites and trash has the Favourites page. When you are signed in Download Saves the original files: one file as itself, several as one zip named after the album. Always Add to album Adds the pictures to another album, as above . When you are signed in Set time Gives the pictures a date and time. Dates and places of pictures covers the dialog. When you may change every selected picture Stack Stacks the pictures, as above . Needs two or more. On an album you may change Set as cover Makes the picture the album's cover. Needs exactly one. On an album you may change Share Shares the pictures Like the album , or gives them Their own sharing , for example to keep a few private in a shared album. Sharing covers the dialog. Greyed out when the selection holds a picture only added here from elsewhere: that picture has the sharing of the place it lives. On an album you may change Set location Says where the pictures were taken. Dates and places of pictures covers it. When you may change every selected picture Label Adds labels to the pictures, in Add labels . Media, Year and labels covers labels. When you may change every selected picture Delete (red) or Remove (orange) Takes the pictures out of this album, as the next section explains. When you may change every selected picture that lives in the album Other pages have most of the same buttons. Stack , Set as cover and Share are the album's own; a person's page has Set as cover too.

A picture in an album either lives there, because it was uploaded or filed into that album, or it was added to the album from elsewhere, and only a link to it is there. The last button of the selection bar treats the two differently: Delete sends a picture that lives in the album to your trash. It leaves every other album it was added to as well, and comes back to all of them if you restore it. Remove takes a picture that was only added to the album out of it. The picture stays where it lives, and in any other album it is in. One picture, many places: Delete acts on the picture itself, Remove only on this album's link to it. The tiles look alike either way; the button tells you which you have. It reads Remove , in orange, when every selected picture was only added here. When any of them lives here it reads Delete , in red: the pictures that live here go to the trash, and the ones only added here are taken out of the album. Neither asks first. EiN says what it did, for example 3 moved to the trash, 2 taken out of this album , and offers Undo , which brings back the deleted pictures and puts the links back. Deleted pictures wait in your trash, under your picture in the top bar → Trash , for 30 days by default ( CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS ); after that they are gone for good. Your profile, favourites and trash covers the Trash page, and Links what deleting and the trash do to links. When you delete a picture, what EiN worked out about it, such as faces and a transcript, goes with it, and comes back with it if you restore it.

p.h: Move a picture to another album
p.x: The web interface has no button that moves a picture from one album to another. Add to album links it into the other album; if you then delete it from the first, it goes to the trash and leaves the other album too. To move pictures, use mv in the terminal , if you may change both albums. mv keeps every link to them working, in other albums, covers and favourites: # in EiN's terminal mv -n "/archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg" "/archive/albums/Erik's archipelago/" A moved picture keeps the sharing it had. To give it the sharing of the album it moved into, select it there, choose Share , then Like the album and Save .

What you did How to undo it Favourite or Unfavourite Undo in EiN's message, or the other button Add to album Undo in EiN's message takes the pictures out again, and files from staging go back to it. An album made in the same step may stay behind, empty; move it to the trash if you do not want it. Delete or Remove Undo in EiN's message, or Restore on the Trash page for what was deleted Move to trash on an album Undo in EiN's message, or Restore on the Trash page Delete on a note Undo in EiN's message, or Restore on the Trash page Edit album No undo: open Edit and change it back Set as cover Choose another picture as the cover Stack Keep separate on each photo, in the viewer's details

p.h: Move an album to the trash
p.x: In the album's header, choose ⋮ , then Move to trash . Nothing asks first. EiN takes you back to the Albums page and says, for example, Sailing in the archipelago moved to the trash , with Undo , which puts the album back and returns you to it. The album waits in your trash with everything that lives in it, and you can restore it from the Trash page for as long as the trash keeps it. The pictures that live in the album leave every other album they were added to, until you restore it. The pictures that were only added to it stay where they live.

When you upload into your staging area, EiN groups the files and suggests albums for them. Those live in your staging area, only you see them, and you decide them on the Staging page. You can open one as an album page ( Open as an album page in staging). It then shows why its pictures were grouped, with Sort in Staging to go back to it, a match percentage, and under ⋮ the choice Keep album as is or Let the organizer manage album . It has no Upload and no Move to trash , and Edit changes only its name and labels. Sorting in staging covers all of it.

What you see Why What to do No Upload , Share or Edit on an album You may look at the album but not change it. Ask its owner, or an administrator, to share it with you so that you can edit it. See Sharing . A placeholder where a picture should be, after an upload Its thumbnail is not made yet. The media service makes it, after the pictures uploaded before it. Wait. Getting your photos in explains why it takes time. Uploaded pictures are not on their day yet Their dates have not been read yet. Reload the page a little later. An album has no dates on its card None of its pictures has a date, and no span is set. Set Starts and Ends in Edit album , or give the pictures a time with Set time . Share in the selection bar is greyed out The selection holds a picture that was only added to this album; it has the sharing of the place it lives. Select only pictures that live here. Share the others where they live. Set as cover is greyed out It needs exactly one picture selected. Select one. Stack is greyed out It needs two or more. Select more. The last button reads Remove , not Delete Every selected picture was only added to this album. Remove takes them out of this album only. To delete a picture, go to the album where it lives. A picture is gone from an album nobody changed Someone deleted it where it lives, or moved that album to the trash. It comes back to every album when it is restored from the trash of whoever deleted it. Nothing in this album has a position, and no device recorded a route while it was taken. on the Map tab No picture has a place, and no route falls within the album's dates. Give pictures a place with Set location ( Dates and places of pictures ), or widen the album's dates. This album holds more than 20,000 entries; 20,000 of them are shown. An album page shows at most 20,000 pictures. Split it into folders or several albums, or search inside it. album: Node already exists in parent … with name: … when you create an album An album or folder of that name is already in /archive/albums . Choose another name.

Everything on this page is a command underneath, and the terminal runs the same commands. A few of them: # in EiN's terminal album create "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" --description "Christmas with Helen and the children" album add "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" "/archive/albums/Ruby's Wellington/IMG_2231.jpg" album set "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" spanStart 2025-12-18 album set "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" next "/archive/albums/Ruby's Wellington" album-stack refresh "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" --dry-run -v album-random An album's path is its folder, /archive/albums/ and the name it was created with; renaming it does not change the path. album , album-stack and album-random have every option in the archive's commands .

Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer an album's pictures open in. Sharing : who sees an album, share links, and keeping some pictures private. Getting your photos in : every way files get in, and what happens to them. Sorting in staging : your private inbox and the albums it suggests. Dates and places of pictures : Set time and Set location . Links : how one picture can be in several albums.

The viewer shows one photo, video or recording at a time, large, with what EiN knows about it beside it. This page is for everyone who looks at pictures in EiN, on a computer or on a phone: how to open the viewer and move through files, what the details panel tells you, and how to work with faces, text in pictures, playback, transcripts and slideshows.

Click any picture in a grid: an album, the Media page, a person's Media tab, your Favourites , a search result. The picture grows out of its tile and fills the screen over the page. With the keyboard, move to a tile with Tab and press Enter or Space . While you are selecting pictures, a click ticks a tile instead of opening it; Albums explains selecting. The viewer walks the list you opened it from, in that list's order. A search hit on something said in a video or a recording opens it at the moment the words are spoken; see Search and the finder . Each file in the viewer has its own address: the page's address with the file added in its fullscreen parameter ( …?fullscreen=%2Fmedia%2F… ), or, opened on its own, /media/ followed by the file's path. You can copy it from the browser's address bar and send it to someone who may see the file. Stepping to another file replaces the address instead of adding to the browser's history, so one press of the browser's Back button closes the viewer and returns you to the page underneath.

The viewer on a computer. The bar under the picture gives the position in the list, the date and the place; the details panel beside it says who took it, who is in it and how old they were that day. On a computer: Top left : the close button (×). Top right : the details button (ⓘ, tooltip Details (i) ), which shows or hides the details panel , and beside it Chat , where the assistant module is installed, which opens the assistant in a drawer beside the picture. You can ask it about the picture you are looking at; see Chatting with the assistant . Left and right edges : arrows to the previous and the next file. The bar under the picture , from left to right: where you are in the list, such as 24 of 26 . The Media page leaves this out, because it loads its feed a part at a time and does not know the whole count; the date and time the picture was taken, such as Saturday, 27 December 2025, 13:16:18 ; the place: the name of the location the picture is linked to, or else the street address read from its GPS position; the heart, Favourite (s) , when you are signed in; Start slideshow ; More (⋮).

The date is shown as precisely as it is known, and no more. A picture known only to the year shows 1975 , one known to the month shows March 2004 , and neither is given an invented day or hour. Point at the date to see where it came from: from the camera clock , from GPS , entered by hand , from Google Photos or a sidecar or from the file name . A scan adds a scan: its scanner’s clocks are not when it was taken . A picture taken in another time zone is shown at the time on the photographer's clock, and the tooltip adds the same moment in your own time, such as 27 Dec 2025, 01:16 your time . Dates and places of pictures explains which date a picture gets and how to change it.

More (⋮) at the right end of the bar holds what you do to the view rather than to the file: Row What it does Pin faces / Unpin faces ( f ) Shows every face box with its name, or hides them again. It reads No faces , greyed out, when none were found. For photos and videos. Show text / Hide text ( t ) Lays the text read from the photo over it. Shown only when text was read. Edit text / Add text Opens the text for writing by hand. Shown on photos you may change. Fullscreen / Exit fullscreen Gives the viewer the whole screen. Download Saves the original file to your device. The file name at the top of the details panel downloads the original too. To download several files at once, select them in the grid and use Download in the selection bar.

p.h: Move between files and close the viewer
p.x: Next file : → , the arrow at the right edge, or swipe left on a touch screen. Previous file : ← , the arrow at the left edge, or swipe right. The list goes round: after the last file comes the first again, and before the first comes the last. To close the viewer, press × at the top left, press Esc , use the browser's Back button, or on a phone swipe down on the picture. The picture shrinks back into its tile, so you see where you were in the grid. Esc first closes whatever lies over the picture: the enlarged map, the text dialog or Edit faces . During a slideshow it stops the slideshow. Only then does it close the viewer.

Photos and videos zoom; recordings do not, and nothing zooms during a slideshow. To With a mouse and keyboard On a touch screen Zoom in or out at a spot Turn the mouse wheel over the spot Pinch Zoom in on a spot, or back out Double-click a photo Double-tap Zoom in a step + or = Zoom out a step - Fit the whole picture again 0 Double-tap Look around a zoomed picture Drag it Drag with one finger Each file opens fitted to the screen. On a touch screen, swiping to the next file waits until the picture is back at its fitted size; until then a one-finger drag moves around the picture. Over text laid on the picture, the mouse wheel scrolls the text; hold Ctrl to zoom instead.

Key What it does ← / → Previous / next file i Show or hide the details f Show or hide the faces t Show or hide the text in the picture s Favourite or unfavourite + or = Zoom in - Zoom out 0 Fit the picture Esc Close: first a layer over the picture or a slideshow, then the viewer Videos and recordings have keys of their own; see Play a video . Press ? to see the shortcuts that work where you are, and see Keyboard shortcuts for every key in EiN.

The viewer takes its phone layout on any touch screen, and in any browser window 768 pixels wide or narrower. On a phone the details are a sheet you pull up from under the picture with a swipe. The date sits in a dark pill centred over the top of the picture, with the time beneath it. The bar under the picture keeps only the position in the list and the place. ⋮ in the top right corner holds Favourite , Start slideshow , the rows of the More menu and Chat . The details panel is closed when the viewer opens. Held upright, swipe up on the picture to pull up the details sheet over the bottom half, and swipe down on it to put it away. Held sideways, the details open as a panel on the right: press Show details beside ⋮, or swipe up, and swipe the panel to the right to close it. Edit faces is not offered on a phone held upright. Gesture What it does Swipe left / right Next / previous file Swipe up Open the details Swipe down Close the details; with the details closed, close the viewer Pinch, or double-tap Zoom a photo Drag with one finger on a zoomed photo Look around it Tap a face Open the person's page, or name an unnamed person; pin the faces to see the boxes A swipe that starts at the very edge of the screen is left to the phone itself, so its own Back gesture closes the viewer. Turning the phone sideways makes the viewer fullscreen, and turning it upright again leaves fullscreen. An iPhone has no fullscreen for web pages, so there the viewer stays as it is. EiN on a phone covers the rest of the interface on a small screen.

On a computer the details panel opens on the right each time you open the viewer. Press the details button (ⓘ) or i to close it while you look; it stays closed until you close the viewer. On a phone you pull it up, as described above. Each part of the panel is a row with an icon at its left. A row appears only when it has something to show. From the top: Row What it shows The file The file name, which downloads the original, and its size. Under it a line of facts: 3200 × 2400 · 7.7 MP · ISO 100 · 1/250 s ; a video adds its length and frame rate, and a recording its length, kbps, kHz and mono or stereo . Then the sharing chip, which says who can see the file ( Sharing ), and the file's labels; a label opens a search for it ( Media, Year and labels ). The cog at the right opens the cog menu . Description What someone wrote about the file. Copies in staging Only for a file of yours still in your staging area: its exact copies and look-alikes. See Duplicates . Transcript For videos and recordings with speech: what is said, line by line. See Read along with a transcript . Camera The device that took it, linking to its page; Owned by whoever owned it then, with the years; Shot by the photographer, when someone has said who. Without a registered device, the make and model the file names. See Devices and GPS tracks . Albums Every album the file is in, with its cover. A file can be in several albums without being copied. People Everyone recognised or tagged in the picture, with their age that day. See People in the picture . Place The location the file is linked to, as a link, the street address, and a small map. Enlarge map opens a large map of the spot. Stack For a photo stacked with others in this album: N stacked photos , or Kept separate , with a thumbnail of each and Front on the one the album shows. Click a thumbnail to see it in the viewer. Make front , Keep separate and Allow stacking are there when you may change the album and every photo in the stack. See Albums . Similar Up to 12 pictures that look most like this one, nearest first, leaving out the picture itself and the rest of its stack. Click one to walk these pictures in the viewer. Show all opens the Media page with every picture like it. Not shown for recordings. Comments Comments on the file, with who wrote them and when. Everyone who can see the file reads them. If you may change the file, write one in Add a comment… and press Comment . The bin beside a comment of your own ( Delete comment ) removes it. Details A folded section for the machine-written facts. See The Details section .

Each person has a badge with their age on the day the picture was taken: 69 years , or 8 months for a child under one. A ~ in front, as in ~44 years , marks an age that is approximate because only the year or month of the person's birth is known. There is no age when the picture has no date or the person has no birth date. Pointing at a name lights up that person's face box on the picture, and pointing at a box lights up the name. Click a name to open the person's page. If you may change the picture and are not sure a face really is the person named, point at the name: a question mark slides in beside it (on a phone it is always there). Press it, Not sure this is <name>? , and either: say who it is: pick someone, or type a name and choose New person: <name> , and press Move ; or press Mark as doubtful to leave it to somebody who knows. The face stays the person's, marked as doubtful until somebody answers, here or on the person's Faces tab (see Doubtful faces ). Beside a doubtful face the question mark is always shown, orange, and asks Is this <name>? , with who marked it, such as "peggy is not sure.": Yes : it is them. The face stays theirs, as a person's decision, and the doubt goes. No, it is… : pick who it is instead, or a new name, as above, and press Move . Withdraw : takes your doubt back without answering it. Readers who may not change the picture see the orange question mark and who marked the face, but cannot answer. Faces that recognition has grouped as one person but nobody has named yet are listed with a crop of the face and a placeholder name, such as Unknown 8F3C81 . Click one to open the review over the viewer, where you name them or say they are someone you already have. People and faces describes the review and how recognition works. A scanned print. The camera row names the scanner it was digitized on, and the two faces nobody has named yet wait under placeholder names; clicking one opens the review where you say who it is.

Details , at the bottom of the panel, unfolds the facts a reader seldom needs. Whether it is open is remembered in this browser, for the next picture and the next visit. Row What it shows Path Where the file is in EiN's tree, such as /archive/albums/cornwall-1968/img20120303_133900582.jpg . Click it to open a terminal tab at the file ( The terminal ). Visitors who are not signed in see the path as text. Text in image The text read from the picture. Text language The language the text was read in, and how sure the reading was. If you may change the file, a menu to choose another; see Read the text in a picture . Type The kind of file, such as image/heic . Taken at The capture time exactly as stored, such as 2025-12-27T13:16:18+13:00 . Taken at (UTC) The same moment in UTC. Time source Where the date came from, in words, and any note left with it. Created , Modified The file's created and modified times. Hashes Fingerprints of the file's bytes, such as sha256 . EXIF tags Every tag the file carries, one per row, or No EXIF recorded .

p.h: Change a file from the cog menu
p.x: The cog at the top right of the details panel ( Edit media ) opens a menu. It is there when you may change the file, and for any signed-in reader for Add to album . Row Who sees it What it does Edit Readers who may change the file Opens Edit file : description, labels and location. See below. Share Readers who may change the file Opens the Share dialog for this file. See Sharing . Add to album Signed-in readers Opens Add to an album . Type part of an album's name to find it, or a name that is not taken to make an album by that name. The file is linked into the album, not copied; a file from your staging area moves into it instead. A message such as 1 added to Christmas in Wellington offers Undo . Edit faces Readers who may change the file, on photos and videos, not on a phone held upright Draw, move or remove face boxes. See Draw or correct a face box . Edit subtitles , Add subtitles Readers who may change the file, on videos and recordings Opens what is said, line by line, beside the video or recording, to correct it. See Correct the subtitles . Rotate left , Rotate right Readers who may change the file, on photos and videos Turns the file a quarter turn. Mirror horizontally Readers who may change the file, on photos and videos Flips the file left to right. A tick shows while it is mirrored. A turn or a flip is kept on the file, for everyone who sees it. EiN moves the face boxes with the picture and makes the smaller versions it shows again. A video is re-encoded by the media service, which takes a while; until it is done the video plays the old way round. To undo a turn, turn it back. The rotate and mirror rows are not offered for a file that cannot be decoded. There is no cropping and no colour editing in EiN.

p.h: Change the description, labels or location
p.x: In the cog menu, choose Edit . The Edit file dialog opens, with the file name under its title. In Description , write what the picture shows or what you know about it. Formatting such as bold and lists is kept. In Labels , pick a label in use or type one. A space starts the next label. To set where it was taken, pick a place in A known location , or click the spot in On the map , or type its coordinates there. The dialog warns: "The new location replaces the position the file carries, for the map and for searching by location." To take the location away, press Clear location . The dialog warns: "The file will have no location, for the map or for searching by location." Press Save . It stays greyed out until you have changed something; Cancel closes the dialog without saving. The date is not changed here. To change when pictures were taken, select them in the grid and use Set time in the selection bar; see Dates and places of pictures .

Face boxes stay hidden until you point at a face; then that face's box and name appear. Pin faces in the More menu, or f , shows every box with its name. They stay pinned as you move from file to file, until you unpin them or reload the page. On a touch screen, where nothing can be pointed at, pinning is the way to see the boxes. Click a named box to open that person's page. Click the box of an unnamed person to open a small field, Who is this? . Type a name and press Enter or the tick. This gives them a name as a person of their own. If they are someone already in the archive, click their placeholder name in the details panel instead and choose the person in the review. A face that belongs to nobody reads Unassigned . A dashed box is a tag: "Tag: a box with a name, not used to recognise faces". It says who is there without helping to recognise them in other pictures. A box drawn by hand is a tag, and so is a found face whose box someone has moved or resized.

p.h: Draw or correct a face box
p.x: Use Edit faces when recognition missed a face, drew the box in the wrong place, or matched the wrong person. It is offered on photos and videos you may change, except on a phone held upright. On a video it pauses the video, and you draw on the frame on screen; the large play button leaves the picture while you draw, and the one on the bar still plays. A box you draw on a video belongs to that moment and shows from half a second before it to half a second after. A box already there can be chosen and removed or given to someone else, but not moved or resized. In the cog menu, choose Edit faces . The bar under the picture reads Draw a new box or select a face , and every box shows. To add a face, drag a box over it. To change a face, click its box. Drag the box to move it, or drag one of the round handles on its edges and corners to resize it. The bar reads Adjust the box, change who it is, or remove it . Under the box, choose: Done to save the box; Cancel to drop your changes to it; the person's name (tooltip Change who this is ) to say who the face is, in the dialog described below; Remove , then Confirm remove , to take the face away. A box you drew is given an unidentified person of its own, and the review opens so you can name them or say they are someone already in the archive. A found face whose box you move or resize keeps its person, but becomes a tag and no longer helps recognition. To leave Edit faces , choose it again in the cog menu, press × in the bar under the picture, or press Esc . The dialog for a face's name is Who is this? , with Now marked as Helen Okafor or Not marked as anyone under the title: Someone I know : pick the person in Who it is , then press Move . Someone new : "the face becomes a new unidentified person, for you to name now or later". Press Move . Let recognition decide : the face is matched again against everyone else. Press Match again . The bar then says what happened, such as Recognition matched the face to Ruby Wrenfield. , Recognition made the face a new unidentified person. or Recognition left the face unassigned: too small or unclear to start a new person. This choice is not there for a tag, which recognition cannot match. Changes you make to faces are decisions by a person, and later recognition runs leave them alone; see People and faces .

p.h: Read the text in a picture
p.x: EiN reads the text in photos: letters, postcards, signs, printed pages, and handwriting in English, Swedish and Finnish. The media service does the reading in the background. A picture still in your staging area is read once it is filed into an album. Show text lays the words read from Peggy's postcard over the picture. The pencil at its top right opens the text for correcting. Show text , in the More menu, or t , darkens the picture and lays the text over it in a typewriter face. Long text scrolls. The row is there only when text was read. The text stays shown as you move from picture to picture, until you close the viewer, so you can page through a scanned letter. It is hidden during a slideshow. Hide text , or t again, takes it away. The text is also under Text in image in the Details section , and search finds pictures by it; see Search and the finder .

p.h: Correct the text, or add it by hand
p.x: In the More menu, choose Edit text , or Add text when nothing was read. With the text shown, the pencil at its top right does the same. The dialog Text in the picture opens: the picture on the left (above, on a narrow screen), which you can zoom to read closely, and a text box on the right. Type or correct the text. Press Save , or Ctrl + Enter . Saving empty text removes it. What you write replaces what was read. It is offered on photos you may change.

p.h: Read the text again in another language
p.x: When the reading came out wrong because EiN took the text for another language, choose the language yourself: Open Details at the bottom of the details panel. In Text language , choose the language. The menu starts at Automatic , which shows what was detected, such as Automatic: English (93%) , and offers Swedish, Finnish, English, Danish, Norwegian, German and French. EiN reads the picture again in that language, and the text follows after a while. Choose Automatic to let EiN tell the language again. Readers who may not change the file see the language without the menu.

A video starts playing when it opens. If your browser blocks that, press play. On a computer, click the picture to pause or play, and double-click it to go fullscreen. A large play button sits in the middle while the video is paused. The controls fade while the video plays and come back when you move the mouse. Control Key What it does Play / Pause Space or k Plays or pauses. Back 10 s j Goes back ten seconds. Forward 10 s l Goes forward ten seconds. Previous chapter , Next chapter Shift + ← , Shift + → Jumps between chapters, when the video has them. Mute / Unmute m Turns the sound off or on. The slider beside it sets the volume, where the browser lets a page do that. The clock Where you are and how long the video is, such as 0:42 / 2:11 , and Chapter 2 of 5 when it has chapters. Subtitles (CC) c Shows or hides subtitles, when the video has a transcript. The tooltip names the language: Subtitles: English (c) . Picture-in-picture p Plays the video in a small window that stays on top, where the browser offers it. Cast to a screen Sends the video to a television or other screen. Shown only while your browser finds one. Fullscreen Gives the player alone the whole screen, with its controls and subtitles. The volume you set is remembered in this browser for the next video or recording. There is no control for the playback speed. On a phone, tap the picture to show or hide the controls. Three buttons sit over the middle of the picture: back ten seconds, play or pause, and forward ten seconds, or previous and next chapter when the video has chapters. More (⋮) on the bar holds Picture-in-picture and Cast to a screen… , where the browser offers them. There is no mute button: use the phone's own volume buttons. On an iPhone, Fullscreen opens Safari's own player, which shows the subtitles when they are on. Elsewhere, a wide video put fullscreen with the player's button turns the screen sideways where the browser allows it.

Click or drag on the timeline to jump. Pointing at it shows the time there and, once the media service has made the video's storyboard, a small frame from that moment. The media service finds the cuts in a video and makes each scene a chapter. A video whose file names the camera or phone that recorded it is taken to be one take, so there only a clear cut makes a chapter, not a lamp switched on or the exposure changing. Chapters show as pieces of the timeline with gaps between them; a video with too many to fit gets a small tick at each start instead. Pointing at the timeline shows the chapter too, such as 1:24 · Chapter 3 . Previous chapter more than two seconds into a chapter goes back to its start, and otherwise to the chapter before. Move to the timeline with Tab to use the keyboard on it: ← and → go back and forward five seconds, Page Down and Page Up go to the previous and next chapter (or a tenth of the video, without chapters), and Home and End go to the start and the end.

A video or recording with a transcript has the CC button. Subtitles start on; once you turn them off, they stay off for the next video or recording in this browser, until you turn them on again. When two or more people speak, each line starts with the speaker's name, in a colour of their own. A voice nobody has named is called Speaker 1 , Speaker 2 and so on.

The face boxes follow the faces as the video plays, and Pin faces works as it does on a photo. In the details panel, a button beside each person shows them: its tooltip reads, for example, Show Ruby Wrenfield at 0:42 · on screen 0:00–0:39, 0:42–1:28 . Pressing it pauses the video on the frame where the face is seen most clearly and keeps a box on the face from there. Press it again ( Stop following Ruby Wrenfield ) to let go.

A recording plays against a picture of its sound. The transcript beside it follows along, and clicking a line jumps there. A recording starts playing when it opens. Its picture is the waveform of the sound, and the waveform is the timeline: the part already played is brighter, a line marks where you are, and a click or a drag on it jumps there. A large play button sits on it while the recording is paused. Under it are play or pause ( Play (Space) , Pause (Space) ), Back 10 s and Forward 10 s , mute and the volume slider (not on a phone), and the clock; at the right end Subtitles (CC) when it has a transcript, Picture-in-picture where the browser offers it, and Fullscreen . With subtitles on, the line being said shows between the waveform and the buttons. Space or k plays and pauses, and j , l , m , c and p work as on a video. Move to the waveform with Tab to use the same keys as on a video's timeline.

The media service writes down what is said in videos and recordings, and works out who speaks when. The transcript appears near the top of the details panel, under the file. Each line starts with its time. The line being said is in bold and is kept in view as it plays. Click a line to jump to that moment. Where the voice changes, the line carries the speaker's name. Above the lines is a chip for each voice, such as Speaker 1 · 1:38 : who it is and how long they speak in the file. The small play button on a chip ( Hear Speaker 1 ) jumps to the start of that voice's longest turn. Click a chip to say who it is. A named voice opens the person's page. An unnamed one opens the review, where you name them or say they are someone already in the archive. A voice that belongs to nobody yet becomes an unidentified person of its own first; this needs permission to change the file.
