A transcript can also read No speech was detected. , or Transcript unavailable. when it could not be loaded.

The transcript is written by a machine, and it mishears: a name, a word in a dialect, a line it invents over a quiet stretch, or one it never heard. You can correct it on a video or a recording you may change. In the cog menu at the top right of the details panel, choose Edit subtitles , or Add subtitles when there are none. The dialog Subtitles opens where the viewer was playing, and pauses it: the video (or the recording's waveform) on the left, above a timeline that shows where every line lies, and the lines on the right (below, on a narrow screen). The line being said is drawn over the picture as it reads now, with your changes, and tinted in the list. Correct a line by typing in it. Each line has its start and end, which you can type ( 1:23.4 , or seconds such as 83.4 ), and a play button that plays just that line and stops. The line you are in has buttons to start or end it at the playhead, split it at the cursor, join it with the next line, and delete it. Add line puts a new line at the playhead. Press Save , or Ctrl + Enter . An empty line is left out. A line that ends before it starts is marked in red and must be fixed first. The keys work while you type in a line, so you can listen and write at once: Key What it does Ctrl + Space , Alt + K Play or pause. Outside a text box Space and k do too. Alt + J / Alt + L Back or forward two seconds. Alt + P Play the line, from its start to its end. Alt + I / Alt + O The line starts, or ends, at the playhead. Alt + N A new line at the playhead. Alt + S Split the line at the cursor. Alt + ↑ / Alt + ↓ The line before, or after. Closing with changes not saved asks first. What you save is what the subtitles, the transcript in the details panel and search show from then on, and EiN keeps it: the file is not transcribed again, not even when the media service's transcription improves. The speakers stay as they were. For a recording or video you reach from a search for words that are said in it, the viewer opens at the moment they are said.

Open the picture to start from, in the album or list you want to show. Press Start slideshow (the play button in the bar). On a phone it is in ⋮. It is greyed out when the list holds only one file. The browser goes fullscreen, if it allows that; if not, the slideshow runs in the window. The close button, the arrows, the details panel and the face boxes go away, and the bar lies over the bottom of the picture. Pinned face names stay on and follow the picture. Each photo stays on screen for Seconds per slide , 3 unless you change it, and fades into the next. With Ken Burns effect on, as it is unless you turn it off, each photo slowly pans and zooms. Videos and recordings play to their end before the next file. One that will not play is skipped after one slide's time. The slideshow follows the list's order and goes round from the last file to the first, until you stop it. There is no shuffle. ← and → still step back and forward. While it runs, the screen is kept from going to sleep. To stop the slideshow, click the picture, press Esc , or leave fullscreen. To change the timing or turn the pan and zoom off, open your picture at the top right, choose Profile , then the Preferences tab, and look under Playback : Setting What it does Default Seconds per slide How long each photo is shown in a slideshow. 3 Ken Burns effect Slowly pan and zoom each photo during a slideshow. on They are yours alone and do not change anyone else's slideshows. See Your profile, favourites and trash , and in the settings reference CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS and CFG_USER_KEN_BURNS .

Press the heart in the bar, or s ; on a phone choose Favourite in ⋮. The heart turns red. Press it again ( Unfavourite ) to take the picture out of your favourites. Your favourites are your own: open your picture at the top right and choose Favourites to see them all, by day. To heart many pictures at once, select them in the grid and use Favourite in the selection bar. Visitors who are not signed in have no favourites and see no heart. See Your profile, favourites and trash .

p.h: What you see depends on who you are
p.x: You are What differs Signed in, and may change the file Everything on this page. Signed in, and may only see the file The cog menu holds only Add to album . You read comments but cannot write them, and see the text language without the menu. No Edit text , Edit subtitles , Edit faces , rotate or mirror. A visitor who is not signed in No heart, no cog menu and no sharing chip. Path is plain text. Someone who opened a share link The pictures without the details panel; the details button and i are not there. Sharing explains who can see what.

p.h: When something is not as expected
p.x: A picture you added a moment ago has no thumbnail, faces, text or transcript yet. The media service works through added files in the background, and the viewer fills in as each step finishes. Until it is done, an administrator sees the Dashboard read Catching up . Text in pictures waits until the file leaves staging. See Getting your photos in . "This rendition could not be played. It may still be transcoding." The version of the video or recording that the browser plays has not been made yet, or failed. Wait a while and open it again. "This browser or device cannot play AV1, the format this video is in." EiN makes its playable videos in the AV1 format, and this browser or device cannot decode it. Use a current browser on another device, or Download the original. "This file cannot be played" , with "The original is damaged, so no preview or playable version could be made from it." The uploaded file itself cannot be read; the reason is under the message. Download it to check the file on your own device. A PDF or a Word file shows nothing. The viewer has no reader for documents. Use Download in the More menu to open the file on your device. Its text can still be found with search; see Supported files . Show text is not in the More menu. No text was read from this picture, or it is a video or a recording. Add the text yourself with Add text , if you may change the file. Start slideshow is greyed out. The list holds only one file. Open the viewer from an album or a longer list. The date or the place is wrong. See Dates and places of pictures .

What the viewer shows and changes can also be done in EiN's terminal : Command What it does media-details <file> Everything the details panel shows about a file. file-set-description --text '…' <file> Sets or clears the description. file-set-text --text '…' <file> Writes the text in a picture by hand. file-set-text-language <file> <code|auto> Reads the text again in a language. file-set-transcript <file> < subtitles.vtt Writes what is said in a video or recording, as WebVTT, by hand. file-set-orientation --rotate cw <file> Turns a file; ccw and 180 too, and --toggle-mirror flips it. star <path> , star -d <path> Marks a favourite, or takes it away. # in EiN's terminal media-details /archive/albums/cornwall-1968/img20120303_133900582.jpg file-set-text-language /archive/albums/cornwall-1968/img20120303_133900582.jpg en

The Media page shows every photo, video, recording and document you may see, and searches them. The Year page shows what one year of the archive holds. Labels are words you put on pictures and albums so that you can find them again. This page is for everyone who browses the archive.

Open Media in the sidebar. The page is headed Media , "Photos, videos, audio and documents", with a search box and its controls under the title. With nothing typed in the box, the Media page is a feed of everything you may see, newest first. The page works in two ways: With the box empty, it is a feed : everything you may see, newest first, in sections by date. With anything typed or picked in the box, it is a search : the best matches first, in one grid without dates. See Search from the Media page .

Each section is headed by its date, such as "29 June 2026", and the number of pictures in it. As you scroll, the date of the section you are in stays at the top of the page. Click a date heading to select everything under it. Click it again to clear the selection. A picture known only to a year, such as a scan dated 1975, sits under the year alone. Pictures with no date at all come last, under Undated . Dates and places of pictures explains where dates come from. Above the feed, a row of round rings shows this day in earlier years: one for each earlier year with pictures taken on today's date, marked "1 year ago", "12 years ago" and so on. A ring plays that year's pictures as a story. Memories, news and events on Home describes it. Once the feed holds more than 120 pictures, a time rail runs down the right edge of the page. Drag it to move through the years; the feed loads the pictures from the date you drag to. Click a picture to open it in the viewer, where the arrows walk through the feed. The viewer's "N of M" counter is not shown here, because the feed loads part of the archive at a time. Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers the viewer. On a phone, in the Default layout, pinch the grid to fit between 2 and 5 pictures across. Files in your staging area are not in the feed, and not in the page's searches, until you file them into an album. See Sorting in staging .

Layout decides how the feed is drawn: Layout How the feed looks Default By day, each picture at its own shape, in rows that fill the width. Days By day, in square tiles: three across on a phone, more on a wider screen. Months By month, in square tiles: five across on a phone, more on a wider screen. Good for getting around a large archive. A search is one grid without dates, so Layout is hidden while you search. Your choice is remembered in this browser, not for your account: another computer or phone starts with Default .

Turn on Show only mine to see only the files you added yourself, the ones uploaded or imported under your account. It narrows searches from the box as well as the feed. With nothing of yours to show, the page says "Nothing you have added yet." The switch is off by default, and like the layout it is remembered in this browser. Visitors who have not signed in do not have it.

Show keeps one kind of file: Choice What is shown All Photos, videos, recordings and documents. Images Photos. Video Videos. Audio Recordings. Documents PDF, Word, OpenDocument, RTF, Markdown, HTML and plain text files. Choosing a kind keeps the feed: the videos alone are still newest first, by date. The kind goes into the page's address ( /media?kind=video ), so a link you copy opens the same view. Documents show as a placeholder tile with no picture; Supported files lists which ones EiN reads the text of.

When the pictures shown carry labels, a row of label pills appears above them, each with the number of pictures that carry it. Click a pill to keep only those pictures: the label becomes a #label chip in the box, and the page turns into a search. Click another pill to narrow further, to pictures that carry both labels. Remove a chip with its × to widen the view again. A label that every picture shown already carries would narrow nothing, so it is left out of the row, as are the labels you have already chosen. Labels explains how pictures get them.

Type in the box, where it says "Filter the media — “Anna sailing 2011”, or type @ to pick someone", and press Enter . On a computer the box has the keyboard as soon as the page opens, so you can start typing at once. Words find pictures by what they show, by the text written in them and by what is said in recordings and videos. "Christmas tree" finds Christmas pictures from every decade, whether or not anyone labelled them. A year in what you type becomes a chip, such as "1998" or "from 2010", and a kind of file, such as "videos", sets Show . With a language model set up, the names of people and places become chips too. @ opens a list of people, locations, labels, devices and albums. Pick one to keep only the pictures that have it: @Peggy Wrenfield , @The cottage at Malpas , #sailing . The picture button beside the box, Search with a picture , finds what looks like a picture from your device, such as a photo of an old print. The results are one grid, best matches first. Each tile shows its score as a percentage, measured against the best match, which is 100%. The search is kept in the page's address, so you can send someone the link and it opens the same search. Remove the chips and empty the box to return to the feed. Search and the finder explains the rest: how the box reads a sentence, the Interpreted filter beside the box, what needs the media service and what a language model adds.

Select pictures as you would in an album: hover over a picture and tick its box, Shift +click to select a range, Ctrl +click ( ⌘ +click on a Mac) to add or remove one, Ctrl + A to select everything loaded, and Esc to clear. On a touch screen, press and hold a picture. ? lists these keys, and Albums describes selecting in full. A bar at the bottom says how many are selected and offers what you may do with them: Button What it does Shown when Favourite / Unfavourite Hearts the pictures, or takes them out of your favourites when all of them are hearted. You are signed in. Download Downloads one file as itself, several as one zip file. Always. Add to album Links the pictures into an album you choose, or one you name there. You are signed in. Set time Sets when the pictures were taken. See Dates and places of pictures . You may change every selected file. Set location Sets where they were taken. See Dates and places of pictures . You may change every selected file. Label Puts labels on them. See Put labels on pictures . You may change every selected file. Delete Moves them to your trash, with Undo in the message that follows. You may change every selected file. On a phone the buttons fold into one Actions menu. Your favourites and your trash are described in Your profile, favourites and trash .

Upload , at the top right of the page, picks files to send, and Upload a folder , under ⋮, picks a whole folder. You can also drop files anywhere on the page: the screen says "Drop files to upload" and "Into staging, folders and all". All three send the files to your staging area, into today's folder of your inbox, and not into the library. They appear on the Media page once you have filed them into an album. You need to be signed in to upload. Getting your photos in explains every way in and what happens to a file afterwards.

Open Year under Explore in the sidebar. The page is headed Year , "Everything from one year", and opens on the current year, or on the year its address names: /year?year=1968 opens 1968. The histogram shows which years hold anything; the slider and the arrows move between them.

There are three ways to move, and they work together: The arrows beside the year. ‹ and › step one year earlier or later. « and » jump to the nearest earlier or later year that holds anything, which saves stepping through the empty years between sparse decades. Pointing at « or » names the year it jumps to, for example "Previous year with entries: 1983", or says "No earlier entries" when there is none; with Albums or People chosen under Show , it counts those instead. The histogram behind the header. Each year that holds anything has a faint bar, taller the more it holds; the chosen year's bar is drawn in blue. The bars grow with the square root of the count, so a year with two albums is still visible beside one with a hundred. The slider along the foot of the header. It has one step for each year that holds anything, plus the current year, so empty years take no room. A few of the years are written under it. Drag the handle and the year at the top follows. The year is kept in the page's address, so you can link to it, and a reload opens the same year. Visiting many years does not fill the browser's history: one press of Back leaves the Year page. The Years section of the Search page lists every year with something in it and opens it here.

The year shows two kinds of card: Albums that hold pictures taken that year. An album with pictures from one December and the January after appears in both years. The card is the one the Albums page draws: the cover, the name, the dates and the number of items. An album with no dated pictures appears in no year, and suggested albums in your staging area do not appear. People born or died that year. A person's card has the badge Born , or Died , with their age added when their birth date is known: Arthur Wrenfield appears in 2014 as Died, aged 83 . Click a card to open the album or the person. Two controls at the right of the box arrange the cards: Control Choices Show All , Albums , or People (births and deaths). Sort Oldest first (the default), Newest first , Name (A-Z) or Most items . With Most items , people come after the albums. Both are remembered in this browser. The histogram and the jump arrows follow Show : with People chosen, they show the years with births and deaths. On a phone, Show and Sort fold into one button with a sliders icon. When a year holds nothing, the page says "Nothing from 1957." and the histogram shows which years do.

p.h: Narrow the year to a person, a place or a label
p.x: The box under the year, "Narrow the year — type @ for a person, location or label", keeps only what has to do with one person, one location or one label. Type @ and the first letters of the name, for example @pegg . Pick Peggy Wrenfield from the list with the mouse, or with the arrow keys and Enter or Tab . Press Enter . The name becomes a chip in the box, and the year keeps: Chip What the year keeps A person Albums holding pictures of them, and their own birth or death. A location Albums holding pictures taken there. A label ( #sailing ) Albums holding pictures that carry the label. You can have one person, one location and one label at a time; picking a second person replaces the first. Words typed without @ keep the cards whose title or description contains them. Remove a chip with its × to widen the year again. The histogram and the jump arrows follow the box as well, so they show the years where that person, place or label appears. When the year you are on has nothing that matches, the page says "Nothing from 1968 matches — the histogram shows the years that do." Use « or » to jump to the nearest year that does. The box narrows what you see without changing the address: a reload, or a link you send, shows the whole year.

A label is one word, such as sailing or christmas , that you put on a picture, an album, a person, a location or a device. A label stays one word: spaces and commas in what you type start the next label, and a slash becomes a hyphen. Labels are shared across the archive, so the labels anyone has used are offered as you type, and the same word is the same label wherever it is. Labels show under the name of what carries them: in an album's, a person's, a location's or a device's header, and in the viewer's details panel.

Select the pictures, on the Media page, in an album, or on a person's, a location's or a device's Media tab. Press Label in the bar at the bottom. In Add labels , type the labels. "Pick a label in use or type a new one. A space starts the next label." Press Add labels . Label is offered only when you may change every selected file. To put labels on a single picture you have open, use its cog menu in the viewer: Edit opens Edit file , which has a Labels field.

p.h: Put labels on an album, a person, a location or a device
p.x: Each of these has a Labels field in its edit dialog, opened with Edit in its header: Edit album , Edit person , Edit location and Edit device . Add a label by typing it, take one off with the × on it, and save the dialog. You see Edit only where you may change the thing. The edit dialogs are also the only place in the web interface where you take labels off. There is no button that takes a label off many pictures at once; in the terminal, label remove does it for one node at a time.

Where you look decides what you find: Where What it finds Click a label wherever it is shown The Search page for that label: albums holding a picture that carries it, and any album, person, location or device that carries it itself. The Media page: pick the label with @ , or click its label pill The pictures that carry the label. The Year page: pick the label with @ The albums of that year holding pictures that carry it. An album's Info tab, under Labels The album's pictures that carry each label, with their count. See Albums . The Labels section of the Search page, before you search Every label in use, most used first, each with its count. A label on an album finds the album on the Search page, but the Media and Year pages look at the pictures themselves: a picture carries a label only when it was put on the picture. The Search page's Labels section also lists suggested labels, drawn outlined with a sparkle: words that at least five pictures look like but that nothing carries yet. Pointing at one says, for example, "A suggested label: 12 pictures look like it, and nothing carries it yet". The words come from a list of things a family archive shows, such as beach , wedding or christmas , in the archive's language ( en or sv , the setting CFG_LANGUAGE ).

Every label is also a folder: /archive/tags/<label> holds a link to each picture, album, person, location or device that carries the label. You can look through it in the terminal, for example with ls /archive/tags/sailing . Links explains links in the tree. A label is kept in two places: on the node that carries it, which the label pills count, and as the link in the folder, which a search for the label reads. The dialogs, label add and label remove keep the two in step, so put labels on and take them off with those, not by adding or deleting links in the folder. When something labelled is deleted, its link in the folder goes with it, and label prune clears any link left pointing at nothing. A label is listed while at least one thing carries it.

p.h: Let EiN suggest where a label belongs
p.x: When you are signed in and the Search page or the Media page asks for exactly one label, a bar headed Looks like and the label appears above the results. EiN learns what the label looks like from the pictures that carry it, and suggests other pictures and albums that look the same. Search for one label, for example by clicking sailing on an album, or by picking #sailing on the Media page. On the Looks like sailing bar, press Show . While EiN learns, the bar says "Learning what sailing looks like…". Look through the suggestions: pictures and albums that do not carry the label yet, the most alike first. Select the pictures that belong and press Label sailing , or select the ones that do not and press Not sailing . An album's card has its own Label and Not sailing buttons. EiN learns from each answer: the model and the suggestions are worked out again at once, and what you marked as not the label is left out of the suggestions from then on. Show all opens the Media page with every picture that looks like the label and does not carry it yet, the most alike first, under the chip Looks like sailing . Hide folds the bar. When the model is good enough to stand on its own, the bar says how many pictures it would add, for example "40 more look like it", before you open it. For a suggested label that nothing carries yet, the bar opens by itself, because the suggestions are all there is. Under the bar, one line says how far to trust the suggestions: What the bar says What it means "Learned from N pictures in N labeled files and albums. Of the labeled pictures held back, it finds N% again." EiN hid some of the labelled pictures while learning and checked how many it found again. The higher, the better. "… Label a few more for it to measure how well it finds them." Too few pictures carry the label to check the model. It still suggests. "Suggested from what "a photo of a christmas tree" looks like. Label pictures of it and it learns from them instead." A suggested label: nothing carries it yet, so EiN goes by what the words describe. "Nothing with this label has a picture to learn from." The label is only on people, places or devices, or on pictures the media service has not looked at yet. "The pictures held back were not found again, so what this label names does not seem to show in the pictures: a person, a trip or a time rather than something seen." The label names something you cannot see, so EiN offers no suggestions. Show what it would suggest shows them anyway. "Nothing else looks like sailing" means that no picture outside the label is alike enough, apart from those marked as not it. Learning works from what the media service has worked out about each picture, so a picture it has not looked at yet is neither learned from nor suggested. Besides the learning you start from the bar, the archive's label-models service relearns every label, and every suggested word, once an hour when something has changed: when pictures gained or lost the label, when something was marked as not the label, or when a week has passed. The web interface has no button to take back a Not ; in the terminal, label-model unreject does.

What you see What it means, and what to do Incomplete answer : "The content match did not answer in time, so these are filename matches only. Try again in a moment." The media service did not answer the search in time, so only file names were searched. Try again shortly. If it keeps happening, tell whoever looks after EiN; The media service is theirs. "No person or location filter matched … — searched those words as description instead." The Media page found no person or place by that name, and searched the words as text. Pick the person with @ instead. "No match for @… — searched as plain text instead." The same on the Year page. Pictures you uploaded are missing from the Media page Files sent with Import media or the Media page's Upload wait in your staging area until you file them into an album; see Sorting in staging . A file that is still being prepared shows a placeholder until its thumbnail exists. An album is missing from a year None of its pictures is dated in that year. Check the pictures' dates; see Dates and places of pictures . "The histogram counts only the first N matches." There is more than the histogram counts, so its bars show part of it. The cards for the chosen year are complete. "Nothing matches that filter." No picture meets every chip. Remove a chip, or choose All under Show . Label , Set time or Delete is missing from the selection bar You may not change every selected picture. Select only your own, or ask the person who shared them. The layout, Show only mine or the Year page's Show and Sort are different on another device They are remembered per browser, not per account.

The Media page, the Year page and labels all run ordinary commands, which you can run yourself in the terminal : # in EiN's terminal search --tag sailing --kind photo,video # pictures that carry a label search 'christmas tree' --kind photo # pictures by what they show timeline --year 1968 --kind album,auto-album,birth,death # what the Year page shows for 1968 labels # every label in use, with its count label add '/archive/albums/Summer 2020' sailing # put a label on an album label remove '/archive/albums/Summer 2020' sailing ls /archive/tags/sailing # the label's folder label-model show sailing # how well the label is learned timeline also takes --person , --location and --tag , as the Year page's box does. The full options are in the reference for search , label , labels , timeline and label-model , and Commands by task lists more.

With the Archive installed, EiN searches your photos, videos, recordings and documents, down to what is in a picture and what is said in a recording, and finds the albums, people, locations and devices they belong to. This page is for everyone who searches the archive in a browser. The finder in the top bar and the Search page itself are EiN's own, and Search and the finder covers them.

Page Where you find it What it finds Search Search under Explore in the sidebar, or Search for "…" in the finder Albums, people, locations and devices: the things pictures belong to Media Media in the sidebar, or Pictures of "…" in the finder The photos, videos, audio recordings and documents themselves Both pages have the same kind of search box. You can write a sentence, pick something exactly with @ , and see what the box understood as chips you can remove one by one. The address in the browser holds the whole search, so a search can be linked, and the browser's Back and Forward step through your searches. Every search finds only what you are allowed to see. Files still in your staging area are left out until they are filed ( Sorting in staging ).

p.h: Find photos, videos, recordings and documents
p.x: The Media page shows everything as a feed, newest first, until you ask it something. Then it turns into a search, with the best matches first in one grid. Open Media in the sidebar. Click the box, Filter the media — “Anna sailing 2011”, or type @ to pick someone , and type what you are looking for, for example Christmas tree . Press Enter , or click the arrow at the end of the box. The results take the place of the feed, the closest first. Each tile shows a match percentage, and a video its length. To see one kind only, choose it under Show : All , Images , Video , Audio or Documents . Click a tile to open it in the viewer . To go back to the feed, empty the box, press Enter and remove any chips with their ×. Nothing in these pictures carries a label or a description: EiN finds the tree by what the pictures show.

p.h: What your words are compared with
p.x: Each search looks in several places at once and puts the results together: What is searched How Try it in the Wrenfield demo What a photo shows, and what a video shows in its frames By meaning; nothing needs a label or a description first Christmas tree , harbour Text in pictures: printed and handwritten letters, postcards, recipe cards, signs By meaning and by its exact words the cottage is ours finds Peggy's postcard from Cornwall in 1968; self-raising flour finds her recipe for scones What is said in videos and recordings By meaning and by its exact words the knife's gone blunt finds Arthur carving the goose at Christmas 1998 Documents: PDF, Word ( .docx ), OpenDocument ( .odt ) and plain text By what their text is about Christmas letter finds the family newsletter from 2019 Descriptions someone wrote By meaning File names By the name DSC_0215 , IMG_0525 A match in something said opens the video or recording at the moment the words are said, not at the start. A name said once in an hour of tape is found by its words. Documents have no preview in EiN and show as plain tiles; Supported files lists which files EiN reads text from.

When words or a picture rank the results, each tile shows a percentage. The best match is always 100%, and every other result shows how it compares with that best one. The number tells you how a result ranks within this search; it is not a measure of how sure EiN is, and the same picture can show a different number in another search.

Show only mine (only when you are signed in) limits the page, both the feed and a search, to the files you added yourself. EiN remembers the choice in this browser, not in your account. The Media page's other controls, its layouts and label pills, are covered in Media, Year and labels .

p.h: Write what you are looking for
p.x: You can type a whole sentence. When you press Enter , the box turns what it understands into chips, each with its own × to remove it, and keeps the remaining words as the description it searches for by meaning. It reads in two passes. Years and kinds , at once, in English and Swedish: A year, such as 1968 . Before or after one: before 1980 or until 1980 , after 2010 or since 2010 , and the Swedish före , innan , efter and sedan . Two years make a span: 1990 1999 . Years from 1800 to next year are read. A kind: photos , pictures , images , videos , films , movies , clips , recordings , audio or documents , and Swedish words such as bilder , foton , filmer , ljud , inspelningar and dokument . On the Media page a kind sets Show ; on the Search page, albums , people and locations do. People, places and words that describe the picture , a moment later, when your EiN has a language model (the assistant module sets one up). A small spinner in the box shows that it is reading. The search already runs on the first pass meanwhile, and runs again when the model has found more. A name that belongs to one person becomes that person. A name several people share becomes a chip ending in … , meaning every person whose name contains it. A place becomes one of your locations , or, for a country or a city that is not one, an Area chip covering it. A word for a relative, such as mother or husband , is not read as a person: the yellow note names it, and it is searched as words. Name the person instead. Some examples on the Media page of the Wrenfield demo: videos 1998 sets Show to Video and adds the chip 1998 , leaving the box empty: every video from 1998. Peggy 1968 adds 1968 at once. With a language model, Peggy then becomes @Peggy Wrenfield , and the box is left empty: every picture of Peggy from 1968. Peggy at the cottage at Malpas in 1968 gives the same two chips and @The cottage at Malpas , so only the pictures that have all three are left. Christmas 1975 adds 1975 and looks through that year's pictures for what looks like Christmas. Without a language model, only years and kinds are read, and the rest is searched as words describing the picture. A name that matched nobody is searched as words too, and a yellow note says so: No person or location filter matched … — searched those words as description instead. The Search page puts it as No person or location matched … — searched as plain text instead. Close the note with its ×. Tip Write a place the way it is named in EiN, or pick it with @ . A word that is only part of a location's name, such as cottage alone, is not taken as that location; the model may then look it up as an area on the map instead. The Interpreted filter shows what happened. A second search adds to the chips already there rather than replacing them. To widen a search, remove a chip; to start again, remove them all.

Chip What it means @Peggy Wrenfield One person, location or device, picked with @ or understood from your words @Okafor… Every person whose name contains these words Area An area on the map, such as a country or a city 1968 , 1990–1999 , from 2010 , up to 1980 A year, a span of years, or a limit #harbour A label @Christmas 1998 An album: only what is in it (Media page) Looks like harbour Pictures that look like the pictures carrying that label Similar , with a small picture Pictures that look like that picture

Beside the box, the Interpreted filter button (an ⓘ icon) opens an account of what is being searched. It appears once there is something to explain, and not on a phone. Row What it shows Description (q) The words searched for by meaning, or none Looks like (like) The picture searched with, in place of words Names (subject-name, AND words) Partial names, and the people each one matched Exact (subject) The people, locations and devices picked exactly Area An area on the map Date (from/to) The year or years Labels (tag) The labels Album/directory The album searched in On the Search page it adds a line saying that people, locations, dates and devices are what a picture has, so an album matches when it holds a picture that does. Open it when a search brings back something unexpected. A word you meant as a description may have been taken as a place, or the other way round; remove that chip and search again.

Type @ and the start of a name. A list opens with the matching people, locations, labels and devices (on the Media page, albums too), each with its kind beside it. The list matches the start of each word of a name, in order, and lets you skip words: @peg wren finds Peggy Wrenfield. Pick one with the arrow keys and Enter or Tab , or click it. The box writes @Peggy Wrenfield . Add more words or picks, and press Enter . Each pick becomes a chip. Esc closes the list without picking. An @ word you type without picking from the list stays in the box as ordinary words, and the yellow note mentions it. The Year page and the Map have boxes of their own that take @ for a person, a location or a label; see Media, Year and labels and Locations and the map .

When words fail you, search with a picture instead: an old print you are holding, or a place you are standing in. On the Media page, click the button beside the box, Search with a picture . Choose a picture on your device, or on a phone take one with the camera. The page shows the pictures that look most like it, nearest first, and the box shows the chip Similar with a small copy of your picture. Chips and Show narrow the answer the same way they narrow words. Typing words and pressing Enter replaces the picture with your words. The picture goes to your EiN and nowhere else, turned upright and made smaller first. EiN keeps it in /tmp , never adds it to the archive, and removes it after 24 hours (the Hours in /tmp setting, CFG_TMP_RETENTION_HOURS ). If it cannot be sent, a red message says the picture could not be sent , followed by the HTTP status. To find pictures like one that is already in the archive, open it in the viewer . Its details panel shows Similar , a strip of the nearest pictures, and Show all opens the same search on the Media page.

Above the results, a row of label pills shows the labels the results carry, each with a count. Click one to add it to the search as a chip, such as #harbour . A label that every result carries is left out, as it would narrow nothing. A label shown anywhere else in EiN, on a picture or an album, opens the Search page for that label when you click it. When you are signed in, a search for exactly one label also offers the pictures that look like that label but do not carry it yet; Media, Year and labels explains how to label them and teach EiN what the label means.

p.h: Find albums, people, locations and devices
p.x: The Search page finds the things pictures belong to. The Search page explains its box, Show and Sort ; with the Archive, Show offers All , Albums , People , Locations and Devices , and an album's card also shows its dates and how many files it holds. What each kind is found by: Kind Found by Try it in the Wrenfield demo Albums Name, description, and what their pictures show album christmas sets Show to Albums and finds the Christmas albums, such as Christmas 1975 and Christmas in Wellington People Name; every word must match the same person helen okafor Locations Name falmouth Devices Name, make, model or serial number lumix finds Peggy's Lumix A person, location, year, device or label in the search narrows albums by their pictures: @Peggy Wrenfield 1968 finds the albums holding a picture of Peggy taken in 1968. A label matches an album that carries it or holds a picture that does.

p.h: Start from people, places, years and labels
p.x: Before you type, the Search page offers places to start: the people and locations with the most pictures, every year, and the labels. Before you type, the Search page shows your Recent searches ( Before you search ), and under them the Archive's rows: People : the people in the most pictures. Locations : up to 16 locations that have a place on the map, as small maps, those placed from the most geotagged pictures first. Years : every year with something in it, each opening that year on the Year page . Labels : every label, the most used first, then suggested labels marked with a sparkle: words that at least five pictures look like although nothing carries them yet. Pointing at one shows A suggested label: N pictures look like it, and nothing carries it yet . See all beside People, Locations and Years opens the People , Locations or Year page. A section with nothing to show is left out. With the assistant installed, it can search for you too: ask it in Chat , and an answer that comes from a search offers Show in search to open it on the Search or Media page.

p.h: What needs the media service and a language model
p.x: EiN's media service reads every picture, recording and document as it arrives, and turns your words into something it can compare with them when you search. A language model reads names out of a sentence. Your administrator installs both; see The media service and The language model . What you do Needs Finding albums, people, locations and devices in the finder The Archive alone Finding files, albums, people, locations and devices by name; @ picks; labels; years and kinds read from a sentence The Archive alone Finding pictures by what they show; text in pictures and speech by meaning; documents; albums by what their pictures show The media service, answering when you search Searching with a picture you choose The media service, answering when you search Finding text in pictures and speech by their exact words The media service to have read them once; not when you search Reading people, places and descriptive words from a sentence, and me or my mother A language model A file is found by what it shows or says only once the media service has looked at it: a picture added a few minutes ago may not turn up by meaning yet. Your administrator's Dashboard reads Catching up while that work goes on. If your administrator chose a hosted provider for the language model, the words you type into a search box are sent to that provider to be read. A place in your words that is none of your locations is looked up on OpenStreetMap's address service, Nominatim, to find its area.

p.h: When the media service is not answering
p.x: On the Media page a yellow note appears above the results: Incomplete answer The content match did not answer in time, so these are filename matches only. Try again in a moment. More lines under it can name other parts that did not answer, such as the picture match. The results come only from what EiN can match without the media service, such as file names. A search with a picture finds nothing, and its line in the note says why. Wait a moment and press Enter in the box again. The media service may be busy or starting. If the note keeps coming back, tell your administrator. Anyone signed in can check first: About EiN , in the menu under your picture, shows the Media service tile as Not answering while it is down. Your administrator finds more on the Dashboard's Media service tab, and The media service covers what to do. Elsewhere you see no note, only less: the Search page still finds albums, people, locations and devices by name, but not albums by what their pictures show. When the language model is slow or away, you see no error either: the search keeps the years and kinds it read and searches the rest of your sentence as words.

The search command answers the same questions as the two pages, in EiN's terminal : # in EiN's terminal search "Christmas tree" --kind photo search --subject-name person:peggy --from 1968 --to 1968 The first finds photos by what they show; the second lists everything with a person whose name contains Peggy, taken in 1968. Its options are in the command reference , the Archive's providers behind it, such as search-media , are in Archive commands , and Commands by task lists the archive's other search commands.

Search and the finder : the finder in the top bar and the Search page. Media, Year and labels : the Media feed, the Year page and labels. Locations and the map : finding pictures by place on the map. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer and its Similar strip. The media service : what reads your pictures, recordings and documents.

EiN finds the faces in your photos and videos and the voices in your recordings, and groups the ones that belong to the same person. This page is for everyone in the family who names those people, corrects what recognition got wrong, and browses a person's pictures.

You do not have to tag anyone for recognition to start. Every photo, and frames sampled through every video, is searched for faces as it arrives, and every face that is found goes through the same three-way decision: It joins a person when it looks enough like faces of that person in other photos, and the comparison clearly favours that one person over everyone else. That person may be named or still unidentified. It starts an unidentified person when it matches nobody, but is clear and large enough to be worth treating as someone new. That person gets a placeholder name such as Unknown 4XK9QM and waits on the Unidentified people page for someone to say who it is. It stays unknown when it is too small or too unsure to start anyone. In the viewer its box reads Unassigned . The next photo of the same stranger finds the first one, sees that it already belongs to an unidentified person, and joins that person instead of starting another. So when you name an unidentified person you name every face in the group at once, and new pictures of them join the named person by themselves from then on. Two faces in the same photo are never made the same person automatically. Voices work the same way across recordings and the sound of videos: a voice that matches nobody starts an unidentified person when it speaks for at least 10 seconds in all in one recording, and two voices in one recording are never made the same person. In a video, a face seen speaking in step with a voice counts as evidence of who is speaking. Recognition decides on its own, and anything a person decides afterwards is kept. The work is done by the media service on your own machine; no photo, face or voice is sent anywhere to be analysed. Without the media service no faces are found, and they are found once it runs again. After a large import it takes a while for every picture to be looked at; the Dashboard reads Catching up until it is done (see Health and the dashboard ). Faces are found in the pictures waiting in your staging area too, before you file them into albums.

Open People in the sidebar, under Browse . Everyone with a name, the most pictured first; the button at the top leads to the people still waiting for one. The header counts the named people ( 19 people ). The filter box ( Filter people… ) matches the name and the full name as you type. N unidentified opens the people recognition found but nobody has named yet. It is there only when there are some. On a phone it is an icon with the count as a badge. Sort offers Most pictured (the default), Name (A-Z) and Name (Z-A) . Your choice is remembered in this browser. A name that starts with ? , a placeholder for someone known only from a family record, sorts after the real names. Each card shows the person's cover picture, their name and how many pictures they are in, or their full name when they are in none. Click a card to open the person's page . The number on a card counts the faces and voices of that person in the library, so a recording they are heard in counts too. Faces and voices in files still waiting in someone's staging area count once those files are filed. When nobody has been named yet, the page says No people yet and "Face recognition finds people in the pictures; name them under Unidentified, or add someone here." with a New person button. You can also find a person from the search box in the top bar, or with @ and their name on the Search, Media, Year and Map pages; see Search and the finder .

Click N unidentified on the People page, or open /people/unknown . Each card is one person recognition put together; typing a name in its box names every face in it. The page is headed Unidentified people : "Faces and voices recognized as the same person, but nobody has said who they are." Under it, N unidentified says how many there are, and N loaded how many the page has fetched so far. Sort offers Most found (the default) and Newest . Found shows only people found at least so many times: Any count , 2+ times , 5+ times , 10+ times or 50+ times . A face and a recording the voice is heard in count one time each. Each card shows one large glimpse and up to three small ones: the best faces first, then round play buttons that play the voice's longest turn. The badges say N faces and heard in N (recordings). Load more (N of M) at the foot fetches the next cards. Both choices are kept in the address, so a link opens the same view. To name someone from their card: Click in the card's Who is this? box and type the name, for example Ruby Wrenfield . Once you type, the box lists the matching people who already have a name. Press Enter , or click one of the listed people, which adds this person to them at once. While it is saved, the box shows a spinner and the card fades in and out until it leaves the page. What happens depends on the name: A new name names the person. They move to the People page with every face and voice they hold, and a message says Named Ruby Wrenfield . The name of someone who already exists adds the faces and voices to that person instead of making a second one, and the message says Added to Ruby Wrenfield . The name must match exactly, apart from capital letters, so pick it from the list rather than typing it differently. Tip Before you name a card you are unsure of, open it. A card shows at most four glimpses; the review shows every face and recording, which is where you notice that two people were put together. When nobody is waiting, the page says "Nobody unidentified. Everyone recognized so far has a name." With a Found filter on, it says, for example, "Nobody unidentified found 5 or more times."

p.h: Look at everything before you decide
p.x: Click a card, anywhere but its name box and its tick box, to open the review. Its title is the placeholder name, with the N faces and heard in N badges beside it. At the top, the Who is this? box ("A new name, or someone you already have") works like the card's. Its button reads Name , or Add to <name> when the name is someone who already exists. Not a person beside it is described in Say what is not a person . Faces shows every face of this person. Click a face to open the photo it came from in the viewer; the arrows then step through the photos of the faces shown. Load more (N of M) fetches more when there are many. Voice ("heard in N recordings") shows a tile for each recording the voice is heard in. The round button plays the voice's longest turn there, and Open in the lightbox opens the recording at that moment. Pick all picks every recording. To pick faces or recordings, tick the box in their corner. Once something is picked, a click on a face picks it too instead of opening its photo; Shift +click picks a range, and Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) picks everything shown. Esc closes an open photo first, then clears what is picked, then closes the review. The review has its own address, /people/unknown?person=<id> , so you can send it to a relative who may know who it is.

p.h: Take some faces out (Split off, Move to…)
p.x: When the review shows faces of more than one person, pick the ones that do not belong. A bar appears with N faces picked and these actions: Action Dialog What it does Split off as someone new Split off N faces? → Split off The picked faces and recordings become a new unidentified person of their own, for you to name afterwards or add to someone. Move to… Move N faces to someone? , then Who they are → Move They move to the named person you pick, and count as decided by a human, so no later pass moves them again. Not a person N faces: not a person? → Unassign and lock They lose their identity and are locked, so recognition leaves them alone. Nothing is deleted. Clear Unpicks everything. When you have picked everything the person holds, Split off as someone new and Move to… are greyed out, with the note "That is everything they have. To give all of it to someone, name them or add them to someone above instead. Not a person removes them."

Recognition sometimes joins two people through one weak resemblance, and four glimpses on a card will not show it. With three faces or more, the review has an Adjust group threshold switch beside Faces (and with three recordings or more, one beside Voice ): Turn on Adjust group threshold . EiN compares every face of this person with every other ("Comparing every face against every other"), once. Drag the How alike slider. The faces are laid out in groups, Largest group first, then Group 2 and onward, each with its number of faces. The slider starts where the comparison suggests the groups part. Tick a group's box to pick all of it, then use Split off as someone new , Move to… or Not a person as above. Only the 30 largest groups are shown; the rest are counted under them ("Move the slider left to bring them up here."). A box someone drew by hand has nothing to compare and is in no group.

p.h: Fold several unidentified people into one
p.x: Recognition often splits one person into a large group and a few small ones. To join them: On the Unidentified people page, tick the box in the corner of each card. Once one is ticked, a plain click on a card ticks it too; Ctrl + A ticks every loaded card and Esc clears. In the bar at the bottom, press Merge . It needs two cards or more. The dialog Merge N into one person? names the one that survives: the card with the most faces, or the older one when two have as many. "<name> survives with all N faces. It keeps its own entry and stays unidentified — name it afterwards." It lists the others with their faces. Press Merge . The other entries are removed, and their faces are marked as decided by a human, so no later pass undoes it. Name the person that is left, from its card or its review. The web interface merges only unidentified people. To fold one named person into another, for example a second Ruby made by a typo, use person-merge in the terminal : faces, voices, events, relations and every other link move to the person you keep, and the other is removed. --dry-run shows what would move without changing anything. # in EiN's terminal person-merge --dry-run /archive/people/ruby-wrenfeld /archive/people/ruby-wrenfield person-merge /archive/people/ruby-wrenfeld /archive/people/ruby-wrenfield The last path is the person who stays. See person-merge in the command reference.

p.h: Say what is not a person
p.x: A poster, a statue, a doll, a pattern in the wallpaper or the back of a head can all be taken for a face. Saying so keeps recognition from trying again: Several cards at once: tick them on the Unidentified people page and press Not a person in the bar. One person: press Not a person at the top of their review. The dialog ( Not a person? , or N: not a person? for several) says what happens: every face and recording they hold loses its identity and is locked, so recognition leaves it alone from now on, and the entry is removed. "The photos and recordings themselves are untouched." Confirm with Not a person . Some faces of one person: pick them in the review and press Not a person in the bar under it. The dialog ( N faces: not a person? ) locks only those, and the person keeps the rest. Confirm with Unassign and lock . For faces wrongly given to someone who already has a name, use Not a face on their Faces tab .

p.h: Name a face in the viewer
p.x: You can also name people while you look at a picture. The viewer describes it fully; in short: Press f , or choose Pin faces in the More (⋮) menu, to show every face box with its name. Hovering a box, or a name in the details panel, lights up the other. Click a named box to open that person's page. Click the box of an unidentified person to get a Who is this? box: type the name and press Enter or the check mark. This always makes a new person, even when someone of that name exists; to add the faces to someone who already exists, use the review instead. In the details panel, under the people in the picture, an unidentified person is listed by a crop of their face and their placeholder name. Click it to open their review over the viewer. On a computer, Edit faces in the cog menu lets you select a box and press its name ("Change who this is"). The Who is this? dialog offers Someone I know (pick them under Who it is ), Someone new (a new unidentified person, for you to name now or later) and, for a face recognition found, Let recognition decide (matched again against everyone except the person it is on now). Confirm with Move or Match again . This is also how you give a name to a face marked Unassigned . In Edit faces you can also drag a new box around a face recognition missed. It becomes a new unidentified person, and its review opens for you to name it. A box drawn by hand names the person in that picture, but is not used to recognise them in others. Edit faces is offered on a computer, on photos you may change.

Someone who is in no picture yet, a great-grandparent for the family tree for example, can be added by hand: Open Create (the plus in the top bar) and choose Person , or press New person on an empty People page. In Create Person , fill in Name (required), and if you like Full name and Gender ( Female , Male , Other or Unknown ). Press Create . The new person's page opens. Look on the People page first, so that you do not add someone who is already there: the dialog does not look for someone of the same name. The address of the new page is made from the name, and if a person already has that address the dialog shows an error instead; give the new person a name that tells the two apart. Later faces only join a person through faces that already belong to them, so a person made by hand gets pictures once you give them a face: add an unidentified person to them by typing their name, or move faces to them with Move to… or Someone I know .

Click a person on the People page, a name in the viewer, or a person in search results. The header places a person in time; the tabs hold everything else. The header shows: their cover picture and name, the full name under it, and "Born as <birth name>" when that is different; a life line: "1934 – 2021 · died aged 86" for someone who has died, "Born 1958 · 68" for someone living. A ~ before the age means it is approximate, because the birth date has no day; where they live now, linking to the location, their contact details (not on a phone; the Info tab lists them), and how many photos they are in, over which years ("34 photos · 1968–2025"); allergies, marked with a warning sign, their labels, and the description. If you may change the person, the header has Share and Edit , and under ⋮ Add event , Split faces… (administrators only) and Move to trash . Share shares the person's page and what hangs off it, not the photos they are in; see Sharing . Move to trash returns you to the People page with "<name> moved to the trash" and Undo . Tab What it shows Timeline Their life by year, the latest first: birth and death, events, moves, partnerships, their children's births, and the albums they appear in. Info Everything recorded about them: Person (Name, Full name, Born as, Gender, Born, Died, Age or Age at death, Photos), Contact , Allergies , Homes with the years, Family (each relative by role) and About . Media Every photo and video they are in, newest first, with the time rail at the side for jumping through the years. Faces Every face of theirs, as a grid of crops. See Correct a person's faces . Heard in Every recording they speak in. See Recordings a person is heard in . Family The family tree. See Family tree, events and homes . Homes Where they have lived, with the years. See Family tree, events and homes . The open tab is kept in the address ( ?tab=faces , ?tab=voices and so on), so you can link straight to it. When there is nothing to show, the Timeline says "Nothing recorded for <name> yet. Add an event to record something.", and the Media tab "No photos of <name> yet. They appear here once tagged, or once a detected face is assigned to them." On the Media tab you can select pictures as in an album. If you may change the person, Set as cover in the selection bar makes the one selected picture their cover; Set time changes the capture time of pictures you may change (see Dates and places of pictures ). On a phone, the tabs show only their icons, except the one that is open, and the header's buttons fold into ⋮. On a phone the same page fits one column; the tab icons are in the same order as on a computer.

The Faces tab shows every face assigned to the person, as crops in a grid. Click a crop to open the photo it came from in the viewer; the arrows step through the photos in the order of the grid. While there are more faces than are loaded, a note says "N of M loaded", and more load as you scroll. A wrong face stands out among the right ones; select it and say who it really is. Select faces as you select pictures in an album: hover a crop and tick its box, Shift +click for a range, or long-press on a phone. The selection bar then offers: Download : the selected crops, as one zip named "<name> faces" when there are several. Set as cover : makes the one selected crop the person's picture. Not <name> : takes the faces off this person. Is <name> : only in the Doubtful view, described below. Not <name> opens the dialog Not <name>? , with the number of faces under its title and four choices: Choice What happens Let recognition decide (the default) Each face is matched again against everyone except this person. It joins whoever it looks like, or becomes a new unidentified person. It is never put back on this person. Someone I know The faces move to the person you pick under Who it is . One new unidentified person All the faces are the same person, not yet named. Name them later from the unidentified list. Not a face They lose their identity and are locked, so recognition leaves them alone from now on. Press Move , or Unassign and lock for Not a face . After Let recognition decide , a short report ( Faces moved ) says where the faces went, for example "2 faces matched to Peggy Wrenfield", "3 faces became unidentified people" or "1 face left unassigned — too small or unclear to start a new person". Press Done . If a face that was the person's cover leaves them, they get a new cover from their remaining faces.

Somebody who is not sure a face is the person can mark it as doubtful in the viewer (see People in the picture ), or with the face-doubt command. The face stays the person's until somebody answers. When a person has doubtful faces, the Faces tab shows a switch: All faces or Doubtful (N) , "Faces somebody is not sure of, or that look more like somebody else". Each doubtful crop is badged with who marked it, for example "asked by peggy". Choose Doubtful (N) . Select the faces that are someone else and press Not <name> . Select the faces that are right and press Is <name> . They stay, as a person's decision. When none are left, the tab says "No doubtful faces of <name> left."

p.h: Recordings a person is heard in
p.x: The Heard in tab lists, under "Heard in N recordings", a tile for each recording the person speaks in, those they speak most in first. The round button on a tile plays their longest turn in that recording. Hovering the name shows the recording's date and how long they speak in it ("speaks 1:42 in it"), and Open in the lightbox opens the recording at their turn. To take a recording off the person, tick its tile and press Not this person (N) . Their voice in it loses its identity and is locked, so recognition does not give it back. Nothing asks first. If the person speaks in no recording, the tab says "Not heard in any recording yet." Naming a voice in a transcript, and seeing who speaks when, is in the viewer .

p.h: Split a person who is really two
p.x: Naming an unidentified person approves every face in it. If it turns out to have held two people, an administrator can take them apart with Split faces… under ⋮ on the person's page. The dialog Split <name> compares the person's faces with each other, more strictly than recognition did. Drag the Similarity slider until the people come apart; the badge says how many groups there are. One group , Split in two , Suggested and Split off all but the largest are shortcuts. For each group, choose Keep , Split off (a new unidentified person; not offered for a group of one face), Merge into… (pick a named person) or Not a person . Every group starts on Keep . Click a face to see the photo it came from; the arrows then step through that group, which is the way to check that the same person keeps turning up. Read the summary at the foot, for example "40 faces stay · 1 new unidentified person", and press Apply to N groups . At least one group has to stay: moving all of them is a rename, not a split. Only the 30 largest groups get a card; the smaller ones stay as they are. A box drawn by hand has nothing to compare and stays where it is.

Press Edit on the person's page to open Edit person . Leave an optional field empty to remove it. Field What to enter Name The name shown everywhere. Required. Full name Their whole name, shown under the name. Birth name The name they were born with, shown as "Born as". Gender Female , Male , Other or Unknown . Born , Died A year, a month or a day: 1934 , 1934-05 or 1934-05-20 . Without a day, their age is shown as approximate. Contact information Add contact adds a row with a Type (for example "Email, phone, address…") and the Details . An e-mail address becomes a link that writes to it, and a phone number one that calls it. Allergies Shown with a warning sign in the header. Description Free text, with Markdown. Labels Words to find the person by. A space starts the next label. Press Save . If something is missing, the dialog says "a name is needed" or "each contact needs both a type and details". Events, parents, partners, children and homes are not in this dialog; see Family tree, events and homes .

A named person without a cover gets one by themselves: the crop of one of their own faces. Faces someone named or confirmed come first, then photos where they are the only face, then clear faces looking into the camera, then the largest. A cover you choose yourself, with Set as cover on the Faces or Media tab, is never replaced by another pick. A cover is replaced only when it no longer works: the picture is gone, or it is the crop of a face that has since been taken off the person, because their card would then show somebody else.

p.h: What EiN keeps of your decisions
p.x: Recognition only decides about faces nobody has decided about. Anything a person says is kept, and no later automatic pass undoes it: You Afterwards Name an unidentified person Their faces count as named by a human. New faces that look like them join them by themselves. Add someone to an existing person, or Merge The faces are marked as decided by a human. Move to… , Someone I know The faces stay with the person you picked. Split off as someone new , One new unidentified person The faces stay together as the new person. Not a person , Not a face , Not this person The faces and voices are locked without a name. Let recognition decide The faces are never matched back to the person you took them from. Is <name> , Yes to Is this <name>? The faces are marked as decided by a human, and the doubt goes. Set as cover Your cover stays, as long as the picture is there and the face is still theirs. Changing the recognition settings does not touch these decisions either.

No faces are found at all. Recognition needs the media service. Ask your administrator to check the Dashboard ; see The media service . A face in a photo has no box. Faces that are very small, blurred or turned far away are not kept. Draw a box around it with Edit faces in the viewer, as described in Name a face in the viewer . One person is spread over many unidentified cards. Tick the cards and merge them , or type the same name into each card's box. An unidentified person holds two people. Open the review and use Group similar faces . For a named person, an administrator uses Split faces… . A person has someone else's faces. Open their Faces tab, select the wrong ones and press Not <name> . A person's card shows more pictures than their page. The card counts faces and voices, so each recording the person is heard in counts too. An action fails. The reason appears in red under the bar or in the dialog. A change you are not allowed to make, to a picture or a person you may only view, is refused; ask whoever owns it, or your administrator. Recognition is too eager or too cautious. An administrator can tune it under Settings → System , in the groups Faces and Voices . Changes apply to faces and voices decided from then on. Setting Default What it decides Face match threshold 0.55 How similar two faces must be before one is attached to a known person. Higher makes fewer wrong matches and more unknown faces. Face winner margin 1.2 How far the leading person must outweigh the runner-up. Higher leaves close calls unknown. Confidence to start a new person from a face 0.7 How sure the detector must be before a face that matches nobody starts a new person. Size to start a new person from a face (px) 48 How large such a face must be: its shorter side, in pixels of the displayed photo. Minimum face confidence , Minimum face size (px) , Maximum head turn (degrees) 0.7, 24, 80 Which detections are kept as faces at all. Speech to start a new person (seconds) 10 How long a voice that matches nobody must speak in one recording, in all, before it starts a new person. Every setting is described in the reference, under Faces and Voices .

This page shows how to record how the people in your archive are related, what happened in their lives and where they lived, and what EiN makes of it: the family tree, the timelines, and the birthdays and anniversaries on the Home page. It is for the family members who keep these records, and it says which parts need an administrator.

Everything on this page hangs off a person's page or a location's page. In the web interface, two of the controls are shown only to an administrator: What Where Who sees the controls Parents, partners and children the person's Family tab administrators only A person's homes the person's Homes tab administrators only A location's residents the location's Residents tab anyone who may change the location Events of a person ⋮ → Add event on the person anyone who may change the person Born and died Edit on the person anyone who may change the person Events of an album, a location or a device ⋮ → Add event on its page anyone who may change it An administrator is someone signed in as admin , or a member of the sudo group who has chosen Administer… in the account menu and entered their password again. See Accounts and groups . Who may change a person or a location is a matter of its sharing; see Sharing . Everyone else reads the tree, the homes and the timelines like any other page, and sees no ⋯ menus on the tree's cards and no Add home button. Note The administrator rule belongs to the web interface only. The same changes are ordinary commands in the terminal , and the assistant can propose parents, partners and events for you; there they need permission to change the people they touch, not administrator rights. See In the terminal .

Open a person and choose the Family tab. The address ends in ?tab=family , so you can link to someone's tree directly. Generations are rows and couples sit side by side, so the tree reads like a family tree on paper. The tree is drawn the way family trees usually are: Generations are rows. Parents and grandparents are above, children and grandchildren below. Couples sit side by side , joined by a line. When the partnership has dates, the year it began is written over the line and the year it ended under it. Each card shows the person's picture, their name and their years: 1934 – 2021 , b. 1958 for someone with only a birth date, d. 2011 for someone with only a death date. The person the page is about has an outlined card and a bold name. Click a name to open that person's page. The tree shows only people you may see. Someone whose page is hidden from you is left out, with the lines to them.

A large family would not fit on a screen, so the tree opens with two generations up and two down from the person, and the partners of everyone drawn. A card with more family behind it has a round chevron on its edge: at the top when there are more parents ("Show <name>'s parents"), at the bottom when there are more children ("Show <name>'s children"). Click one and the tree loads one more generation that way: the parents above the card, or the children below it. The chevron then turns round ("Hide <name>'s parents" or "Hide <name>'s children"), and clicking it folds those relatives away again. Two things are not drawn until you ask: Brothers and sisters. The tree walks up from the person and down from the person, so their siblings appear once you open the chevron on one of their parents' cards. A partner's own family. A husband's or wife's parents belong to another tree. Open the chevron on the partner's card to bring them in.

The tree moves inside its own box, as a map does, so the rest of the page stays where it is. Drag it with the mouse or one finger. Scroll over it to zoom around the pointer, or pinch with two fingers or on a trackpad. A double click or double tap on the space between the cards zooms in there; hold Shift to zoom out. The buttons in the box's top right corner: Button What it does Full screen Opens the tree in a window that fills the screen; Leave full screen closes it. Fit the whole family Shrinks the drawing until all of it fits the box. Centre on this person Moves back to the person the page is about. Hidden while the whole family is fitted.

There is no brother or sister relation to record. Two people are siblings when they share a parent: give both the same two parents and they are brother and sister, give them one parent in common and they are half-siblings. In-laws and step-parents also follow from the ties you record: the partner of someone's parent is their stepfather or stepmother, and the parent of someone's partner is their father-in-law or mother-in-law. Set each person's Gender with Edit (see Edit a person ) so that EiN can say father or mother rather than parent.

p.h: Add a parent, partner or child
p.x: You need administrator rights for this in the web interface; see Who may change what . Open the person's Family tab. Find the card of the person you are adding to. It can be any card in the tree, not only the person the page is about. Click ⋯ on that card and choose Add parent , Add partner or Add child . The dialog asks the question: "Whose child is <name>?", "Who is <name> with?" or "Who is a child of <name>?". Leave Someone already here selected and pick the person in Who . Type part of a name to narrow the list. For a parent or a child, choose the Kind . For a partner, choose the Relationship and, if you know them, the dates in From and Until . Press Add . The tree, the person's header and their timeline are read again at once. The tree opens again as it first did, two generations up and two down, so a relative added further out shows once you open the chevrons to it again. Each tie joins two people. Add child gives the child one parent: if both partners of a couple are the child's parents, add the child from the other partner's card as well, or add the second parent from the child's own card. Adding a partner links no children. Warning Choose Someone already here , not Someone new , in this dialog. Someone new makes the person outside the archive's people folder: they are not listed on the People page, their card in the tree does not open their page, and their birthday never reaches the Home page. To add someone who is not in the archive yet, a great-grandmother for example, first create them with Create → Person (see Create a person by hand ), then add them here with Someone already here .

Kind Use it for Blood A birth parent. This is the default. Adoptive A parent by adoption, as Jon and Kiri Wrenfield are to Leo. Step A step-parent you want drawn as a parent, above the child. Foster A foster parent. The tree draws every kind of parent alike. The kind shows in the words EiN uses for the tie, such as "adoptive father" or "stepmother", when the assistant or person-how-related says how two people are related. A step-parent does not have to be recorded as a parent at all: the partner of a parent is already a stepfather or stepmother.

Relationship is Partner or Married . From and Until take a year, a month or a day: 1972 , 1972-05 or 1972-05-20 . Leave Until empty while the two are together. The dates do more than label the line in the tree: From puts "<A> and <B> married" (or "became partners") on both people's timelines on that date. Until puts "<A> and <B> parted" on both timelines. Leave it empty when the partnership ended with a death: the death date already ends the anniversaries, and an Until on the day of death makes both timelines say the two parted that day. From with a full date makes the anniversary come round on the Home page: "Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married". A partnership dated only to a year or a month, such as Thomas Wrenfield and Rachel Moore's from 2008-05 , has no day to come round on. See Birthdays, memorials and anniversaries . To add or correct the dates of a partnership that is already recorded, choose Add partner again, pick the same partner, and fill in From or Until . EiN updates the dates of the partnership you have instead of adding a second one, and keeps its Relationship as it was. To change the Relationship or to clear a date, remove the relation and add it again.

Problems show in a red box in the dialog, which stays open so you can correct them. People are named there by the last part of their page's address, such as Helen_Okafor . Message What it means "pick somebody, or create them" Who is empty. "person-set-parent: refusing to add parent: <a> is a descendant of <b>" The tie would make someone their own ancestor. Check who is the parent. "person-set-parent: <a> is already a parent of <b>" The tie is already there. "person-set-partner: <a> and <b> are already partners" The partnership is already there, and no dates were given to update. "person-set-partner: invalid from date '…' (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])", or the same with to A date is not written as a year, a month or a day. "person-set-partner: partnership end is before start" Until is earlier than From .

On the Family tab, click ⋯ on the card of one of the two people and choose Remove a relation… . The dialog lists their ties to the people on screen, such as "Arthur Wrenfield — partner" or "Helen Okafor — child". Choose one. Press Remove . The tie goes both ways, so this removes it from both people. Neither person is deleted, and nothing goes to the trash: to undo it, add the relation again, with its kind and dates. Only ties to people drawn in the tree are offered. If the dialog says "Nothing to remove — no relations of theirs are on screen.", open the chevrons until the other person's card is shown.

There is no page in the web interface that answers this. Ask the assistant , for example "How is Ruby related to Peggy?". Its answer can carry a small tree of only the people on the line between the two, with a Full screen button.
