In the terminal , person-how-related answers in English or Swedish: # in EiN's terminal person-how-related /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield /archive/people/Ruby_Wrenfield person-how-related /archive/people/Erik_Wrenfield /archive/people/Rachel_Moore Ruby Wrenfield is Peggy Wrenfield's granddaughter Rachel Moore is Erik Wrenfield's stepmother Add --lang sv after the two people for the Swedish word.

An event is a dated note on a person: a wedding, a move abroad, a graduation, a birth or a death. Open the person's page, click ⋮ in the header and choose Add event . Choose the Type : Generic , Birth , Death , Marriage or Engagement . Type the Date as 1956 , 1956-06 or 1956-06-16 . Write the Description , with Markdown if you like. Its first line becomes the event's title on the timeline. Written by names the person who wrote the text. It starts as you, when your account is linked to a person; clear it or pick someone else. Press Add event . It becomes available once there is a date or a description. Type What else it does Generic Nothing more: it is an entry on the person's timeline. Birth With a date, it sets the person's Born , replacing what was there. Its description joins the "<name> was born" entry on the timeline. Death With a date, it sets the person's Died , replacing what was there. Its description joins the "<name> died" entry. Marriage Counts in the Marriages by month chart on the Statistics page. It does not record a partnership; see Record a wedding . Engagement Counts in the Engagements by month chart. Things to know: An event without a date is kept but placed on no timeline , since there is nothing to place it by. Give it a date to see it. Without a description , the timeline shows a name made from the type and the date, such as marriage-1956-06-16 . Write a first line that says what happened. A person's events cannot be changed or removed in the web interface once added. An administrator, or anyone who may change the person, can do it in the terminal: the events are files in the person's events folder. # in EiN's terminal ls /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield/events trash put /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield/events/event-1999 trash put moves the event to your trash, where you can restore it; see Your profile, favourites and trash .

A wedding is best recorded in two parts, because each part feeds a different place: The partnership , with Add partner , Relationship Married and the full date in From . It puts the wedding on both people's timelines and brings the anniversary to the Home page every year. A Marriage event , if you have more to say, with the same date and a description such as "Married at Islington Town Hall". It carries the story, and counts in the Statistics chart. When the event and the partnership fall on the same day, the timeline of the person who has the event shows the two as one entry; the partner's timeline shows the partnership.

p.h: Events of albums, locations and devices
p.x: Albums, locations and devices have Add event under ⋮ too, for someone who may change them. Their events are always generic, and need both a Date and a Description . On an album , the date starts as the first day with pictures and no event yet. The event stands as a note among that day's pictures, signed "— <writer>", or with the name of the account that added it when it has no writer. If you may change it, a pencil on the note opens Edit event , where you change the date, the text or the writer and press Save , or press Delete . A deleted event goes to your trash, and the message "Event moved to the trash" has Undo . On a location or a device , the event appears on its Timeline tab. It cannot be changed in the web interface afterwards.

A person's Timeline tab is put together from what is recorded about them and their family. You do not add entries to it directly. Her death, her moves and the end of her marriage all come from records on her page and her family's, not from entries typed into the timeline. Entry Where it comes from "<name> was born", "<name> died" Born and Died , with any Birth or Death event The event's title Their dated events "<name> moved to <location>", "<name> left <location>" Their homes, on the Moved in and Moved out dates "<A> and <B> married", "became partners", "parted" Their partnerships' From and Until "<child> was born", with "Child of <name>" Their children's Born An album The albums with pictures of them A location's Timeline tab shows its residents moving in and out, its own events and the albums with photos taken there. When it has none, it says "Nothing recorded at <location> yet. Residents with dates, and albums with photos taken here, appear on its timeline." A person's Born and Died also put them on the Year page for those years, with a "Born" or "Died, aged N" badge; see Media, Year and labels .

Where someone lived is one record seen from two sides: the person's Homes tab lists their homes, and each location's Residents tab lists the people who lived there. A change on either side shows on both.

p.h: Add a home to a person
p.x: You need administrator rights for this in the web interface. Open the person's Homes tab. It says "Where <name> has lived, and when." Press Add home . Choose Location already here and pick it in Location , or choose New location and type a Location name . Fill in Moved in and, if they left, Moved out : 1972 , 1972-05 or 1972-05-20 . Leave Moved out empty while they live there. Press Add home . A new location made here has only its name. It has no place on the map until someone opens it and gives it an address or a position; see Locations and the map . Each row shows the location, which opens its page, and the dates as they were entered: 1956 – 1999 , since 1983 , until 1999 , or dates unknown . A home with a moved-in date and no moved-out date is marked current . Homes without a moved-out date come first, then the others, the latest move first. To correct the dates , press the pencil on the row, change Moved in or Moved out , and press Save changes . The dates you leave are the new ones: emptying Moved out makes it a current home again. To remove a home , press the bin on the row, then Remove under "Remove <location> from this home history?". The location itself stays. A person with no homes shows "No homes recorded."

p.h: Add a resident to a location
p.x: The Residents tab of a location works the same way, from the other side, and anyone who may change the location can use it. Open the location and choose the Residents tab. It says "Who has lived at <location>, and when." Press Add resident . Choose Person already here and pick them in Person , or choose New person and type their Name . A new person made here is an ordinary person on the People page. Fill in Moved in and Moved out , and press Add resident . The pencil and the bin on each row correct the dates and remove the resident, as on the Homes tab; the question there is "Remove <name> from the residents of <location>?". A location with nobody recorded shows "No known residents."

The dates are what turn a home into moves: A home with a moved-in date puts "<name> moved to <location>" on the person's timeline and on the location's. A moved-out date adds "<name> left <location>". A home without dates says where someone lived and nothing about when. It is listed on the Homes and Residents tabs as dates unknown and on the person's Info tab, but on no timeline. A home without a moved-out date counts as where the person lives now, even with no dates at all: the person's header shows it, and the location's header lists them under its current residents. Give a moved-out date to every home somebody has left.

The form stays open with the reason in a red box: Message What to do "pick a location, or create one", "pick somebody, or create them" Pick one in the list, or switch to New location or New person . "a location name is needed", "a name is needed" Type the name. "that name has no letters or digits to make a path from" Use a name with letters or digits in it. "person-set-home: --from '…' is not a date (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])" Write the date as 1972 , 1972-05 or 1972-05-20 . "person-set-home: moved out … before moving in …" Moved out is earlier than Moved in . "person-set-home: … already exists (use --update to change the dates)" The home is already recorded. Close the form and use the pencil on its row.

p.h: Birthdays, memorials and anniversaries on the Home page
p.x: The Events panel on the Home page lists what comes round in the next 30 days and what came round in the last 7, under Today , Coming up and Recently . It is filled from the dates on this page, so what it shows depends on what you record: On the Home page Comes from Needs Birthdays: "<name> turns N", or "would have turned N" after their death the person's Born a full date, 1934-08-22 Memorials: "N years since <name> died" the person's Died a full date; only on round years Anniversaries: "<A> and <B> — N years married" or "… years together" a partnership's From a full date; Married says married, Partner says together A date known only to the year or the month never comes round, since it has no day. Round years, the 5th, 10th, 15th and 20th and then every 10th, are shown in bold, and they are kept first when there are more than 16 entries. Birthdays stop after the 110th. An anniversary comes round up to the year of the Until date or of the first partner's death, and for 75 years at most. Someone born on 29 February appears only in leap years. Birthdays and memorials come from the people on the People page. Memories, news and events on Home describes the panel itself, and the Statistics page with its charts of births, engagements, marriages and deaths by month.

Everything on this page is also a command, which an administrator or a power user can run in the terminal or over SSH . The commands need permission to change the people and locations they write to; they do not ask for administrator rights. # in EiN's terminal person-set-parent /archive/people/Leo_Wrenfield /archive/people/Kiri_Wrenfield --kind adoptive person-set-partner /archive/people/Jon_Wrenfield /archive/people/Kiri_Wrenfield --kind married --from 1996-02-03 person-set-home --from 1996 /archive/people/Jon_Wrenfield /archive/locations/Kelburn person-add-event -- type marriage -- date 1956-06-16 --body 'Married at Islington Town Hall' /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield person-family-tree /archive/people/Peggy_Wrenfield Give person-set-parent , person-set-partner and person-how-related the two people first and the flags after them: placed before the people, a flag's value is taken for a person. Command What it does person-set-parent Adds a parent; the child comes first. --kind blood|adoptive|step|foster . person-set-partner Adds a partnership, or updates the dates of one. --kind partner|married , --from , --to . person-remove Removes the tie between two people, from both sides. person-set-home Records a home with --from and --to ; --update rewrites the dates of one already there. person-remove-home Removes a home, from both the person and the location. person-add-event Adds an event to a person, album, location or device. person-info Shows a person's dates, relatives, homes and events, the undated ones too. person-family-tree Prints ancestors and descendants as text. person-how-related Names how two people are related. person-timeline Prints a person's timeline. person-check Looks for broken ties, impossible dates and loops in the tree: person-check /archive/people . events Prints what the Home page's Events panel shows. You can also tell the assistant a parent, a partnership or an event the archive should record, for example "Leo was adopted by Jon and Kiri". It proposes the command, and nothing changes until you press Run ; it runs as you, with your permissions. Homes are not among the commands it is pointed to, so record those on the Homes or Residents tab.

There is no ⋯ on the cards, or no Add home button. These are shown only to administrators. Ask one to make the change, or, if you are in the sudo group, choose Administer… in the account menu first. A relative is missing from the tree. Open the chevron on the nearest card that is shown; siblings and a partner's family appear only then. If there is no chevron, the tie is not recorded, or the relative's page is hidden from you. A card in the tree opens "Person not found." The person was made with Someone new in the relation dialog, outside the archive's people folder. Remove the relation, create the person with Create → Person , and add the relation again with Someone already here . The stray person stays under /people , where an administrator can delete it in the Nodes explorer or the terminal. A birthday or anniversary does not show on the Home page. Check that the date has a day, that it falls within the next 30 days or the last 7, and for an anniversary that the partnership has a From date. When more than 16 entries fall in the window, the rest are left out; round years are kept first. A move is not on the timeline. The home has no dates. Press the pencil on its row and fill in Moved in . Someone shows a home they left long ago as where they live. That home has no moved-out date. Add one.

This page is for everyone in the family who works with places: the homes, cottages, churches and towns where pictures were taken and people lived. It covers the Locations page, creating a location and drawing where it lies, how pictures join a location by themselves, and the Map page, where pictures, locations and GPS tracks are drawn together. How one picture gets its position, and how you correct it, is on Dates and places of pictures .

A location is a named place in the archive, such as "The cottage at Malpas", "Highbury" or "London". It has a name and, if you give them, an address, a city and a country, a description, labels and the people who lived there. Where it lies on the map is one of three shapes: Shape What it is Where it comes from Pictures inside join it Point One spot, with no size Coordinates typed or clicked when the location is created No Circle A centre and a radius Drawn by hand, or worked out from the location's address or linked pictures Yes Polygon An outline with three or more corners Drawn by hand Yes A location with a circle or a polygon does work for you: Pictures whose position falls inside it are linked to it. The viewer shows the location's name for them, and its Media tab lists them. Typing @ and the location's name finds those pictures in search and on the map, and narrows the Year page to what holds them. An album's Info tab lists the locations of its pictures under Places . Staging names the albums it suggests after the location most of their pictures are linked to, or else the nearest location within 500 m. People's homes are locations too, so a location's page shows who lived there; see Family tree, events and homes . Locations are kept under /archive/locations in the tree .

Open Locations in the sidebar, under Browse . Each card shows where the place lies and where that position came from. The header counts the locations, for example "16 locations", and has these controls: Control What it does Filter locations… Narrows the cards as you type, by name and address. Case and accents do not matter. Show All (N) or Needs location (N) , the locations with no place on the map. It appears only while at least one location has none. Sort Name (A-Z) or Name (Z-A) . This browser remembers your choice. Each card shows a small map of where the location lies, or a crossed-out pin when it has no place yet, then its name, its address and one of these badges: Badge Means set by hand Someone drew its shape or typed its coordinates from N photos Its circle was worked out from N geotagged photos linked to it from address Its circle comes from looking up its address N suggestions The address lookup found candidates but was not sure; you pick one on its page Click a card to open the location. A location has no cover photo to choose in the web interface; its card shows the map. With no locations at all, the page says "No locations yet" and "Homes, churches, summer houses: locations where people lived or pictures were taken.", with a New location button when you are signed in. A filter that matches nothing says No locations found matching "<text>" .

You need to be signed in. Press the plus ( Create ) in the top bar and choose Location . On an empty Locations page, New location does the same. See The Create menu . The Create Location dialog opens with a map beside the fields. Type a Name , for example The cottage at Malpas . It is the only field you must fill in. If the place has an address, type it under Address as it was written down: street and number, postcode and town. The hint reads "Looked up on the map when no coordinates are given, and again whenever it is edited." If you know exactly where it is, click the map under Coordinates , or type Latitude and Longitude . A marker shows the spot. Press Create . The location's page opens. What happens next depends on what you gave: Coordinates make the location a point, set by hand. An address you typed is kept as written and not looked up. An address and no coordinates : EiN looks the address up in the background, a few seconds after you press Create . Reload the location's page to see the answer: a circle with a radius of 50 m on the building, a list of suggestions to choose from, or still "No location set yet." when nothing matched. See Where a location's position comes from . Only a name : EiN looks up the name the same way. A name such as Falmouth brings suggestions at best, because a name has no house number or postcode to confirm the answer. Tip A point is an exact spot with no area, so no picture joins it. For a home, a church or a town, give the location a circle or a polygon; see Draw a circle or a polygon . A point can be turned into a circle there too. If the dialog says "Give both latitude and longitude, or neither.", fill in the other half or empty both. The page's web address is made from the name, /locations/the-cottage-at-malpas for the example, so two locations whose names give the same web address cannot both exist. When the dialog reports an error for that reason, choose another name.

p.h: Where a location's position comes from
p.x: A location gets its place on the map from the first of these that gives one: Set by hand. A circle or polygon drawn in Edit location , or coordinates given when the location was created. Nothing else ever moves it. Its pictures. When at least two geotagged pictures are linked to the location directly, by hand in the terminal, EiN puts a circle around them, as wide as they spread. A picture far from the rest is left out, and pictures spread wider than 25 km give no circle. Pictures that joined the location because they lie inside its shape do not count. Its address. EiN asks OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service where the address is, or where the name is when there is no address. EiN uses the answer by itself only when the answer is a building, the house number or postcode you wrote agrees with it, and no answer that ranks almost as high lies more than 250 m away. The location then gets a circle with a radius of 50 m, and its City and Country are filled in. A less certain answer is kept as up to five suggestions for you to choose from. Source Badge on the card Line on the Info tab Set by hand set by hand "Set by hand" Its pictures from N photos "Derived from N geotagged photos spread over N m" Its address from address "Geocoded from the address" An address is looked up in Sweden first, and in the rest of the world when Sweden has no match. A location with only a name is looked up worldwide. For a place abroad, write the town and the country in the address, so that a street of the same name in Sweden does not win. When you change the address of a location that was placed from its address, EiN looks up the changed address. If it cannot be placed with certainty, the location loses its old position and shows suggestions instead, or "No location set yet." when nothing matched. A location placed from its pictures stays where its pictures are, and a location set by hand keeps its shape whatever the address says.

The Info tab shows the shape that decides which pictures belong here, and where that shape came from. The header shows the location's name and address, the people who live there, and its labels. If you may change the location, it also has Share , Edit and a ⋮ menu with Add event and Move to trash . On a phone all of these are in the ⋮ menu. Sharing a location works as for anything else; see Sharing . Tab What it shows Info The map with the location's shape, its details and its current residents. The page opens here. Timeline Residents moving in and out, the location's own events, and the albums with photos taken there Media The pictures linked to the location, newest first, in month sections Residents Everyone recorded as having lived there, with their dates The page's web address keeps the tab, for example /locations/the-cottage-at-malpas?tab=media , so you can link straight to it.

The map shows the location's circle, polygon or point. The button in its top-right corner switches between Map , Dark map and Satellite . Details lists the address as written, the full address the lookup found when that differs, the city and country, the description, the shape ("Polygon, 6 points", "50.24400, -5.02700 · radius 300 m", or the coordinates alone for a point), and where the position came from. Current residents lists the people living there, each with when they moved in, such as "since 2021", or "dates unknown". All residents opens the Residents tab. With nobody recorded, the card says "No known residents."; when everyone recorded has moved out, it says "Nobody lives here now, as far as the archive knows." A location with no place says "No location set yet." under the map. If you may change the location, Location on map beside it opens Edit location .

The Media tab lists every picture linked to the location; see How pictures join a location . You can select pictures and open them in the viewer as in an album, and the selection bar offers Set time . With nothing linked, the tab says "No photos here yet. Geotagged photos inside its area are linked to it automatically." For a location with no place yet, it says "No photos here yet. Once it has a location, geotagged photos inside its area are linked to it automatically."

When the lookup found candidates but was not sure, the Info tab shows numbered pins on the map and a Suggested locations card: "Geocoding was not confident enough to place this automatically. Pick the right one, or set it by hand." Each row has the place's full name, its kind (such as city or house ) and its coordinates. Pointing at a row lights up its pin, and the other way round. Open the location's Info tab. Click the numbered pin that looks right, or its row in the list. The location gets a circle with a radius of 50 m at that spot, marked "Geocoded from the address", and the suggestions disappear. If none of them is right, press None of these under the map or None of these — place it by hand under the list. Both open Edit location , where you draw the shape yourself. Only someone who may change the location can pick a suggestion. Everyone else sees the list.

p.h: Draw a circle or a polygon
p.x: You need permission to change the location. Open the location and press Edit , or Location on map when it has no place yet. The Edit location dialog has the fields on one side and On the map on the other. Choose Circle or Polygon above the map. Draw the shape: Circle : click the map to place the centre. The circle starts with a radius of 250 m. Drag the pin to move it, and drag the round handle on its right-hand edge to make it larger or smaller. Polygon : click the map once for each corner. Drag a corner to move it, click one of the small handles halfway along a side to add a corner there, and right-click a corner to remove it. A polygon needs at least three corners. Press Save . The hint under the map repeats how the chosen mode works. When the location has suggestions, they show on this map as numbered pins, for reference only. After Save , the location is "Set by hand". Within a few seconds, the library's pictures inside the shape are linked to it, and pictures it no longer covers are let go. Open the Media tab to see them. Make the shape cover everywhere pictures of the place were taken: the garden, the jetty below the house, the whole village. A circle from an address is only 50 m around the building. Good to know: Switching between Circle and Polygon clears what you drew. To start a shape again, switch to the other mode and back. Clicking the map does not move a circle that is already there. Move it by its pin. A location that is a point opens as a circle of 250 m around it. Move the pin or the handle and press Save , and the location becomes that circle. The dialog cannot take a location off the map. That is done in the terminal; see In the terminal . If saving fails, the dialog stays open with the reason: "a polygon needs at least three corners" or "a location needs a name".

p.h: Change a location's name, address or description
p.x: Press Edit on the location. The Edit location dialog has these fields beside the map: Field Notes Name Required. A changed name shows everywhere; the page's web address stays the same. Address "As it was written down. A changed address is looked up on the map again, unless the location was set by hand." City Filled in when EiN places the location from its address by itself. You can type it yourself. Country As for City . Description Free text, with Markdown. Labels One word each. A label on a location opens a search for that label when clicked. Emptying a field other than Name removes it. Save stays greyed out until you change something. After an address change, EiN says "Saved. The new address is looked up in the background; a location set by hand is kept." Reload the page after a few seconds to see where the lookup put it.

You do not file pictures into a location. EiN links them by these rules: A picture inside a shape is linked to it. A picture in the library with a position, from its GPS or set by hand, that falls inside a location's circle or polygon is linked to that location. This happens when the picture gets its position, and again whenever the location's shape changes. A picture has one location. When it falls inside several shapes, as a picture taken in Highbury lies inside both Highbury and London, it goes to the location whose centre is nearest. London's Media tab therefore does not list the pictures linked to Highbury. A point contains nothing. A location that is only a point collects no pictures. A changed shape moves the links. Pictures the shape no longer covers are let go, or go to another location that covers them. A link made by a person stays. A link made by hand in the terminal is never replaced by one of these. To put pictures in a location, give them a position inside it. Select them, press Set location and choose the location under A known location : the pictures take the location's centre as their position, and join it when it has a circle or a polygon. The steps are in Set the place of pictures .

The Residents tab lists everyone who has lived at the location. Anyone who may change the location can add residents and correct their dates there with Add resident , choosing Person already here or New person and giving Moved in and Moved out . A resident without a Moved out date counts as living there, and appears under Current residents and in the header. The same records are a person's homes, seen from the other side: see Add a resident to a location . Under ⋮, Add event writes a dated note on the location, which appears on its Timeline tab. A location's event needs both a Date and a Description ; see Events of albums, locations and devices .

p.h: Move a location to the trash
p.x: If you may change the location, open ⋮ and choose Move to trash . EiN returns you to the Locations page and says "<name> moved to the trash", with Undo . You can also restore it from Trash in the account menu, for as many days as an administrator keeps the trash; see Your profile, favourites and trash .

Open Map in the sidebar, under Explore . The map fills the page, with no header. Pictures, locations and the routes that devices recorded share one map, narrowed by the search box and the years under it. The map draws three things: Pictures with a position that you may see, gathered into piles. Pictures in staging are left out until they are filed. Locations that have a place, as pins. GPS tracks that devices recorded. Opened from the sidebar, the map starts over Gothenburg in Sweden, whatever your pictures show. Zoom out to find them, or keep a bookmark of the view you use; see Share or bookmark a view .

Drag the map to move it, and zoom with the mouse wheel or by pinching. The map has no zoom buttons, and clicking a pile never zooms: it opens the pile. A small spinner in the top-left corner shows while the map reads what is in view.

A single picture is drawn as its thumbnail, and pointing at it shows its file name. Click it to open the viewer . The arrow keys then move through the other single pictures on the map. A pile is several pictures close together, drawn as one of them with the count on it. Pointing at it says "N photos — click to browse". Click it to open N photos here : the pictures behind it in month sections, with the spot's coordinates under the title. Open one in the viewer, or select pictures as in an album. The browser's Back, or a phone's back gesture, closes it and leaves you on the map. List the N photos in this view , the button with four squares in the top-right corner, opens every picture in view the same way, titled "N photos in this view". It shows while pictures are drawn and the view holds some. Piles depend on the zoom: zoom in, and a pile splits into smaller piles and single pictures.

p.h: Locations and tracks on the map
p.x: Location pins stand at each location's centre. Click a pin to open the location's page. The pins are hidden while the search box narrows the map; the years do not hide them. Tracks are the routes devices recorded, as coloured lines, one colour per day. Each track has three colours of its own that its days take in turn, so two days in a row differ, and other tracks use other colours. Pointing at a line shows the device's name and the day. Tracks are always drawn in full: the years and the search box narrow the pictures only. How tracks get into EiN from GPX files is on A device's track .

The funnel button at the top of the right-hand corner is the Show menu: Choice Draws All Pictures, locations and tracks Media Pictures only Locations Location pins only Tracks Tracks only While one layer is chosen, the button shows that layer's icon instead of the funnel.

The button under it, Map style , opens a column of previews, each showing the place you are looking at in one style. Pointing at a preview names it, and clicking it changes the map: Style What it is Map OpenStreetMap's street map, the default Dark map A dark grey map from Esri Satellite Aerial photographs from Esri The maps on a location's page and on an album's Map tab have their own style button in the corner, with the same three styles.

Under the search box is a slider for the years, with the first year of the range drawn at its left and the last at its right. Drag either handle, and the map reads again when you let go. While the slider narrows the map, the two years turn white; with both handles at the ends, nothing is narrowed. Only years with pictures take room on the slider, so the decades most pictures come from get most of its length.

The box at the foot of the map reads "Search this view — type @ for a person, location or label". Type what you are looking for. Words find pictures by what they show or contain, as on the Media page. @ opens a list of people, locations and labels to pick from: type @peg and choose Peggy Wrenfield, for example. Press Enter or the arrow at the right of the box. Nothing changes while you type. The map then draws only the matching pictures in view and hides the location pins. For words, the 500 best matches in view are drawn. The box takes one person, one location and one label; when you pick a second person, the last one counts. A location finds the pictures linked to it. Except on a phone, an info icon beside the box shows what the box understood. To show everything again, empty the box and press Enter . Finding pictures by what they show needs the media service; see What needs the media service and a language model .

The address bar holds the whole view, so a bookmark or a link you send opens the same map, and a reload keeps it. These parts of the address are the map's: Part What it holds c The centre, as latitude and longitude z The zoom layers Which of media , locations and tracks are on; absent for all from , to The years base The map style; absent for Map q , person , location , tag What the search box holds For example, /map?c=50.244,-5.027&z=14&layers=media&from=1968&to=1975 shows the pictures taken around the cottage at Malpas from 1968 to 1975. Every address of the web interface is listed on Addresses in the web interface .

p.h: Where the maps and addresses come from
p.x: The map pictures and the address lookups come from outside services. Your photos, videos and recordings are never sent to them. What From What is sent The Map style, and the small maps on cards OpenStreetMap's tile servers, tile.openstreetmap.org Your browser asks for the map squares of the area you look at The Dark map and Satellite styles Esri, server.arcgisonline.com The same A location's position from its address OpenStreetMap's Nominatim, nominatim.openstreetmap.org The machine EiN runs on sends the location's address, or its name Pictures' street addresses Nominatim The machine EiN runs on sends each picture's coordinates Without an internet connection, the maps have no background, while pins, thumbnails and tracks are still drawn, and addresses cannot be looked up. For administrators: the public Nominatim service answers one request a second, and EiN paces its own requests to that. The environment variable NOMINATIM_SEARCH_URL points the address lookups at another Nominatim server, such as one of your own; see Environment variables .

Locations are ordinary nodes, and these commands work on them in the terminal . Each links to its reference entry. Task Command List the locations with their coordinates location-list See a location's shape position-get <location> Give a location a point or a circle ( --polygon for a polygon) position-set <location>/position --lat=… --lng=… [--radius=…] Take a location off the map position-set <location>/position --clear Mark a shape as set by hand, as Save does geocode-location <location> --drawn Look an address up again, even for a placed location geocode-location --force <location> Place a location again from its pictures or its address location-locate --force <location> Change the name, address, city, country or description location-update Link the pictures inside a location's shape at once location-link-media --location <location> To turn the point "Islington Town Hall" into a circle with a radius of 150 m, the way the dialog does it: # in EiN's terminal position-set /archive/locations/Islington_Town_Hall/position --lat=51.5416 --lng=-0.1028 --radius=150 geocode-location /archive/locations/Islington_Town_Hall --drawn Write negative coordinates with = , as --lng=-0.1028 , so they are not read as an option. How to link one picture to a location by hand is in Dates and places of pictures .

A location stays at "No location set yet." The lookup found nothing for its address. Edit the address so it has a house number, a postcode, the town and, abroad, the country, or draw its shape yourself. It shows suggestions although the address is right. The address has no house number or postcode to confirm the answer, or two places share the name. Pick the right one, or press None of these and draw it. Its circle is on the wrong building or in the wrong town. Draw it yourself with Edit . A shape set by hand is never moved by a lookup. Pictures taken there are not on its Media tab. Look for the cause in this order: the location is a point, which contains nothing: give it a circle or a polygon; the pictures have no position: give them one with Set location , as in Set the place of pictures ; they lie inside another location whose centre is nearer, such as a house inside a town, and are on that location's Media tab; they were linked to another location by hand or by the import, which is never replaced; they are still in staging: file them into an album first; you drew the shape a moment ago: wait a few seconds and open the Media tab again. The page shows the old position after you changed the address. The lookup runs in the background. Reload the page after a few seconds. A location set by hand does not move for an address. Edit, Share and the ⋮ menu are missing. You may not change this location. Ask whoever owns it to share it with you; see Sharing . The map is grey, with thumbnails and pins but no streets. Your browser cannot reach the tile servers: you are offline, or a network filter blocks tile.openstreetmap.org or server.arcgisonline.com . The Map page shows no pictures. It opens over Gothenburg; zoom out. Check that Show is on All or Media , that the year slider's handles are at the ends, and that the search box is empty. The location pins are gone from the map. The search box narrows the map, or Show is on Media or Tracks . A track ignores the year slider. Tracks are always drawn in full; only the pictures are narrowed.

Dates and places of pictures : a picture's position, street address, and Set location Family tree, events and homes : homes, residents and events Devices and GPS tracks : the devices whose tracks the map draws Search and the finder : finding pictures by location with @ Albums : an album's Map and Info tabs Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the place section of the details panel

A device is a camera, phone, scanner, camcorder or GPS tracker that took pictures or recorded routes for your archive. This page is for family members and administrators who register devices, say who owned them, set their clocks right and bring in GPS tracks.

p.h: What registering a device gives you
p.x: EiN reads the camera's name out of every picture, but until the camera is registered as a device that is all it knows: the viewer shows the make and model the file names, and nothing else. Once a device is registered, the pictures it took are linked to it, and: the viewer's camera line names the device, links to its page and says who owned it (see The details panel ); the device's page gathers everything it took, who owned it and when, and the route it recorded; an album's Info tab lists the devices that took its pictures (see Albums ), and the Search page finds devices and narrows albums by them (see Search and the finder ); the device's Timezone , Scanner or digitizer and Video times in UTC settings correct the dates of every picture it took; the GPS route it recorded, its track, is drawn on the maps.

When a file arrives, EiN reads what the camera wrote into it: the make (the EXIF tag Make ), the model ( Model ) and, when the camera writes one, its serial number ( SerialNumber , InternalSerialNumber or DeviceSerialNo ). Some camcorders write the make and model as DeviceManufacturer and DeviceModelName instead. These three together are the file's fingerprint , and EiN looks for the registered device that has the same one: a device with the same serial number; otherwise, a device with the same make and the same model. The device's name plays no part. The make and model are compared exactly as the camera writes them, so a device registered with the make Nikon does not match files that say NIKON CORPORATION . EiN does this once, when it first reads the file. A device you register afterwards does not claim the files that arrived before it; Link existing media on its page finds them (see Link the pictures it took before it was registered ). Two things a fingerprint cannot do: Tell two phones of the same model apart. A serial number identifies one camera body; a make and model identify only a model line, and most phones write no serial number. If two people in the family have the same phone model, EiN cannot tell their pictures apart, and all of them are linked to one of the two devices. Match a file that names no camera. Many messaging apps remove the make and model from the pictures they send, and a file without them matches nothing. You can link such files by hand in the terminal (see From the terminal ). A device's fingerprint has nothing to do with the fingerprints EiN takes of the pictures themselves to find copies; those are described in Duplicates .

Open Devices in the sidebar, under Browse . Every registered device with the picture that stands for it; the badges show at a glance which ones carry a serial number, a time zone or the scanner setting. The header counts the registered devices ( 13 devices ). The filter box ( Filter devices… ) matches the name, make, model and serial number as you type. Show switches between Registered (N) and Unregistered , the cameras EiN has seen in the pictures that match no registered device. Sort offers Name (A-Z) (the default), Name (Z-A) and Make / model . Your choice is remembered in this browser. It has no effect on the unregistered list. Each card shows the device's cover, its name, its description or else its make and model, and badges: the serial number, the time zone, scanner and video UTC . Click a card to open the device's page . When nothing is registered yet, the page says No devices registered yet : "The cameras and phones that took the pictures. Unregistered lists the ones the archive has already seen." with Show unregistered and, when you are signed in, New device .

p.h: Register a camera EiN has already seen
p.x: The quickest way to register a camera is from the pictures it took. On the Devices page, choose Show → Unregistered . The first time in a visit, EiN looks through the files it has read for cameras that match nothing registered. The list reads: "Cameras found in the indexed media that match nothing in the registry. Registering one lets its photos be linked to it, and its timezone and owners apply." Find the camera. Each card shows a suggested name (the model, with the make in front when the model does not start with it, such as Canon EOS 7D or Panasonic DMC-TZ1 ), the make and model, the serial number when there is one, and how many files it took ( N files ). The cameras with the most files come first. Click Register on its card. The Register Device dialog opens with Name , Make , Model and Serial number filled in from the files. Change Name to what the family calls the camera, such as David's 7D . Leave Make , Model and Serial number as they are: they are what the files are matched on. Under Timezone , choose the time zone its clock was set to, and turn on Scanner or digitizer or Video times in UTC if they apply (see Clocks, time zones and scanners ). Click Register . The device's page opens. On its Info tab, click Link existing media . The files the camera took are linked to it, and a message says, for example, "Linked 412 files and updated dates on 37." Rescan at the top of the unregistered list looks again, for instance after a large import. When every camera is registered, the list says "Every camera the media names is registered (N files matched)." With many unknown cameras it shows the most used ones and says "Only the most-used cameras are listed; there are more."

p.h: When a card says "registered as …, but unmatchable"
p.x: Sometimes a device with the camera's name already exists, but without the make, model or serial number its files carry, so nothing is matched to it. Its card then has the badge registered as <name>, but unmatchable and the button Add fingerprint instead of Register , because registering would make a second copy of a camera EiN already knows. Click Add fingerprint . EiN writes the make, model and serial number from the card into the existing device and links the files they identify. When it is done, a message says "Linked N files to <name>." or "<name> now carries the fingerprint, but no unclaimed files matched it." This is quick for a camera with a serial number and slow for one known only by its make and model, which can take minutes in a large archive. The button is there only if you may change that device; otherwise the card has no button.

Register a device by hand when EiN has not seen it in any picture yet: a GPS tracker, a scanner before the scans arrive, or a camera whose files you are about to import. Open the Create menu (the plus in the top bar) and choose Device , or click New device on an empty Devices page. The Register Device dialog opens. Fill in the fields below. Only Name is required. Click Register . The device's page opens. Field What to enter Name What the family calls it, such as Helen's scanner . The name also gives the device's folder in the tree, so two devices cannot have the same name. Make "As the camera writes it in exif: what files are matched on." For example Canon . Model "As the camera writes it in exif." For example Canon EOS 5D Mark III . Serial number "Tells one body apart, where make and model tell only the model." Optional. Timezone "The zone its clock was set to." Optional. Scanner or digitizer "Its EXIF device dates describe digitisation, not when the photograph was taken." Video times in UTC "Its videos keep their recording time in UTC, as phones do." To copy the make and model exactly, open a picture the camera took in the viewer and open Details at the foot of the details panel. Among the EXIF tags it lists are Make , Model and, when the camera writes one, SerialNumber (see The Details section ). A device without a serial number and without both a make and a model is never matched to any file. Its page says so: "No serial and no make/model — nothing is matched to this device automatically; device-link --device links files to it by hand." Anyone signed in can register a device. Changing it afterwards, with the buttons this page describes, is offered to whoever may change it, which the device's Share dialog shows and sets (see Sharing ).

Click a card on the Devices page, or the device's name in the viewer. The page's address is /devices/ and the device's folder name, such as /devices/Jons_eTrex , and a tab other than Info adds ?tab= with the tab's name, such as ?tab=track . A device's page opens on its settings, with the button that links the pictures it took before it was registered. Under the name, the header shows the current owners (up to three, then "and N more"), how many files the device took and in which years, such as 75 files · 2025–2026 ( N+ files when counting stopped at its limit), and the device's labels. For those who may change the device, the corner has Share and Edit , and the ⋮ menu has Add event and Move to trash . On a phone they are all under ⋮. Tab What it shows Info The page opens here. The Settings card lists Make, Model, Serial number, Timezone, "Capture dates: Scanner dates suppressed" for a scanner, "Video times: UTC", and the description; with nothing but a name it says "Nothing recorded beyond the name." Below it, Link existing media , and beside it Current owners with All owners . Timeline The device's history: when each owner started and stopped using it, the events written on it, and the albums holding pictures it took. Media Every file linked to the device, by date. Select pictures to act on them from the selection bar, for example Add to album or Set time (see The selection bar ). Track The route the device recorded (see A device's track ). Owners Everyone who has owned it, with the dates (see Say who owned a device ). The Media tab is the place to correct a camera whose clock was wrong: select its pictures and use Set time , as Dates and places of pictures describes. Move to trash sends the device to your trash, and the message's Undo brings it back (see Your profile, favourites and trash ).

p.h: Link the pictures it took before it was registered
p.x: Files are linked to their device when EiN first reads them. A camera registered afterwards leaves its older pictures unclaimed, and so does a device whose make, model or serial number you change later. Open the device's page. The Info tab opens. Click Link existing media . The card explains: "Files are linked to their device when they are indexed. A camera registered afterwards leaves its older photos unclaimed; this finds them by fingerprint and attaches them." Wait for the message, such as "Linked 412 files and updated dates on 37.", or "Nothing new to link or update — every matching file already has this device policy." Linking also dates the files again by the device's settings, which is what "updated dates" counts. Files that are already linked to another device are left with it. The card is shown only to those who may change the device, and only when the device has a serial number or both a make and a model. A device with a serial number is linked quickly; one known only by its make and model can take minutes in a large archive.

On the device's page, click Edit . The Edit device dialog opens. Change what you need: Name , Make , Model , Serial number , Timezone (a list of time zones you can type in, such as Pacific/Auckland ), Scanner or digitizer , Video times in UTC , Description and Labels . Click Save . A changed Timezone , Scanner or digitizer or Video times in UTC re-dates every file already linked to the device, and the page says "Re-dated N linked files.", or "Removed scanner dates from N linked files." when you turned the scanner setting on. A changed Make , Model or Serial number decides only which files arriving from then on are linked to the device. Click Link existing media afterwards to link the files already in the archive.

Three settings tell EiN how to read a device's dates. Each one applies to every file linked to the device, and changing it re-dates them. Timezone : the time zone the camera's clock was set to. A camera's clock writes a time without a zone, and EiN reads it in this zone, with the summer time of the year the picture was taken. A zone the camera wrote into the file itself comes first. Without a Timezone , EiN uses the archive's own time zone. Set it for a camera bought abroad, or one left on home time during a trip: Helen's Coolpix stayed on London time when she took it to Wellington, and with its Timezone set to Europe/London , EiN reads its clock as London time and gets the moment of each picture right. Scanner or digitizer : the device's clock records when a file was scanned, not when the photograph was taken, so EiN does not date pictures by it. Pictures with no other date stay undated until someone gives them one. Files brought in through a staging category of the kind Scans are treated as scans whatever device made them; this setting matters for scans uploaded straight into an album, copied in over SFTP, or already in the library. Video times in UTC : phones keep their videos' recording time in UTC. Turn this on for a phone whose videos come out off by its time zone. Dates and places of pictures explains how EiN chooses a picture's date and time zone, and Date scans of old prints and slides how scans are dated.

A device can have several owners over the years. The viewer lists them under the camera's name, each with the dates, such as Owned by Ruby Wrenfield (2023–), so you can tell whose camera it was when a picture was taken. On the device's page, open the Owners tab: "Who has owned <name>, and when." Click Add owner . Under Person , choose the person. Fill in From and To as a year, a month or a day: 2005 , 2005-06 or 2005-06-20 . Leave To empty while they still own it, and leave both empty if you do not know the dates. Click Add owner . The list shows the current owners first, then the earlier ones, with their dates: "2019 – 2023", "since 2019", "until 2023", or "dates unknown". A current owner with a start date has the badge current . Use the pencil beside an owner to change the dates ( Save changes ), and the bin to remove them; EiN asks "Remove <person> as an owner of <device>?" before it does. An owner without a To date counts as a current owner, in the page's header and on the Info tab's Current owners card. Dated ownership appears on the Timeline tab, as "<person> started using <device>" and "<person> stopped using <device>". A date that is not a year, month or day is refused with a message ending in "is not a date (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])".

p.h: Write something on a device's timeline
p.x: To keep a story with a device, such as where it was bought or when it broke, add an event: On the device's page, open the ⋮ menu and choose Add event . Fill in Date (such as 2005-06-15 ) and Description ("What happened"). Both are needed. Written by is you unless you choose someone else. Click Add event . The event appears on the device's Timeline tab. Events are described in full in Family tree, events and homes .

The picture on a device's card and behind its page's header is its cover: the newest picture linked to it, by the date it was taken. The cover moves on by itself as newer pictures are linked. A device that took only videos, such as a camcorder, gets the poster frame of its newest video once that video has been processed; recordings are never used. The card of a device with no pictures shows a placeholder with its initials. The web interface has no button to choose a device's cover. In the terminal you can link a picture as the device's coverPhoto yourself, and a cover chosen this way is kept. In the demo, Ruby's iPhone is the folder /archive/devices/ruby-iphone : # in EiN's terminal ln -sf /archive/albums/wellington-christmas-2025/IMG_0650.HEIC /archive/devices/ruby-iphone/coverPhoto To go back to the automatic cover, remove the link with rm /archive/devices/ruby-iphone/coverPhoto and run device-cover /archive/devices/ruby-iphone .

The route a GPS-capable device recorded is its track. It shows on the device's Track tab, on the Map page with its Tracks layer (see Locations and the map ), on the Map tab of every album whose dates it falls in (see Albums ). The Track tab draws the route on a map, each day in its own colour, and adds it up: Figure What it is Points How many recorded positions the track holds. Days On how many days it recorded. Distance The length of the route in kilometres, added up day by day, so the gap between one day's end and the next day's start is not counted. Duration The time from the first point to the last, in hours and minutes. It includes the time between trips, so a track that holds several trips shows the whole span. Under the figures are the times of the first and the last point. A long track is drawn from a thinned copy; the line then ends with "drawn from a thinned copy of the track", and the distance comes out a little shorter than the route really was. A device with no route says This device has recorded no track . EiN draws a track on the maps; it does not use it to give a position to pictures that have none. To place those, see Dates and places of pictures .

p.h: Upload a GPX file to a device's track
p.x: A GPX file is the format GPS trackers and tracking apps save routes in. If you know which device recorded a file, upload it on that device's page: Open the device's page and the Track tab. Click Upload GPX and choose one or more .gpx files. Wait for the message: "N new points added to the track", or "The track already had every point in it". The button is offered to those who may change the device. EiN reads the recorded track points of the file, each with its time; points with a time the track already has are not added twice, so uploading the same file again changes nothing. The GPX file itself is not kept, only the points.

A GPX file that arrives in your staging area, by Import media , the Media page's Upload or copying over SFTP (see Getting your photos in ), is not treated as a picture. EiN reads which device the file says recorded it and adds the route to that device's track; the file then goes. The file names its device in its creator attribute or in one of its <name> entries. It matches a registered device when one of these holds, as whole words, the device's name, its make and model together, or its serial number. Capital letters and punctuation do not count. A file whose creator reads Garmin eTrex 30x joins the device with the make Garmin and the model eTrex 30x ; in the demo, Ruby's tracks say Apple iPhone 15 and join Ruby's iPhone. When a file names no registered device, or more than one, it waits for you: Open Staging in the sidebar. A yellow box titled Needs you says "1 GPS track waits for the device that recorded it." (or how many). Click Choose device . The Inbox's Files tab opens with the card Routes waiting for a device : "These GPX files do not name a device the archive knows. Say which device recorded each, and its route joins that device's track." Beside each file, choose the device in the Device list and click Import . If the device is not registered yet, register it first (see Register a device by hand ) and open the card again; a waiting file is not tried again by itself. Waiting files are kept in your staging area's routes folder, /home/<you>/staging/routes/ . Sorting in staging describes the staging area.

What you see Why What to do The viewer shows only a make and model where the camera's name should be. The camera is not registered, or it was registered after the picture arrived. Register it from Unregistered , or click Link existing media on its page. A device's Media tab says "Nothing is linked to this device yet. If it was registered after the media was indexed, use “Link existing media”." The device was registered after its pictures arrived. Click Link existing media on the Info tab. The Media tab says "Nothing is linked to this device yet, and nothing can be: give it a serial number, or both a make and a model." The device has no fingerprint. Edit it, fill in Make and Model exactly as the files have them, then click Link existing media . Link existing media finds nothing, but pictures from the camera are missing from its page. The make or model differs from what the files say; the files are linked to another device; or they name no camera at all. Compare with the Make and Model in the viewer's Details . For files linked elsewhere or naming no camera, use device-relink --force or device-link --device in the terminal. Pictures from two people's phones are mixed up on one device. The phones are the same model and write no serial number. EiN cannot tell them apart. Link one person's pictures by hand with device-link --device . A camera's pictures are some hours off. Its clock was set to another time zone. Set its Timezone ; see Clocks, time zones and scanners . A phone's videos are off by exactly its time zone. The phone keeps video times in UTC. Turn on Video times in UTC for it. Scans are dated to the day they were scanned. The scanner is not registered with Scanner or digitizer . Register it with the setting on, or turn it on in Edit device . Registering says device-create: /archive/devices/…: already exists . A device with that name exists already. Punctuation such as an apostrophe is left out of the folder name, so Davids 7D and David's 7D clash. Choose another name, or open the existing device. Edit , Link existing media , Add owner or Upload GPX is missing. You may not change this device. Ask the person who registered it, or an administrator. Upload GPX gives a message ending in "no track points found". The file holds no recorded track points, only a planned route or waypoints. Use the file the device recorded while it moved. A GPX file sits in an album as an ordinary file. It was uploaded straight into the album, where GPX files are not read as routes. Upload it on the device's Track tab, then delete the file from the album.

Each device is a folder under /archive/devices ; ls /archive/devices lists their names, and its route is the child track . The commands below are in the archive command reference , and every one takes --help . Task Command List the cameras seen but not registered device-scan Register a device device-create --name <name> --make <make> --model <model> , with --serial , --timezone , --digitizer or --quicktime-utc Change a device's settings device-update <device> --timezone <zone> , or --clear <field> Show a device and its owners device-info <device> Link the files a device took before it was registered device-relink <device> ; --dry-run reports first, --force takes files from another device, --all does every device Link files to a device by hand device-link --device <device> <file or folder>… Add an owner, or change the dates device-set-owner <device> <person> --from <date> --to <date> , with --update to change Remove an owner device-remove-owner <device> <person> Add a GPX file to a device's track track-stage <gpx> --device <device> Bring a device's automatic cover up to date device-cover <device> , or --all Registering Jon's GPS tracker, making him its owner and adding a route copied into your home folder: # in EiN's terminal device-create --name "Jon's eTrex" --make Garmin --model "eTrex 30x" --timezone Pacific/Auckland device-set-owner /archive/devices/Jons_eTrex /archive/people/Jon_Wrenfield --from 2021 track-stage " $HOME /tararua-walk.gpx" --device /archive/devices/Jons_eTrex device-create prints the device's folder, /archive/devices/Jons_eTrex , and track-stage removes the GPX file once its points are in the track. See Commands by task for the rest of the archive's commands.

Locations and the map : the Map page and its Tracks layer. Dates and places of pictures : how a picture's date, time zone and place are chosen. Getting your photos in : every way files, GPX tracks among them, get into EiN. Sorting in staging : the staging area where waiting routes are. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the camera line in the details panel.

t: Memories, news and events on Home

p.x: With the Archive installed, Home shows pictures taken on this day in earlier years, the albums people made lately, and the birthdays and anniversaries around today, and the Statistics page shows when in the year births, weddings and deaths fall. This page is for everyone who uses EiN. Home's layout and the rest of the Statistics page are EiN's own, and Home and statistics covers them. News lists the albums made lately and Events what comes round in the next month. On this day is missing here because nothing was taken on that date in earlier years. The Archive fills all three of Home's sections. Like everything on Home, they show only what you may see: an album or a person that is not shared with you does not appear.

On this day is a row of round pictures, one for each year that has pictures taken on today's date, newest year first, up to 8. Under each ring it says how long ago that was, such as "1 year ago" or "12 years ago", and the year. The picture in the ring is the first one taken that day. This year counts too, so a picture taken today has a ring of its own, "0 years ago". When there are more rings than fit, swipe the row sideways, or scroll it with a trackpad. The row counts pictures in albums only. Pictures still in your staging area, and pictures with no date, are not part of it, and neither are pictures you may not see. When no year has anything for today, the section is not shown at all. The same rings stand above the feed on the Media page; see Media, Year and labels .

Press a ring. The story opens over the whole window, on black. At the top, a thin bar for each picture of that year fills as the picture shows; each picture stays 5 seconds. Under the bars it says how long ago it was, such as "7 years ago", and the date, such as "25 December 2019". The story plays that year's pictures in the order they were taken, up to 24 of them, then moves on to the next earlier year with pictures from this day, through up to 30 years that have pictures. After the last picture of the oldest year, it closes. To With a finger or the mouse With the keyboard Go to the next picture Tap or click anywhere but the left third → Go back a picture Tap or click the left third ← Pause, and play again Hold your finger or the mouse button down, and let go to play on; or press Pause , then Play Space See the pictures in the viewer Open in the lightbox Close the story Close Esc Open in the lightbox opens the story's pictures, from every year, in the viewer at the picture you were on, with the details panel and everything else the viewer offers; see Viewing photos, videos and recordings . A few things work differently from a slideshow in the viewer: The 5 seconds are fixed. Your Seconds per slide preference applies to the viewer's slideshow only; see Watch a slideshow . Each picture pans and zooms slowly whatever your Ken Burns effect preference says. On a device set to reduce motion, the pictures stay still. A video shows as a still from it, and a recording as an empty slide. Use Open in the lightbox to play them. While a picture is still loading, its bar waits, so a slow picture still gets its full time. While the story plays, your screen is kept from going to sleep.

News is a timeline of the albums people made lately, newest first, up to 8. Each entry reads "<who> added <album>", for example "Helen Okafor added Christmas in Wellington", with how long ago under it: It says When the album was made "just now" less than an hour ago "3h ago" less than a day ago, in hours "yesterday" one day ago "4 days ago" up to a week ago "2 weeks ago" up to a month ago a date, such as "12 Jul 2025" longer ago, in your browser's date format Under it is a row of the album's pictures, as many as fit and at most five, the last one marked with how many more the album holds, such as +21 . Click the album's name or any of the pictures to open the album. Beside each entry is the portrait of the person whose account made the album, when the account is linked to a person in the archive; otherwise a picture icon. See Your profile, favourites and trash . What makes an entry: An album is made. Every way of making one counts: Create → Album , New album while adding pictures, and filing a group from staging as a New album or New private album . See Create an album and Sorting in staging . The time is when the album was made. Adding pictures to an album, renaming it or changing its dates does not bring it back to the top. Only albums in the album list count : folders inside an album, and the albums staging suggests to you, do not. An album moved to the trash leaves the news. When nothing has been added yet, News says "Nothing has been added yet" and "What people add shows up here.", and when you are signed in the Archive offers Import media under it; see Import media .

Events is a card of what comes round every year, for the days around today. How the card groups its entries, how far it looks and how it says when each falls are on Home and statistics . Each entry shows the face of the person it is about, or both partners' faces for a wedding anniversary. Click it to open the person's page.

Kind Comes from When it shows It reads Birthday A person's Born date Every year, up to the age of 110 "Helen Okafor turns 68"; after the person's death, "Arthur Wrenfield would have turned 95" Memorial A person's Died date Only in milestone years "5 years since Peggy Wrenfield died" Wedding anniversary The From date of two partners' relation Every year, up to and including the year the relation ended ( Until ) or the first of the two died, and for at most 75 years "Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married"; "… years together" for Partner , "… years engaged" for a relation whose kind is engaged Each of them needs a full date, with year, month and day. A date known only to the year or the month, such as 1934 or 1934-05 , has no day to come round on, so it makes no entry. Someone born on 29 February has a birthday entry in leap years only. The first entry is the first anniversary: nobody "turns 0". Birthdays and memorials are read from the people on the People page. A Marriage event on a person's page does not make an anniversary; the From date on the partner relation does.

A milestone is the 5th, 10th, 15th and 20th year, and then every 10th: 30, 40, 50 and so on. A milestone shows in bold, and milestones are the entries kept when the card runs out of room. Memorials appear only on milestones; birthdays and wedding anniversaries appear every year.

In the Wrenfield family's archive, the Events card on 20 January 2026 shows four entries, the milestones in bold: Group Entry When Coming up Grace Price turns 40 in 5 days Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married in 2 weeks Thomas Wrenfield turns 65 in 4 weeks Recently 5 years since Peggy Wrenfield died 3 days ago

Birthdays and memorials: open the person, press Edit , and type Born or Died as a full date, such as 1958-05-03 . See Edit a person . Wedding anniversaries: give the partner relation a From date, such as 1996-02-03 , when you choose Add partner on the person's Family tab, and an Until date if it ended for another reason than a death. Choose Married under Relationship for "years married". In the web interface this takes an administrator. To date a partnership that is already recorded, choose Add partner again and pick the same partner. See Partnerships and their dates .

p.h: Life events on the Statistics page
p.x: The Archive adds the Events section to the Statistics page , above EiN's own Nodes section. Each chart folds every year into twelve months, so you see when in the year births, weddings and deaths fall. It has four charts: Births by month , Engagements by month , Marriages by month and Deaths by month . Each has a bar for every month from Jan to Dec, counting all years together, as the line "All years" under it says. Rest the pointer on a bar to read its count, such as "Mar: 2". The number at the top right is the total. It also counts dates known only to the year, which are in no month's bar, so the bars can add up to less than the total. Births and Deaths count the Born and Died dates of people. Engagements and Marriages count the Engagement and Marriage events written on people's pages. A wedding written on both spouses counts twice, and a partnership dated only by a From date on the relation does not count. See Record a wedding .

What you see Why, and what to do On this day is missing No picture in the albums you may see was taken on today's date in another year. Pictures still in staging and pictures without a date do not count; file them into an album and check their dates, see Dates and places of pictures . A picture turns up under the day before or after The day is counted in UTC, so a picture taken close to midnight can fall on the neighbouring day. A picture known only to a year or a month counts from the start of that period, so it can turn up on 1 January or the first of the month, or the day before in a time zone east of UTC. The story says "Nothing was taken on this day in earlier years." There are no pictures you may see from that date, for example when the story was opened from a link for another day. An album you added pictures to is not in News News shows when an album was made, not when pictures were added to it. An entry reads "Somebody added …" EiN could not tell which account made the album, for example because that account is gone. A birthday or memorial is missing The Born or Died date needs a day, the person must be on the People page, and birthdays stop at 110 years. Memorials show only in milestone years. The card also holds at most 16 entries, milestones first. A wedding anniversary is missing The partner relation needs a From date with a day. Anniversaries stop after the relation's Until year, after the year one of the two died, and after 75 years. A Marriage event alone does not make one. Events is a day out, or On this day shows yesterday's pictures Home takes today's date from your computer or phone. Check its date and time zone. The Marriages chart shows twice as many weddings as there were Each wedding was written as an event on both spouses, and each event counts. See Life events on the Statistics page .

Home's onthisday , news and events commands gather what every installed module offers; Home and statistics shows how to run them. The Archive's part comes from onthisday-media , news-albums and events-anniversaries . events --today 2026-01-20 in the Wrenfield family's archive prints the example above. A * marks a milestone: 2026-01-17 3d ago * 5 years since Peggy Wrenfield died 2026-01-25 in 5d * Grace Price turns 40 2026-02-03 in 14d * Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married 2026-02-19 in 30d Thomas Wrenfield turns 65 onthisday prints one line for each year, such as 2019 Pictures taken on 25 December 2019 , and news one line for each album, such as 2026-10-11 18:02 Helen Okafor added Christmas in Wellington . The Archive has more commands about the family's dates: # in EiN's terminal timeline --kind birth,death,anniversary # the family's history, looking back from today dayinhistory 12-25 --years 20 --per-year 1 # the pictures of a day, by path person-stats # the counts behind the Statistics page's Events charts timeline is the archive's history, newest first: albums, births, deaths, birthdays, wedding anniversaries, events, moves and GPS tracks. It looks back from today, never ahead, and stops a person's birthdays at their death. By default it lists only milestone birthdays and anniversaries; --birthdays all and --anniversaries all list every year. --kind , --year , --person , --location and --tag narrow it. The full options are in the reference for timeline , dayinhistory , person-stats , onthisday-media , news-albums and events-anniversaries .

Home and statistics : the Home page and the Statistics page themselves. Family tree, events and homes : dates of birth and death, partners and their dates, and events on a person's page. Media, Year and labels : the Media feed with the same rings, and the Year page. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer and its slideshow. Albums : making the albums that fill News. Sharing : who sees which albums and people.

EiN keeps any file you give it. What it works out from a file depends on what kind of file it is: a photo gets thumbnails, faces and a date, a video also gets a version your browser can play, and a document has its text read for search. This page is for everyone who brings files into EiN. It lists the formats EiN recognises, what it makes from each, and what happens to the rest.

p.h: What EiN does with each kind of file
p.x: Kind Formats What EiN works out Photos JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, WebP, AVIF, GIF, BMP, camera RAW date, place, camera, thumbnails, faces, text in the picture, what it shows, look-alikes Videos MP4, MOV, M4V, MTS and M2TS, MPG, AVI, MKV, WebM, 3GP, FLV date, place, camera, a playable version, a preview clip, chapters, faces, what is said and who says it, look-alikes Recordings M4A, MP3, WAV, FLAC, Ogg and Opus, AMR date, a playable version, a picture of the sound, what is said and who says it, the same recording twice Documents PDF and plain text the text, for search; the text of scanned pages too Sidecar files Google Takeout JSON, XMP nothing of their own: they give their picture its date, place and caption GPS tracks GPX the route, added to the track of the device that recorded it Zip files ZIP in staging, expanded into the files it holds Everything else any file kept as it is, and nothing more The work happens in the background after a file arrives, and each part shows up when it is done; Getting your photos in explains the order. A file you upload into staging is read once it arrives, but the text in pictures and documents is read only when you file it into an album.

p.h: How EiN tells what a file is
p.x: EiN looks at the first bytes of a file, not at its name. A JPEG photo named IMG_0412.png is still a JPEG photo, and a file with no extension at all is recognised the same way. It makes no difference whether the file came in with Import media , an upload into an album, or by dropping it on a page. A file copied in over SFTP is the exception: when EiN knows its extension, such as .png , .docx or .md , the type that extension names is the one it keeps, and only a file with an extension EiN does not know is recognised by its first bytes. The name decides in two cases, because the bytes say too little: Camera RAW files. Most RAW formats look like a TIFF picture from their first bytes, so EiN goes by the extension, such as .NEF or .CR3 . Capital or small letters do not matter. Sidecar files. A text file ending in .json is JSON data, and one ending in .xmp is an XMP sidecar, not a document to read. Once the media service has read a photo, video or recording, the type it reports is the one EiN keeps. To see what EiN made of a file, run mime in the terminal; see In the terminal .

EiN recognises JPEG, HEIC and HEIF (what iPhones take), PNG, TIFF, WebP, AVIF, GIF and BMP, and the camera RAW formats below. For each photo, EiN: reads its date, its GPS position and the camera or phone that took it; see Dates and places of pictures and Devices and GPS tracks ; makes thumbnails and screen-sized copies in the AVIF format: a square of 320 pixels, and copies that fit inside 512, 800, 1,600 and 2,560 pixels. These copies are never larger than the photo, so a small one gets only the sizes up to its own; finds the faces in it ( People and faces ); reads any text in it, printed or handwritten, so that search finds it ( Read the text in a picture ); works out what it shows, so that you can search for "a dog on a beach"; takes a fingerprint, which finds copies, look-alikes and bursts ( Duplicates ). Text in a photo is read, handwriting included, and search finds the picture by it.

EiN takes the RAW files of these cameras: Extension Camera .cr2 , .cr3 , .crw Canon .nef , .nrw Nikon .arw , .sr2 Sony .raf Fujifilm .orf Olympus .rw2 , .raw Panasonic .pef Pentax .dng Adobe DNG, used by many cameras and phones .x3f Sigma .mrw Minolta .dcr , .kdc Kodak .3fr Hasselblad .iiq Phase One .erf Epson .srw Samsung .rwl Leica A RAW file gets everything a JPEG gets. EiN develops it for the thumbnails; a RAW file whose sensor data cannot be read is shown from the JPEG preview the camera put inside it. Faces and text are read from that preview too. A RAW file and the JPEG the camera saved beside it stay two pictures; when EiN finds them to be duplicates, it suggests keeping the RAW, as the better format ( Which copy is kept ).

EiN recognises MP4, MOV (what iPhones and many cameras record), M4V, MTS and M2TS (AVCHD camcorders), MPG, AVI, MKV, WebM, 3GP and FLV. For each video, EiN: reads its date, its GPS position and the camera or phone that recorded it; makes a still for its tile and the poster shown before it plays; makes a version your browser plays, at most 1920 × 1080 pixels, in the AV1 format inside an MP4 file, with the sound at 128 kbit/s; makes a silent clip of up to 20 seconds that plays when you point at the tile.
